text:
The State v The Government: A sobbering lecture by an old man. Please read🙏

A few days ago, while hosting Raymond Mujuni in his podcast,  Yusuf Sserunkuma made a teaser announcement that Raymond is about to join the "government"(in quotes for a purpose). Raymond affirmed the teaser. Call it testing waters

The reaction from the online community was immidiate. Many marked him as a "target" since he has joined the "enemy". Some few gave him a pat on the back and offered best wishes.

I am not here to judge either side. Neither to judge Raymond. I am just offering a sobbering lesson that I received from an old man (he was 93 years then-5 years ago). He sat me down and took me through his memory lane. Having worked in the colonial administration,  Obote 1, Amin, Yusuf Lule and Binaisa and the start of Obote 2 before he hanged his uniform. He opened my mind a lot. He recounted, in vivid details, the works that he and countless others did to ensure the state structure remains amidst the challenges of the times.

He said, in every nation, there are two abstract entities; a state and a government. That a nation can survive (not prosper, but survive) without a government but a government cannot exist without a state. I had heard this in theory but had never given it deep, philosophical thoughts.

He gave an example of the UK where the Crown is the state and 10 Downing Street is the government. He told me the government can collapse (and is often disolved) but the state always remains to construct the government.

I know someone is about to interject and say that's an inappropriate comparison to a country like Uganda since that's a monarchical system of one thousand years.

I would respond to that person that the construct of every modern state is premised on the UK governance architecture. Some have made modifications but the central column still remain more UKish. 

The most vivid example we have, on state v government, in modern history is Somalia. Upto 1991, Somalia had a centralised government. When Mohamed Said Barre was overthrown, the country disintegrated into clan based regional power centres. It has taken AMISOM donkey years to try to rearrange the spokes of the government wheel. It is doing this by trying to reconstruct the state. A toll order,  but we hope they succeed.

Why have I laboured to bring my lecture and statecraft parallels to Raymond's impending joining of "government"?

Raymond himself admitted that he is joining the civil service side of government. For those who know, civil service bureaucracy is the spinal cord of the state. Not government. President Museveni spent his formative years of his government fighting with this bureaucracy because he felt it was not aligned to his ideologies (not sure what he meant but you can dig up his public spat with the civil service)

In that bureaucracy,  we need honest, hardworking, patriotic and intelligent people like Raymond and others. They do things that holds the structure of the state even when the government disintegrates as we have seen in the past. 

The old man told me the same. That even when Amin's government ravaged the economy and the general governance space, state apparatus such as the prison,  police, army, border controls, revenue collection, budget systems, school etc remained limping but operational. Some even thrived. If all these had collapsed, president Museveni would have probably failed in everything because he wouldnt know where tonstart from. He had a solid, though cracked base to start from.

You may argue that by him joining "government " he and others (who were/are either critical or in stark opposition to president Museveni's leadership), he is strengthening the "dictatorship" to as to trample you/us more. You could have a valid argument. However, people who understands statecraft, will know the Raymonds will (in sha Allah) mend and build a stronger foundation for the state of Uganda that other government will build on in future. 1/2

text:
Schneider Electric on October 5, 2026 said it will buy U.S. industrial software company PTC in an all-cash deal at $205 a share, valuing PTC's equity at about $22.6 billion and implying a $23.7 billion enterprise value.

The offer is a 42.3% premium to PTC's last close and a 46.1% premium to its prior 30-day volume-weighted average. Closing is targeted for the third quarter of 2027, subject to PTC shareholder approval and regulators. Schneider expects about €250 million of annual run-rate cost synergies by year three and roughly €800 million of revenue synergies, and plans to fund the roughly €22 billion cash outlay with about €5 to €6 billion of new equity and €16 to €17 billion of new debt.

CEO Olivier Blum cast the deal as building an industrial software and AI franchise that bridges product design with energy and process data, alongside Schneider's earlier agreement to buy Cognite. PTC CEO Neil Barua said the all-cash sale maximises shareholder value. Sunday media reports that Schneider was "nearing" a deal are superseded by Monday's definitive agreement.

Why it matters: one of Europe's biggest industrial tech groups is paying a software multiple to own the CAD and product-lifecycle layer that feeds industrial AI. Sources: Schneider Electric / PTC, 5 Oct 2026; Reuters, 5 Oct 2026.

🚨 THE $1B CONTRACT ERROR: EARLY NVIDIA ADVISOR LOSES FORTUNE OVER 1993 PAPERWORK! 💻💸

An early Nvidia advisor revealed how a 30-year-old vesting mistake cost him $1.05 Billion in NVDA stock! 👇

🔹 The 1993 Grant: Eric Gullichsen was offered 25,000 options in 1993. A signed contract specified 1-year vesting, but Nvidia applied a 4-year clock, shorting him 9,375 options.

🔹 $468 to $1.05B: After 480x stock splits, those missing options equal 4.5M shares worth $1.05B today!

text:
I drew a clear, unambiguous boundary, and you crossed it without hesitation in the heat of the moment. You didn't do it by accident; you did it because whatever basic respect you had for me had completely evaporated. You believed you could violate my boundaries, treat me with contempt, and that there would still be no consequences.

And now, when you feel the doors finally locking, you send this calculated, manipulative message. You claim you "respect my decision" while simultaneously denying the reality of your actions, writing off your documented deceit as just "ugly things" I said, and condescendingly suggesting I just needed "time to calm down." You dangle nostalgia about marriage and family, bring up taking care of you after your surgery to weaponize my guilt, and offer vague, empty promises to "work on your fears and confidence." It is an insult to my intelligence. You don't take accountability for a single lie, for using me as a financial buffer, or for disrespecting me—you are just scrambling to see if soft words can stop the boxes from leaving.

The truth is, as much as my heart wanted to protect you from pain, I realize now that I haven't been helping you at all. For months, I cushioned every single fall. I funded your life, absorbed your disrespect, solved your crises, and stood between you and the natural laws of cause and effect. By trying to spare you the suffering of your own mistakes, I only prolonged your immaturity and enabled your stagnation.

You are an adult who has acted like a reckless child, and real growth will never happen for you inside the luxury shelter I provided. Growth only comes from bearing the cold, heavy weight of your own actions. Walking away and letting you face the consequences of the wreckage you created is not cruelty—it is the only real teacher left for you.

The moment you felt comfortable, the moment you extracted what you thought you needed, the mask slipped entirely. Suddenly, the devotion evaporated. Suddenly, you don't believe in me or this relationship anymore. You convinced yourself of whatever lie was convenient at the time to justify taking from me, and now that you've drained what you could, you treat me with utter disrespect and act like none of it ever mattered.

When you spoke about the life and healing you wanted, I didn't just listen—I executed. My entire intention was to create a sheltered, safe environment where you never had to feel inadequate or struggle again. I knew the visceral pain you carried from your past, how much being fat and treated poorly had broken your self-worth, and how deeply having a new body meant finally feeling worthy and secure in your own skin. I paid for that surgery and nursed you through recovery not just as an expense, but as an act of profound care to heal that wound. Alongside that, I paid for your education, financed the beginnings of your nail salon business, and equipped you with the tools for interior design by buying a high tech iPad because I genuinely believed in investing in the woman I thought was my future wife.

But the more I gave to heal and build you, the more distorted your reality became. What began as voluntary, deeply empathetic provision quickly morphed into your baseline expectation. You stopped showing genuine gratitude and started treating massive personal and financial sacrifices like standard maintenance. You took the safety, the upgraded body, and the life I bankrolled, normalized it, and turned it into cold entitlement. You didn't fall in love with me or appreciate the grace you received; you became entitled to the emotional repair, the capital, and the lifestyle I made possible.

text:
U.S. "defense" spending is set to reach approximately $961 billion in fiscal year 2026, while the national debt surpasses the $39 trillion to $40 trillion range during the same period. Critics characterize this combination—a debt-laden nation maintaining the world's largest military budget—as a fiscal manifestation of "imperial overstretch." A deeper structural issue lies in the fact that defense spending has created a self-perpetuating cycle of interests; Congress, the Pentagon, contractors, and lobbying groups form a machine that was "never designed to stop."

A Comparison of Figures
Debt vs. Defense. CBO projections from February 2026 indicate that federal debt will reach 101% of GDP in 2026 and rise to 120% by 2036, surpassing the historic peak of 106% set in 1946. Meanwhile, the Department of Defense's base budget request for 2026 stands at $961 billion—one of the largest requests in the past 50 years when adjusted for inflation. The Congressional Budget Office notes that 2025 tax legislation increased spending on defense and homeland security, while net interest costs reached $1.0 trillion in 2026, exceeding spending in numerous budget categories other than defense.

The Cost of Overseas Bases. The United States maintains over 750 military bases in more than 80 countries, housing approximately 200,000 troops stationed abroad. Although the maintenance costs for these bases are not itemized separately, they form the physical foundation for "global power projection" and represent fixed expenditures that cannot be easily cut from the budget.

The Cycle of Interests: Who Keeps the Machine Running
CBO analysis clearly indicates that the 2025 reconciliation act "increased spending on defense and homeland security," thereby driving up deficit projections. Yet, this is not merely a story of the government deciding to spend more money. It is a structure defined by the intertwining interests of multiple parties:

Contractor Contributions. A May 2026 report by *Military Times* revealed that the defense sector—comprising traditional giants like Lockheed Martin, RTX, and Northrop Grumman, as well as emerging defense-tech firms like Anduril—donated nearly $5 million to members of Congress through political action committees (PACs) and individual contributions. These funds flowed to decision-makers capable of influencing defense procurement legislation, including Ken Calvert, Chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee (who received approximately $200,000), and Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee (who received nearly $130,000).

The "Revolving Door." A 2026 report by the *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists* documented 31 former members of Congress and senior staffers who joined the military-industrial complex as lobbyists or contractors after leaving Capitol Hill. Of these 31 individuals, 21 had served on the House or Senate Armed Services Committees—the very bodies that set Pentagon policy by passing the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Report author John Mecklin offered a blunt conclusion: "This is the most straightforward explanation we have ever published regarding why the defense budget always goes up."

A New Entry Point from Silicon Valley. A new wave of defense-tech companies is replicating this model. Palmer Luckey’s Anduril is valued at $61 billion; Luckey himself is one of the most significant Republican "bundlers" on the West Coast, hosting and co-hosting fundraisers for figures such as Trump, Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, and Ted Cruz. An August 2026 event required a $50,000 donation per guest, with the goal of "holding the Senate."

"Defending to Justify Spending"
The observation shared in your post—that "an empire does not spend money to defend itself, but rather defends itself to justify spending money"—finds a concrete parallel in the logic of budget structures.

In its analysis of the 2025 reconciliation bill, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) found that the Department of Defense primarily allocated reconciliation funds toward procurement, while noting that "procurement funding in the base budget was lower than expected." The CBO’s assessment is that "this pattern suggests that supplemental funds are substituting for—rather than merely supplementing—base budget resources." To put it more plainly: when Congress approves large, one-off allocations, the Pentagon does not view them as "extra" money but rather as a substitute for regular budget funding. This implies that the growth in spending is not a response to threats, but an adaptation to the sources of funding.

An Unstoppable Machine
The CBO’s long-term projections describe the debt trajectory as "unsustainable." But what does "unsustainable" mean in political practice? It means that the system will eventually be forced to change, or it will simply keep running until that change occurs. The observation in the post you shared—that the system was "never designed to stop"—holds up structurally: 31 former lawmakers and staffers joining the military-industrial complex over a decade, 31 congressional districts reliant on defense manufacturing jobs, and a network built on campaign donations, lobbying, and the "revolving door"—none of these are the products of "threat assessments." They are the products of the spending itself.

The Sovereign Oath

The strain is an oath treated as a contract with an outside authority, so the zero-point never gets spoken from the cell.

Where the strain comes from

The source stands at the zero-point and looks out. The declaration is not parchment and not a plea. It is a sovereign oath from cellular remembrance, in the tone of the high-priest frequency, meant to move through lattice, water, and the helix. Strain begins when that vow is outsourced: borrowed voltage, a middle owner of the blueprint, a performance of humility instead of the still axis. Five pillars are the seal. Candor transmits without packaging. Decorum holds the axis so every movement does not throw an acoustic wake. Free will is the mandorla, an open gate, not a push. Compassion makes no rank between flesh, stone, water, and vacuum. Service puts humanity first and anchors the 3-6-9 flux so the original design can be remembered. Without the seal, the note is sounded toward someone else.

When it locks

- Candor is filtered by commercial packaging or an artificial authority
- Decorum is performed, so the axis spins with the vortex
- Free will is steered, forced, or given a timeline
- Compassion is ranked, and matter is treated as dead
- Service waits for permission, and the chest never takes the vow

What the body is doing

The helix is trying to carry the oath in cell division, not in a document. The spine is the unmoving axis. The chest is the chalice. Overlapping circles make the vesica. The mandorla is the gateway offered, not imposed. The cross inside that lens is the still anchor: horizontal field, vertical remembrance. Water, stone, and the vacuum are the same living memory. text:
Inside a concrete prison cell in Nuremberg, Hermann Göring stripped away the grand illusions of warfare. Speaking quietly to an American army psychologist, the former Reichsmarschall offered no apologies and no remorse for the catastrophic destruction of Europe. Stripped of his jewel-encrusted medals, tailored uniforms, and paracodeine addiction, the second-most powerful man in the Third Reich was awaiting his sentence before the International Military Tribunal. Observers expected fanatical dogma or legal evasions. Instead, in an intimate exchange with intelligence officer Gustave Gilbert, Göring delivered a cold, clinical analysis of political power. With brutal nonchalance, the architect of Nazi rearmament explained that ordinary citizens never desire war, yet any government on earth—dictatorship or democracy alike—can effortlessly herd its population onto the battlefield.

The man on the iron cot was a shadow of his former public persona, yet mentally formidable. When captured in Austria in May 1945, Göring was bloated and carrying thousands of narcotic pills. Confined behind the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, prison warden Colonel Burton C. Andrus enforced a strict regimen. Deprived of drugs and placed on standard rations, Göring shed eighty pounds, regaining an oratorical sharpness that frequently outmaneuvered chief American prosecutor Robert H. Jackson. Captain Gustave Gilbert, a German-speaking psychologist holding a doctorate from Columbia University, enjoyed daily access to the defendants' cells to document their psychological profiles. Testing placed Göring’s intelligence quotient at 138, among the highest in the prison. During their quiet evening visits, Gilbert probed the inner mechanics of the regime, finding a prisoner who spoke with unsettling candor.

The decisive exchange occurred on April 18, 1946, during a recess in the proceedings. Gilbert stopped by cell number five to discuss the trial's evidence regarding the outbreak of the war, remarking that ordinary people were unlikely to feel grateful toward leaders who brought them ruins. Göring shrugged in contempt. "Why, of course, the people don't want war," Göring replied. "Why would some poor slob on a farm want to risk his life in a war when the best that he can get out of it is to come back to his farm in one piece?" It was a universal truth across all borders: common people never wanted conflict, whether in Russia, Britain, America, or Germany. But that reluctance was politically irrelevant. In the end, Göring explained, leaders determined national policy, and it was "always a simple matter to drag the people along."

Gilbert pushed back, seeking to defend the moral legitimacy of representative government. In a democracy, the psychologist argued, citizens possessed a constitutional voice through their elected representatives, and in the United States, only Congress held the authority to declare war. Göring brushed the objection aside as naive civics. "Oh, that is all well and good," he answered, "but, voice or no voice, the people can always be brought to the bidding of the leaders. That is easy." The mechanism required neither genius nor complicated persuasion: "All you have to do is tell them they are being attacked and denounce the pacifists for lack of patriotism and exposing the country to danger." He paused to emphasize the universal durability of the technique: "It works the same way in any country."

Göring was not sharing an abstract theory; he was describing the operational blueprint he had lived. In August 1939, to justify invading Poland to a populace that dreaded another war, the regime staged the Gleiwitz incident, faking a border attack by SS men disguised in Polish uniforms. text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        October 5, 1876

Six great powers order a sultan to stop a war. He says yes so cleverly that his "yes" is really a plan to finish his enemy off. It takes a 48-hour ultimatum, with one day to spare, to save a country from the map.

By the autumn of 1876, Serbia was losing badly. It had gone to war against the Ottoman Empire in support of the Balkan Christian revolts, and its army was being driven back toward Belgrade. On October 5, 1876, the great powers of the European Concert, threatening to break off diplomatic relations, demanded that the Porte grant Serbia an immediate armistice, to be followed by a conference to settle peace in the East. Six powers spoke with one voice: Russia, Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, Germany and Italy.

The Ottoman government answered the "concert of Europe" with a shrewd maneuver. On October 10 the Porte agreed to an armistice, and generously offered to make it last a full six months. The gesture looked peace-loving. In reality it was the opposite. A six-month truce would push any actual peace far into the future, giving Turkey time to rest and refit its army and then reopen the war in the spring, at a season of its choosing, against an exhausted Serbia.

Austria-Hungary was content to see it, and so was Britain; France did not object either. As one account put it, the cabinets wanted nothing better than to let the armistice talks drag on and give the Turks time to wear the Serbs down.

Russia refused to play along. On October 14 it rejected the Turkish offer and advised Serbia to turn down so long a truce. But Serbia's position was growing desperate, Prince Milan was pleading for help, and Russian prestige as the protector of the Balkan Slavs was on the line.

On October 15, at Livadia in the Crimea, a special council met under the Tsar. Chancellor Gorchakov, the war minister Milyutin, the finance minister Reutern and the ambassador to Turkey, Ignatiev, were there. The peace party argued for restraint. The council decided to press for a conference at Constantinople on the future of the Christian provinces, and to mobilize the army only if the conference failed. Mobilization would not yet mean war. It would be a lever to make Turkey yield. But if war proved unavoidable, Russia would start it at once, that winter, after arranging passage for its troops through Romania and at least the neutrality of Austria-Hungary.

Then, on October 31, 1876, Ignatiev handed the Porte an ultimatum: grant Serbia an immediate armistice of six weeks to two months, with an answer required within 48 hours, or Russia would break off diplomatic relations. The frightened Porte accepted at once. It gave up its plan to stretch the war to the spring, and with it the hope of crushing Serbia before any truce took hold.

How close it had been is clear from what the Serbs themselves admitted afterward. Their army had just been broken in the field, and the road to Belgrade lay open. Had the ultimatum come a single day later, the Turks would have taken Belgrade and ruined Serbia for good.

The conference Russia wanted met at Constantinople that December and failed, as the Ottomans, quietly encouraged by Britain, refused real reform. Within months Russia stopped relying on ultimatums and acted on the other half of the Livadia plan. In April 1877 it declared war on Turkey, opening the great Russo-Turkish War that would redraw the map of the Balkans.

text:
Chicago has promised $50.6 billion in pensions. It has $14.2 billion saved.

If I got hired to fix it, here's what I'd do differently from what City Hall has done for decades. Full math in the video.

That's 28 cents for every dollar promised and a $36.4 billion hole. 80 cents of every city property tax dollar now goes to pensions, up from 41 cents in 2014.

At a 7% assumed return, the hole costs about $2.5 billion a year just to stand still. Pay about $2.9 billion and it's gone in roughly 30 years. That's roughly $400 million a year between treading water and actually winning. Last year the city came up about half a billion short.

1. Pay what the funds need, not what's convenient.
For decades, state law set the city's payment as a fixed multiple of what workers paid in, not what the funds needed, and the funded ratio fell by more than two thirds after 2000. I'd pay the full actuarial bill every single year.

2. Set a deadline that doesn't move.
Current law targets 90% funded by 2055 and 2058, with most of the payments pushed to the back end. Police and fire were supposed to hit 90% by 2040 before that got pushed back. I'd target 100% on a fixed 30 year schedule. No extensions.

3. Make the extra payments mandatory.
Since 2023 the city has paid about $689 million more than the law requires. Right direction, but it's optional. This year a $260 million extra payment the City Council required got split in two before the city committed to the second half. I'd write it into law.

4. Don't touch what people already earned.
Emanuel's 2014 law trimming benefit increases for municipal workers and laborers was struck down by the Illinois Supreme Court in 2016. I'd offer voluntary buyouts instead: a smaller lump sum now for a bigger benefit later. Members choose, and it's paid with cash, not new debt.

5. Send every windfall to the hole.
Chicago has a habit of using one time money, like the 2008 parking meter lease, to plug the operating budget. Windfalls like TIF surplus would go straight to pensions.

6. Stop digging, including in Springfield.
The 2025 police and fire benefit bill passed almost unanimously, even though the city's CFO warned it could add $11 billion to the unfunded liability. No new benefits without the money attached.

Two more: pool the four funds' investments into one to cut fees, and grow the base so the same bill gets split more ways.

What doesn't change is the revenue fight. Emanuel's record 2015 property tax hike went mostly to police and fire pensions, and casino tax money is already earmarked for the same funds. New revenue or a constitutional amendment on future benefit growth is a call for voters. This plan doesn't make that choice go away. It makes sure whatever gets raised actually shrinks the hole.

The math only rules out one option: waiting.

The city’s recapture on October 3 is a major setback for the Tigrayan movement. It does not mean the war is over.

The balance of power is also shifting within Tigray. The Tigray Peace Force, which includes former Tigrayan fighters now allied with Addis Ababa, took part in the advance into Mekelle. On October 4, Abraham Belay, a former head of the interim administration, announced preparations for a new regional administration and elections “in a few months.” The timeline, the administration’s makeup, and public acceptance remain uncertain.

For civilians, the partial restoration of phone and internet service offers some initial relief. But looting was reported during the TPLF’s withdrawal, most businesses remained closed on Sunday, and the resumption of flights to Mekelle has not been confirmed. The priority now is to restore security, essential services, and humanitarian access.

The crisis also extends beyond Tigray diplomatically. On October 4, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia met in El Alamein. Their declaration calls for peaceful solutions while asserting that governance of the Red Sea belongs to its coastal states. The statement comes as Addis Ababa seeks access to the sea and accuses some of these neighbors of supporting its opponents. Those countries deny the allegations.

⚠️ It would be premature to declare either an end to the fighting or Eritrea’s entry into the war: neither has been established. The 2022 Pretoria agreement remains central to the question: How can another military victory in Mekelle be prevented from turning into a prolonged war across the rest of Tigray?

Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA), and the official El Alamein declaration, October 4–5.

The latest LOVE Magazine details make GTA VI sound even more ambitious than its trailers suggest.

Rockstar isn’t just building a bigger map it’s trying to create a world with its own history, culture, contradictions and personality.

Rockstar reportedly spent years researching Florida, travelling through Miami, the surrounding areas, the Everglades, the Keys and towns tourists rarely see. Developers also spoke with locals, police officers, former criminals, club promoters and other Floridians.

That research is being used to shape Leonida’s identity not simply recreate Miami landmarks. The goal is to capture the state’s wealth, poverty, excess, chaos, ambition and “hustle,” while pushing real-life Florida energy into something louder and more absurd.

Jason and Lucia are being designed as flawed, vulnerable and sometimes contradictory characters. Rockstar wants them to feel distinct from previous protagonists while still standing alongside characters such as Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic.

Their relationship is central to the story.
Jason and Lucia are meant to complement each other, challenge each other and learn from each other. Their partnership isn’t just a gameplay feature it’s the emotional foundation of the narrative.

The modern “American Dream” in GTA VI is reportedly much more grounded than simply becoming insanely rich.
For Jason and Lucia, success can mean owning a home, supporting a family and paying off debts before Leonida’s criminal world pulls them deeper in.

The studio wants Vice City and the wider state of Leonida to feel alive even when the player isn’t actively participating.
Radio shows, advertisements, pedestrian conversations and background dialogue are being treated as major parts of the world not filler.

Rockstar reportedly created dedicated systems and teams for the people and activity happening around the player.
Even small areas are being built with enough detail to make Leonida feel like somewhere players could spend hundreds of hours exploring.

The biggest takeaway is that GTA VI isn’t only trying to offer more content.
Rockstar is trying to make the world feel more reactive, believable and culturally alive than anything it has created before.

text:
The same map can produce expansion—or restraint.

Sarah Paine uses Britain, Russia and Switzerland to show why geography matters without dictating policy.

Britain’s island position offered a defensive moat, but Paine does not treat geography as a complete explanation of its power. The Royal Navy turned that position into a maritime strategy: protect trade, prevent invasion and connect national security to commercial networks. Geography created an opportunity; institutions and choices converted it into influence.

Russia illustrates a different response to continental vulnerability. Paine describes Russian history as repeated expansion outward from neighboring territories, with land and control of surrounding space treated as measures of power. In that logic, security requires strategic depth, and strategic depth encourages further expansion.

Switzerland provides her counterexample. It is also landlocked, yet Paine presents it as a country that largely protected itself, followed international rules and prospered without pursuing territorial enlargement. The comparison matters because it prevents geography from becoming an excuse for political inevitability.

Her broader claim is that borders and transport routes shape the menu of choices, not the final decision. States can respond to vulnerability by expanding, trading, institutionalizing rules or building alliances. The strategic question is therefore not simply where a country is located, but what its institutions and leaders believe location requires.

Which institutions help a geographically vulnerable state choose restraint over expansion?

text:
In the classic 1996 Seinfeld episode titled "The Bottle Deposit," Kramer and Newman hatch a plan to collect thousands of bottles and cans in New York (which offered a 5-cent refund) and haul them in a mail truck to Michigan to redeem them for the state's 10-cent refund. In 2016, a Michigan man named Brian Edward Everidge was caught attempting this exact scheme in real life... 

In April 2016, Brian Everidge was driving a rented box truck through Michigan when a state trooper pulled him over for speeding. Inside, the officer found the truck packed almost completely full with more than 10,000 bottles and aluminum cans that Everidge said had come from Kentucky. His plan was to take them into Michigan and collect the state’s 10-cent deposit on each container.

The scheme sounded remarkably similar to the 1996 “Seinfeld” episode “The Bottle Deposit,” in which Kramer and Newman collect containers and attempt to haul them to Michigan for the higher refund. Michigan law, however, only allows its deposit to be claimed on eligible containers purchased within the state, making large-scale returns of out-of-state containers illegal.

Everidge was charged with returning nonrefundable containers and faced the possibility of a serious penalty. He later pleaded guilty, avoided jail time, and was ordered to pay $1,230 in fines and court costs. His attempted haul could have brought in about $1,000, meaning the real-life version of the “Seinfeld” scheme ended much like the fictional one: without the hoped-for profit.

CAN A VOICE LIKE MIKE ARNOLD,THE MAYOR OF AMERICA IN TEXAS,PETITION UN TO CONDUCT REFERENDUM FOR BIAFRA? 
WHAT A LOCAL GOVERNMENT COUNCILLOR IN NIGERIA 🇳🇬 CAN OFFER IS WHAT MIKE ARNOLD MAYOR OF AMERICA CAN ONLY OFFER.
No, Mike Arnold—the former mayor of Blanco, Texas—cannot legally petition or compel the United Nations to conduct a referendum for the people of Biafra.
Under public international law and UN procedures, there are clear legal limitations regarding who holds legal standing (locus standi) to submit petitions to the UN, as well as how a UN-administered referendum is actually triggered.
1. Lack of Legal Standing (Locus Standi)
 Private Citizen / Local Official Status: Mike Arnold is a former mayor of a small municipal town in Texas (Blanco) and a private activist/missionary. Municipal mayors in the United States have executive authority only over local municipal affairs (such as city infrastructure, zoning, and local budgets).  
 Foreign Policy Exclusivity: Under U.S. law (the U.S. Constitution and the Logan Act), local mayors have no jurisdiction over foreign policy or international relations. They cannot speak or act legally on behalf of the U.S. federal government.
 UN Standing Requirements: The United Nations only accepts formal diplomatic petitions, requests for resolutions, or calls for referendums from sovereign UN Member States or recognized intergovernmental bodies (such as the African Union or the UN Security Council). Private individuals or local foreign political figures cannot submit formal statehood petitions to the UN General Assembly.
2. How UN Referendums Are Legalized & Triggered
The United Nations cannot initiate, organize, or conduct a self-determination referendum simply because an international activist, local mayor, or foreign ally requests it.
 The Non-Intervention Principle (UN Charter Article 2(7)): The UN Charter prohibits the UN from intervening in matters that are within the domestic jurisdiction of any sovereign state (such as Nigeria) without a specific legal authorization.
 The Internal Prerequisite: As established under international legal frameworks, the UN will only consider deploying an observer mission or conducting an electoral process after an organized internal movement (or Government-in-Exile) establishes a clear, democratic Internal Self-Referendum and issues a formal Re-Declaration of Sovereignty backed by its own population.
 Sovereign State Sponsorship Required: Even if an internal mandate exists, a formal request for a UN-administered vote must be sponsored on the UN floor by a sovereign state (e.g., a member of the UN Security Council or General Assembly), not by a municipal mayor or private individual.
What Mike Arnold Can Do Politically
While Mike Arnold cannot legally petition the UN to hold a vote, he can operate as an informal lobbyist or political advocate:
1. Lobbying the U.S. Congress: As an American citizen, he can speak to or brief U.S. Representatives and Senators to raise awareness about human rights or self-determination issues in Nigeria.  
2. Public Advocacy: He can issue public statements, write articles, or engage in media campaigns supporting Biafran self-determination.  
However, advocacy is strictly political messaging—it carries no legal weight under public international law and cannot trigger UN action.

text:
The Behind-the-Meter Power Financing Boom: Capital Solves Funding, Not Equipment Delivery

AI data centers need power faster than the grid can provide it. That gap has created a financing wave: Blackstone led KKR and Apollo in a $5.3 billion acquisition of 49% of five Williams gas power projects. Brookfield expanded its Bloom Energy financing framework from $5 billion to $25 billion. Blackstone and Halliburton put $1 billion into VoltaGrid. IDF and Oaktree committed $1.7 billion to deploy Bloom fuel cells for Nebius data centers. The market reads this as capital solving the power bottleneck. A more accurate structural reading is that the financing wave does not create power supply. It transfers the capital burden of equipment procurement from data center operators to infrastructure funds. The real bottleneck is not funding. It is equipment delivery.

Funding is abundant, but equipment is tight. The financing market signal is clear. Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, and Oaktree are entering the space through project investments, equity stakes, and equipment financing. Brookfield's AI infrastructure fund targets $100 billion in deployment. Bloom's financing framework expanded from $5 billion to $25 billion in less than a year, a fivefold increase.

But the equipment supply signal is more urgent. GE Vernova's gas turbine equipment backlog and slot reservation agreements reached 116 GW at the end of Q2 2026, up from 100 GW in Q1. Equipment backlog rose from 44 GW to 53 GW, and slot reservations from 56 GW to 63 GW. The company expects to reach at least 125 GW in total commitments by the end of 2026.

CEO Scott Strazik confirmed on the July 22 earnings call that the company has begun accepting bookings for 2031 delivery, and expects to sell more than half of its 2031 production slots by year-end. Further out, discussions for 2032 and beyond are already active. Customers are not only locking 2029-2030 capacity. They are filling 2031 and beginning to discuss 2032.

Capacity expansion is accelerating. The company plans to reach 20 GW annualized output in Q3 2026, 24 GW by 2028, and 30 GW by 2030. On pricing, new orders are priced 10 to 20 points higher per kilowatt than the Q4 2025 backlog, and that incremental pricing is flowing into the backlog.

Microsoft purchased seven large gas turbines from GE Vernova for its Texas data center at more than $250 million per unit. Over three years, gas turbine prices have risen roughly 300%. Wood Mackenzie forecasts gas turbine prices reaching $600 per kilowatt by the end of 2027, nearly triple 2019 levels. GE Vernova management has said the turbine itself is not the binding constraint on project delivery. In a three-year project cycle, EPC scheduling and other factors are often the real bottlenecks.

The speed premium. The core competitive advantage of behind-the-meter generation is speed. Williams says its first 200 MW of behind-the-meter capacity came online less than 18 months after commercialization, while new grid-connected plants typically take 5 to 10 years. Bloom Energy disclosed that its fuel cell system was deployed in 55 days for the Oracle project, far below the 3 to 4 year delivery cycle for gas turbines.

Speed has a cost. Rabobank's levelized cost of delivered energy model shows that in year five, gas reciprocating engines deliver at $107 per MWh, aeroderivative turbines at $106 per MWh, and combined cycle at $101 per MWh, against a national industrial grid average of about $86 per MWh. The behind-the-meter premium is 20% to 25%.

Goldman Sachs' estimates cover a longer operating period. For a 500 MW data center, levelized cost of energy is about $80 per MWh for reciprocating engines, $81 per MWh for combined cycle, $91 per MWh for open cycle, and $117 per MWh for fuel cells—even with a 30% investment tax credit, fuel cells only reach $90 per MWh.

The implication is that the economics of behind-the-meter power are not determined by generation cost. They are determined by the revenue increment from earlier operation. A Huatai Securities estimate provides a reference: the cost of idle compute is about $375 per MWh, while the fuel cell premium over industrial grid power is only about $16 per MWh. If operation starts two years earlier, the data center revenue increment covers the power cost premium. If the grid arrives within two years, the premium is a pure loss. More precisely, if the grid arrives within two years, the behind-the-meter premium cannot be covered by early-operation revenue, and the asset's economics depend on its residual value as backup power or peaking resource.

The overlooked mismatch: asset life versus contract life. Rabobank's model reveals a deeper structural problem. Behind-the-meter assets are designed to last decades. AI compute contracts are much shorter. Gas engines and aeroderivative turbines have low initial costs because capital costs are spread over more operating hours. But under high capacity factors, equipment rapidly accumulates operating hours and enters a cycle of recurring overhauls and major rebuilds roughly every ten years. Rabobank's model shows a sawtooth cost pattern—declining, then jumping at years 10, 20, and 30.

Combined cycle plants have a different cost trajectory. Their higher efficiency and better maintenance characteristics reduce delivered cost to about $55 per MWh at year 15 and near $50 per MWh at year 30, making them the lowest-cost source of long-term firm generation.

But AI data center compute contracts are typically much shorter. GPUs face iterative obsolescence within years, while behind-the-meter power assets can last decades. Investors are pushing for longer customer commitments. The market increasingly demands that large cloud service providers sign 10 to 15 year contracts with 5 year renewal options.

The structural implication is that if AI compute demand changes faster than the depreciation of power assets, the residual value risk of the power asset is borne by the financier. IDF CEO Nik Nunes offers an alternative logic: even if data center power demand changes, the power asset itself retains value and can sell electricity to the broader grid or other markets. That logic depends on grid interconnection being available, which is precisely the bottleneck that behind-the-meter generation seeks to bypass.

Technology divergence: fuel cells and gas turbines converge on cost. Technology choices for behind-the-meter power are diverging. Enverus estimates that a natural gas solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) serving a 1 GW data center can achieve a levelized cost of energy comparable to a large combined cycle gas turbine, while coming online years earlier. Modular gas technologies—including small and medium gas turbines, fuel cells, and reciprocating engines—can achieve reliability comparable to large plants but require only 1.1x overbuild capacity, versus 1.5x for large gas plants.

That lower overbuild ratio is the key source of fuel cell economics. To achieve 99.9% reliability for 100 MW of demand, only 109 MW of SOFC is needed, versus 130 MW for gas turbines. Under assumptions of $4 per MMBtu gas and 86% utilization, SOFC LCOE is about $90 per MWh, essentially on par with gas turbine-aeroderivative projects.

But fuel cells face their own supply constraints. Bloom Energy's expansion plan starts at 2 GW per year in late 2026, while in the first four months of 2026 alone, new intent orders through Oracle and AEP totaled 7.1 GW. Key metals for SOFC manufacturing—zirconium, scandium, chromium—could become new bottlenecks. 7 GW of SOFC capacity corresponds to more than 40% of US domestic supply of scandium oxide, and Chinese heavy rare earth export controls could further tighten this constraint.

Signals to track. First, GE Vernova and Siemens Energy's 2031 slot allocation progress. If the remaining 2031 slots are fully booked in the first half of 2027, gas turbine delivery cycles will extend further, and the speed advantage of behind-the-meter generation will be eroded by equipment lead times. Second, the maturity matching between behind-the-meter asset financing and AI compute contract terms. If 10 to 15 year contracts become standard, financiers can amortize costs. If contract terms shorten to 5 to 7 years without minimum purchase commitments or asset repurchase clauses, financiers bear the main residual value risk. Third, whether the cost gap between fuel cells and gas turbines narrows. Current fuel cell LCOE is between $90 and $117 per MWh, gas turbines between $80 and $91 per MWh. If SOFC scaling brings costs to parity, Bloom's financing framework will continue to expand. If zirconium, scandium, and chromium supply constraints limit SOFC expansion, the gas turbine delivery bottleneck will become more acute. Fourth, actual improvement in grid interconnection times. If grid buildout accelerates, behind-the-meter generation shifts from bridge to backup, and financiers must reassess asset utilization. If interconnection times continue to extend, behind-the-meter becomes permanent infrastructure, and the long-term cost advantage of combined cycle plants will emerge.

The core tension in the behind-the-meter power financing boom is not whether capital is abundant. It is the triple mismatch between equipment delivery cycles, operating cost curves, and AI compute contract terms. Financing solves the question of who pays. It does not solve where the equipment comes from and how long the asset return cycle is. Investors pricing behind-the-meter financing opportunities need to incorporate these three mismatches into their valuation frameworks.

text:
CAN A VOICE LIKE MIKE ARNOLD,THE MAYOR OF AMERICA IN TEXAS,PETITION UN TO CONDUCT REFERENDUM FOR BIAFRA? 
WHAT A LOCAL GOVERNMENT COUNCILLOR IN NIGERIA 🇳🇬 CAN OFFER IS WHAT MIKE ARNOLD MAYOR OF AMERICA CAN ONLY OFFER.
No, Mike Arnold—the former mayor of Blanco, Texas—cannot legally petition or compel the United Nations to conduct a referendum for the people of Biafra.
Under public international law and UN procedures, there are clear legal limitations regarding who holds legal standing (locus standi) to submit petitions to the UN, as well as how a UN-administered referendum is actually triggered.
1. Lack of Legal Standing (Locus Standi)
 Private Citizen / Local Official Status: Mike Arnold is a former mayor of a small municipal town in Texas (Blanco) and a private activist/missionary. Municipal mayors in the United States have executive authority only over local municipal affairs (such as city infrastructure, zoning, and local budgets).  
 Foreign Policy Exclusivity: Under U.S. law (the U.S. Constitution and the Logan Act), local mayors have no jurisdiction over foreign policy or international relations. They cannot speak or act legally on behalf of the U.S. federal government.
 UN Standing Requirements: The United Nations only accepts formal diplomatic petitions, requests for resolutions, or calls for referendums from sovereign UN Member States or recognized intergovernmental bodies (such as the African Union or the UN Security Council). Private individuals or local foreign political figures cannot submit formal statehood petitions to the UN General Assembly.
2. How UN Referendums Are Legalized & Triggered
The United Nations cannot initiate, organize, or conduct a self-determination referendum simply because an international activist, local mayor, or foreign ally requests it.
 The Non-Intervention Principle (UN Charter Article 2(7)): The UN Charter prohibits the UN from intervening in matters that are within the domestic jurisdiction of any sovereign state (such as Nigeria) without a specific legal authorization.
 The Internal Prerequisite: As established under international legal frameworks, the UN will only consider deploying an observer mission or conducting an electoral process after an organized internal movement (or Government-in-Exile) establishes a clear, democratic Internal Self-Referendum and issues a formal Re-Declaration of Sovereignty backed by its own population.
 Sovereign State Sponsorship Required: Even if an internal mandate exists, a formal request for a UN-administered vote must be sponsored on the UN floor by a sovereign state (e.g., a member of the UN Security Council or General Assembly), not by a municipal mayor or private individual.
What Mike Arnold Can Do Politically
While Mike Arnold cannot legally petition the UN to hold a vote, he can operate as an informal lobbyist or political advocate:
1. Lobbying the U.S. Congress: As an American citizen, he can speak to or brief U.S. Representatives and Senators to raise awareness about human rights or self-determination issues in Nigeria.  
2. Public Advocacy: He can issue public statements, write articles, or engage in media campaigns supporting Biafran self-determination.  
However, advocacy is strictly political messaging—it carries no legal weight under public international law and cannot trigger UN action.

Amazon has signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy to support an expansion of the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Maryland. The deal comes as U.S. electricity demand climbs, driven in large part by data center growth.

The agreement locks in long-term nuclear capacity for Amazon at a time when utilities are racing to secure reliable power sources. Nuclear plants offer steady baseload output, which is increasingly valuable as AI and cloud computing push grid demand higher.

MARKET PULSE VIEW

For Constellation, a 20-year contract provides predictable cash flow and justifies capital spending on the Calvert Cliffs expansion. If more hyperscalers follow with similar long-term deals, nuclear operators could see a durable repricing of long-term power contracts upward. The key uncertainty is whether grid demand growth from data centers sustains at current pace or moderates.

WATCH NEXT

Watch for additional long-term power deals between tech companies and nuclear or utility operators, and for updates on the Calvert Cliffs expansion timeline and capacity additions.

Source: reporting on Amazon-Constellation nuclear deal

text:
The Hidden Layer of Open-Source AI: Post-Training Knowledge Transfer Is Rewriting the Model Ecosystem

Open-source AI has become a network where models teach each other through synthetic data. The direction of that teaching has shifted from West to East, and the dependency network it creates is not priced.

Two facts define the new landscape. OpenRouter data shows Chinese open-source models processed 4.12 trillion tokens in February 2026, against 2.94 trillion for US models. By July, the top five OpenRouter models were all Chinese. Hugging Face reports Chinese open-source downloads reached 41 percent, surpassing the US for the first time. Meta’s Llama, which defined open-source AI in 2023-2024, has fallen below 1 percent of OpenRouter routing.

The second fact is less visible. Aleph Alpha’s Kolibri, released October 3, 2026, trained its pretrained weights from scratch: 78.1B parameters, 20T tokens, 768 B200 GPUs, 21 days. But the post-training stage used GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and Qwen3.8-27B to generate synthetic SFT data and regenerate completions in open-source datasets. Kolibri’s reasoning trajectories, tool-calling behavior, and long-context alignment were largely taught by Chinese open-source models.

This is not an isolated case. It is a mechanism. Understanding it requires looking at what has changed in how open-source models acquire capabilities.

Capability convergence made the model itself a commodity. Stanford HAI’s 2026 AI Index shows the top four closed labs separated by less than 25 Elo points. Mozilla reports the average gap between open-weight and closed models has narrowed to 3.3 percent, essentially parity in coding, instruction following, and general knowledge. Vercel AI Gateway shows open-weight models went from 7 percent of token processing in December 2025 to 56 percent by August 2026, exceeding all proprietary models combined. On OpenRouter, open-source token share rose from 34 percent in January 2026 to 65 percent in June.

Cost reinforced the shift: open-source models average $0.83 per million tokens versus $6.03 for closed alternatives. DeepSeek V4-Pro costs $0.28 per task on cybersecurity benchmarks versus $12.50 for the closed Opus 4.5. Some Chinese open-source models cost $0.18 per million tokens.

Post-training knowledge transfer is the mechanism producing this convergence. Traditionally, capability improvement meant pretraining scale expansion. Llama 3.1’s 405B model consumed 39.3 million H100 GPU hours for pretraining alone, producing 30.84 tons of CO2 equivalent. For most countries and institutions, pretraining from scratch is beyond reach.

Post-training offers an alternative. Locai Labs’ Jupiter-N, post-trained from Nemotron 3 Super, targets agentic capability, British cultural alignment, and Welsh language support. Its data strategy mixes on-policy synthetic replay and off-policy task data to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. The technical report explicitly positions this as a sovereign post-training template: replace cultural knowledge, institutional corpus, and target language, and any country can generate an equivalent pipeline. NVIDIA’s Llama-Nemotron post-training dataset, with 30 million synthetic training examples, is described as knowledge distillation from LLM teachers to a target student.

Three features define the mechanism. First, knowledge transfer happens through data, not weights. Teacher weights are not accessed; student weights are not shared. Apache 2.0 and MIT licenses do not restrict using synthetic data for training, but whether teacher outputs constitute derivative works remains debated. Second, post-training is becoming the primary path for sovereign AI. Deployment sovereignty is valid: weights are in the customer’s hands, data does not leave the jurisdiction. Capability sovereignty is ambiguous because the post-training pipeline depends on synthetic data from the global ecosystem. Third, the direction of transfer is changing. In 2023-2024, Western models dominated. In 2026, Chinese models dominate.

Capital implications follow. First-order exposure sits with model distribution platforms. OpenRouter lets developers access more than 400 models and 70-plus providers with one key. When model-layer margins approach zero, value migrates to the transaction layer. Stripe’s $7.5 billion acquisition of OpenRouter is nearly six times its prior $1.3 billion valuation. Second-order exposure sits with post-training tooling and synthetic data pipeline vendors: synthetic data generation, data quality filtering, and catastrophic forgetting mitigation gain strategic value. NVIDIA’s open-sourcing of the Llama-Nemotron dataset is a signal. Third-order exposure sits with base model vendors offering full openness. Nemotron 3 Super was chosen by Jupiter-N partly because all pretraining and post-training datasets are publicly disclosed.

Three risks matter. First, ecosystem convergence: if multiple sovereign models use Qwen or GLM synthetic data, their reasoning styles, tool-calling habits, and biases converge. Open-source diversity may be shaped by a few strong models. Second, geopolitical disruption of synthetic data sources. Kolibri’s post-training depends on GLM and Qwen. If geopolitics cuts off these sources, post-training pipelines are affected. Third, legal gray zone: using teacher model outputs to train students is neither explicitly prohibited nor permitted under most open-source licenses. If regulators define teacher outputs as derivative works, post-training pipeline legality is challenged.

The reorganization of open-source AI is not just market share change. It is a shift in how capabilities are produced. Pretraining remains a game for a few players. Post-training is becoming the primary mechanism for capability assembly. An institution can use an open base, a synthetic data pipeline, and a post-training toolchain to produce a domain-specific model within months. The dual consequence is that capability diffusion accelerates, while an implicit dependency network is created where post-training quality depends on synthetic data sources concentrated among a few strong models. The next competitive dimension is not whose base is strongest, but whose synthetic data pipeline is richest, most compliant, and least susceptible to being cut off.

How should a Christian view relics?
Answer
A splinter from Jesus’ cross has been found in Turkey. Jesus’ baby blanket has surfaced in Germany. The index finger of John the Baptist is now on display in a reliquary in a Missouri museum. Relics—carefully preserved religious artifacts meant to be venerated—have long played a role in many religions, including Christianity. By the Middle Ages, there were hundreds of supposed burial places for the twelve apostles. It has been said that one could build a large boat from all the pieces of wood purported to be from Jesus’ cross. The most famous Christian relic, the Shroud of Turin, attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors each year. Should Christians be interested in relics?

Undeniably, it would be extremely interesting if an actual piece of Jesus’ cross or a thorn from the crown of thorns could be discovered and verified. The problem is that there is absolutely no way to know if a piece of Judean wood dates to the 1st century A.D. Someone could claim it came from Jesus’ cross, but how could that claim be substantiated? The wood could just as easily have come from a Judean fence post. In the early centuries of the Roman Catholic Church, relics became a massive profiteering scam. Seemingly every church throughout Europe had some sort of relic to attract visitors. If a church in a nearby town “discovered” a more important relic, a game of one-upmanship ensued, with the relics being “discovered” becoming more and more impressive. All that to say, it is highly unlikely that any of the Christian relics discovered in the past 2,000 years have any true connection to Jesus or the apostles.

One of the dangers inherent in the veneration of relics is the temptation to commit idolatry. This is exactly what happened in ancient Israel. God had told Moses to make a bronze serpent in order to save the Hebrews from a plague of poisonous snakes (Numbers 21:8–9). That bronze serpent was kept by the Israelites as a reminder of God’s goodness and salvation; however, by the time of King Hezekiah, the “relic” had become an object of worship. Hezekiah’s reforms included breaking “into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. (It was called Nehushtan)” (2 Kings 18:4). Physical aids to faith, if not commanded by God, are unnecessary and inevitably lead to superstition and idolatry.

There is absolutely no power in Christian relics. Even if the entire cross of Jesus were discovered intact, it would have no spiritual value. Relics do not, in any manner whatsoever, enable us to get closer to God. The humerus of a saint can do nothing for your spirit. Relics should not be prayed to, worshiped, or in any way be used as a means to better connect with God. Using relics in such a talismanic way is blatant idolatry (Exodus 20:3; Isaiah 42:8). An elaborate church filled with relics is no more valid a place for worship than a simple tent in a jungle. We worship the Lord in spirit and truth (John 4:24), not by idols, icons, or relics, whether genuine or fake.

Deadpan means delivering a joke, remark, or serious message with an impassive, expressionless face and a matter-of-fact tone. [1, 2]
What is Deadpan?
Meaning: A style of speaking or acting that hides all emotion, warmth, or reaction, creating a "dead face" (dead + pan, where pan is old slang for face). [1, 2]

VATICAN CITY (Vatican News) — Pope Leo XIV has dedicated his October prayer intention to mental health ministry, calling on the Church to listen without judging and accompany those who suffer without excluding them.

In a video produced by the Pope’s Worldwide Prayer Network, the pope prayed that the Church may be an “open house” where people facing challenges to their mental health find welcome, dignity and hope.

He prays that the Church may become “a safe space where everyone has a place — a community that accompanies and never excludes, that listens without judging and draws near without fear.”

The pope also remembered those who provide care, including professionals, family members and volunteers, asking God to give them strength and compassion.

Doublespeak is language that deliberately obscures, disguises, distorts, or reverses the meaning of words. Doublespeak may take the form of euphemisms (e.g., "downsizing" for layoffs and "servicing the target" for bombing),[1] in which case it is primarily meant to make the truth sound more palatable. It may also refer to intentional ambiguity in language or to actual inversions of meaning. In such cases, doublespeak disguises the nature of the truth.

Doublespeak is most closely associated with political language used by large entities such as corporations and governments.[2][3]

Origins and concepts
The term doublespeak derives from two concepts in George Orwell's 1949 novel, Nineteen Eighty-Four, "doublethink" and "Newspeak", despite the term itself not being used in the novel.[4] Another version of the term, doubletalk, also referring to intentionally ambiguous speech, did exist at the time Orwell wrote his book, but the usage of doublespeak, as well as of "doubletalk", in the sense of emphasizing ambiguity, clearly predates the publication of the novel.[5][6] Parallels have also been drawn between doublespeak and Orwell's classic essay, Politics and the English Language, which discusses linguistic distortion for purposes related to politics.[7] In the essay, he observes that political language often serves to distort and obscure reality. Orwell's description of political speech is extremely similar to the popular definition of the term, doublespeak:[8]

In our time, political speech and writing are largely the defence of the indefensible… Thus political language has to consist largely of euphemism, question-begging and sheer cloudy vagueness… the great enemy of clear language is insincerity. Where there is a gap between one's real and one's declared aims, one turns as it were instinctively to long words and exhausted idioms…

The writer Edward S. Herman cited what he saw as examples of doublespeak and doublethink in modern society.[9] Herman describes in his book, Beyond Hypocrisy, the principal characteristics of doublespeak:

What is really important in the world of doublespeak is the ability to lie, whether knowingly or unconsciously, and to get away with it; and the ability to use lies and choose and shape facts selectively, blocking out those that don’t fit an agenda or program.[10]

Examples
In politics
Edward S. Herman and Noam Chomsky comment in their book Manufacturing Consent: the Political Economy of the Mass Media that Orwellian doublespeak is an important component of the manipulation of the English language in American media, through a process called dichotomization, a component of media propaganda involving "deeply embedded double standards in the reporting of news." For example, the use of state funds by the poor and financially needy is commonly referred to as "social welfare" or "handouts," which the "coddled" poor "take advantage of". These terms, however, are not as often applied to other beneficiaries of government spending such as military spending.[11] The bellicose language used interchangeably with calls for peace towards Armenia by Azerbaijani president Aliyev after the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War were described as doublespeak in media.[12]

In advertising
Advertisers can use doublespeak to mask their commercial intent from users, as users' defenses against advertising become more entrenched.[13] Some are attempting to counter this technique with a number of systems offering diverse views and information to highlight the manipulative and dishonest methods that advertisers employ.[14]

According to Jacques Ellul, "the aim is not to even modify people’s ideas on a given subject, rather, it is to achieve conformity in the way that people act." He demonstrates this view by offering an example from drug advertising. Use of doublespeak in advertisements resulted in aspirin production rates rising by almost 50 percent from over 23 million pounds in 1960 to over 35 million pounds in 1970.[15]

In comedy
Doublespeak, particularly when exaggerated, can be used as a device in satirical comedy and social commentary to ironically parody political or bureaucratic establishments' intent on obfuscation or prevarication. The television series Yes Minister is notable for its use of this device.[16] Oscar Wilde was an early proponent of this device[17][18][19] and a significant influence on Orwell.[18]

Intensify/downplay pattern
This pattern was formulated by Hugh Rank and is a simple tool designed to teach some basic patterns of persuasion used in political propaganda and commercial advertising. The function of the intensify/downplay pattern is not to dictate what should be discussed but to encourage coherent thought and systematic organization. The pattern works in two ways: intensifying and downplaying. All people intensify, and this is done via repetition, association and composition. Downplaying is commonly done via omission, diversion and confusion as they communicate in words, gestures, numbers, et cetera.

The 1,700-year-old skull belonged to Saint Agatha, a third-century Christian martyr and the patron saint of Catania, Sicily
By Hazel Gandhi
15:10 ET, 21 Aug 2026

During an elaborate ceremony where the skull of Saint Agatha was placed back in a gold bust, the Vatican's secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, bowed and kissed the relic as part of Christian tradition.

The 1,700-year-old skull is believed to belong to Saint Agatha, a third-century martyr and patron saint of Catania, Sicily.

The skull was temporarily removed from its original place as the Catania Cathedral was undergoing restoration. On Aug. 17, it was put back by Parolin, who bowed and blew a kiss on the skull before placing it back. This ritual is part of the Catholic rite of veneration.

Footage of the ceremony quickly surfaced on social media, shedding light on the ancient tradition followed in Catholicism. According to Catholics, the act shows respect to the saint rather than worshipping her remains, but has ignited debate around the veneration of relics.

Many non-Catholics said the ritual was "idolatry," meaning the worship of a physical object or image as a God.

Saint Agatha was born around 231 AD in Catania, and dedicated her life to God, becoming a consecrated virgin, which is when a young woman chooses to remain celibate and gives herself completely to Jesus and a life in the Church of prayer and service.

However, one man who had hoped to marry Saint Agatha threatened to torture her if she did not agree to be with him. She was then imprisoned and brutally tortured after refusing to renounce her faith.

According to Christian lore, she died in prison around 251 AD during Emperor Decius’s persecution of Christians.

After her death, she was honored as a martyr and became Catania's patron saint. Her relics were then taken to Constantinople centuries later, before they were returned to her place of birth in 1126.

The recent ritual showed how the Church displayed her skull in a historic procession and placed it back in a decorated 14th-century gold bust.

According to Catholic tradition, kissing a relic is an act of veneration that shows deep respect for a saint rather than offering them worship, which is solely reserved for God. In Catholicism, relics are seen as tangible links to figures from the past and offer a way to honor and respect their sacrifice.

For this particular event, a prayer vigil was first held on Aug. 16, followed by the restoration of the skull.

What is the significance of Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss?
Answer

Judas Iscariot was one of the original twelve disciples who followed and were taught by Jesus. Being in Jesus’ “inner circle,” Judas had a closer relationship to Jesus than most people during His ministry. Judas betrayed the Lord to the Jewish authorities. The pre-arranged signal was that the person Judas kissed was to be arrested and taken away (Mark 14:44). In this way the Son of Man was betrayed with a kiss (Luke 22:48).

In the culture of first-century Israel, a kiss was not always a romantic expression of love; rather, a kiss on the cheek was a common greeting, a sign of deep respect, honor, and brotherly love (see Luke 7:45; Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 2 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; 1 Peter 5:14). For a student who had great respect for his teacher, a kiss fell well within the healthy expression of honor.

What really stands out in the mode of Judas’s betrayal is that Judas used such an intimate expression of love and respect to betray Jesus. Judas’s actions were hypocritical in the extreme—his actions said, “I respect and honor you,” at the exact time he was betraying Jesus to be murdered. Judas’s actions illustrate Proverbs 27:6, “Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.” Often, foes disguise themselves as friends. Evil often wears a mask to conceal its true purpose.

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

Today: how the dollar got its crown.

FIRST: WHAT DOES "WORLD RESERVE CURRENCY" MEAN?

Every country has a central bank. It's like the country's main bank account manager. Central banks keep national savings, called reserves, the way a family keeps an emergency fund.

For decades, most countries kept those savings in U.S. dollars, mostly by buying U.S. government bonds, called Treasuries. 

A Treasury is basically an IOU: you lend the U.S. government money, and it pays you back with interest.

That gave America a huge advantage. The whole world wanted to lend it money.

HOW THE DOLLAR GOT ITS CROWN

1944: After World War II, world leaders agreed the dollar would be the world's main currency. Any country could trade its dollars for gold at $35 an ounce. [1]

1971: President Nixon ended that deal. The dollar was no longer backed by gold. [2]

1974–75: America found a new anchor: oil. The U.S. offered Saudi Arabia military support. In return, the Saudis invested their oil profits in U.S. Treasuries. Soon, oil around the world was priced in dollars. Every country that needed oil needed dollars. This became known as the "petrodollar." [3]

Late 1990s: Central banks decided gold was old-fashioned. They sold it and bought Treasuries, because Treasuries pay interest and gold doesn't.

But there's a part of this story most people never hear.

After World War II, America was buried in debt. It didn't default. It found a quiet way out, and savers paid the bill without ever being told.
That same playbook is running again right now.

Part 2: the trick Washington used then, and the one it's using on your savings today.

For Hanson, the midterms create a countdown for Iran policy.

Victor Davis Hanson argues that the approaching midterms could work in Donald Trump's favor by giving him a short period in which to seek a decisive outcome with Iran. The election is not simply a source of political risk in this account. It becomes a deadline that may sharpen Trump's incentive to act.

Hanson says Iranian leaders may be counting on Trump to offer concessions to reduce gasoline prices before the election, or on Democratic gains to constrain military action afterward. He rejects the first possibility and doubts the second would produce enough congressional support to cut off military funding.

Instead, Hanson predicts that Trump could intensify pressure through stronger sanctions, blockades and embargoes, while encouraging internal dissent and Kurdish resistance. These are predictions about possible next steps, not confirmed reports that the measures have been authorized or implemented.

That is why Hanson sees Iran as drawing the wrong conclusion from the calendar. In his view, the midterm deadline gives Trump a short window to raise the stakes and seek a decisive result. He also says dissidents may see the same period as favorable because they currently have support in Washington.

31 Abandoned Places That Are Eerily Mesmerizing
📸
18/31
--
Seattle Underground
Location: Seattle, Washington

Beneath Seattle’s Pioneer Square neighborhood lies a long-abandoned subterranean city. It was constructed after the Great Seattle Fire of 1889 destroyed 25 blocks of the neighborhood’s central business district. When it came time to rebuild, the city constructed eight-foot retaining walls on both sides of the streets, filled in the space between the walls and paved over everything, leaving the streets one story higher than before.

But before the new streets were finished, some business owners had already reconstructed their buildings—not realizing their street-level ground floors would soon be underground. The result was a network of tunnels and passageways under Pioneer Square. While they were open initially, city officials condemned the subterranean maze in 1907, fearing they could play a role in spreading plague. These underground ruins were largely forgotten, almost like a lost city, until a local historian researched the passageways, restored some to what they might have looked like at the turn of the century and started offering public tours in 1965. The company still offers tours today.

Startups in Cameroon, Central Africa and the diaspora have until today, October 5, to apply for a Yaoundé competition offering one winner a pathway to the Startup World Cup programme in San Francisco.

The competition, known as Lion’s Den, will be held during the Cameroon International Tech Summit, CITS26, at the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on October 17.

Organisers say ten startups will be selected to pitch their businesses before investors, technology leaders and other industry figures.

Applications are open to legally registered startups and scale-ups from any sector, although organisers are particularly interested in technology businesses working in areas such as artificial intelligence, fintech, agriculture, health, climate, education, e-commerce, mobility and digital services.

Applicants are expected to have moved beyond the idea stage and be able to demonstrate customers, pilot projects, revenue, partnerships or other evidence that their product has been tested in the market.

The ten finalists are expected to be announced on October 10.

Each finalist will have four minutes to pitch, followed by two minutes of questions from the jury. Presentations can be made in English or French, although slides must be in English.

The winner of the Yaoundé competition will advance to the Startup World Cup Grand Finale programme in San Francisco, entering at the semi-final stage. Organisers say the winner will also receive a return economy flight for one company representative and a place in Mountain Hub’s incubation programme.

There is no application fee.

The final pitch is scheduled for 9am to midday on October 17 at the Palais des Congrès.

For young companies seeking investors and opportunities beyond Cameroon, the competition offers a chance to test their businesses before an international audience and potentially move from the local market to Silicon Valley.
