text:
An Iranian Threat, 3 Vans and a Phone Call: Behind the Mystery at a U.K. Air Base

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 12:48 min
Published 03OCT2026 & Updated 04OCT2026
By Michael D. Shear, Eric Schmitt, Megan Specia, and Adam Goldman
https://t.co/ChdUDBfCD5
Michael D. Shear and Adam Goldman reported from London, Megan Specia from Fairford, England, and Eric Schmitt from Washington.

A mysterious call last Sunday near a military base used by the U.S. set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty in Britain.

The three white vans navigated through a picturesque stretch of rural England in the middle of the night, winding toward a British air base that America is using to wage war on Iran.

It was 12:45 a.m. on Sunday when one of the men inside the vans 

— for reasons still not clear — 

dialed emergency services, giving authorities their first sign that a terrorism plot they had received intelligence on almost two weeks earlier might be in motion.

The police scrambled an urgent, armed response, speeding to the scene and arresting the man and four associates. 

A grainy photo later leaked to the media showed the five men sitting shirtless on the side of a road, their hands bound behind their backs.

Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford
https://t.co/T0efWnPSQc
29SEP2026 Olivia Ireland & Leigh Boobyer, West of England

Why the man called the police remains the subject of debate among investigators trying to unravel what happened that night, security officials from several countries told The New York Times. They asked for anonymity because the inquiry remains open.

It is one of many puzzles that the authorities have yet to piece together.

The call did set off a cascade of events, including the arrest of the men on suspicion of terrorism, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives, and a national security meeting convened by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. 

He said later that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part.”

But a part in what, exactly? Mr. Burnham and other British authorities have offered few answers. The vans contained no explosives when the police searched them. 

And within a day, all five men were released on bail, the kind of treatment typically given to common criminals, rather than terrorism suspects. 

The authorities could also have been hamstrung by the need to keep evidence classified and thus unable to be cited in criminal court.

The police have cast a wide net in trying to find those responsible for hiring the men, whom one official described as “unwitting chumps.” 

U.S. and British officials believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, has rejected the accusations.

This account is drawn from interviews with investigators, local officials and residents as well as security officials in Britain, Germany, Israel and the United States who had knowledge of warnings about a plot to target U.S. bases in Britain and Europe. 

Some officials declined to reveal details of the case. 

Others conceded that the full story remains hazy, even to them. 

Most spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing the sensitive nature of the investigation.

For Britain, the events of the last six days have been a vivid — if at times mystifying — reminder that the American- and Israeli-led war against Iran that began eight months ago has the potential to do more than raise the price of oil.

In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for their actions. 

“Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory,” the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces.”

Officials found no concrete signs the men in the vans were in the final stages of an attack.

Then, over the weekend, commanders received new information, which one U.S. official said was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced last month but with specific details and greater urgency. 

The U.S. rapidly withdrew all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from the air base, two U.S. officials said on Sunday, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
05OCT2026
By Eric Schmitt 
https://t.co/nUA7uo65Cn
The withdrawal came with unusual speed, following what U.S. officials said were threats of an Iran-based plot against the installation.
A military airplane taking flight in an airfield with a lightly cloudy sky in the background.

Vague warnings
In mid-September, U.S. military commanders received a chilling warning from American and other Western intelligence agencies, according to U.S. officials briefed on the information. 

R.A.F. Fairford, the base in southern England primarily used by the United States Air Force to deploy some of its largest bombers, was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.

The map locates the R.A.F. Fairford air base, outside of the city of Fairford, in southern England, northwest of London.

The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. 

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. 

Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.

The warnings were general. Analysts could not pin down a date or concrete details about the plotters, other than concluding they were guided and supported by Tehran. Base commanders in Britain raised security levels, already elevated since the start of the war with Iran.

Residents of the nearby town of Fairford, and the villages of Kempsford and Whelford, began noticing changes. There were “rumbles that things were being moved around the base in terms of protection and levels of warnings,” said Dom Morris, a local councilor.

On Sept. 16, 11 days before the episode at the base, a resident posted in a private neighborhood Facebook group that he had seen something unusual: a man in a balaclava running through the village around 9 p.m. At least three other villagers said they had seen a masked man wearing black. It was unclear if they were speaking about the same person, or who it was.

Across Europe, concern among officials was surging. 

According to a senior U.S. official, Israel warned Germany that American bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.

On Sept. 23, four days before the events at R.A.F. Fairford, an Iranian-backed media site posted comments from Yahya Rahim Safavi, former chief commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. 

According to SITE Intelligence Group, which tracks the online activity of jihadist organizations, Mr. Safavi condemned Europe as a “logistics hub” for America’s war on Iran, naming air bases that U.S. forces have used to conduct the war, including Ramstein in Germany, Aviano in Italy and Fairford.

But without concrete intelligence about a specific target or timing, there was little the authorities could do — except tighten security and wait.

A plot emerges
That changed, dramatically, last Sunday.

A local farmer returning home from a party found her driveway blocked by the three white vans.

“I looked at it and thought, ‘That is not real,’” the farmer, who declined to be identified, later told BBC News. 

She told reporters she saw eight to 10 people in masks running.

At 1:36 a.m., she said, she called 999, the British version of 911, and later said she believed her call “foiled whatever plans they had.”

The police timeline suggests, however, that she made her call about 50 minutes after the man in the van. It isn’t clear whether the people she saw were the suspects, or security operatives responding to the initial alert.

“This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation,” Vicki Evans, the deputy assistant commissioner for Britain’s counter terrorism police, said later on Sunday, adding, “Our activity is in the interest of national security.”

By Monday, however, the case took a surprising turn.

The men were released on bail, a rare outcome for terrorism suspects. The police said later they had discovered some gasoline, but no explosives, in the vans. Laurence Taylor, Ms. Evans’s supervisor, told reporters the men were “subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation.”

Behind closed doors, officials were trying to determine the suspects’ role, and whether Iran was using them to undermine Britain’s willingness to let the United States use its bases. It is not yet clear how much investigators have learned from the men about their plans.

Were they a diversion from another attack that was in the works? Had they been intercepted before they could link up with other confederates? Or was the episode an elaborate hoax designed to sow fear and create propaganda?

Some intelligence officials believed the initial call by one of the five men was part of a plan to distract the police while a broader plot unfolded. Others thought it was more likely that the five men were low-level criminals, one of whom called when they realized they had been hired to do something serious.

Mr. Taylor shared little about the investigation in his statement on Monday. But he hinted at the complexity of the case.

“Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity,” he said, “often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain.”

Assessing future risks
The head of MI5, Britain’s domestic security agency, has warned for years about Iran-backed plots, which have often involved targeting opponents using local criminals.

“Iranian state actors make extensive use of criminals as proxies — from international drug traffickers to low-level crooks,” Ken McCallum, the group’s director general, said in 2024. Iranian journalists and dissidents in Britain have received death threats and been physically attacked.

When he was prime minister of Britain, Keir Starmer initially refused to let the Trump administration use R.A.F. Fairford for strikes on Iran, saying he would not join “regime change from the skies.” 

But he later gave permission for what he called “defensive” operations, and American B-52 and B-1 planes loaded with bombs began flying to Iran from Fairford. Mr. Burnham has continued the policy.

After Mr. Starmer announced the change on March 1, Iranian proxies appeared ready to act against a wider range of targets in Britain. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer group in London were set on fire. Molotov cocktails were thrown at several synagogues in the middle of the night.

The goal appeared to be to stoke fear in the Jewish community, while signaling that Britain’s changed posture had consequences. 

The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, or Hayi, which, U.S. prosecutors said, is a front for Kataib Hezbollah, a U.S.-designated terrorist group and one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in Iraq. 

A commander from the group was charged in the United States in May with leading the attacks and other incidents in Europe as part of a retaliation campaign by Tehran.

In April, Hayi posted a video claiming that the Israeli Embassy in London would be attacked by drones carrying dangerous substances. Suspicious items, including two jars of a powdered substance, were found in the nearby Kensington Gardens. A huge police response was triggered, involving chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear teams. But the police later concluded that there had been no attack on the embassy and the powdered substance was not hazardous.

An actual assault on an American air base in Britain would be a drastic escalation, officials said.

By the end of the week, the evacuated families had returned to their homes and a 1,300-foot cordon around where the vans had been was taken down. But concrete barriers were installed around the entrance of R.A.F. Fairford. As the investigation continued, the police arrested a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian citizen in London, on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He, too, was released on bail.

Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting from Washington.

Michael D. Shear is the chief U.K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U.S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Megan Specia reports on Britain, Ireland and the Ukraine war for The Times. She is based in London.

Adam Goldman is a London-based reporter for The Times who writes about global security.

A version of this article appears in print on Oct. 4, 2026, Section A, Page 12 of the New York edition with the headline: A Threat, 3 Vans and a Shadow War in a Corner of England.

Automated turrets offer another layer of defense. Machine vision can help detect and track fast-moving targets, while automation shortens the engagement cycle.

text:
$ONEN: Headquartered in West Palm Beach, Florida, the company positions itself as an independent power developer. Its strategy involves deploying natural gas units and energy storage systems for rapid implementation, supplemented by advanced Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) in the long term, to provide high-density baseload power to data centers, hydrogen facilities, industrial sites, and the grid, while securing long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). The industry backdrop is characterized by surging electricity demand from AI data centers and a race across the Southeastern U.S. (particularly Louisiana) to secure transmission capacity, industrial parks, and computing infrastructure sites. While the nuclear power narrative is gaining momentum, natural gas combined with energy storage remains the only solution capable of grid interconnection within two to three years; SMRs require site selection, environmental impact assessments, and U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing—a process spanning a decade. ONEN sits at the very beginning of this value chain: it holds site control intentions but currently lacks permits, disclosed off-takers, and operating revenue.
On September 23, 2026, the company completed its merger with Hennessy Capital Investment Corp. VII and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ONEN around September 24. It closed at approximately $1.87 on October 2, with a market capitalization of roughly $200–$230 million; the stock has fallen about 82% over the past 52 weeks, with insiders holding approximately 74% of shares and institutions holding about 4%. In pre-market trading on October 5, the price briefly touched approximately $1.95.

Product and Qualification Highlights
The company’s offering is not currently operational power plants, but rather a portfolio of three projects in Louisiana totaling approximately 5 GW under development. This includes "Amberjack," a standalone, scalable multi-unit SMR complex targeting up to approximately 1 GW of advanced nuclear capacity. Site control has been secured, and the project has entered the technical and environmental assessment phase, with preparations underway for pre-application discussions with the NRC. The company has clarified that current activities do not equate to NRC site approval, reactor licensing, environmental permits, or a finalized engineering plan; specific reactor designs, investment budgets, commercial operation dates, and power customers have not yet been determined. Cayman: ~2.88 GW of natural gas-fired generation paired with ~700 MW / 2.88 GWh of energy storage, with the potential to co-locate a data center campus. A binding Letter of Intent (LOI) for site control was signed with a local landowner group in late August 2026; the site is located near RiverPlex MegaPark, northeast of the area where SpaceX is currently expanding its infrastructure. The current plan does not include nuclear power.
Barracuda: ~1.2 GW of modular natural gas generation, ~300 MW / 1.2 GWh of four-hour energy storage, and up to ~1 GW of critical IT data center capacity; deployment can be phased based on customer demand and grid interconnection conditions.

Core Investment Thesis: The narrative aligns with the pressing issue of power shortages: AI data centers require 24/7 power; gas-fired generation plus storage offers a near-term solution, while SMRs represent a long-term option.
The Louisiana portfolio combines ~4 GW of gas-fired generation and up to 1 GW of nuclear capacity on a single platform; securing a major customer for either project could drive significant valuation upside.
The stock price has retreated significantly from its highs during the initial listing hype; the market cap of ~$200 million reflects the value of "5 GW under development" options rather than operational assets.
High insider ownership aligns interests with project advancement; however, the low public float and limited institutional holdings make the price susceptible to one-sided volatility driven by news flow.

Short-term target price: $1.60–$2.30

Central Michigan Kept NFL Star Antonio Brown on the Rails
The star wide receiver's erratic behavior only started after he left the Chippewas for the NFL

By Alex Deimel @AlexDeimel1 

Every professional sport has that one player who is way more famous for performances off the field than for their performance on it.

When it comes to Antonio Brown, that line is quite blurry.

Controversy has surrounded the former NFL wide receiver for a long time. From tearing off his jersey in the middle of a game while playing for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, to several allegations of sexual abuse and domestic violence, Brown seems to have lost his mind years ago.

His decision-making reeks of head trauma, but little controversy followed him while he played college football at Central Michigan.

Brown walked on to the Chippewa football team in 2007 after wide receivers coach Zach Azzanni offered him a tryout. Before that tryout, Brown had been expelled from Florida International University for an altercation with campus security, prompting Azzanni to reach out.

Mount Pleasant seemed to suit the Florida-born star. It seems the only point in Brown’s career where he didn’t get into any legal trouble was at Central Michigan. Though he initially struggled with punctuality, he won the MAC Freshman of the Year award and All-American honors before declaring for the NFL draft.

Although his antics prior to CMU suggest Brown was destined for the looney bin from the jump, it’s equally likely that Brown endured enough helmet-to-helmet contact during his time with the Chippewas.

Brown’s YouTube highlight titled “The Game That Got Antonio Brown Drafted” shows several instances where, despite excellent jukes, Brown was blown up by Georgia defenders.

Brown led the Chippewas in receiving yards that game despite multiple helmet-to-helmet blows. Eight years later came the infamous Vontaze Burfict head-to-head knockout hit during a Bengals and Steelers wildcard matchup, which many consider to be the inciting incident for Brown’s mental struggles.

Brown’s legal troubles began in 2018 when he threw furniture from his 14th-floor apartment and nearly killed a 22-month old. In between that and multiple sexual assault allegations in 2019 came some 100 mph+ speeding tickets.

Brown has dug the hole deeper for himself. In 2020, the Hollywood, Florida, police stated they no longer wanted Brown to be involved with their youth league after they were called to his home for multiple domestic incidents.

His public incidents since then have ranged from everything including public exposure to most recently second-degree attempted murder, which he recently pled no contest to in order to receive probation instead of going to prison.

Interestingly, around the time of his release from the New England Patriots, Brown re-enrolled at Central Michigan in 2019, graduating in 2023.

Considering Michigan seems to be the one state in which he never got in any legal trouble, it might make sense for him to come back.

💰 At the 2021 Cyber Symposium, Mike Lindell claimed he had data proving China hacked the 2020 election. He offered $5 million to anyone who could prove that data was not real election data. Robert Zeidman, a computer expert and Trump supporter, took up the challenge.

Zeidman submitted a report arguing that the data "unequivocally does not contain packet data of any kind and do[es] not contain any information related to the November 2020 election."

A 2023 arbitration panel ordered Lindell to pay Zeidman the $5 million. Lindell challenged the award in court. A federal judge in Minnesota upheld the ruling in 2024.

An appeals court overturned the ruling in July 2025; the judges said the arbitrators looked beyond the strict wording of the contest rules when they made their decision. In January 2026, the Supreme Court refused to hear Zeidman's appeal.

Current status: in August 2026, a federal judge sent the case back to the same arbitration panel for a new decision. This time the panel must stick only to the exact wording of the contest rules, nothing else.

Zeidman won the arbitration in 2023. Whether that legally entitles him to the $5 million is still being decided.

text:
An Iranian Threat, 3 Vans and a Phone Call: Behind the Mystery at a U.K. Air Base

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 12:48 min
Published 03OCT2026 & Updated 04OCT2026
By Michael D. Shear, Eric Schmitt, Megan Specia, and Adam Goldman
https://t.co/ChdUDBfCD5
Michael D. Shear and Adam Goldman reported from London, Megan Specia from Fairford, England, and Eric Schmitt from Washington.

A mysterious call last Sunday near a military base used by the U.S. set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty in Britain.

The three white vans navigated through a picturesque stretch of rural England in the middle of the night, winding toward a British air base that America is using to wage war on Iran.

It was 12:45 a.m. on Sunday when one of the men inside the vans 

— for reasons still not clear — 

dialed emergency services, giving authorities their first sign that a terrorism plot they had received intelligence on almost two weeks earlier might be in motion.

The police scrambled an urgent, armed response, speeding to the scene and arresting the man and four associates. 

A grainy photo later leaked to the media showed the five men sitting shirtless on the side of a road, their hands bound behind their backs.

Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford
https://t.co/T0efWnPSQc
29SEP2026 Olivia Ireland & Leigh Boobyer, West of England

Why the man called the police remains the subject of debate among investigators trying to unravel what happened that night, security officials from several countries told The New York Times. They asked for anonymity because the inquiry remains open.

It is one of many puzzles that the authorities have yet to piece together.

The call did set off a cascade of events, including the arrest of the men on suspicion of terrorism, the frantic evacuation of 85 homes, a bomb disposal robot searching the vans for explosives, and a national security meeting convened by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. 

He said later that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part.”

But a part in what, exactly? Mr. Burnham and other British authorities have offered few answers. The vans contained no explosives when the police searched them. 

And within a day, all five men were released on bail, the kind of treatment typically given to common criminals, rather than terrorism suspects. 

The authorities could also have been hamstrung by the need to keep evidence classified and thus unable to be cited in criminal court.

The police have cast a wide net in trying to find those responsible for hiring the men, whom one official described as “unwitting chumps.” 

U.S. and British officials believe the operation is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps or a separate military headquarters in Tehran. Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, has rejected the accusations.

This account is drawn from interviews with investigators, local officials and residents as well as security officials in Britain, Germany, Israel and the United States who had knowledge of warnings about a plot to target U.S. bases in Britain and Europe. 

Some officials declined to reveal details of the case. 

Others conceded that the full story remains hazy, even to them. 

Most spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing the sensitive nature of the investigation.

For Britain, the events of the last six days have been a vivid — if at times mystifying — reminder that the American- and Israeli-led war against Iran that began eight months ago has the potential to do more than raise the price of oil.

In July, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards issued a statement warning that allowing the United States to use the base “makes London responsible” for their actions. 

“Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory,” the statement said, “is a legitimate target for our forces.”

Officials found no concrete signs the men in the vans were in the final stages of an attack.

Then, over the weekend, commanders received new information, which one U.S. official said was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced last month but with specific details and greater urgency. 

The U.S. rapidly withdrew all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from the air base, two U.S. officials said on Sunday, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
05OCT2026
By Eric Schmitt 
https://t.co/nUA7uo65Cn
The withdrawal came with unusual speed, following what U.S. officials said were threats of an Iran-based plot against the installation.
A military airplane taking flight in an airfield with a lightly cloudy sky in the background.

Vague warnings
In mid-September, U.S. military commanders received a chilling warning from American and other Western intelligence agencies, according to U.S. officials briefed on the information. 

R.A.F. Fairford, the base in southern England primarily used by the United States Air Force to deploy some of its largest bombers, was the target of a potential Iran-backed attack.

The map locates the R.A.F. Fairford air base, outside of the city of Fairford, in southern England, northwest of London.

The murky outlines of a plot had been pieced together through a combination of intercepted communications, informants and other intelligence. 

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said his intelligence officials also warned their British counterparts of a probable Iranian-sponsored attack, though they did not provide a specific target. 

Follow-up attacks were likely to include drones, the confidential assessments warned.

The warnings were general. Analysts could not pin down a date or concrete details about the plotters, other than concluding they were guided and supported by Tehran. Base commanders in Britain raised security levels, already elevated since the start of the war with Iran.

Residents of the nearby town of Fairford, and the villages of Kempsford and Whelford, began noticing changes. There were “rumbles that things were being moved around the base in terms of protection and levels of warnings,” said Dom Morris, a local councilor.

On Sept. 16, 11 days before the episode at the base, a resident posted in a private neighborhood Facebook group that he had seen something unusual: a man in a balaclava running through the village around 9 p.m. At least three other villagers said they had seen a masked man wearing black. It was unclear if they were speaking about the same person, or who it was.

Across Europe, concern among officials was surging. 

According to a senior U.S. official, Israel warned Germany that American bases there were at heightened risk, noting Spangdahlem and Ramstein in particular.

On Sept. 23, four days before the events at R.A.F. Fairford, an Iranian-backed media site posted comments from Yahya Rahim Safavi, former chief commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. 

According to SITE Intelligence Group, which tracks the online activity of jihadist organizations, Mr. Safavi condemned Europe as a “logistics hub” for America’s war on Iran, naming air bases that U.S. forces have used to conduct the war, including Ramstein in Germany, Aviano in Italy and Fairford.

But without concrete intelligence about a specific target or timing, there was little the authorities could do — except tighten security and wait.

A plot emerges
That changed, dramatically, last Sunday.

A local farmer returning home from a party found her driveway blocked by the three white vans.

“I looked at it and thought, ‘That is not real,’” the farmer, who declined to be identified, later told BBC News. 

She told reporters she saw eight to 10 people in masks running.

At 1:36 a.m., she said, she called 999, the British version of 911, and later said she believed her call “foiled whatever plans they had.”

The police timeline suggests, however, that she made her call about 50 minutes after the man in the van. It isn’t clear whether the people she saw were the suspects, or security operatives responding to the initial alert.

“This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation,” Vicki Evans, the deputy assistant commissioner for Britain’s counter terrorism police, said later on Sunday, adding, “Our activity is in the interest of national security.”

By Monday, however, the case took a surprising turn.

The men were released on bail, a rare outcome for terrorism suspects. The police said later they had discovered some gasoline, but no explosives, in the vans. Laurence Taylor, Ms. Evans’s supervisor, told reporters the men were “subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation.”

Behind closed doors, officials were trying to determine the suspects’ role, and whether Iran was using them to undermine Britain’s willingness to let the United States use its bases. It is not yet clear how much investigators have learned from the men about their plans.

Were they a diversion from another attack that was in the works? Had they been intercepted before they could link up with other confederates? Or was the episode an elaborate hoax designed to sow fear and create propaganda?

Some intelligence officials believed the initial call by one of the five men was part of a plan to distract the police while a broader plot unfolded. Others thought it was more likely that the five men were low-level criminals, one of whom called when they realized they had been hired to do something serious.

Mr. Taylor shared little about the investigation in his statement on Monday. But he hinted at the complexity of the case.

“Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity,” he said, “often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain.”

Assessing future risks
The head of MI5, Britain’s domestic security agency, has warned for years about Iran-backed plots, which have often involved targeting opponents using local criminals.

“Iranian state actors make extensive use of criminals as proxies — from international drug traffickers to low-level crooks,” Ken McCallum, the group’s director general, said in 2024. Iranian journalists and dissidents in Britain have received death threats and been physically attacked.

When he was prime minister of Britain, Keir Starmer initially refused to let the Trump administration use R.A.F. Fairford for strikes on Iran, saying he would not join “regime change from the skies.” 

But he later gave permission for what he called “defensive” operations, and American B-52 and B-1 planes loaded with bombs began flying to Iran from Fairford. Mr. Burnham has continued the policy.

After Mr. Starmer announced the change on March 1, Iranian proxies appeared ready to act against a wider range of targets in Britain. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer group in London were set on fire. Molotov cocktails were thrown at several synagogues in the middle of the night.

The goal appeared to be to stoke fear in the Jewish community, while signaling that Britain’s changed posture had consequences. 

The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, or Hayi, which, U.S. prosecutors said, is a front for Kataib Hezbollah, a U.S.-designated terrorist group and one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in Iraq. 

A commander from the group was charged in the United States in May with leading the attacks and other incidents in Europe as part of a retaliation campaign by Tehran.

In April, Hayi posted a video claiming that the Israeli Embassy in London would be attacked by drones carrying dangerous substances. Suspicious items, including two jars of a powdered substance, were found in the nearby Kensington Gardens. A huge police response was triggered, involving chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear teams. But the police later concluded that there had been no attack on the embassy and the powdered substance was not hazardous.

An actual assault on an American air base in Britain would be a drastic escalation, officials said.

By the end of the week, the evacuated families had returned to their homes and a 1,300-foot cordon around where the vans had been was taken down. But concrete barriers were installed around the entrance of R.A.F. Fairford. As the investigation continued, the police arrested a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian citizen in London, on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. He, too, was released on bail.

Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting from Washington.

Michael D. Shear is the chief U.K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U.S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Megan Specia reports on Britain, Ireland and the Ukraine war for The Times. She is based in London.

Adam Goldman is a London-based reporter for The Times who writes about global security.

text:
The petrodollar won't die in a Treasury meeting. It'll die in the Strait of Hormuz. And I think the first crack shows up in the Gulf.

Since Feb 28 the Gulf has been a war zone. Iran choked Hormuz for weeks, hit tankers, even hit Fujairah in the UAE. In March a senior Iranian official floated letting tankers through only if the cargo was traded in yuan. Then came reports of Iran charging transit tolls in yuan.

Now look at who actually got through. Chinese tankers, broadcasting Chinese ownership and Chinese crew. Beijing leaned on Tehran to let Qatari LNG and crude move.China buys over 80% of Iran's oil. Nobody else has that kind of leverage over Tehran. Not Washington. Not Moscow.

So think like a Gulf oil minister.
The old deal was simple. Price oil in dollars, get American security. This year that security didn't stop missiles hitting your terminals or your tankers sitting stranded for months.

Now imagine Beijing walking in with a different offer:

"Sell to us in yuan. We're your biggest buyer anyway. And Tehran won't touch your facilities or your ships."

That's the petroyuan. It isn't a currency pitch. It's a protection pitch. Same model as 1974, different guarantor.

How I think it plays out:

China-bound cargoes go first, settled in yuan, quietly.
Smaller Gulf producers test it before Riyadh does.
Saudi hedges. Some yuan, mostly dollars, for years.
Digital rails like mBridge do the plumbing so nobody touches SWIFT. The dollar isn't going anywhere tomorrow. The riyal is still pegged to it. The yuan isn't fully convertible and Beijing runs capital controls. A US naval blockade has cut Iran's exports to almost nothing, Gulf crude through Hormuz is back near prewar levels, and Gulf states are making more money right now than before the war.

So this isn't a switch flipping. It's a slow leak.
But a reserve currency rests on one question: who keeps the oil moving safely?

 For 50 years the answer was Washington. In 2026, for the first time, Gulf capitals are seriously asking whether it still is.

Which Gulf state blinks first?

text:
A month out from the midterms, most polling says Democrats can retake the House and cut the Senate gap. It guarantees nothing for Ukraine.

Three problems are already visible.

First, the heavyweights are leaving. The Democrats who carried the hardest pro-Ukraine fights for years are ending their congressional careers.

Friends remain in both parties, but the new Congress loses those who did not flinch when the votes got hard.

Second, the primaries showed where the party is drifting. Progressives and democratic socialists beat moderates across multiple states.

Some voiced solidarity with Ukraine. Others offered vague lines about preferring diplomacy over weapons.

Most barely mentioned Ukraine at all and campaigned on Palestine instead.

Third, even Ukraine's remaining friends will often vote otherwise. Democrats stay in opposition to Trump for the next two years.

Passing Ukraine aid will require negotiating with a president who must sign the bills. Many Democrats will refuse to hand him a win.

We already saw it on the Graham sanctions bill, when most House Democrats voted no and the quiet argument was that supporting Ukraine was worth less than denying Trump a political gift.

Republicans had the same disease in 2023 and 2024, when "we support Ukraine, but" meant refusing to boost Biden before an election. Now the roles flip.

Bipartisan support survives. The good news is that.

But it will not convert into decisions unaided. The Ukrainian government, diplomats, diaspora, advocacy groups, and every delegation that visits Washington will have to activate it.

Ukrainians learned to speak Republican over the last few years. Now they need to remember how to speak Democrat.

Washington wants superintelligence. Futures want a nap.

Nasdaq 100 futures -0.18%, S&P 500 -0.09%, Dow -0.09%. That's a barely red tape on a morning full of headlines that would usually move things a lot more.

Start with $NVDA. DBS says its P/E plus roughly 70% expected earnings growth next year means AI tech is nowhere near bubble territory. That's the cleanest bull case there is: if earnings compound that fast, the multiple shrinks on its own even if the stock goes nowhere. The catch is that 70% is a forecast, not a print, and the stock is already priced for it. A quarter that merely meets it is a sell-the-news risk. The real test is whether capex from $MSFT $GOOGL $AMZN $META keeps climbing into 2027. Trump's new federal "superintelligence task force" gives the story a policy tailwind, but a coordination body is a narrative, not a purchase order. After TSMC jumped more than 3% in Taipei today, $TSM ADRs have a head start, and $AVGO and $AMD should follow the same AI bid at the open.

Deal of the morning is $CHRW buying $RXO for $17.25 a share in cash and stock. Freight brokerage has been stuck in a long downcycle, and consolidating near the bottom is the classic move. RXO should trade up toward the offer minus a spread for the stock piece, while CHRW holders will want to see how much dilution they eat and how fast synergies show up. Truckers like $JBHT and $XPO could catch a sympathy bid on the consolidation read.

Then there's the part nobody seems to be pricing. The fight over the Bab el-Mandeb is still going, Saudi Aramco's CEO says total crude supply is down nearly 3 billion barrels with commercial inventories below 6 billion, and OPEC+ left November quotas unchanged. That's a tight market with no extra barrels on the way. Good for $XOM $CVX $COP, and bad for anyone betting that cooling rate-hike fears are a straight line.

AI keeps the Nasdaq bid, and crude is the one thing that can flip the whole tape. Own the growth, but hedge the oil.

text:
You treated a foreign minister telling the American ambassador to “get out of the kitchen” as background noise, and the objection to it as the scandal.

Lamola did not offer a policy rebuttal. He delivered a personal dismissal: if Bozell will not keep talking on Pretoria’s terms, he should leave. That came after months of démarches aimed at the ambassador for saying in public what Washington has said in private - that expropriation without compensation, race-based empowerment rules, the refusal to treat “Kill the Boer” as hate speech, and the non-answers on farm murders are why the relationship is collapsing. Objecting to the insult is then cast as the undiplomatic act. The sequence is the point Bozell made. You answered it with a metaphor about a toddler.

Diplomacy has limits when one side uses “dialogue” as a substitute for answering. The US set out specific asks, waited, got what it regards as a non-response, and moved to visa restrictions. An ambassador stating that the time for endless process is over is blunt. A minister answering with “get out of the kitchen,” then expecting another lecture on manners when the bluntness is returned, is reckless. It is also arrogant: Lamola speaks as if ANC foreign-policy instincts are the settled position of the Government of National Unity. They are not. Coalition partners did not mandate him to personalise a fight with Washington or to treat criticism of domestic policy as interference that must be formally protested three times in nine months.

The cost lands on South Africa, not on Bozell’s tone. Trade, investment, market access and security cooperation are the things being put at risk by a minister who confuses sovereignty with immunity from consequences. If anyone in this exchange needs correcting, it is the man who turned a stalled negotiation into a public slight and then acted surprised that relations keep worsening. Lamola is a hazard.

text:
Possible Plague Crisis in Siberia: Five Hospitals Placed Under Quarantine After Lab Tech Dies Following Test Tube Accident Containing Plague Bacteria | Jim Hoft, The Gateway Pundit

A 28-year-old technician at Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute is dead, nearly 200 people are under medical observation, and five hospitals in the region have been reportedly slammed shut for quarantine, while the Kremlin’s health agency insists this is nothing but “pneumonia of unknown origin.”

The Moscow Times identified the dead woman as Darya Shipilova, a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

She was hospitalized in Shelekhov on September 29 with severe pneumonia, placed on a ventilator, and died on October 1, overnight into October 2, by some accounts.

The account that set off the alarm: Shipilova told medical staff she had accidentally broken a test tube of live Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, while handling samples on September 25. That is four days before she was admitted, DW reported.

Meduza, citing regional media, reported both that version and a competing claim that she fell ill after a trip. Neither has been officially confirmed.

Alexei Tsydenov, head of neighboring Buryatia, went further than Irkutsk officials were willing to go. He publicly said the woman had died of plague, then edited the post to say she “may have” died of it.

Irkutsk’s own governor, Igor Kobzev, would only call it a “particularly dangerous infection” and convene an emergency anti-epidemic commission.

On October 4, Russia’s consumer watchdog Rospotrebnadzor denied she died of plague at all. The official line, reported by bne IntelliNews and CNN: “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”

A commission claimed no accident involving pathogenic microorganisms had occurred at the institute. Contacts, officials said, were testing negative and showed no symptoms.

According to Charter97’s report citing the regional outlet People of Baikal, three Irkutsk city hospitals, Hospitals No. 1, No. 3, and No. 10, along with the Ivanomatreninskaya Children’s Hospital and a maternity hospital were reportedly placed under quarantine.

Those reports have not been independently confirmed by Russia’s federal health authorities, and officials have offered conflicting accounts of what exactly killed Shipilova.

Meanwhile, workers at the massive Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov have been ordered to wear masks as a precaution.

CNN reported that plant director Artem Fominikh acknowledged that “many rumors and conflicting reports” were circulating and confirmed the mask requirement.

At least 197 people who may have crossed paths with Shipilova were identified. About 189 of them were hospitalized for observation, 114 in one facility, 63 in another, 12 at the anti-plague institute itself, according to figures carried by The Moscow Times, REN TV, and bne IntelliNews. As of the latest official statements, no secondary cases have been confirmed.

Pneumonic plague is the form that matters. It is the only form that spreads person to person, through respiratory droplets. The CDC says the incubation period after inhalation can be as short as one day.

The World Health Organization puts the usual window at one to seven days. Untreated, it is frequently fatal, and the clock for antibiotics is measured in hours, not days. A September 25 broken vial and a September 29 collapse sit squarely inside that window.

Shelekhov is not a village. It is an industrial town built around the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant, a Rusal facility with more than 2,000 workers.

Plant director Artyom Fominykh ordered a mask protocol and told employees, in a Telegram post reported by bne IntelliNews and The Moscow Times: “God protects the cautious.” He urged anyone with symptoms to get medical help immediately — while admitting the town was awash in contradictory reports.

A nearby town administration briefly told residents to avoid Shelekhov, then deleted the post. Public events in Irkutsk were canceled.

text:
🧵

The ‘exodus’ that keeps arriving

How one billionaire’s move became a ‘failed state’ by breakfast

Late on Saturday 3 October, a story about an 88-year-old billionaire began spreading on @X. Ten minutes after one account posted it, Adam Brooks was telling his followers that Britain was “bleeding out”.

The facts underneath were modest. A spokesman confirmed to The Times and to LBC that David Reuben had moved from his Holland Park home to Monaco over the summer. He gave no reason. Reuben shares second place on the Sunday Times Rich List with his brother Simon, who, LBC reports, moved to Monaco decades ago. That much is news.

At 23:03 the @X account GB Politics reported that Reuben had quit the UK “amid tax fears”. The spokesman had given no such reason. The post had 160,100 views by Monday morning. At 23:13 Brooks quote-posted it with a verdict: “The exodus continues... Britain is bleeding out.”

Brooks, who describes himself on @X as a GB News and TalkTV panellist and has more than 450,000 followers, routinely takes aim at anything he regards as left-leaning or “woke”. In August he presented Westminster council’s draft licensing policy as something it was not, a pattern I examined in detail at the time (see my less measured next tweet). His post about Reuben reached 79,400 views.

At 04:23 the controversial prediction-market platform Polymarket, a betting operator rather than a newsroom, put out its own version under a “JUST IN” banner, adding that Reuben was “joining a growing exodus of ultra-wealthy residents”.

By breakfast Ben Graham, who describes himself on X as a Reform UK member and a Free Speech Union member, had linked Reuben to the hedge fund manager Chris Rokos and diagnosed “a country heading towards becoming a failed state”.

Within a few hours, a confirmed move with no stated motive had acquired a motive, a trend, a national wound and a prognosis of state failure. None of those additions came from Reuben or his spokesman. Each was supplied by someone passing the story on. The speed matters. The framing didn’t wait for a reason or explanation. It provided them.

This piece looks at how that happens. It’s the latest turn in a story I first examined in 2025 (see second tweet below), when the “millionaire exodus” rested on figures from a firm that sells residence and citizenship by investment. That firm has since stopped publishing them. The figures went, but the frame stayed.

It’s true that some very wealthy people have left Britain, and several say tax changes were a reason. Lakshmi Mittal and Nassef Sawiris have relocated, and Rokos is reported to be moving his tax residence to Greece. Richard Gnodde and Christian Angermayer have also been reported as leaving. These departures are real and worth reporting.

What we lack is any reliable measure of scale. The Sunday Times Rich List counted 157 sterling billionaires in 2026, down from a peak of 177 in 2022. But the list cannot separate people who left from people whose fortunes fell below £1 billion. It also keeps British nationals on the list regardless of where they now live. Its compiler, Robert Watts, called this year’s edition “a tale of two exoduses”. The Press Association’s syndicated copy then reported “an ongoing exodus of wealth from the UK” without qualification: a compiler’s interpretation became a news agency’s fact.

The best official data points the other way, with an important caveat. The non-dom regime, which let UK residents with a permanent home abroad avoid UK tax on overseas income, was abolished in April 2025 and replaced with a four-year exemption for new arrivals. HMRC’s July 2026 release covers the year to April 2025, the regime’s final year. Non-dom and deemed-domiciled taxpayers fell by about 1,200 to 81,900, while their tax and National Insurance liabilities rose 9% to £13.6 billion.

About 9,000 taxpayers “flowed out of the non-domiciled taxpayer population” in 2024-25, down from 11,200 in 2023-24. That count includes people who stopped claiming the status as well as people who left the country. Because these figures end the month the regime was abolished, they cannot settle the question. The first real test comes with HMRC’s 2027 release.

Ministers have repeatedly told Parliament the Government does not hold data on how many wealthy people have left. Treasury answers note there is “no single agreed definition of a high net worth individual”.

Nobody in this debate has the number, yet some write as if they do.

For two years the anchor figure was Henley & Partners’ claim that Britain would lose a net 16,500 millionaires in 2025, the largest outflow it had ever recorded. Henley sells residence and citizenship by investment. Its estimates came from New World Wealth, a small South African consultancy.

The Tax Justice Network argued that the observations the report claimed to make were impossible to make. Tax Policy Associates applied forensic accounting tests and concluded the report should be treated as marketing material until independently audited.

In June 2026, Henley’s new report dropped New World Wealth and stopped publishing country migration counts. According to the Tax Justice Network, the report now acknowledges that other studies found departure rates among high earners to be “modest”. Henley still presents Britain as a country under competitive pressure, but it no longer puts a number on the flight.

The 16,500 circulates regardless. Fortune repeated it in July 2026, six weeks after Henley stopped publishing country counts. When one statistic falls away, the frame finds another: the Rich List, a millionaire count from the free-market Adam Smith Institute, a forthcoming New World Wealth report trailed in the Spectator, and now tax-form filings.

The press regulator has already ruled on one version of this move. On 18 January 2025 the Express ran the headline “Rachel Reeves has ‘made one huge mistake’ - and ‘now we have the proof’”, opening with the claim that since Starmer and Reeves took office, “thousands of millionaires have left Britain, new figures reveal”. The figures were New World Wealth’s.

In July 2025 IPSO found they were provisional forecasts for the whole of 2024, “based on year-to-date HNWI movements to June 2024”, before Labour took office and before the October 2024 Budget. It upheld a breach of the accuracy clause for presenting forecasts as confirmed departures and found that the paper’s own clarification had repeated an inaccuracy. The required correction could run as a footnote. The headline had already done its work.

Not all coverage runs this way. The Financial Times greeted the July HMRC figures with the headline “Data suggests fears of UK ‘non-dom’ exodus overblown”. In January 2025, the Bloomberg Opinion columnist Matthew Brooker argued that the UK ultra-rich exodus was “less than meets the eye”. Careful, more nuanced and accurate reporting does exist, but what follows examines the outlets and political accounts where the exodus frame dominates, and how they routinely outrun that more cautious work.

Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) treats news as a set of choices: what is said; what is left out; who speaks; and how events are made to mean something. Four concepts from CDA and sociology more generally help here, and each can be seen at work in what follows.

The first is ‘recontextualisation’, Theo van Leeuwen’s term for how a social practice is transformed as it moves into a new text. Details are dropped, purposes are added and evaluations are attached. The Reuben chain is a small, clear example.

The second is Teun van Dijk’s ‘ideological square’. Discourse tends to emphasise our good qualities and their bad ones, and to play down our bad qualities and their good ones. In ‘exodus’ coverage the very wealthy become “wealth creators” and “top taxpayers”, government measures become a “tax raid”, and inconvenient facts quietly drop out.

The third is the ‘primary definer’, from Policing the Crisis by Stuart Hall, Chas Critcher and their co-authors. Accredited sources set the first definition of a story, and everyone after them has to argue against it. Here the primary definers are the Rich List compiler, consultancies selling relocation, advisory firms that commission surveys, and a chorus of unnamed wealth advisers. Official data enters late, low down, or not at all.

The fourth is the ‘moral panic’, as developed by Stanley Cohen and later by Critcher: a disproportionate reaction in which a threat is amplified, folk devils are named, and pressure builds for a policy response. I use it at the end as an analogy rather than a diagnosis, because the exodus story borrows its structure while reversing its roles.

The most consistent move is collectivisation: single cases turned into a movement. When Bloomberg reported Rokos’s plans in September, the shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith called his decision “just the latest manifestation of the ongoing wealth exodus”. City AM headlined that Rokos “joins UK wealth exodus”. One person had moved, and the copy described a crowd.

The Reuben case shows the same move at speed. Polymarket’s “growing exodus” and Graham’s “mass exodus of Britain’s wealthiest” each rest on two names. When a reply asked Graham why the very rich worry so much about tax, he did not withdraw the tax framing. He replaced it with national decline: Reuben, he said, could see Britain moving towards “a failed state”. When one explanation is challenged, the frame keeps its conclusion and changes its explanation.

On 28 September, The Telegraph reported that 69,300 taxpayers filed a P85 in 2025-26, under the headline “Record 69,000 workers flee high-tax Britain in a year”. A P85 is the form people use to tell HMRC they are leaving the UK, mainly so they can claim back income tax. The figure came from an FoI request by the accountancy firm UHY Hacker Young.

The article itself describes the P85 as a form “expats must submit if they wish to claim back income tax”. “Expat” is a telling choice. It is commonly reserved for affluent professionals abroad and withheld from the care workers, builders and cleaners who cross the same borders and are called migrants. Here it lends the leavers a status the data cannot show: the published count says nothing about income, or about how long people stay away. The form is a refund mechanism, not a census of the wealthy, and many high earners, who report through Self Assessment, may never file one.

The article nonetheless asserts that many of those leaving are likely to be wealthy, though the data records no incomes. The government warned that the comparison runs through pandemic-affected years, which is exactly where the chart begins.

The next day the Express ran the same figure, the same expert quotes and the same government response under a new headline: “Nightmare for Andy Burnham as 69,000 workers abandon UK”. It added, without support, that many of those leaving are high-profile millionaires. GB News ran the same data and told readers that “the true scale of the exodus is almost certainly larger”.

Across three outlets, a count of refund forms became workers fleeing, then millionaires abandoning the country, then a nightmare for a Prime Minister who had been in office for barely ten weeks. No step in that sequence added evidence. Each added certainty.

The clearest sign that the story is written backwards is that the outlet, not the person leaving, provides the reason.

GB News is backed by the hedge fund founder Sir Paul Marshall, worth an estimated £875 million according to the 2024 Sunday Times Rich List, and by the investment firm Legatum. According to Press Gazette, the channel had lost £131 million since its 2021 launch by May 2025, losses underwritten by its parent company, All Perspectives. Marshall also agreed in September 2024 to buy the Spectator for £100 million.

In January, GB News headlined that “UK’s billionaire exodus continues as Wales’ richest man flees the country”. The man was Sir Michael Moritz, who planned to take German citizenship. The article itself reported his reasons: rising antisemitism, and growing support for populist right-wing movements in Britain and America. It also reported that he had told The Times his decision was driven by political anxiety “rather than a desire to avoid paying taxes”. The headline filed him under the exodus anyway, and the article added a consultancy estimate of non-dom departures. A man leaving partly out of fear of the populist right became evidence for a story the populist right tells.

In June, GB News reported that “Rachel Reeves tax raids cause surge in millionaires fleeing” to the Isle of Man. The evidence was estate agents reporting more enquiries. The example was Tyson Fury, who moved after home invasions at his Morecambe property. A week later a GB News YouTube video was titled “Labour’s wealth tax is causing millionaires to FLEE Britain”. The title reports, in the present tense, the effect of a tax that did not even exist then, and does not exist now.

On 4 October GB News reported David Reuben’s move under the headline “Britain’s second-richest man quits UK for Monaco - with Labour blamed”. The article never says who blamed Labour. The spokesman had given no reason. The passive voice lets the blame arrive without anyone having to make it.

Look at who gets counted: Jim Ratcliffe moved to Monaco under a Conservative government, years before Labour took office. Sir Michael Moritz said he was leaving because of antisemitism and the rise of the populist right, and that it was not about tax. Tyson Fury moved after his home was broken into. The Independent’s report on Reuben listed Sir Lewis Hamilton and Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou among “other departing wealthy figures”. Stelios has lived in Monaco since 1990, according to his own foundation’s biography, and Hamilton has been reported as a Monaco resident for more than a decade.

Yet all of them are offered as evidence that Labour’s taxes are driving the rich away. Precisely when someone left, and why they say they left, makes no difference to whether they are counted.

Before each of the last three Budgets, the professional services firm S&W has published a survey of 500 business owners asking whether they would consider leaving if taxes rose. In October 2024, the figure was 48%. In November 2025, it was 41%. This month it is 50% if capital gains tax rises, and 51% for a wealth tax. The survey combines “somewhat agree” with “strongly agree”.

“Would consider” measures an attitude. It does not record a single move. The survey is commissioned by a firm that advises the people it surveys, and it returns every autumn as a warning to the Chancellor. This Is Money’s headline told Burnham a capital gains tax raid “would send banks and UK business owners fleeing overseas”. The business-owner survey it cited found that 50% would consider leaving if capital gains tax rose. The headline’s certainty is not in the survey.

The most revealing move appears in the most careful piece in the sample. On 4 October the Business Times in Singapore ran a Straits Times analysis by Jonathan Eyal. To his credit, Eyal says neither the government nor its critics has accurate figures, and he dismisses Henley’s number. But then he writes: “The economic impact of such an exodus is not in doubt.”

He goes further with the HMRC data. Rising tax receipts from non-doms, he suggests, may show the rich are preparing to leave by selling assets, and he offers a 58% rise in capital gains liabilities as a hint. HMRC’s release had already described that rise as “consistent with broader trends” in receipts ahead of the capital gains changes announced in the October 2024 Budget. Eyal leaves this out. On his reading, falling receipts would prove flight and rising receipts would prove imminent flight. No evidence could count against the claim.

The Spectator’s economics editor, Michael Simmons, handles the same release selectively in his guide to “fleeing Britain”. He notes that newly arrived non-doms fell from 10,000 to 8,600. From the same release, he leaves out that the number leaving the non-dom population fell from 11,200 to 9,000 over the same two years, and that tax paid rose. That is van Dijk’s square in miniature. He concedes that “Official figures on Britain’s wealth exodus are limited”, then argues that wealth advisers’ anecdotes settle the matter anyway.

The shifting comparator is revealing too. Rokos’s reported £330 million tax bill appears in a different unit depending on who is describing it. Andrew Griffith converted it into 7,380 nurses and also into the contributions of 38,000 average taxpayers, the figure Michael Simmons used in the Spectator. GB News, followed by Jonathan Eyal, put it at 21,000 average households, using an average family tax bill of £15,700.

While each conversion is defensible on its own terms, what really matters is what they do. Each turns one man’s tax bill into a loss the reader can picture: hospital wards without nurses, streets of households whose tax must now be replaced. That makes a private relocation feel like a direct cost to the public. And all of them assume the whole £330 million simply disappears. 

None of the pieces examines that assumption, or notes that GB News’s own report described the year in question as exceptional, with his firm’s profits almost tripling and his pay reaching £477 million.

The comparator changes with the speaker, but the effect is the same: a single, unusually large tax year becomes a permanent hole that ordinary people must fill.

Omission is as telling as emphasis. The Times reported in March that the Reuben brothers had given £100,000 to Reform UK. None of the posts about David Reuben’s move mentioned it. I make no claim about what any poster knew. The observable fact is that a recent Reform donor’s relocation was presented as an indictment of a Labour government, largely by Reform UK supporters.

GB News’s report on Rokos noted, further down, that he gave £1.9 million to the Conservatives before the 2015 election, and that Alan Howard, who moved to Switzerland last year, is a Conservative donor. The departures most often cited as verdicts on Labour include past donors to the Conservatives and to Reform. That doesn’t make their reasons illegitimate, but it does complicate the picture of neutral wealth creators driven out by a hostile government.

On 20 September, Richard Tice posted that Britain should “celebrate & retain our wealth creators & entrepreneurs”, linking a Telegraph column praising Ratcliffe. Ratcliffe has been tax resident in Monaco since well before Labour took office. Tice’s own phrase, “Tories then Labour”, concedes the point. Sawiris, often listed as a casualty of Labour policy, told the FT: “You can’t blame Labour.” He blamed “10 years of incompetence” by the Conservatives. Departures that do not fit the timeline are absorbed into it anyway.

On 28 July, Nigel Farage posted that “the biggest taxpayers are leaving the UK in droves”, linking a Telegraph report on the free-market Adam Smith Institute’s millionaire count. One sentence performs two conversions. A fall in the number of millionaires becomes people leaving. And millionaires, a wealth measure that includes homes and pensions, become “the biggest taxpayers”, an income-tax measure.

Six weeks later, Reform announced £36 million each from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, the largest donations in British political history.

In April, Delo had written in the Telegraph that he was moving back from Hong Kong so he could keep giving after a planned cap on overseas donations. In September, Tice could not give a date for Delo’s return but said compliance had been checked. Harborne, long described as Thailand-based, appeared on the June electoral register at a Hampshire address, and his lawyers say he complied with the law. Under the rules then in force, a British citizen on the electoral roll could donate without living here.

The party announcing the flight of wealth had banked £72 million from two men whose UK residence is asserted but not dated. Coverage that treats every departure as a verdict on the government had no comparable frame for that.

The moral panic is an analogy here, not a finding, but it clarifies the shape of the story.

Cohen’s classic panic has a vulnerable public, a threatening group cast as folk devils, and moral entrepreneurs demanding action. The exodus story borrows that structure and reverses the roles. The group ‘at risk’ is the very wealthy, presented as an endangered resource: golden geese, wealth creators, the top 1% who pay a quarter of income tax. The ‘folk devils’ are the Treasury, wealth-tax advocates and, increasingly, a named Prime Minister. The ‘moral entrepreneurs’ are the think tanks, wealth managers, commentators and opposition politicians, many with a commercial or political stake in the outcome.

The analogy pays off with Critcher’s attention to how panics resolve. In January 2025, after weeks of exodus headlines built on the Henley figures, Rachel Reeves softened the non-dom changes at Davos. The Times headline read: “Rachel Reeves to relax non-dom tax rule amid millionaire exodus”. The coverage presented the concession as a response to a flight measured by numbers Henley has since stopped publishing.

With John Healey’s first Budget due on 28 October and a wealth tax not ruled out, the cycle is now running again. The frame has already moved policy once. That is reason enough to test it before it moves policy again.

I’m not denying that some wealthy people are leaving, or that some say policy is why. The 2025 reform extended inheritance tax to worldwide assets after ten years’ residence, which is harsher than the 2017 changes. Academic work by Advani, Burgherr and Summers found only modest emigration after 2017, but that may understate the response this time.

I also accept that the counter-frame overreaches at times. Campaigners’ claims that the government was simply “hoodwinked”, and polling commissioned by advocacy groups, deserve the same scrutiny I apply here. Until HMRC publishes in 2027, the defensible verdict is that the exodus is unproven. It is neither a proven myth nor a proven rout.

Four questions will take apart most versions of the story:

- Did the person who left give the reason now attached to them?

- Does the number count people actually moving, rather than refund forms, survey attitudes or fortunes that fell below a threshold?

- Does the piece report HMRC’s figures on arrivals, departures and tax paid, not just the ones that fit?

- Does it say who produced the estimate, and what they sell?

If the answers are no, it is amplification rather than reporting. Put those questions to the next exodus headline, or to whoever is sharing it.

Journalists can separate the confirmed move from the supplied motive in the first sentence, and put the official figures, limited as they are, above the anecdote.

Editors can ask why a refund-form count or a “would consider” survey is leading the page when ministers have told Parliament the Government does not hold data on how many wealthy people have left.

Politicians and wealth advisers are entitled to argue that tax changes do damage. They should not expect an unaudited marketing figure, or two named moves, to pass as a measured “national exodus”.

None of this requires waiting for the 2027 figures. It only requires asking what each claim actually counts.

An unproven exodus is exactly what the coverage examined here will not allow. A story that should carry a question mark arrives every week with an exclamation mark. The evidence keeps shifting: from Henley to the Rich List, from survey intentions to refund forms, from one billionaire to the next. The conclusion stays fixed: the rich are fleeing, and the government is to blame.

When a conclusion survives every change in its evidence, the evidence was never what held it up. It is worth asking what does, and on whose behalf.

text:
Steve Jobs put his feet on the table and asked what Morgan Stanley does. It still won Apple's IPO and took home $2.5 million.

Not the big check at that closing.

The small bank beside it already owned Apple shares. It took home $25 million.

Jack Wadsworth was the partner Jobs asked. He told him the firm's last IPO was in 1962, and Morgan Stanley worked alone: it had just turned down a billion dollar IBM bond rather than share it with Salomon. For Apple he talked his partners into sharing.

Apple priced at $22 in December 1980, and Massachusetts banned its people from buying.

The 26 minute video attached to this post is Wadsworth on camera, filmed for the Computer History Museum in 2019. The deal from the banker's chair: the split, the price, the state that called it overpriced.

Watch 3:30, when Jobs asks what Morgan Stanley does.

At 8:41 he gives the split and says there's something wrong with these numbers. At 12:43 Boston bans it, then a week later lets its people in at 28, he remembers. At 21:40 Markkula hears $22 and says: God bless you, Jack.

A banker's cut is a slice of the price. H&Q had bought in before there was one.

Apple's 4.6 million shares sold at $22 and closed the first day at $29. That is $32 million to whoever got an allocation.

Every IPO still seats people that way: funds before the price, banks for a fee, their clients at the offer, you at the first trade. His 1980 rule was an account a year old and a million dollars.

A listing opens 30% up and you think you were late. You were never on the list.

He says a pop is fine if owners keep most of the company. I don't buy it: that gap was Apple's money, handed to the bank's richest clients.

On the next IPO you want, divide the first trade by the offer price on the prospectus cover. That is what your seat cost.
