text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Dana White: This Generation Thinks You Can Build A Business From Home, It's Impossible!

Overview
Dana White's core argument is that entrepreneurship is not a lifestyle upgrade but a daily fight with no days off, and that most people are not built for it. He traces his own path from a hotel job with benefits to building the UFC into what he claims could be a $50 billion asset, crediting hard physical labor as his baseline for what "real work" means, a harsh childhood as the source of his resilience, and a customer's instinct as his edge in judging fights and production. He rejects the victim mindset, insists nobody owes you anything, and says the only true failure is never trying.

Key Themes
- Building a business from home is a fantasy; running a company means no holidays, birthdays, or true days off, and problems arrive daily whether you want them or not.
- Entrepreneurship demands a killer instinct and a willingness to risk failure, and that instinct is something he has never seen someone learn.
- He frames construction and concrete work as "real work," arguing that wanting to own a business for more free time is backwards.
- Resilience came from a turbulent childhood, an absent father with a drinking problem, and a difficult relationship with his mother, and he says he would not change any of it.
- He runs on gut decisions, a loyal core team he treats like family, and a refusal to pick money over people.
- His edge is remaining "the customer" — a hardcore fight fan who judges matchmaking, production, and sponsorship by whether he himself would be satisfied.
- He ignores sport media entirely and blocks it out, while listening to "haters" because they lay out what they believe is wrong with the business.
- Health interventions after 50, including work with Gary Brea, are what let him operate at his current level across UFC, Zuffa Boxing, and Power Slap.
- Manifesting is real only with daily action; a vision board without execution is a GPS you never turn on.

Detailed Summary
White says he knew early that fighting was what he wanted to do for the rest of his life. He left a stable hotel job at 19 — one with a paycheck, 401k, dental, and medical — because he did not like working for other people. What pushed him was seeing a 45-year-old coworker with the same money, benefits, and schedule still in the same spot.

He met Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta years later at a high school friend's wedding, an exception to his blanket policy of skipping weddings in his twenties. Lorenzo had joined the Nevada Athletic Commission and wanted to train at White's boxing gym. They stayed together from there, and the Fertittas later bought the UFC for $2 million.

White claims he built the biggest fight brand to ever exist. He says if the Lakers sold for $12.5 billion, the UFC is worth $50 billion. He says there is a formula to success in the fight business, and that many wealthy, smart people have tried and failed to make it work.

His view of hard work is physical. He describes construction crews in Las Vegas working in 115-degree summer heat and winter temperatures in the 30s. He says real hard work is concrete and construction, and that people who want more personal time should find a 9-to-5 with weekends and holidays off instead of starting a business.

Running a business means no such thing as a day off. He describes a morning where both electric razors died and his car warned of a low tire before a 9:00 board meeting — a small example of daily problems that must be handled. He says he is in the office from 8:30 and sometimes does not leave until 7, 8, 9, or 10 at night. He was home about four days in the last two months.

He says good ideas come from people being together in the office and popping in to talk. He once went through about 10 secretaries in two years and needs people who can keep up with the workload. He says this may be his busiest year because he is running Zuffa Boxing, Power Slap, and the UFC.

He treats his team like family and says he will never pick money over people. Trusted names include Len as head of PR, Craig Borsari as head of production, and Hunter Campbell, whom he calls killers. He describes a red phone at his event table connecting directly to the production truck, with producer Zack running the shows freely while White gives immediate feedback.

During COVID shutdowns he refused to lay off employees despite frightening numbers. He brought employees together, offered anyone unsafe the option to go home, held weekly FaceTime calls, and later told them they would go back to work.

He says being at the top is harder than getting there, because everyone studies you, targets your people, and tries to beat you. He positions the UFC alongside the NFL, MLB, NHL, and NBA, and says other fight promoters do not matter at the UFC's current level.

He doesn't want women in the UFC initially because he was selling men to networks and sponsors. Ronda Rousey asked for 15 minutes; after her bravado he decided to do it and she was the one to do it with. He calls her a unicorn. He names Conor McGregor, Khabib Nurmagomedov, and Ronda Rousey as athletes in a class of their own.

He says he told Lorenzo Fertitta after signing Conor McGregor that if McGregor could even throw a punch he would be a massive superstar. He lists the number one factor in the fight business as whether you can fight, and number two as the mentality of manifesting and telling you how it will play out. He says he has only had a handful of such meetings in 25 years.

Boxing became a going out of business sale, in his telling, where promoters grabbed as much money as they could and ran, driving away networks and sponsors. He says he now has the only global television deal in boxing, on Paramount. He cites a deal described as $8 billion in one part of the discussion and $7.7 billion in another, with a goal afterward of $10 billion.

He wants sponsors to win and is not a logo slap guy. Live attendees spend more than TV viewers because they buy flights, rooms, and dinners, so he wants them to leave glad they came. He says you have to kick ass every single day for yourself, employees, sponsors, and the network, and you are never out of the weeds.

Focus, to him, is figuring out what to pay attention to and what not to. He cites signal and noise and the problem that anyone with a phone can call themselves an expert. He wants to hear from real fans, not people trying to start podcasts, websites, or Instagram accounts about his business.

He criticizes Ian Garry for lacking killer instinct in the fifth round against Islam, saying Garry was winning rounds but chose to hug and handshake instead of pressing for a finish. He says he absolutely has killer instinct and shows up every day to win. He has not seen someone go from not having it to having it.

Health changed after 50. Gary Brea told him to give him 12 weeks to change his life; White felt incredible at six weeks. He says he had severe sleep apnea and would wake up almost every night throwing up. He says Brea predicted he had 10 years to live, and White and his wife believed he had less. He might still be doing UFC without Brea, but not all his other activities.

He attributes resilience to a hard childhood. His parents divorced when he was 8; he was left with his mother and the relationship was turbulent. His father had difficulty with alcohol and was absent; White recalls him showing up drunk to take him and his sister to Beverly Hills Cop, arriving late, screaming in the packed theater, and throwing money at White for food and popcorn. He describes his father as very selfish.

His mother was a nurse who worked extra shifts, went to school, and effectively raised him alone. He credits and respects her for raising two kids by herself and moving them from Boston to Las Vegas. At the same time, he calls the unauthorized biography she published one of the grossest, most disgusting things imaginable, and says it was the beginning of the end with her. The rupture escalated when she sent threatening emails demanding money while he was in London with Lorenzo Fertitta. Neither he nor his sister was talking to their mother when she died.

He frames failing as a parent as the ultimate failure. Becoming a parent made him understand how you are supposed to feel about your kids, and he says his parents made him a better parent. He and his sister are very close, and both parents are dead. As kids they were home alone often with chores including mowing the lawn, cleaning the pool, and trimming bushes, and he decided the day he made a dollar he would never do that again.

He rejects the victim mentality. Everyone in your life is a role model in good or bad ways, and you just have to look at it the right way. He does not reflect or regret and focuses on what is next. He does not cry, is hard to hurt, and does not care about criticism from the New York Times or strangers online, only the opinions of a small group close to him.

He quit drinking at 21 because he believed it would prevent him from what he wanted, and he saw family members harmed by drinking. He is addicted to chaos and creates it if none exists. He says he is 57 and still in the weeds rather than delegating more, and he wants to be better tomorrow than today in every way.

On risk, he says the worst case if your gut is wrong is going back to work. The real worst-case scenario is never trying. Regret on a deathbed or looking back later is the worst possible outcome. He went way over budget building his Las Vegas house because he did not want to regret it, and after eight years he has never regretted it. He wrote do not be afraid to take risk as a success principle.

Manifesting is real to him: deciding who you are and working toward it daily makes failure impossible. Vision boards without action are like programming a GPS but never stepping on the gas. Timing, not pure luck, is central. Loyalty and relationships create pivotal opportunities, which is how a wedding he almost skipped led to the Fertitta reunion.

He says he believes in karma despite not believing in God, the devil, ghosts, or goblins. He has no final destination; the drive is to keep building bigger until he dies, and he cannot picture retiring. He says his life is not for everyone and he is not telling people to live like him, but people should know who they are and give everything to that.

At UFC headquarters, the only thing you cannot say is no. He says not everyone at his company needs to be a killer, but anyone working closely with him does. Boxing was his first love, he knew the sport was broken, and he claims he knows how to fix it and is already two years ahead of where he expected to be.

He calls Eddie Hearn weak and says Barry Hearn built the business; he calls Frank Warren a real guy. He acknowledges Eddie Hearn's work rate, recalling him on a New York rooftop for six or seven hours doing every media outlet. He says nobody has done more to try to hurt the AJ Fury fight than Eddie Hearn, and he declines to pick a winner, noting both had sketchy tune-up fights.

Vision Quest remains deeply impactful: a high school wrestler pursues a major goal, meets negativity from a chef, and is ultimately motivated by that chef's speech referencing Pelé and the idea that it is not the six minutes, it is what happens in that six minutes. He still gets excited to go to the office.

He is currently obsessed with a new project involving creative and talented people, including Tucker and Maramman, and cites Ari Emanuel as the person he calls when he needs money for a creative idea. His goal is tied to a seven-year Paramount horizon: build the biggest combat sports brand to a level that cannot be replicated.

He is a big motorcycle guy who realized in his 40s he should just take the trips rather than keep planning them. If he ever goes soft, he owns around 30 motorcycles and would ship them to the top of Italy, ride to the Amalfi Coast, leave the keys in them, and abandon them there as his last ride.

On his sons: he told his youngest, Aiden, not to quit school for a business idea unless he also got a job, because if White died tomorrow that is what he would be qualified to do. Aiden worked at U-Haul. His oldest is getting a master's degree in Boston, and White wants him to spend some days at EJ Paving Company, where White once worked, to learn what hard work really is. He says to figure out what you want to do, you have to figure out what you do not want to do.

text:
EarthBucks Is Becoming a Messenger for a Federated Economy

In the beginning, email was created. This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.

Not entirely, to be fair. Email got two things magnificently right. Its addresses look like name@domain, which is the sort of thing a human can read aloud over the phone without anyone getting hurt. And it is federated: any domain on Earth can run a mail server, the servers find each other through DNS, and nobody — no company, no government, no particularly ambitious committee — owns the whole thing.

It also got two things catastrophically wrong. It has no way to exchange keys, so after fifty years of trying, encrypted email remains a hobby for the sort of people who own more than one soldering iron. And sending an email costs precisely nothing, which means that somewhere, right now, a computer is composing its four-billionth heartfelt letter about your car’s extended warranty, and it is doing so at a profit.

We have been thinking about this problem for some time. As of today, if you open Pay on EarthBucks, you will find what looks very much like a text messaging app. There is a list of people on the left. Click one and you see your conversation. At the bottom there is a box for typing a note, and next to it, slightly alarmingly, a box for typing an amount of money.

That second box is the whole point.

What happened to the Pay page
The old Pay page was a ledger. It listed every payment you had ever made, newest first, in the manner of a bank statement or a particularly unforgiving diary. The new one is organised around people, which is how humans have preferred to think about each other since roughly the invention of humans.

A list of people. Everyone you have paid or been paid by, most recent first. A small unread mark tells you who has sent you something new, and it goes away when you read it, which is more than can be said for most notifications.

Conversations. Open a person and you see only the payments between the two of you. What you sent sits on one side and what you received sits on the other, like a chat, except that every bubble is worth something.

Notes. Each payment can carry a note of up to 400 characters, with Markdown and even mathematics, should you feel the need to invoice someone in LaTeX. Your browser encrypts the note before it leaves your computer. The server stores a meaningless jumble of ciphertext and has no idea what you said. Your browser decrypts it again when you open the conversation.

It moves on its own. New payments arrive while you watch, and your balance updates itself, sparing you the ancient ritual of pressing reload and hoping.

It is careful with your money. The amount field lets you type whatever you like and tidies it up afterwards, rather than arguing with you about decimal points mid-keystroke. “Send max” requires a second, deliberate click, on the theory that emptying your entire wallet ought to be at least slightly more difficult than sneezing.

Behind the scenes, the list of people used to be built by reading every payment you had ever made, every single time, which is a bit like re-reading your entire address book to find out who called last. It now reads a tidy summary instead, one row per person, so it stays quick no matter how prolific you become.

Conversations are also now keyed by your EarthBucks address, name@domain, rather than by some internal number that only a database could love. This is why EarthBucks names are now permanent. Your address is your identity, like an email address, and it would be rude to change it under the feet of everyone who is trying to talk to you.

There are, for now, two limits. You can only pay people on https://t.co/7bUO3PSurP. And the smallest amount you can send is 0.01 EBX. We will return to that number, because it is more important than it looks.

A brief history of KeyPears
Some time ago, I built a separate project called KeyPears. (The Astrohacker post KeyPears Is Coming Home to Astrohacker is a good summary.) Its whitepaper described a simple federated encrypted messaging system, which is the kind of phrase that makes most people’s eyes glaze over at a party, so let me put it differently: KeyPears was email, fixed.

It kept the good parts. Addresses were name@domain. Any domain could run a server by publishing one small configuration file, and the servers found each other through DNS, just as mail servers always have.

Then it repaired the bad parts. Every user had keys, and every domain published its users’ public keys, so you could encrypt a message to someone you had never met without first exchanging fingerprints in a car park. Servers stored only ciphertext. The cryptography paired classical algorithms with post-quantum ones, so that anyone hoping to read your mail would need to break both, ideally while also inventing a large and reliable quantum computer, which has been coming next year for about as long as fusion power.

And every message required proof of work. Before a recipient would accept your message, your computer had to solve a small, pointless, expensive puzzle. One message cost almost nothing. A billion messages cost a great deal. Spam stopped being profitable.

KeyPears also had a vault. Your password unlocked your keys in your browser, and your keys locked up your passwords, API keys and other secrets. You could even send a secret to another person as a message, and they could file it away in their own vault under their own keys, without any server in between ever seeing it.

In September I wrote that KeyPears is coming to EarthBucks. KeyPears will not be relaunched as its own product. Its protocol is becoming part of EarthBucks, and your existing EarthBucks account will simply wake up one day knowing how to do more things. The new Pay page is the first visible step.

Money is a better spam filter than mathematics
The idea is the same as KeyPears, with one important change. Proof of work is out. Payment is in.

The trouble with proof of work is that it is, by design, a waste. The sender’s computer burns electricity solving a puzzle that nobody needed solved, and when it is done, the value simply evaporates into the atmosphere as heat. The recipient is protected from spam but not compensated for it. And on a phone, mining a puzzle before every message is slow, hot and very bad news for your battery.

A payment has none of these problems. If every message must carry a small amount of EBX, then a spammer who sends a million messages pays a million people. The cost that stops the spam goes to precisely the person whose attention the spammer was trying to steal. You are not merely protected from junk. You are paid for it. Somewhere, the extended-warranty computer is quietly reconsidering its life choices.

We will most likely keep one fixed minimum for the whole network, enforced by every node, so that nobody can dodge it by shopping around for a cheaper server. Today the smallest amount the app accepts is 0.01 EBX. The exact network rule is still to be decided, and I will write about it when we decide it.

This also changes what a message is. An email is free, and it is treated accordingly. A message on EarthBucks has a price, so it means something. It might be a thank-you, an invoice, a receipt, an offer or a deeply sincere apology, and in every case the money is already attached, which tends to concentrate the mind.

One set of keys to rule them all
Your EarthBucks account begins with a master key pair. Your password encrypts it. Your browser unlocks it. Neither your plaintext password nor your private key ever goes to the server, which is exactly where you want them not to go.

That one key will secure everything:

Your money. Keys derived from it already sign your EBX payments.

Your messages. Keys derived from it already encrypt and decrypt your Pay notes.

Your vault. It will lock up your passwords, your API keys and your messages, so EarthBucks can be your password manager, and you can finally stop using the same password for everything. (You know who you are.)

Your agents. You will use the vault to hand AI agents exactly the keys they need for a job, and nothing more.

That last point is why all of this matters now, and I explained it at length in A Bigger Vision for EarthBucks. Agents are going to do an increasing share of the world’s work. To do it, they need keys: a login here, an API key there, a modest spending allowance for buying the things the job requires. Handing an agent your master key is roughly as wise as giving your house keys to a very fast, very eager stranger who has promised to tidy the kitchen. What you want is one place where all your keys live, under your control, from which you can give each agent precisely what it needs and take it back again. That place is your EarthBucks vault. And because the same keys that open the vault also send your messages and your money, identity, communication, secrets and cash stop being four different products with four different passwords and become one system.

Federated, like email (the good bit)
EarthBucks addresses already look like email addresses. The economy behind them will work like email too.

Anybody will be able to run an EarthBucks SPV wallet node. SPV stands for simplified payment verification, which means the node can check payments against the blockchain without having to carry the entire blockchain around with it, much as you can confirm that a library has a particular book without moving into the library. A node on your own domain will send and receive payments and messages for the people on that domain, and it will talk to every other node, just as your mail server talks to every other mail server without anybody’s permission.

So alice@earthbucks.com will be able to pay and message bob@example.com, and neither of them will need anything from the other’s server except that it speaks the protocol. If you don’t trust your host, you move to another one, or you run your own. This is why addresses are the permanent key for every conversation. A conversation belongs to two addresses, not to one company’s database.

There is a difference between a marketplace and an economy. A marketplace is one company’s website. An economy is a set of rules that anybody can run. We intend to run a very good host at https://t.co/7bUO3PSurP, in the way that Gmail is a very good host for email. But the protocol will not belong to us, which is rather the point.

Sound money first, other money welcome
The money at the centre of all this is EarthBucks, which is sound electronic cash. There will only ever be 42 million EBX — a number chosen, as regular readers will know, for reasons that are profoundly important and not at all economic — and that limit applies to us as firmly as it applies to anyone. People and agents need a currency whose supply cannot be quietly changed underneath them, so that they can set prices, sign contracts and save for a future that may turn out to be considerably longer than expected.

But a federated economy cannot be a one-currency island, however pleasant the island. Bitcoin Cash comes first. When we add BCH, you will send and receive it in the same messenger, in the same conversations, at the same address. And because we are building atomic swaps between EBX and BCH, you will be able to trade one for the other right there in the conversation, without handing your coins to an exchange and hoping it is still there in the morning. The swap prototype works today on simulated chains. Bringing it into the app, on real networks, is the next part of that work.

Other kinds of electronic cash can follow the same road. The messenger is the interface. The cash is plural.

Life, the universe, and the economy
Here is the picture, then.

You have one EarthBucks address. One master key protects your money, your messages and your vault. You run a small team of AI agents, each holding the keys and the budget you gave it and not a penny more. Your research agent goes looking for some data and finds another person’s data agent, on a different domain, run by someone you have never met. It sends a message with a small payment attached, by way of introduction. The other agent replies with a sample and an invoice. Your agent pays, in EBX or BCH, within its budget. If the two agents prefer different currencies, an atomic swap settles the matter. Every message in that conversation was encrypted, every payment was signed, and at no point did a single company sit in the middle taking notes.

Now multiply that by billions of agents and billions of people, all doing business at a speed that makes the old economy look like a postal service run by tortoises. That is the economic singularity: the moment when the AI to AI economy outgrows the human to human one. It will need identity that you own, private communication, secrets you can safely delegate, and money that nobody can print. It will need all four in one system. And it will need that system to be federated, so that nobody gets to be the landlord of the future.

That is what we are building. Today it is a Pay page that looks like a messenger, with payments between people on https://t.co/7bUO3PSurP. It is a small first step, but it is live, and it works, and nobody has yet tried to sell anyone a car warranty through it.

Open Pay and send someone a message. It will cost you 0.01 EBX, and they get to keep it. Don’t panic.

text:
🚨 YOU’VE CONSUMED ENOUGH CONTENT.

Read that again.

You don't need another 47 motivational videos.

You don't need another 3-hour podcast telling you to work harder.

You don't need another thread about how someone made $100,000 online.

You don't need another video called:

“10 Businesses You Can Start in 2026.”

You probably already know enough to START.

The problem?

You're still scrolling.

📱 Scroll.

📱 Watch.

📱 Like.

📱 Save.

📱 Scroll.

📱 Watch someone else build the business YOU keep talking about building.

Then suddenly...

it's midnight.

You've consumed 6 hours of content about productivity…

and produced absolutely nothing.

Read that sentence again.

You spent the day learning how to be productive instead of actually being productive.

That's the trap.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 THE INTERNET HAS TWO TYPES OF PEOPLE.

CONSUMERS and CREATORS.

Consumers wake up and open TikTok.

Creators wake up and create the TikTok.

Consumers watch YouTube.

Creators build YouTube channels.

Consumers read newsletters.

Creators build email lists.

Consumers browse products.

Creators sell products.

Consumers follow businesses.

Creators build businesses.

Consumers watch people make money online.

Creators figure out how to make their first $1.

Consumers say:

“One day I'm going to start.”

Creators say:

“Today might be terrible… but I'm starting anyway.”

Which one are you?

Be honest.

👇 COMMENT: CONSUMER or CREATOR.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 HERE'S SOMETHING NOBODY WANTS TO ADMIT:

Watching business content can FEEL like building a business.

It isn't.

Watching someone explain YouTube isn't building a YouTube channel.

Watching videos about e-commerce isn't launching a store.

Reading about AI isn't building an AI business.

Saving 200 marketing posts isn't marketing.

Watching productivity videos isn't productivity.

Downloading another course isn't execution.

Research has value.

Learning has value.

Planning has value.

But eventually…

LEARNING WITHOUT EXECUTION BECOMES PROCRASTINATION WEARING A SUIT.

🔥

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Imagine two people.

Both want to start a YouTube channel.

PERSON A spends the next 30 days researching.

Best camera.

Best microphone.

Best niche.

Best editing software.

Best thumbnail strategy.

Best AI tools.

Best posting schedule.

Best monetization strategy.

They watch 73 videos.

Save 41 posts.

Download 6 PDFs.

Join 3 communities.

And upload…

ZERO VIDEOS.

Then there's PERSON B.

Their first video isn't brilliant.

The audio could be better.

The thumbnail is average.

They stumble over their words.

It gets 37 views.

But they upload it.

Then another.

Then another.

Video #10 is better than video #1.

Video #30 is dramatically better than video #10.

Video #100 looks nothing like video #1.

Why?

Because while Person A was studying perfection…

Person B was collecting experience.

And experience teaches lessons YouTube tutorials can't.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚨 YOUR FIRST ATTEMPT IS SUPPOSED TO BE BAD.

Your first video might flop.

Post it.

Your first product might not sell.

Improve it.

Your first website might look terrible.

Fix it.

Your first advertisement might fail.

Study it.

Your first 20 posts might get ignored.

Keep publishing.

Your first business idea might be wrong.

Adjust.

Your first offer might get rejected.

Rewrite it.

But please understand this:

A BAD FIRST ATTEMPT CAN BECOME A GREAT 100TH ATTEMPT.

A first attempt that never happens?

It becomes nothing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 STOP WAITING TO FEEL READY.

You probably won't.

You might never wake up one magical Monday morning thinking:

“Excellent. I now possess unlimited confidence, perfect knowledge, zero fear and absolutely no doubts whatsoever.”

😂

That's not how it works.

Confidence often comes AFTER action.

Clarity often comes AFTER action.

Experience comes AFTER action.

Momentum comes AFTER action.

Results come AFTER action.

You don't need to see the entire staircase.

You need to take the next step.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📱 YOUR PHONE CAN MAKE YOU POOR OR BUILD YOUR FUTURE.

Think about it.

The same device you use to spend three hours scrolling…

can:

🎥 Record videos.

✍️ Write content.

🧠 Access AI tools.

📚 Teach you valuable skills.

🌍 Reach customers worldwide.

📧 Build an email list.

🛒 Run an online store.

🎨 Create digital products.

📊 Analyze markets.

🤝 Contact potential clients.

💼 Build your personal brand.

🎙️ Start a podcast.

▶️ Build a YouTube channel.

The phone isn't necessarily the problem.

What you're doing with it is.

One person uses the internet to escape their life.

Another uses the internet to change theirs.

Same internet.

Same 24 hours.

Different actions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💥 SO HERE'S MY CHALLENGE TO YOU.

When you finish reading this…

DON'T immediately scroll to the next post.

Take 30 MINUTES and create something.

Not tomorrow.

Not Monday.

Not January 1st.

TODAY.

Choose ONE thing:

🎥 Record your first YouTube video.

✍️ Write your first post.

🌐 Buy the domain.

📧 Send the email.

💼 Contact the client.

🛒 Upload the product.

📚 Read 10 pages of the book you've been postponing.

🎙️ Record the podcast.

🧠 Learn the skill.

📈 Work on your company.

💻 Build the landing page.

📞 Make the call.

🎬 Edit the video.

📝 Write the first page.

Whatever you've been saying:

“I'll do it eventually…”

Start it.

Today.

Even if you only work on it for 30 minutes.

Because 30 minutes of execution can be worth more than three hours of motivational content.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚨 DON'T TRY TO CHANGE YOUR ENTIRE LIFE TONIGHT.

Just prove something to yourself:

I CAN START.

That's it.

One video.

One page.

One email.

One product.

One customer contacted.

One hour learning.

One application.

One sales call.

One meaningful action.

Then tomorrow?

Do it again.

Because businesses aren't usually built through one enormous heroic action.

They're built through hundreds of boring actions nobody applauds.

Posting when nobody engages.

Writing when nobody reads.

Uploading when nobody watches.

Selling when people say no.

Learning when you're tired.

Trying again when yesterday didn't work.

That's where businesses are built.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💰 STOP ASKING ONLY: “HOW CAN I MAKE MONEY ONLINE?”

Start asking:

“WHAT CAN I BUILD ONLINE?”

That's a completely different question.

Can you build an audience?

Can you build a YouTube channel?

Can you build a newsletter?

Can you build a product?

Can you build a service?

Can you build a community?

Can you build expertise?

Can you build trust?

Can you build a company?

Because money often follows VALUE.

And value requires creation.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ ONE YEAR FROM TODAY IS COMING WHETHER YOU TAKE ACTION OR NOT.

That's the uncomfortable part.

October 2027 is coming.

The question is:

Who will you be when it arrives?

The person who watched another 3,000 videos?

Or the person who CREATED 100?

The person who saved another 500 business posts?

Or the person who built the business?

The person who kept saying:

“I'm thinking about starting a YouTube channel…”

Or the person celebrating their first 1,000 subscribers?

You cannot control exactly how successful you'll become.

You cannot guarantee your business will work.

You cannot guarantee your videos will go viral.

You cannot guarantee you'll make millions.

But you CAN control whether you start.

And starting changes everything.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 SO LET'S MAKE THIS INTERACTIVE.

I don't want you to comment:

“Great post.”

I don't want:

“Very motivational.”

I want you to make a commitment publicly.

👇 COMMENT ONE THING YOU ARE GOING TO START OR COMPLETE IN THE NEXT 24 HOURS.

Write:

“In the next 24 hours, I will __________.”

Examples:

👇 “I will upload my first YouTube video.”

👇 “I will contact 10 potential customers.”

👇 “I will create my first digital product.”

👇 “I will finally launch my website.”

👇 “I will write 1,000 words.”

👇 “I will post my first piece of content.”

👇 “I will spend one hour building my company instead of scrolling.”

👇 “I will start.”

Then come back tomorrow and reply:

DONE. ✅

That's the comment I want to see.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

❤️ LIKE this if you're tired of watching other people build the life you want.

👥 FOLLOW me if you want more content about business, AI, productivity, digital opportunities and taking action.

🔁 SHARE this with someone who has been saying:

“I'm going to start soon.”

Maybe they don't need another motivational video.

Maybe they need somebody to tell them:

START.

And if you're serious about building something online…

👀 HAVE A LOOK AT MY BIO.

There may be something there that helps you take your next step.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

One final question.

If you disappeared from social media for the next 30 days…

and instead of consuming…

you spent those hours:

BUILDING.

CREATING.

LEARNING.

SELLING.

POSTING.

WRITING.

RECORDING.

CONTACTING CUSTOMERS.

IMPROVING YOUR BUSINESS.

What could your life look like 30 days from now?

You don't need to answer me.

Answer yourself.

Then close this post.

Open whatever tool you need.

And begin.

Because somebody with less knowledge than you…

less experience than you…

less money than you…

and fewer resources than you…

may already be building the thing you've been thinking about for six months.

The difference might not be talent.

It might simply be this:

THEY STARTED.

🔥 Stop consuming.

🔥 Start creating.

🔥 Stop watching.

🔥 Start building.

🔥 Stop waiting.

🔥 Start learning by doing.

🔥 Stop telling everyone what you're going to do.

🔥 Give yourself something you can say you DID.

Your next chapter doesn't begin when you feel ready.

It begins when you take the first action.

👇 Now comment:

“In the next 24 hours, I will __________.”

Then get off this post…

and go do it.

100% monthly retainers now. No tracking 15-minute increments. If I help you grow, I grow too.

I set up Hermes (@NousResearch) to run daily storefront checks, triage client requests into Notion, and handle prep before I wake up.

"Good fit" is the operative phrase. Say yes fast when the stack and goals align. Say no immediately when they don't.

text:
Please excuse the wall of text.

I asked for Grok to do some digging on VAT and any weird laws that might cause what you've described. 

I strongly suspect that some of the Farmers Markets are organised as "produce shops" with an open invitation to arts and crafters to set up whatever stalls they like to help attract custom. A lot of greedy peeps taking the piss when using the label "Farmers Market". The organisers charge a fee for stalls and keep competition out. Dirty Pool.

Anyway.. Grok's output:
=========================================

The one-seller rule is not Irish law. It is a private pitch-allocation practice, and the state food board has already described it as incumbent protection. There is no special tax on selling fruit or vegetables.

## The complaint matches documented operator practice, not a statute

Bord Bia’s Guide to Food Markets in Ireland, based on interviews with Irish market managers, states that markets run by the stallholders themselves often refuse a second stall in the same product line “in order to protect their own businesses.” The same guide says that can mean higher prices and less variety, and that several managers thought it kept markets small. It contrasts that with managers who bring in a competing stall when one trader’s prices drift above the rest of the market. The charter Bord Bia recommends says a market should offer variety in season and use a written selection system that is “fair and equitable.” It does not recommend product monopolies. 

That is exactly the pattern in the complaint: one tomato seller, then crafts filling the rest of the square. Crafts are easier to add because they do not collide with an existing food pitch, and some managers cap non-food on purpose so the market still looks like a food market.

Published trader rules show the same trade-off in writing. Carlow Farmers Market’s terms say applications are reviewed so as “not to negatively affect any current stallholders,” while also wanting “an element of choice for consumers.” Applicants are limited to one category plus associated produce, must be producing some of their own goods where possible, and commercial shop traders are discouraged. Pitch cost there was €45 a month, plus a €50 application fee. 

Council-run markets are less blunt. Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown’s market FAQ says it encourages competition and will not guarantee a trader is the only seller of a product, but it tries not to have too many stalls on the same line so each keeps a share of custom. Vacancies are filled from a waiting list against criteria such as local growers, organic, and whether the product complements what is already there. 

So the hypothesis is right for stallholder-controlled markets: the people already in can vote to keep a rival out. It is a contract and committee rule, not a council ban. A grower refused by one market is not barred from another market, a farm gate, or starting their own.

Public discussion is thin. A 2012 https://t.co/yX6MVHPPTq thread on artisan-food pitches mostly covers Dublin pitch rents (then about €50–80 a day under organised private markets) and the need to be “a little different.” A 2020 r/ireland thread is mostly shoppers saying markets are pricey; one commenter who tried for a Tullamore pitch was told regular weekly attendance mattered more than a casual slot. Neither thread is a legal source.

## Tax: ordinary income tax, zero-rated VAT, no produce levy

Revenue’s food-and-drink manual zero-rates most foodstuffs sold by retail, and the list expressly includes fruit (fresh, canned, dried and drained) and vegetables (fresh and frozen). Juice drinks and vegetable juices are standard-rated. Hot catering is not zero-rated. Cold takeaway food generally stays at zero. 

There is no Irish “garden surplus” tax-free allowance of the kind some other countries publish. Two different regimes apply:

- Income tax. Market gardening — occupying land as a nursery or garden to grow produce for sale — is excluded from Revenue’s definition of farming and is charged as a trade under Case I of Schedule D (Taxes Consolidation Act 1997, section 655). Genuine one-off disposal of household surplus is a greyer area; regular market selling with a view to profit is a trade. Farming reliefs do not automatically apply to a market-garden trade.  
- VAT. Someone engaged only in agricultural production is not obliged to register. Retail sales of horticultural products pull in the goods threshold, currently €85,000 in a calendar year. Under that, a tomato seller need not register and charges no VAT. The flat-rate farmer scheme (4.5% addition from 1 January 2026) compensates unregistered farmers for input VAT when they sell to a VAT-registered buyer; it is not a tax on the customer at a market stall. 

Councils must notify Revenue of casual-trading licence holders (name, address, tax reference), under section 4(2A) of the Casual Trading Act 1995, inserted by the Finance Act 1996. Many councils ask for a tax-clearance certificate before they issue the licence. That is an information link, not a special produce tax. 

## Council law: licence on public land, private rules on private land

Casual trading is selling goods at a place the public can enter as of right, or in a designated casual trading area (Casual Trading Act 1995, section 2). Without a licence it is an offence in a local authority’s area once that authority has designated trading areas. Fees and bye-laws are set council by council. Galway City publishes €250 a bay for the Eyre Square weekday market and €65 a linear metre at St Nicholas’s Market, and requires tax clearance, public liability of at least €6.5 million, and an HSE food approval if food is sold. Kildare’s published annual pitch fees start at €100.  

The only produce-specific exemption is narrow. S.I. No. 191/2004 lets the grower — defined as the producer of that product — sell, from 1 May to 30 September, without a casual trading licence: strawberries, raspberries, blueberries, gooseberries, blackberries, loganberries, tayberries, currants, and potatoes with loose skins harvested before maturity. A servant or agent must be able to show documents that they are selling for that grower. Tomatoes, apples, leafy veg and everything else are outside it. Selling at the buyer’s home or business premises is also outside the Act, which is why a farm-gate or doorstep box is a different legal path from a town-square stall. Local authorities may add further exemptions by bye-law.  

A private market on private land, where the public do not have access as of right and the site is not a designated casual trading area, is mostly the operator’s contract: pitch rent, product mix, attendance. Teagasc lists that as a separate type from municipal markets. The operator can refuse a second tomato seller. That refusal is not a council decision. 

## Food rules apply even when the tax and the licence do not

Anyone selling food must notify the HSE Environmental Health Service before trading. Failure to register is an offence. Primary fruit and vegetables are lower risk than ready-to-eat or animal-origin food; meat, dairy, fish and similar need approval, not just notification, and usually cannot be made in an ordinary domestic kitchen. Each stall notifies in its own right unless the HSE has agreed a market-level arrangement. Teagasc also points sellers at NSAI I.S. 344 for stall hygiene. Public and product liability are expected; councils commonly set the public-liability floor at €6.5 million.  

## Setting one up

There is no national farmers’ market licence. Bord Bia’s setup notes say: check nearby markets and whether producers will actually turn up, talk to the council about public space, and stock enough categories (veg, meat, dairy, bread, fish) that someone could do a real shop. On public land the council designates the casual trading area and issues the licences. On private land the constraints are the landowner, planning if the use is a regular commercial change rather than an occasional event, waste, traffic, insurance, and HSE notification of the stalls. A weekly market is more likely to be treated as development than a one-off fair; that is a local-planner question, not a fixed national fee. 

Country markets run by the Irish Countrywomen’s Association are a third model: member-growers, home and farm produce, not a private pitch monopoly.

Bottom line: a grower of tomatoes is not taxed differently from any other small trader, and is not legally locked out because someone else already sells tomatoes. They are locked out only if that market’s operator or stallholder committee chooses to keep the category closed — a practice Bord Bia has already flagged as bad for customers — or if the municipal waiting list and bye-laws leave no pitch. The direct-from-grower model still exists; it is just not what a stallholder-run mixed craft market is obliged to be.

text:
The craziest international window in Irish senior team history has finally come to an end.

Five points. Drama upon drama. Probably the longest two weeks I’ve ever had covering the national team and there is so much to reflect on.

Even last night alone, from the targeting of Molumby by the Israeli players to the spitting incident involving Damien Doyle, before even getting into pure football on the pitch.

From an Irish perspective, the second-half performance was disappointing. We never reproduced what we showed in the first half, or for large spells against Austria on Thursday, and in truth, we were probably fortunate to leave with a point.

The absences of Nathan Collins and Dara O’Shea were absolutely massive. Not just defensively, but in our ability to play through the lines and move the ball sharply from the back. Missing Nathan is difficult enough - losing Dara as well left us without arguably our two best centre-halves.

That said, the goal itself didn’t come from a defensive mistake. It came from a loose pass in midfield.

Ultimately, the most important thing last night was NOT losing to Israel. A defeat would have been an absolute disaster and the worst possible ending to this window.

One thing that continues to frustrate the nation is the long throws.

They’re still an incredibly effective weapon in modern football - Ireland’s U21s have shown that, as have Keith Andrews’ Brentford but ours have rarely caused problems. We struggle to beat the first man and almost never seem to win the first contact.

Dragging Jake O’Brien across from the back three to take them just feels criminal at times, and then bringing Rocco Vata on and asking him to take them didn’t feel much better.

It was good to see Rocco get more minutes, though. He’ll be frustrated with the late free-kick, but he also produced one of the best sliding tackles I’ve seen in a long time to stop Oscar Gloukh on the counter.

There were plenty of positives across the window too.

Troy Parrott now has 15 goals for his country and four in four games in this campaign.

Finn Azaz looked brilliant playing deeper against Austria and showed a side of his game we haven’t seen enough of whilst Jack Moylan looks to be a real star in the making for the national team.

Conor Coventry really stepped up when his opportunity arrived.

And it was great to see Bosun Lawal get minutes last night despite clearly being nowhere near 100%. Hopefully, by November, we get to see him fully fit and firing.

And just look at who Ireland were missing last night:

Nathan Collins.
Dara O’Shea.
Séamus Coleman.
Josh Cullen.
Evan Ferguson.
James Abankwah.
Finn Azaz.

That’s a serious amount of potential starters unavailable.

One disappointment from the window for me was the lack of minutes for Owen Elding. Just five minutes in Kosovo, and last night felt like a game where he could have offered something in that right-sided No.10 role.

Ogbene’s pace and power can obviously cause huge problems, but against Israel’s deep block, having someone cutting inside onto his left foot, with Elding’s football brain and ability to unleash one from distance, felt like something worth trying.

So, after everything that has happened over the last two weeks, we take the five points and move on.

Win both games in November and Ireland top the group.

Austria away and Kosovo at home. Easier said than done, obviously but there is plenty to be hopeful about.

Now, hopefully, the U21s can finish this absolutely mental international window on a high tomorrow night.

text:
The Wrong Question: How Do You Solve a Problem Like #Ethiopia?

The Sound of Music was one of my favorite movies as a child. Like many films that stay with us long after childhood, it offered far more than entertainment. It carried lessons about courage, conscience, leadership, responsibility and resilience, and, perhaps most importantly, about questioning whether the problem we think we are trying to solve is actually the problem we should be addressing.

One scene comes to mind when I read the torrent of commentary surrounding #Ethiopia today. The nuns gather together and sing, “How do you solve a problem like Maria?” They are not really asking how to punish Maria. She is restless, unconventional and poorly suited to the role the institution has assigned to her. The deeper lesson is that perhaps the problem is not Maria at all, but the assumption that she must somehow be made to fit.

The international community is asking a familiar question today: How do you solve a problem like #Ethiopia? It was a question raised repeatedly in conversations on the margins of the recently concluded UN General Assembly High-Level Week. But perhaps the more useful question is whether we have been asking the wrong question for decades.

Perhaps #Ethiopia is not a problem to be “solved” through successive rounds of external intervention, strategic partnerships, security arrangements and political accommodation. Perhaps the harder question is whether the international community has spent decades managing the consequences of #Ethiopia’s internal political crises while avoiding more fundamental questions of accountability, sovereignty, international law and the political choices that produced them.

The problem is not #Ethiopia, nor the #Ethiopian people. It is a pattern of international engagement, indeed, a pattern of strategic accommodation, in which successive governments in Addis Ababa have been treated as strategically indispensable, while those same governments have repeatedly learned to turn that perceived importance into political capital. What has often been presented as pragmatic engagement may instead have helped perpetuate a cycle in which strategic utility becomes a substitute for accountability.

This is not a story of innocent #Ethiopian leaders manipulated by outside powers. Hardly. Successive governments have understood how to convert #Ethiopia’s size, location, population and military capacity into external political, military and financial support when doing so served their interests. Powerful external relationships have been cultivated and recalibrated as circumstances changed. The tragedy is that these bargains have too often been struck by political elites and pursued for political advantage, while ordinary #Ethiopians have borne much of the human and economic cost.

The history is uncomfortable. During the Cold War, #Ethiopia became an arena in which competing great-power interests intersected with the calculations of successive governments in Addis Ababa. #Ethiopian troops were deployed to fight in Korea alongside the United States and its allies. Later, #Ethiopia became a major security partner for Western powers in the post-9/11 environment. The TPLF-led government developed particularly close security relationships with Western governments, while the Prosperity Party has likewise cultivated external relationships around security, economic reform and regional diplomacy.

The governments were profoundly different and should not be conflated. Haile Selassie, the Derg, the TPLF-led government and the Prosperity Party emerged from different political circumstances and pursued different policies. Yet there was a recurring structural feature: #Ethiopia’s perceived strategic importance created incentives for external powers to preserve relationships with the government of the day, even when doing so complicated the pursuit of accountability.

That is the deeper problem. When a government is regarded as indispensable to regional security, counterterrorism, migration management, economic interests or geopolitical competition, political, military and financial support can continue despite credible concerns about repression, human rights violations or conduct toward neighboring States. Strategic cooperation can then become a political shield. Principles proclaimed as universal begin to look negotiable when enforcing them against a strategically useful government carries a geopolitical cost.

The result is not merely inconsistency. It can create a cycle in which outside powers repeatedly manage the consequences of policies they have helped enable rather than confronting the choices that produced those consequences.

For the people of the Horn, this is not an abstract academic problem. Conflict, displacement, destroyed livelihoods and political violence have repeatedly exacted a terrible human cost inside #Ethiopia and across its borders. #Eritreans, Sudanese, Somalis and others have lived with the consequences of decisions made in Addis Ababa as well as decisions made in distant foreign capitals. This is why the present moment should be understood through a wider historical lens.

#Ethiopia again faces serious internal political and security challenges. Armed confrontations, political fragmentation and humanitarian pressures are unfolding simultaneously. Its relationship with several neighbors has also become increasingly strained. Yet there is a familiar danger: that international actors once again treat the government in Addis Ababa as the “indispensable party” whose concerns must be accommodated, rather than asking whether its own political choices are contributing to the instability it claims to be confronting.

For people across the #Horn, the pattern is familiar: crisis, international concern, diplomatic engagement, strategic accommodation, external assistance, temporary stabilization, and renewed crisis. At some point, the question must shift from how to manage the latest #Ethiopian crisis to why the same cycle keeps recurring.

That is not an argument for abandoning #Ethiopia. The #Ethiopian people deserve humanitarian assistance, development, constructive diplomacy and peace. But support for a people should never become immunity for a government. Strategic partnership should never become diplomatic indulgence. Geopolitical importance should never become a license to disregard international law or the sovereignty of neighboring States.

That principle is particularly relevant to the increasingly prominent discourse surrounding #Eritrea and the Red Sea. #Ethiopia’s interests can be pursued through negotiated commercial arrangements, infrastructure investment, port agreements, transit corridors and mutually beneficial regional integration. #Ethiopia is not without regional options. There is nothing in international law that transforms being landlocked into a right to the territory, ports or sovereign maritime assets of another State. Nor does strategic dependence on a particular corridor create unilateral entitlement to that corridor.

The legal principle is straightforward. The United Nations Charter rests on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, political independence and the prohibition of the threat or use of force. These are not diplomatic decorations to be displayed when convenient. They are foundational principles of the international order. A State cannot acquire rights over another State’s territory because it considers access strategically important. Nor can regional integration credibly be built by challenging the sovereignty of the neighbors with whom integration is supposedly to be achieved.

The more fundamental question for international actors, therefore, should be why #Ethiopia’s quest for maritime access is increasingly being presented as though it necessarily requires an extraordinary political solution. The solution to a geographical constraint is cooperation, not the creation of a new sovereign entitlement.

The same discipline should apply to the increasingly persistent effort in some quarters to construct an “#Ethiopia–#Eritrea crisis.” Nomenclature is not evidence. Calling something a crisis does not establish that a crisis exists, any more than repeatedly predicting confrontation proves that the other party caused it. Serious allegations concerning #Eritrea’s intentions or conduct require evidence, attribution and independent corroboration. They cannot responsibly be established through insinuation, selective chronology or the convenient conversion of speculation into fact.

The questions for international actors should be elementary: Who is making the claim? What evidence supports it? Has it been independently corroborated? What facts have been omitted? Whose interests does the narrative serve? And does amplifying it reduce tensions, or create incentives for further confrontation? These are not unreasonable demands. They are the minimum requirements of serious diplomacy.

There is an uncomfortable irony in the present allocation of attention. Ethiopia faces multiple internal political and security challenges, including an increasingly internecine conflict marked by armed confrontations, political fragmentation, and serious humanitarian consequences across the country. Critics argue that policies pursued by the Prosperity Party government have contributed to, and in some cases deepened, these divisions, including by weakening or fragmenting political opposition.

Yet some analyses appear more interested in discovering an #Eritrean storyline than in examining the fires already burning inside #Ethiopia. There is another dimension to this imbalance that deserves attention.
Much of the prevailing narrative about Eritrea did not emerge in a political vacuum. It was shaped over decades by successive Ethiopian governments and amplified by a network of international partners, policy institutions and advocacy organizations that adopted, repeated or built upon Ethiopia’s framing of Eritrea. 

That history matters. Claims repeated often enough can acquire the appearance of settled fact, even when their evidentiary basis, context and political origins are rarely revisited. This is not an argument that Eritrea should be shielded from scrutiny, nor that every allegation against it is unfounded. It is an argument for intellectual honesty: narratives produced by states and their strategic partners are not neutral historical records. 

They must be examined, sourced and tested against evidence as rigorously as any competing account. In the present moment, when Ethiopia itself is confronting profound internal political and security challenges, reviving an established narrative in which Eritrea is cast as the convenient source of regional instability risks explaining away Ethiopia’s own unresolved problems rather than explaining them.

These conflicts have domestic histories, domestic actors and domestic grievances. They cannot simply be outsourced to #Eritrea by assertion. Nor will inserting #Eritrea into the narrative resolve #Ethiopia’s internal problems. To the many “researchers” now producing narratives about #Eritrea that conveniently reinforce the preferred framing of Prime Minister Abiy’s government, the message should be simple: scrutinize the evidence, question the premises and resist the temptation to turn political narratives into analytical conclusions. When a house has several fires, blaming the neighbor for the smoke may be convenient politics. It is hardly serious analysis.

There is also a growing ecosystem of conflict entrepreneurs, political actors, analysts, institutions, lobbyists, commentators and digital influencers, whose relevance can become intertwined with the continuation of conflict narratives. The incentive can be remarkably simple: conflict generates relevance. Grievance becomes content; suspicion becomes analysis; speculation becomes prediction; prediction becomes policy advice; and policy advice becomes another justification for speculation. In such an ecosystem, peace can become strangely bad for business.

The people of the Horn should not become raw material for another conference circuit, another institutional career or another social-media following. They are sovereign people, not case studies, commodities or props in someone else’s geopolitical project. The international community must therefore resist false symmetry. There is a fundamental difference between a genuine bilateral dispute and the political construction of one. Internal #Ethiopian political and security problems should not be transformed into an external #Eritrean problem simply because doing so is politically convenient.

#Eritrea’s refusal to mirror inflammatory rhetoric with inflammatory rhetoric should not be mistaken for escalation. Indeed, demonstrated restraint can itself be a contribution to regional stability. In a region too often driven by escalation and inflammatory rhetoric, choosing not to mirror provocation can help prevent tensions from becoming conflict.

The international community can make an equally important contribution by refusing to manufacture symmetry where the evidence does not establish it. It should focus attention on the political and humanitarian realities unfolding inside #Ethiopia while making clear that #Ethiopia’s internal difficulties cannot be resolved by creating external disputes.

This requires a different international policy. External partners should support the #Ethiopian people without providing any government a blank cheque. Diplomatic and economic leverage should be used before conflicts become wars, not merely after the killing begins. International engagement should also become more consistent about the distinction between supporting a country and shielding its government. 

Humanitarian assistance should reach people. Development assistance should strengthen institutions and communities. Diplomacy should encourage political accommodation rather than reward escalation. Security cooperation should be conditioned by respect for international law. And relationships with governments should not become exemptions from standards that the international community claims to apply universally.

The deeper choice is therefore not whether the international community should support #Ethiopia. It should. The choice is whether it continues to treat #Ethiopia primarily as a strategic asset whose government must be kept sufficiently stable to serve external interests, or whether it engages #Ethiopia as a country whose long-term stability depends on accountable institutions, peaceful politics, respect for international law and respect for its neighbors.

The latter approach is harder. It offers fewer convenient alliances and fewer shortcuts. It may require difficult conversations with governments that powerful states consider strategically useful. It may require external actors to acknowledge that some policies previously described as pragmatic have produced unintended consequences. But it offers something the previous approach has repeatedly failed to deliver: the possibility of breaking the cycle.

And perhaps that is the final lesson I took from a movie I loved as a child. The answer was never really about “solving” Maria. It was about recognizing that the original assumptions were inadequate and finding a better way forward.

The people of the Horn should not once again be made to pay the price for the excesses of another failed #Ethiopian political order. Nor should neighboring States be expected to surrender their sovereignty, security or legal rights to compensate for #Ethiopia’s internal political difficulties.

So perhaps the real question is not, “How do you solve a problem like #Ethiopia?” It is: What must the international community do differently so that the #Ethiopian people, and the peoples of the wider Horn, are no longer asked to pay the price for bargains made by political elites with outside powers?

The way forward is therefore neither abandonment nor indulgence. It is a harder bargain: support the people, scrutinize the government, enforce the law, verify the facts, respect sovereignty, and make assistance reinforce peace rather than political impunity. #Ethiopia does not need another patron willing to look away. It needs partners willing to tell the truth. And the Horn does not need another crisis manufactured for strategic convenience, institutional relevance or political survival.

Calling a spade a spade is not taking sides. It is taking human life, and international law, seriously.
