text:
VOLUNTEERS
(RADIO ZAVTRA)

6 (271)
Date: 09 February 1999
Taking part in the Zavtra radio programme are military correspondent and conflict analyst Alexander Borodai, historian Oleg Airapetov, and Zavtra contributor and Interior Troops officer Igor Strelkov.

ORIGINS

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
On the threshold of the third millennium, almost all of Eurasia, and especially the territory of the former USSR, has become a zone of relatively small-scale military conflicts — so-called “regional wars.”

One of the most characteristic features of these conflicts is the participation not only of regular military formations, but also of people who, for one reason or another, voluntarily take up arms.
These people are described in different ways — sometimes as mercenaries, sometimes as volunteers.

The democratic media habitually use the cliché “dogs of war,” applying it not only to the notorious “White Tights,” but also to those who fought for Russian national interests, for the violated honour of the state in Ossetia, Transnistria, Abkhazia and Chechnya.

And to those who helped the Serbian “brothers” resist the attacks of Croats and Bosnian Muslims nurtured by NATO sponsors and trained by Western instructors.

Yandarbiyev, in a recent interview with Nezavisimaya, claimed that Russian troops in Chechnya consisted mainly of “mercenaries recruited from prisons,” whom Chechen “civilians” could decapitate with a clear conscience.

Fear of the “brutalised mercenaries” is carefully cultivated by the liberal press, which tries to frighten the ordinary citizen with the image of an armed Russian passionary.

We intend to discuss and examine volunteering as a social phenomenon, as a unique feature of contemporary Russian life.

So, who are these volunteers?

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
One can speak of volunteering not merely as a social phenomenon, but also as a historical and ideological one.

The first volunteer movement in Russia emerged in connection with the Balkans — the participation of Russian volunteers in the Greek uprising led by Ypsilantis.

The first volunteers numbered only in the dozens, but among them were some rather remarkable personalities.

One could mention Khomyakov, one of the fathers of Slavophilism, although he was intercepted by the border guards and was therefore unable to take part in the fighting.
This first movement was also the first to be reflected quite widely in classical Russian literature.

We can recall that Pushkin, the man to whom we owe the emergence of the Russian literary language and whose bicentenary will soon be celebrated throughout the country, portrayed types of volunteers in several of his works, including Kirdjali and The Shot.

From the outset, however, we should distinguish between volunteering aimed at participation in external conflicts and volunteering that occurs in internal conflicts, in civil war.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Generally speaking, volunteering is a phenomenon highly characteristic of the Russian people and of Russian military culture.

Today we are talking about volunteering as it existed when Russia already possessed not only a regular army but was also beginning to become a “civil society,” if we use the terminology of Marx or Tönnies, when the distinction between soldiers and civilians was determined not merely by social estate but also by law.

But Russian volunteer warriors are a phenomenon typical of the whole of Russian history.

Peresvet and Oslyabya were volunteers; the militia of Minin and Pozharsky was also a volunteer militia.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I will probably express a somewhat pessimistic thought.

It seems to me that during the Time of Troubles the volunteer movement was only weakly connected to the regular army.
The first militia was purely voluntary and disintegrated because of poor organisation and conflicts between its Cossack and noble components.

The second volunteer movement, of course, already claimed a nationwide role.

A “Council of All the Land” was established.

People genuinely gathered and went to defend Moscow — the Third Rome — Rus', and the Orthodox faith.

These were the people directly addressed by Patriarch Hermogenes in his appeal:

“You were Russian Orthodox people, but now I do not know what to call you.”
Apparently, the unwillingness to become former Orthodox believers and former Russian people was transformed into free will — the will to defend one’s Fatherland.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
True volunteers always number only in the dozens, perhaps hundreds.

But often they become the catalyst for powerful movements, and their names remain in history.

Now, when Russia finds itself in a critical situation, such defenders are needed more than ever.

Yet precisely now the term “volunteer” is hardly used at all.

People who voluntarily go to war for ideological reasons are portrayed by the mass media as mercenaries.

I would like to draw a clear and distinct dividing line: what is a mercenary, and what is a volunteer?

In this particular case, I think we need to discuss not even the moral distinction, but, if you like, the legal one, because the new version of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation offers a rather severe interpretation of the volunteer movement.

IGOR STRELKOV (GIRKIN):
Yes, of course. There is Article 359, which provides for serious criminal punishment for mercenary activity.

The article explicitly states that a mercenary is a person acting for the purpose of obtaining material remuneration who is not a citizen of a state participating in the armed conflict or hostilities, does not permanently reside on its territory, and is not a person sent there to perform official duties.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
One famous nineteenth-century diplomat said that in the dark forest of international law there are neither murderers nor murdered — only corpses.
The same can be said here about the new version of the Criminal Code, because it quite clearly attempts to subsume volunteers under the concept of mercenarism as well.

What, for example, constitutes material remuneration?

As far as I know, Russian volunteers who fought in Serbia and in Republika Srpska — one of whom is present here in the studio, namely Igor — did receive certain provisions.

But can the mere fact of receiving money, food or rations, something natural to any military organisation or unit, really be treated as material remuneration?

There has to be a clear boundary between mercenarism and volunteering.

Mercenarism is a means of obtaining profit, of earning money, and mercenarism has already been condemned by international organisations; there are relevant provisions within the UN framework.

Can someone who receives a bowl of rice or a packet of cigarettes per day for defending his ideals really be called a mercenary?

IGOR STRELKOV:
In this respect, the war in Serbia is particularly illustrative.

A clear line can be drawn between the volunteers and Russian servicemen who served in Bosnia as members of UN forces.
For comparison, at different times and during different periods, volunteers received between 150 and 300 German marks.

At the final and most difficult stage of the war, volunteers received thirty dinars a month, which in present-day terms is less than 300 roubles at the current exchange rate.

At the same time, contract soldiers serving in Russian Army UN units received between 900 and 1,200 US dollars per month.

Yet the first were considered mercenaries — at least that was how they were described by the press and portrayed on television — while the latter were regarded as servicemen honourably carrying out their duty on the territory of a foreign state.
There are known cases in which servicemen in Chechnya who wished to transfer to a UN contingent had to pass a special selection process.

There were quite a lot of them, because 900 dollars seemed such an enormous amount to an ordinary soldier that some people were prepared to go anywhere and do anything for that money.

FOR OUR BROTHERS

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Across the enormous post-Soviet space, which includes not only the territories of the fifteen former Soviet republics but also former allied states such as Yugoslavia, numerous armed conflicts have erupted during the past ten years.

And it must be said that the outcomes of these conflicts were determined not by the participation of regular armed forces, but precisely by volunteer formations and mercenary formations.

The first Russian war begun and won by volunteers was the Transnistrian War.

All of us here today were in that war at one time, and we remember who made up the battalions of the Transnistrian army that fought what were then called the “Romanian invaders.”

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I think we should make a small clarification.

The initiator of the war was not the volunteer units but the regime in Chișinău, which was attempting to impose an ethnocracy throughout the territory of the former Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic.

It is characteristic that this regime was led by former officials of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
But the people of Transnistria resisted that regime.

The volunteers only began to be drawn into the conflict during the second, if not the third, stage.

IGOR STRELKOV:
But why should the local inhabitants not be regarded as volunteers?

There was no mobilisation as such in Transnistria.

The Transnistrian Guard was likewise staffed by volunteers.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Yes, Transnistria is famous for its volunteer traditions.

Even in Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s army, which liberated Ukraine from the Poles and other foreigners, the regiments of Ataman Bohun, recruited from inhabitants of that region, were considered the most reliable.

And at the beginning of the Russian Civil War, Colonel Drozdovsky’s detachment was formed in Tiraspol and Iași, later giving rise to the famous White Guard division.

They sang about that unit:

“From Romania on campaign came Drozdovsky’s glorious regiment,
to save the people it marched to fulfil its difficult duty.”
OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I think we have by now more or less identified the dividing line between a volunteer and a mercenary.

A volunteer is someone who goes to war for ideological reasons.

His motives are not material; his motives are spiritual.

He defends his own ideals.

If you like, he goes to war in order to destroy war.

A mercenary, by contrast, goes to war exclusively for material considerations; he lives by war.
If we recall one of the hymns of French mercenaries, it contains the words:

“Long live death, long live war, long live the valiant mercenary.”

I do not think any volunteer would agree to repeat the words of that French mercenary hymn.

That is the whole difference.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
When the war began in Transnistria, the exhausted Russian people, worn down by the disasters of the twentieth century — this super-ethnos — demonstrated that it was not yet completely dead, that it was still capable of certain vital impulses.

The cause of those impulses was a sense of dignity, a sense of ethnic solidarity.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
That is a profound and correct observation.
If we examine the history of the volunteer movement, at least outside Russia, we see that its social and ideological structure is extremely diverse.

People go there with completely different, and often opposing, views.

It was the same in Transnistria.

There were nationalists, communists and internationalists.

There were Russian nationalists and Ukrainian nationalists.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
I remember that reconnaissance in our company was commanded by a Ukrainian nationalist.

A trident was displayed on the stock of his assault rifle.

One of his subordinates was a Russian Orthodox ultramonarchist nicknamed “Kolya the Emperor.”

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
If we look at the volunteer movement of 1876, on the eve of the liberation war, we see that a very mixed assortment of volunteers gathered in Serbia.

There were monarchists, supporters of a Great Russia, liberals, and supporters of the revolutionary-democratic movement, often hostile to one another.
Why did they go there?

It seems to me that the initial impulse behind the volunteer movement, whose core is formed by passionaries, comes from protest against the reality a person sees at home but cannot change.

Secondly, there is an idealistic element.
He goes somewhere where this opposing ideal supposedly exists.

While the first motive can easily be translated into practice, the second is connected with romantic ideas and is doomed to collapse, because as a rule an ideal is incompatible with real life.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
In Transnistria one could observe how many people experienced the collapse of their ideals and transformed from volunteers into mercenaries.

In fairness, it must be said that by no means everyone who came to fight in Transnistria was a pure volunteer.

Alongside ideologically motivated fighters who tried, with weapons in their hands, to establish a higher truth and obtain justice for the Russian people, there were also quite a few outright lumpen elements.

Practically every platoon included characters nicknamed “Odessa.”

Transnistria is only a few dozen kilometres from Odessa, after all, and many such brave Odessans poured into this relatively prosperous territory simply in order to profit and loot.

I should say that the Transnistrian War was not the hardest war, so there was room there for criminals as well.

Many subsequently became professional mercenaries and went immediately afterwards to Karabakh, for example, or to Abkhazia.

But look at how tragically the fates of those who went to fight in Karabakh and Abkhazia developed.

Many people who had sat in the same trench in Transnistria later found themselves in opposing trenches and on opposing sides in those wars for various reasons.

Some went to fight for Azerbaijan, while others went to help the Christian Armenians.

IGOR STRELKOV:
I know people who went there not because of ideology.

Many of them said they were going there to gain experience that would later be useful to them here in Russia.

And those wars were much more serious than the Transnistrian War.

The losses were greater.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
What Igor has just said reminds me of an episode from Churchill’s biography, since Churchill was also a volunteer.

During the Greco-Turkish War he wrote to his mother asking her to obtain letters of recommendation for him.

There was a sentence along these lines:

“If you obtain letters of recommendation to the Greeks, I will go and fight for the Greeks; if you obtain them to the Turks, then I will fight for the Turks, because what I need is precisely this combat experience.”

For an officer, for a professional serviceman, it is natural to want to acquire this kind of experience.

But if we return once again to the distinction between mercenarism and volunteering, we can recall the 1970s and the end of the colonial conflicts in Africa.

At that time it seemed that the era of mercenaries was drawing to a close.

And every mercenary claimed to be going off to defend one idea or another.
The fact is that an ideological component is always present among mercenaries.

But it is not their principal motivation.

It serves as a cover.

text:
The door was sealed to the dying. Compassion opened it. Neglect kept it open.

Canada removed the requirement that death be reasonably foreseeable. Track 2 now covers people with disabilities who are not dying. Disability is a Charter-protected ground under section 15. Offering death as the reliable service, while the supports required to live remain chronically underfunded, does not fulfill that protection. It narrows it.

In 2024 Track 2 recipients were far more likely to self-identify as disabled, and Ontario coroner data shows they disproportionately come from poorer neighbourhoods with unstable housing. Supports that might relieve the suffering are offered in a minority of cases. MAID is funded and timely. Disability income often is not.

Poverty is not an eligibility criterion. Once disability qualifies someone, the suffering produced by missing supports can be treated as reason enough. Autonomy requires alternatives. When death is the reliable service and living is not, the choice is no longer clean.

Canada abolished the death penalty in 1976 because the state taking a life raised a moral question it would no longer answer with a rope. The question did not retire. It returned as a medical procedure, with cost savings attached and the paperwork arranged so the intervention disappears. Ontario instructs providers to record only the underlying illness or disability and to make no reference to MAID or the drugs on the medical certificate of death. Manner of death is to be certified natural where that option exists. A state that administers the death does not require the death certificate to say so. The savings stay quiet because the record does.

39. One Day in Kaito's Body

Jerry had always believed that power was something a king should be careful with. A crown could command armies, but true power could destroy a kingdom if placed in the wrong hands. So when he suddenly woke up in Kaito's body, his first instinct was disbelief. His reflection was no longer his own. His senses were sharper, his heartbeat strangely quiet, and every sound around him seemed impossibly clear. Then he lifted his hand—and the chair across the room flew toward him.

Telekinesis.

Jerry stared at it in silence. "Well... this is going to be interesting." For the first few hours, Jerry experimented with Kaito's abilities. His telekinesis allowed him to move objects without touching them, while his werewolf-vampire nature gave him incredible speed and physical strength. He raced through the forests surrounding Virelia, moving so quickly that the world seemed frozen around him. For once, he could experience the kingdom from a perspective no ordinary human could. But Jerry did not spend the day simply enjoying his newfound abilities. He remembered what it meant to be King. There were citizens struggling in distant villages, soldiers exhausted from patrols, and old infrastructure that had been neglected because repairing it would take weeks. So Jerry decided to use Kaito's powers for something useful. He used telekinesis to lift fallen trees blocking roads, repair damaged structures, and transport heavy supplies that normally required dozens of workers. With his supernatural speed, he traveled across the kingdom in minutes, personally checking on villages that had rarely seen their King. Yet there was one final thing he wanted to do. That evening, Jerry stood atop the palace tower, overlooking Virelia. For one day, he had possessed enough power to become almost unstoppable. And strangely, he realized that the greatest lesson was not about what he could do.

43. The King in the Mirror

Jerry had always believed that a crown could change a person. He simply never expected it to change him. The night was unusually quiet in Virelia. After another exhausting day of council meetings, disputes between noble families, and reports from the kingdom's borders, Jerry returned to his chambers alone. He removed his crown and placed it upon the table. For a moment, he simply stared at it. Then he walked toward the mirror. He expected to see the same man who had entered the room that morning. Instead, he froze.

“I turned around and didn’t recognise the person in the mirror.”

The reflection looked exhausted. His eyes no longer carried the carefree warmth they once had. They were sharper now, weighed down by decisions that could determine whether people lived peacefully or suffered. Jerry touched the mirror.

"When did I become this person?"

He remembered the boy he had once been—the one who loved music, wandered through the kingdom without guards, and believed that every problem could be solved if people simply listened to one another.

Now, he was King. Every decision came with consequences. A wrong judgment could destroy a family. A careless treaty could start a war. A moment of weakness could make thousands lose faith in him. Jerry wondered whether becoming a good King meant losing the person he used to be. Then his eyes fell upon the crown. He picked it up but did not place it on his head. Instead, he smiled faintly. Perhaps the person in the mirror wasn't a stranger after all. He was simply the version of Jerry that had survived everything the crown demanded of him. Jerry looked at his reflection again. "I haven't changed completely," he whispered. "I've just learned how much I have to protect." He finally placed the crown upon his head.

Gardeners offered him vegetables. Citizens stopped to pet the strange royal bunny. For the first time, Jerry experienced Virelia without anyone knowing he was their King. Jews had lived there for centuries in small communities, then larger numbers returned from the 1880s under Ottoman & British law. They bought land legally, mainly from absentee landlords (e.gLebanese Sursock family) & those sales often put Arab tenant farmers off the land. By 1947 Jewish ownership approximately 6–7 %of the Mandate at the time held by Britain 
after the Ottomans. The UN plan offered a Jewish state & an Arab state. Jewish leaders accepted it. Arab leaders & the surrounding Arab states rejected it & said they would stop a Jewish state by force. Britain left due to it being untenable financing British army out there. Then when Israel declared independence it was invaded by the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq & Lebanon. It defended itself & finished the war holding more than the partition had given it.
About 700,000 Arabs left or were driven out in that war. The main cause was the fighting & Israeli military operations. There were also some expulsions, fear after killings, & local Arab orders to move women, children & the elderly out of the way. Arab radio often told people to stay put &  Arab states mostly refused to take the refugees in.
Haj Amin al-Husseini collaborated with Nazi Germany, met Hitler, broadcast propaganda & tried to block Jewish refugees reaching Palestine. 

Later Israeli governments offered a Palestinian state on Gaza plus roughly approximately 95% of the West Bank with land swaps but Palestinian leaders did not agree to this. Israel left Gaza in 2005 & Hamas took over, kept firing rockets, built tunnels mainly for its fighters & placed operations among civilians. Earlier bombings & rockets from the West Bank led Israel to build the barrier and the iron dome which intercepts rockets but these can still cause damage which mainly hits Arab towns in Israel. These rockets also misfire and come down in Palestinian Territory. These Israeli Settlements in the West Bank there are widely treated as illegal; Israel has cited security, history & high ground as its reasons. So the Wst bank does keep control of who goes in & out there are Israelis living in the West Bank as there are Arabs living in Israel. No Jews live in Gaza. There is a surrounding wall the length of Gaza that separates the Palestinians from Israel as there is a blockade on the side of Egypt. So Arab states also controls who goes in & out of Gaza. Before October 7th 2023 Palestinians were provided with work permits but since the attack Israel site security being the reason why these have been revoked. 

On 7 October 2023 Hamas & allied groups broke the border, attacked communities & a music festival, killed about 1,200 people mostly civilians, & took roughly 250 hostages. They filmed killings, burnings & sexual violence & called it the start of ending Israel.
Israel went to war to break Hamas’s army & rule in Gaza, free the hostages & stop another attack on that scale. It closed the crossings & went in by air & ground. Hamas kept firing rockets, fighting from tunnels under civilian areas & holding hostages there. Israel destroyed much of the tunnel network & killed many commanders & fighters, but Hamas remained. Some hostages were freed in negotiated pauses, some were killed in captivity or rescue attempts, & some were still missing into 2025 & 2026.
Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry reported Palestinian deaths in the tens of thousands without separating fighters from civilians. Israel estimated many thousands of militants killed. Large parts of the housing, hospitals & infrastructure were destroyed. Israel said this followed from Hamas siting military assets among civilians; aid agencies & critics said the firepower & aid limits caused excessive harm. Both were visible.
Talks through Qatar, Egypt & the United States produced short pauses & partial exchanges, but no deal that disarmed Hamas or met its demand for full withdrawal. By late 2026 major ground fighting had eased in places, Hamasstill present, lower-level attacks 👇

He continues:

"𝑂𝑢𝑟 𝑚𝑜𝑠𝑡 𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑐 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔: 𝑈𝑔𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑎 𝑖𝑠 𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑐𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑎𝑚𝑜𝑢𝑛𝑡𝑠 𝑜𝑓 𝑔𝑜𝑙𝑑—$8.9 𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑙𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑡ℎ 𝑖𝑛 12 𝑚𝑜𝑛𝑡ℎ𝑠 𝑡ℎ𝑟𝑢 𝐽𝑢𝑛𝑒—𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑎 𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚 𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙𝑒𝑑 𝑇ℎ𝑎𝑏𝑎 𝐼𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑠 𝑖𝑠 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑏𝑙𝑒 𝑓𝑜𝑟 𝑛𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑙𝑦 ℎ𝑎𝑙𝑓."

This is shown in the graph below.

What is going on here? I summarised a list from tweets of three different people, and I use the word "allegedly" to protect myself. The detailed tweets and articles can be found in the comment section. Each element in the list can be researched with few searches. 

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐭𝐬: 𝐖𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐧𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐲𝐨, 𝐠𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐬𝐦𝐮𝐠𝐠𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐦, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐟𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬.

- Gold as the Sudanese Rapid Support Front (RSF)’s Lifeblood (Background): Gold is described as the RSF’s lifeblood: the RSF controls Darfur mines, mills ore, and smuggles gold out. The sanctioned Dagalo family, who fund the RSF, have deep ties here. The RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo has held meetings with the exact same presidents we used to see Chivayo rubbing shoulders with. 
  
- Ruto’s Alleged RSF Ties (2025): President Ruto of Kenya faces accusations of RSF ties mostly tied to gold smuggling. Kenya and Tanzania are transit hubs for the gold to the UAE.
  
- US Eyes on Chivayo (2025): The US allegedly had eyes on Chivayo; his visa was revoked years ago; Michael J. Kavanagh's articles suggest America “whispered” to President Emmerson Mnangagwa recently.
  
- Chivayo as a Front (2025):  There are claims Chivayo was a front; only one person controls that kind of liquid cash because they can’t use standard banking channels.

- Then on 30th September 2026, Wicknell Chivayo's helicopter crashed.
  
- The Elimination Claim (After 30 September 2025): There are claims Chivayo was eliminated because he knew too much/the net was closing; “no loyalty amongst thieves and criminals.” There are questions raised about the two choppers during the time of the accident. Out of the 2 choppers, senior pilots failed to navigate the weather, while junior pilots in a less sophisticated chopper were fine.
  
- The Mansion Lockdown (After 30 September 2025): After Chivayo’s helicopter crash, the army allegedly swarmed and locked down his mansion in Zimbabwe with no family/friends allowed in.
  
- The Mysterious Digging (After 30 September 2025): Neighbors allegedly complained of mysterious digging; tunnels collapsed, causing cracks in neighboring homes.
  
- The Hoarded Billions (After 30 September 2025): Chivayo allegedly hoarded billions in gold, diamonds, and cash; the Tanzanian president allegedly offered mercenaries to help secure the house.
  
- The $4 Billion Weapons Shipment (July 2025):  Weapons shipment rumoured to be worth up to $4 billion; investigators have not officially named the financial backer, but all eyes  points to Chivayo.
  
- Malawi Cleaning House (October 2025):  Malawi is “cleaning house”; Zimbabwe allegedly cut off the “single explosive link” to terrorism funding.
  
- The Phiri Arrest (2 October 2026): General Phiri from Malawi, a man with close ties to Chivayo, is accused of involvement in property deals linked to “terrorism”—in plain terms, helping arm Sudanese rebels with heavy weaponry. Bail terms for Phiri: a K10 million cash bond, two sureties of K20 million each, grounded in Malawi, and report to police once a month.

- The Zimbabwe Encounter (3 May 2026): President Cyril Ramaphosa faced intense public scrutiny after being photographed with controversial businessman Wicknell Chivayo during a working visit to Zimbabwe. On 6 May 2026, the Presidency maintained that Ramaphosa had no prior knowledge that Chivayo would be present.
  
- The Dagalo Meeting (4 January 2024): President Ramaphosa drew diplomatic criticism for hosting Sudanese Rapid Support Forces (RSF) leader General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti) in Pretoria. South Africa said the engagement was part of tentative regional peace efforts aimed at ending Sudan’s civil war.

- Just days before the Chivayo helicopter crash, Open Secrets ZA (@OpenSecretsZA) lodged a formal criminal complaint with the Hawks regarding suspicious cross-border financial transactions involving Wicknell Chivayo. These investigations focus heavily on multi-million-rand illicit flows and inflated election tenders linked to the South African printing firm Ren-Form, which has also previously secured major contracts with South Africa’s IEC and the elections in Zimbabwe.

text:
The explanation of chapter 2 of the Prophet Zechariah

Good morning, Ladies, Young Ladies and Gentlemen,
Please find attached the explanation of chapter 2 of the Prophet Zechariah:

⚖️Zechariah 2:1 Then I looked up and saw a vision. Behold, there were four horns.

Behold: the first horn was Pharaoh of Egypt; the second horn was the alliance between Eglon, King of Moab, and the sons of Ammon and Amalek; the third horn was the alliance between the leaders of the Philistines and the Ammonites; the fourth horn was the alliance between Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, the ruler of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who struck down the children of Israel

Exodus 1:15 The king of Egypt said to the midwives of the Hebrew women—one of whom was called Shiphrah and the other Pua—
Exodus 1:16 “When you assist the Hebrew women in childbirth, look at the two stones. If it is a son, put him to death; if it is a daughter, let her live.”
Exodus 1:22 Pharaoh then gave this order to all his people: “Every son that is born, cast him into the River, but let every daughter live.”
Exodus 14:5 When it was reported to the king of Egypt that the people had fled, the attitude of Pharaoh and his officials towards the people changed. They said, ‘What have we done, letting Israel go from our service!’
Exodus 14:9 The Egyptians set out in pursuit and caught up with them as they were encamped by the sea—all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, his horsemen and his army—near Pi-Hahiroth, opposite Baal-Zephon.

Judges 3:8 Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; he delivered them into the hands of Kushan-Rishathaim, king of Edom, and the Israelites were enslaved to Kushan-Rishathaim for eight years.
Judges 3:12 The Israelites again began to do what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord strengthened Eglon, king of Moab, against Israel, because they were doing what was evil in the sight of the Lord.
Judges 3:13 Eglon gathered the Ammonites and the Amalekites, marched against Israel, defeated them and captured the City of Palms.
Judges 3:14 The Israelites were enslaved to Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years.

Judges 4:1 After Ehud’s death, the Israelites once again began to do what was evil in the sight of the Lord,
Judges 4:2 and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.
Judges 4:3 So the Israelites cried out to the Lord. For Jabin had 900 iron chariots and had oppressed the Israelites severely for twenty years.

Judges 6:1 The Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Midianites for seven years,
Judges 6:2 and the hand of Midian was heavy upon Israel. To escape from Midian, the Israelites took refuge in the clefts of the mountains, in caves and in strongholds.
Judges 10:7 Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and into the hands of the Ammonites.
Judges 10:8 From that year onwards, for eighteen years, they crushed and oppressed the Israelites—all the Israelites who lived beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites in Gilead.

1 Samuel 12:9 But they forgot the Lord their God, and he delivered them into the hands of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who waged war against them.

1 Samuel 12:10 They cried out to the Lord: ‘We have sinned,’ they said, ‘for we have forsaken the Lord and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. Now deliver us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you!’
1 Samuel 12:11 Then the Lord sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah and Samuel; he delivered you from your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety. (No years given)

Judges 13:1 The Israelites again did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.

2 Kings 13:3 Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against the Israelites, and he delivered them into the hands of Hazael, king of Aram, and into the hands of Ben-Hadad, son of Hazael, all that time.
2 Kings 13:4 But Jehoahaz sought to appease the Lord, and the Lord answered him, for he had seen the oppression that the king of Aram was inflicting on Israel.
2 Kings 13:5 The Lord raised up a deliverer for Israel who rescued them from the hand of Aram, and the Israelites lived in their tents as before. (No years)

2 Kings 17:20 And the Lord cast off the whole house of Israel; he humbled them and delivered them to plunderers, until at last he cast them far from his presence.
2 Kings 17:21 For he had severed Israel from the house of David, and Israel had proclaimed Jeroboam son of Nebat king; Jeroboam had led Israel astray from the Lord and caused them to commit a great sin.
2 Kings 17:22 The Israelites imitated the sin that Jeroboam had committed; they did not turn away from it,
2 Kings 17:23 until at last the Lord cast Israel away from his presence, as he had foretold through his servants the prophets; he exiled the Israelites from their land to Assyria, where they remain to this day’
(No years)

⚖️Zechariah 2:2 I said to the angel who was speaking to me, ‘What are these horns?’ He replied, ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah (Israel) and Jerusalem.’

According to the Book of Jeremiah, the deportation of the Judeans took place in three stages (Jeremiah 52:28–30). The first was in the time of Jehoiachin (c. 624 BC, before the Resurrection of the Saviour), following the defeat of the Kingdom of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar II; the Temple in Jerusalem was then partially plundered and the majority of the citizens were taken away.

Eleven years later, in c. 614 BC, following a revolt against the Neo-Babylonian Empire during the reign of Zedekiah, the city was completely razed to the ground and a further, smaller-scale deportation ensued.

Finally, Jeremiah records a third exile five years later, in 609 ± BC.

⚖️Zechariah 2:3 Then the Lord showed me four smiths.

Four ‘king-builders’: Alexander, Ptolemy I Soter, Ptolemy II Philadelphus and Ptolemy III Euergetes I, under whose rule the children of Israel lived

In Tevet 361–Elul 360 BC, Alexander took possession of Judea and Samaria.
A king-builder, Alexander founded some twenty cities, the most important and best known of which was Alexandria in Egypt.

The Battle of Gaza took place in 339 ± BC, against the backdrop of the Wars of the Diadochi, pitting Ptolemy, satrap of Egypt, against Demetrius, son of Antigonus the One-Eyed, ruler of Asia. It resulted in Ptolemy’s victory. Judea was brought under Ptolemaic rule.
Ptolemy I Soter was the great builder of the city of Alexandria, which he made his capital.
After the Battle of Ipsus in c. 328, which saw the death of Antigonus, at the instigation of Seleucus the allies refused to hand over Coele-Syria to him permanently; from then on, it became the subject of a major rivalry – the Six Syrian Wars – between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids.

Ptolemy II Philadelphus, son of Berenice I, who had been co-ruler since around 312, succeeded his father in 310. He waged the First Syrian War, extended Ptolemaic rule into Cilicia and Caria, but lost control of Cyrenaica following the defection of his half-brother Magas. Ptolemy II undertook major public works, notably in Alexandria, which became one of the greatest metropolises of the Mediterranean.
Seventy-two Jewish scholars produced a Greek translation there of all the Israelite books, both sacred texts and secular narratives; this translation, in their honour, was named the Septuagint.

Ptolemy III Euergetes I, the younger son of Ptolemy II, succeeded him following a betrayal by his elder brother. He opposed the Seleucids during the Third Syrian War, marching as far as Babylon. He intervened in the affairs of Greece by allying himself first with the Achaean League and then with Sparta. His reign marked the territorial zenith of Ptolemaic Egypt.
He commissioned the construction of a library in the Serapeum, amongst other places, which complemented the Library of Alexandria.
According to the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, Ptolemy III Euergetes I and one of his sons, Ptolemy IV Philopator, having emerged victorious – from which conflict? – offered sacrifices in Jerusalem.

Ptolemy IV Philopator, son of Berenice II, defeated Antiochus III at the Battle of Raphia in 244 BC or thereabouts, thereby regaining all his possessions in Coele-Syria with the exception of Seleucia in Pieria.
He was more concerned with luxury and entertainment than with the affairs of his kingdom and his people. His reign saw the beginning of the decline of Ptolemaic Egypt.

Following the Fifth Syrian War, around 228 ± BC, Antiochus III took control of Judea. Relations between the Seleucids and the Judeans were initially harmonious.
But in 215 ± BC, the Seleucids were defeated by the Romans during the Antiochian War. The Treaty of Apamea stripped Antiochus of his possessions in Asia Minor and required him to pay a colossal indemnity to Rome. This financial burden marked the beginning of the disintegration of the Seleucid Empire. From then on, Antiochus no longer had the means to bestow gifts upon his subjects. He was tempted to plunder the temples, which at that time served as deposit banks.

⚖️Zechariah 2:4 And I said, ‘What do these signify?’ He said to me, ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one dared to lift up his head; but’

In 202 ± BC, Joshua, the brother of Onias III, the high priest of the Jews—who went by the Greek name Jason—plotted with the new king, Antiochus IV, who granted him the right to transform the city of Jerusalem into a new Greek city, a polis.

1 Maccabees 1:14 So they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, in accordance with the customs of the nations,
1 Maccabees 1:15 had themselves circumcised again and renounced the holy covenant in order to join with the nations. They sold themselves to do evil.

1 Maccabees 1:20 Having thus defeated Egypt and set out on his return journey in the year 143, he marched against Israel and Jerusalem with a mighty army.
1 Maccabees 1:21 Having entered the sanctuary with arrogance, Antiochus removed the golden altar, the lampstand of light with all its accessories,
1 Maccabees 1:22 the table of showbread, the libation vessels, the cups, the golden censers, the veil, the crowns, and the golden decoration on the façade of the Temple, from which he stripped all the plating.
1 Maccabees 1:23 He took the silver and gold, as well as the precious vessels, and seized the hidden treasures he found.
1 Maccabees 1:24 Carrying everything off, he returned to his own country; he shed much blood and uttered words of extreme insolence.
1 Maccabees 1:25 There was great mourning throughout the land of Israel:
1 Maccabees 1:26 Leaders and elders lamented, young maidens and young men wasted away, and the beauty of the women faded.
1 Maccabees 1:27 The newlywed groom sang a dirge; seated in her chamber, the bride went into mourning.

1 Maccabees 1:29 Two years later, the king sent the Mysarch to the towns of Judah; he came to Jerusalem with a formidable army.
1 Maccabees 1:30 He made falsely conciliatory speeches to the inhabitants and won their trust; then he fell upon the city unawares, dealing it a terrible blow, and put many of the people of Israel to death.
1 Maccabees 1:31 He plundered the city, set it on fire, and destroyed its houses and its city wall.
1 Maccabees 1:32 His men took the women and children captive and seized the livestock.
1 Maccabees 1:33 Then they rebuilt the City of David with a great and very strong wall, fortified with mighty towers, and made it a citadel.
1 Maccabees 1:34 They settled there a band of sinners, a rabble, and fortified themselves there;
1 Maccabees 1:35 they stockpiled weapons and provisions there, deposited the spoils from Jerusalem which they had gathered, and it became a dreadful snare.
1 Maccabees 1:36 It was an ambush for the holy place, a constant and evil adversary to Israel.
1 Maccabees 1:37 They shed innocent blood around the sanctuary and defiled the holy place.
1 Maccabees 1:38 Because of them, the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled, and the city became a settlement of foreigners; it was alien to its own offspring, and its own children abandoned it.
1 Maccabees 1:39 Its desolate sanctuary became like a wilderness; its festivals turned to mourning, its Sabbaths to derision, and its honour to contempt.
1 Maccabees 1:40 Its humiliation was commensurate with its glory, and its greatness gave way to mourning.

⚖️(Zechariah 2:4) ‘These have come to terrify them, to cut down the horns of the nations that were raising their horns against the land of Judah in order to scatter it.’

Around 195 BC, Mattathias and his sons took action.

1 Maccabees 2:15 The king’s officials charged with enforcing apostasy came to the town of Modin for the sacrifices.

1 Maccabees 2:19 Mattathias replied in a loud voice: “Even if all the nations within the king’s empire were to obey him, each abandoning the worship of their forefathers and conforming to his decrees,
1 Maccabees 2:20 I, my sons and my brothers will follow the covenant of our forefathers.”
1 Maccabees 2:21 May God preserve us from abandoning the Law and its observances!
1 Maccabees 2:22 We will not heed the king’s commands. We will not deviate from our religion, neither to the right nor to the left.”
1 Maccabees 2:23 As soon as he had finished speaking, a Jew stepped forward, in full view of everyone, to offer a sacrifice on the altar at Modin, in accordance with the king’s decree.
1 Maccabees 2:24 At this sight, Mattathias’s zeal was kindled and his heart burned within him. Seized by righteous anger, he ran forward and cut his throat upon the altar.
1 Maccabees 2:25 As for the king’s officer who was forcing people to sacrifice, he killed him at the same time, then tore down the altar.

1 Maccabees 2:45 Mattathias and his companions went about destroying the altars
1 Maccabees 2:46 and forcibly circumcising all the uncircumcised children they found throughout the land of Israel.
1 Maccabees 2:47 They drove out the insolent, and their undertaking prospered in their hands.
1 Maccabees 2:48 They wrested the Law from the hands of the nations and kings and rendered the sinner powerless.

1 Maccabees 3:1 Judas, called Maccabeus, his son, rose up in his stead;
1 Maccabees 3:10 Apollonius gathered together pagans and a strong contingent from Samaria to wage war against Israel.
1 Maccabees 3:11 Judas learnt of this and went out to meet him; he defeated him and killed him. Many were struck down and killed, and the rest fled.

1 Maccabees 3:23 When he had finished speaking, he sprang upon them unawares. Seron and his army were routed.
1 Maccabees 3:24 They pursued them down the slope of Beth-horon to the plain. About 800 men were killed, and the rest fled to the land of the Philistines.

1 Maccabees 4:5 Gorgias, for his part, having arrived at Judas’s camp by night, found no one there and began to search for the Jews in the mountains, for, as he said: ‘They are fleeing before us.’
1 Maccabees 4:12 The foreigners looked up and, seeing the Jews marching against them,
1 Maccabees 4:13 they came out of the camp to do battle. Judas’s soldiers sounded the trumpet
1 Maccabees 4:14 and engaged the enemy. The nations were routed; they fled towards the plain,
1 Maccabees 4:15 but all the enemies who were in the rear fell by the sword. The pursuit reached Gazara and the plains of Idumea, Azotus and Jamnia: about 3,000 men perished there.

1 Maccabees 4:28 The following year, however, Lysias mustered 60,000 elite troops and 5,000 horsemen in order to defeat the Jews.
1 Maccabees 4:29 They came into Idumea and encamped at Beth-zur. Judas went out to meet them with 10,000 men.
1 Maccabees 4:34 A battle ensued, and as many as 5,000 men from Lysias’s army fell in hand-to-hand combat.

⚖️Zechariah 2:5 Then I looked up and saw a vision. Behold, there was a man, and in his hand was a measuring line.

Judas was so merged in God that he had great power in his hand

1 Maccabees 4:35 Seeing the rout of his army and the fearlessness of Judas’s soldiers, who were prepared to live or die courageously, Lysias set off for Antioch, where he recruited foreigners to return to Judea with more troops than before.
1 Maccabees 4:36 Then Judas and his brothers said: ‘Behold, our enemies have been crushed,

⚖️Zechariah 2:6 I said to him, ‘Where are you going?’ He said to me, ‘To measure Jerusalem, to see how wide and how long it is.’

let us go and purify the sanctuary and perform the rededication.’
1 Maccabees 4:37 The whole army gathered together and they went up to Mount Zion.
1 Maccabees 4:38 There they saw the holy place desolate, the altar desecrated, the gates burnt down, bushes growing in the courtyards as if in a wood or on a mountain, and the chambers destroyed.
1 Maccabees 4:39 They then tore their clothes, mourned deeply, and sprinkled ashes on their heads.
1 Maccabees 4:40 They then fell face down on the ground and, at the sound of the trumpets, cried out to Heaven.

⚖️Zechariah 2:7 And behold, the angel who was speaking to me stepped forward

Judas is called an angel in Zechariah’s vision

1 Maccabees 4:41 Judas ordered men to fight those in the Citadel until he had cleansed the sanctuary.
1 Maccabees 4:42 Then he chose priests who were blameless and zealous for the Law,
1 Maccabees 4:43 who purified the sanctuary and cast the defiled stones into an unclean place.

⚖️(Zechariah 2:7) and another angel came forward to meet him.

1 Maccabees 4:44 They deliberated on what to do with the altar of burnt-offerings, which had been desecrated,
1 Maccabees 4:45 and it occurred to them to tear it down, lest it should become a source of shame to them, since the pagans had defiled it. They demolished it
1 Maccabees 4:46 and laid the stones on the Mount of the Tabernacle in a suitable place, whilst awaiting the coming of a prophet who would give his ruling on the matter.

⚖️Zechariah 2:8 He said to him, ‘Run, speak to that young man.

1 Maccabees 4:47 They took uncut stones, in accordance with the Law, and built a new altar modelled on the previous one.
1 Maccabees 4:48 They repaired the sanctuary and the interior of the Tabernacle and consecrated the courtyards.
1 Maccabees 4:49 Having made new sacred vessels, they brought the candelabrum, the altar of incense and the table into the Temple.
1 Maccabees 4:50 They burnt incense on the altar and lit the lamps of the candelabrum, which shone within the Temple.
1 Maccabees 4:51 They placed the loaves on the table, hung up the curtains and completed everything they had set out to do.

⚖️(Zechariah 2:8) and say to him: ‘Jerusalem must remain open, because of the great number of people and livestock within it.’

In 191 ± BC, the Jewish festival of the Dedication, Hanukkah, was celebrated for the first time in the Temple, which had been restored to Jewish worship alone.

1 Maccabees 4:52 On the 25th day of the ninth month—called Kislev—in the year 148, they rose at daybreak
1 Maccabees 4:53 and offered a lawful sacrifice on the new altar of burnt offerings which they had built.
1 Maccabees 4:54 The altar was consecrated to the sound of hymns, zithers, lyres and cymbals, at the same time and on the same day that the pagans had desecrated it.
1 Maccabees 4:55 The whole people prostrated themselves in worship, then raised their praise to Heaven, which had led them to victory.
1 Maccabees 4:56 For eight days they celebrated the rededication of the altar, offering burnt offerings with joy, together with the sacrifice of communion and thanksgiving.
1 Maccabees 4:57 They adorned the façade of the Temple with golden wreaths and shields, refurbished the entrances and the chambers, and fitted them with doors.

⚖️Zechariah 2:9 As for me, I will be for her – declares the Lord – a wall of fire all round,

1 Maccabees 4:60 At that time they built high walls and strong towers all round Mount Zion, lest the nations should come and trample these places as they had done before.
1 Maccabees 4:61 Judas stationed a garrison there to guard it. He fortified Beth-zur so that the people might have a stronghold facing Idumea.

1 Maccabees 5:4 He also remembered the wickedness of the sons of Baian, who were a snare and a trap to the people through the ambushes they laid for them on the roads.
1 Maccabees 5:5 Having trapped them in their towers, he laid siege to them and pronounced them accursed; he set fire to the towers and burnt them down with all those inside.

1 Maccabees 5:28 Suddenly, Judas led his army along the road to Bosora through the desert. He captured the town and, after putting all the males to the sword and gathering all the spoils, he set it ablaze.

1 Maccabees 5:35 He then turned against Alema, attacked it, captured it, and, after killing all the males and gathering the spoils, he set it ablaze.

1 Maccabees 5:65 Judas and his brothers went to war against the sons of Esau in the southern region; he took Hebron and the surrounding villages by force, demolished its fortifications and set fire to the towers of its walls.

1 Maccabees 5:68 Judas then marched on Azotus, a district of the Philistines; by God’s power, he overthrew their altars, set fire to the carved images of their gods, subjected the towns there to thorough plunder, and returned to the land of Judah.

⚖️(Zechariah 2:9) ‘and I will be his Glory.’

Yahweh was the Glory of Eleazar, surnamed Auârân, and of Judas Maccabee

1 Maccabees 6:18 The people of the Citadel were besieging Israel around the sanctuary and were doing their utmost to harm them at every opportunity, and to support the pagans.
1 Maccabees 6:19 Determined to wipe them out, Judas summoned all the people to lay siege to them.
1 Maccabees 6:20 They gathered together and laid siege to the Citadel in the year 150; they built batteries and siege engines.
1 Maccabees 6:21 But some of those under siege broke through the blockade, and with them were some godless Israelites,
1 Maccabees 6:22 who went to the king and said to him, ‘How long will you delay in bringing us justice and avenging our brothers?’

1 Maccabees 6:28 At these words, the king flew into a rage and summoned all his friends, the commanders of his army and his field marshals.
1 Maccabees 6:29 Mercenary troops also came to him from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.
1 Maccabees 6:30 The total strength of his forces amounted to 100,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry and 32 elephants trained for battle.
1 Maccabees 6:31 They came through Idumea and laid siege to Beth-zur, which they besieged for a long time using siege engines. But the defenders, launching sorties, set the city ablaze and fought valiantly.
1 Maccabees 6:32 Then Judas set out from the Citadel and went to camp at Beth-Zachariah, opposite the royal camp.
1 Maccabees 6:33 The king, rising early in the morning, led his troops in a swift advance along the road to Beth-Zachariah, where the armies took up their battle positions and sounded the trumpets.
1 Maccabees 6:34 Grape and blackberry juice was laid out in full view of the elephants to rouse them to the attack.
1 Maccabees 6:35 The beasts were distributed amongst the phalanxes. Beside each elephant were stationed a thousand men clad in chain mail and wearing bronze helmets, not to mention 500 elite horsemen assigned to each beast.
1 Maccabees 6:36 These horsemen anticipated every movement of the beast and accompanied it everywhere without ever straying from its side.
1 Maccabees 6:37 On each elephant, as a defensive structure, a sturdy wooden tower was secured with straps, and in each were the three warriors fighting from the animals, in addition to their mahout.
1 Maccabees 6:38 As for the rest of the cavalry, the king deployed them on both flanks of the army to harass the enemy and cover the phalanxes.
1 Maccabees 6:39 When the sun’s rays struck the golden and bronze shields, the mountains were illuminated and shone like burning torches.
1 Maccabees 6:40 Part of the royal army took up position on the mountain heights and another part below; they advanced in a solid and orderly formation.
1 Maccabees 6:41 All were dismayed at the clamour of this multitude, the sound of their marching and the clang of their weapons—a vast and mighty army indeed.
1 Maccabees 6:42 Judas and his men advanced to engage the enemy, and 600 men from the king’s army were slain.

text:
US Military Uses Xbox-Style Controllers to Operate Laser Weapons in Strait of Hormuz | Wonderful Engineering

The U.S. military is moving high-energy laser weapons closer to routine battlefield use, deploying directed-energy systems to counter drones and other aerial threats in the Strait of Hormuz. The development highlights a shift in modern air defense, where laser technology could offer a more cost-effective way to tackle inexpensive drones.

Some operators reportedly use modified Xbox-style controllers to aim and operate the systems, offering a familiar interface for precise targeting and rapid adjustments. The approach reflects an effort to make sophisticated weapons easier to operate, rather than requiring personnel to learn entirely new control layouts.

Unlike conventional missiles, high-energy laser weapons use concentrated beams of light to damage or disable targets. Sensors first detect and track an incoming threat before the system directs its beam toward a specific point. The laser must remain focused on that location for a period known as dwell time, allowing heat to accumulate and damage critical components.

Depending on the target and the weapon’s capabilities, the concentrated energy can disrupt sensors, damage electronics, or weaken structural components. This makes lasers particularly attractive for counter-drone operations, where disabling a relatively small aircraft may be sufficient to neutralize the threat without launching an expensive missile.

The technology has become more practical as electrical power systems, target-tracking sensors, beam control, and compact laser hardware have improved. The U.S. Army has also committed nearly $500 million to bring a new generation of high-energy laser weapons into production, signaling a move beyond laboratory experiments toward operational systems.

Jared Keller, author of the Laser Wars newsletter, described the technology as weaponized light that remains focused on a target for several seconds to destroy it. He also highlighted the Army’s major contract as a significant step toward fielding combat-ready laser weapons.

However, lasers are not expected to replace conventional weapons entirely. Their effectiveness depends on factors such as available power, atmospheric conditions, target characteristics, and the time required to maintain the beam on a target. Missiles, guns, electronic warfare, and directed-energy systems are therefore likely to operate alongside one another.

The growing use of laser weapons could ultimately change the economics of air defense, particularly when militaries face large numbers of low-cost drones.

text:
West wasn’t  short of ideas. They were short of a method that produced a state.

By the 1950s American Protestantism still had doctrine, guilt, and Sunday, but the mystical strand — the part that claimed you could know God directly — had been trimmed back for centuries. What was left felt moral and institutional. Psychology, the other place inner life might have gone, had mostly become behavior or illness. And the postwar bargain was material: house, car, job, and a low-grade emptiness that the suburbs couldn’t name. Vietnam and the bomb made the emptiness sharper. A culture very good at making things had almost no language for what a person was for.

India arrived, in translation, as the missing technology. Meditation and yoga were practices, not beliefs. A guru was someone who seemed to have done the practice and come out the other side. The Gita and the Upanishads offered a cosmology — reincarnation, non-duality, action without clinging to fruits — that didn’t require joining a church. Huxley had already packaged this as the “perennial philosophy,” one truth under every religion, which let a secular Westerner take the method and leave the temple.
The psychedelic years intensified it. LSD gave a temporary version of what the books described. When the trip wore off, people wanted the permanent version, and the books said India had it. That is why Alpert went, and why Jobs, a decade later, followed Be Here Now to a dead guru’s ashram. They were not looking for a better theology. They were looking for a way to sit still until something quieter than analysis showed up.

What they often skipped was the rest of the culture: caste, ritual obligation, the guru’s authority, the fact that village life was not a meditation retreat. 

They imported the technique and the aphorism, and left the social world that had produced them. Krishnamurti, raised inside that import business, spent his life saying the technique still wasn’t enough.

text:
When the 66 books are read with attention to typology, they form a single coherent picture. Clusters of connections appear across law, history, poetry, prophecy, and letters. The same themes recur: the Passover lamb, the suffering servant, the temple, exile and return, shadow and fulfillment. These threads run through roughly forty authors over fifteen centuries and still land on the same arc.

The Limits of Academic Explanations
Historical and academic attempts to account for this coherence are highly complex. They demand extensive specialized knowledge and years of study. Even when carefully presented, these accounts often remain unconvincing to skeptics, who can point to unresolved uncertainties, competing theories, or the influence of human institutions.

Tracing every stage, every regional variation, and every remaining scholarly debate requires prolonged technical study and still leaves room for disagreement. The simpler tests that follow do not replace scholarship; they offer a direct way to examine the observed coherence without first requiring mastery of that apparatus.

The Puzzle Test
Picture a puzzle set on a table with no image as a reference, but whose 66 or so pieces have one consistent style, one set of colors, one narrative direction. A piece showing a spaceship with aliens does not belong. It is set aside not by decree but because it fails to fit. In the same way, certain writings produce no matching pattern. They remain outside the picture.

Signal Versus Noise
The better test is signal vs noise. The 66 books generate a clear, repeated signal. Other ancient texts produce disconnected material that does not advance or complete the pattern. The claim is not that nothing else was ever written. The claim is that only these books carry the signal with this degree of consistency.

Survivorship and Selection
Survivorship bias is often raised as an explanation: the coherent texts were simply the ones people kept copying. That accounts for elegance but not for the rest of the evidence. These books do not flatter the communities that preserved them. They repeatedly condemn Israel’s kings, priests, and people. They expose human nature rather than accommodate it. In addition, the depth of the connections remains largely unseen by most readers even though the letter to the Hebrews already makes the structure explicit.

Self-Critique and Depth
Ordinary cultural filtering tends to retain what is useful, flattering, or easy. A collection that is self-critical, complex, and still not exhausted is harder to explain by simple survival or selection. The text keeps accusing its own keepers and still yields layers that most readers have not fully traced.

The Bible Interprets Itself
The same coherence points to another feature: the Bible interprets Itself. Typological links, cross-references, and fulfillments are already present in the text. One passage illuminates another without requiring an external system of doctrine, tradition, or study notes to supply the meaning. The books function as a self-contained library. Aids may be helpful for language or history, but they are not required for the internal logic to become visible. The signal is already there.

Conclusion
Taken together, the interlocking typology, the consistent signal across centuries, the refusal to flatter its own keepers, and the self-interpreting character of the collection form a pattern that ordinary human filtering does not easily account for.

When the text is allowed to interpret itself, prophetic passages reveal their meaning and fulfillment within the Bible’s own framework and timeline. When contemporary events and modern technology are forced into the text instead, the result is anachronism: prophecies are made to speak of attack helicopters, implantable chips, nuclear conflict, and other present-day images that the original writers never addressed.

text:
Interesting model here per the 8-K and $AEP release

>WULF agrees to pay estimated financing costs associated with construction of Kentucky Power's ($AEP) planned 760MWs combined cycle generation facility at Big Sandy.
>WULF offers to provide $100M in winter bill credits for Kentucky Power's residential customers over the first 10 years off the contract (estimates this will equate to ~$25 per month during winter heating season per customer, with credits beginning in 2029)
>Agreement includes collateral requirements from WULF (announced upsizing the senior secured revolver this morning, from current $250M)
>Kentucky Power will seek regulatory approvals later this year

"Paying the interest costs on 760MW of new gas generation". Here's how it likely works:

Kentucky Power is a regulated utility. It earns a regulator-approved return on plants once they're running, charged to customers through rates. While a plant is being built, the utility is borrowing and spending but collecting nothing. Normally it books those financing costs as AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction), adds them to the plant's price tag, and customers pay them later.

WULF appears to be covering that cost instead. The exact mechanics aren't disclosed yet: interest only or the utility's full return, paid as incurred or as a lump sum. Our guess, could be $100-300M over the build, depending on structure. AEP gets paid sooner, the plant goes into rates cheaper, and existing customers don't fund a plant built for a data center. Looks to be in line thematically with what the White House has demanded.

This is not behind-the-meter because WULF won't own the plant. It will pay tariff rates like any other customer, plus this carry. Expect it to pass through to the tenant in the lease. The Public Service Commission filing later this year will likely reveal more details.

Bets considered by Joe Duffy:

🔥 MONDAY, OCTOBER 5 — FREE PLAYS 🔥

🏈 NFL

FREE PLAY — ATLANTA +1.5 over NEW ORLEANS — 8:15 ET

Atlanta has the strongest system profile in this matchup. The primary angle says to fade early-season favorites coming off poor previous seasons. That system is 368-269 ATS, 57.8%, for +72.1 units. New Orleans qualifies as the favorite, putting the Falcons on the system side.

There is additional system corroboration based on yards-per-point differential. Teams with a substantially worse yards-per-point margin are 174-116 ATS, 60.0%, +46.4 units with a 14.6% ROI. The road-specific version is 83-45 ATS, 64.8%, +33.5 units with a 23.8% ROI. Neither secondary angle carries enough units to drive the wager independently, but both reinforce the much larger +72.1-unit system.

The personnel matchup provides the strongest fundamental reason to back Atlanta. New Orleans is without linebacker Kaden Elliss and defensive ends Carl Granderson and Anfernee Jennings, while linebacker Pete Werner is questionable. Those losses are concentrated in the front seven against the strength of Atlanta's offense.

Bijan Robinson gives the Falcons a direct way to exploit it. Atlanta has been one of the league's most productive rushing teams, and its outside-zone concepts are particularly well suited to attacking New Orleans. The Saints have struggled badly defending those concepts, creating an opportunity for Atlanta to control the game through Robinson rather than requiring Michael Penix Jr. to carry the offense.

The matchup also gives Penix opportunities when Atlanta throws. New Orleans uses Cover 3 extensively, a coverage against which Penix has produced strong efficiency. The absence of Granderson and Jennings also compromises the Saints' ability to create pressure without committing additional defenders.

Drake London becomes particularly important. His target share with Penix has been substantial, and a successful Robinson-led ground game can force New Orleans to devote additional resources to the box, creating favorable opportunities for London on the perimeter.

New Orleans faces a much more difficult rushing matchup. Atlanta enters allowing only 47.7 rushing yards per game, the best mark in the NFL. The Saints are also without Travis Etienne Jr., removing their leading early-season runner. Alvin Kamara is available, but New Orleans may have difficulty establishing enough conventional rushing success to keep Tyler Shough out of obvious passing situations.

The public information is the primary concern. Atlanta is an underdog receiving the majority of spread tickets. Our worldwide contrarian indexes therefore point toward New Orleans, and a public underdog carries substantially more contrarian significance than an equivalently supported favorite.

The market also opened around Atlanta +2.5 and is now approximately +1.5. We generally prefer fading that type of movement rather than following it. A respected sharp also has a significant position on New Orleans -1.5.

Those are meaningful negatives. However, the +72.1-unit league-wide system, two additional profitable systems and Atlanta's substantial rushing matchup advantage provide enough independent support for a free play.

There is no outdoor weather concern because the game is inside the Superdome.

🎯 Play to: ATLANTA +1.5. Pass at pick'em.

⚾ MLB

FREE PLAY — UNDER 6.5 CHI WHITE SOX/CLEVELAND — 5:00 ET

The pitching matchup and one active historical system point toward a low-scoring game.

One of our systems applies when both teams enter off particularly low-scoring games. The historical results favor the UNDER. Chicago is coming off a 3-0 victory, creating the appropriate low-scoring setup for today's matchup.

Gavin Williams provides the strongest organic support. His home report card is excellent. Williams has a 2.84 ERA and 1.04 WHIP in Cleveland, with 150 strikeouts in 107.2 home innings.

His recent home work has also been strong. Across recent home starts against Oakland, Chicago and Detroit, Williams surrendered only four earned runs over 18 innings while striking out 27.

Anthony Kay isn't nearly as strong, particularly on the road, which is why the extremely low 6.5 keeps this strictly in the free-play category.

The system support and Williams' home profile make the UNDER the preferred free total.

🎯 Play to: UNDER 6.5.

⚾ MLB

FREE PLAY — CHI WHITE SOX +136 over CLEVELAND — 5:00 ET

Chicago offers the better value on the early moneyline.

The Luck Gap receives no consideration. Chicago is +7.53 and Cleveland +4.07, a difference of only 3.46 games. This late in a 162-game season, a gap below six is irrelevant and is excluded entirely from the handicap.

The meaningful support comes from postseason systems and price.

One of our postseason systems backs teams coming off a victory after the opening game of a playoff series. Chicago qualifies after taking Game 1, 3-0.

Chicago also enters in excellent form, having won eight of its last 10. The White Sox have already demonstrated that they can compete successfully in this pitching matchup and shut Cleveland out in the series opener.

The principal concern is Williams. His 2.84 home ERA and strong strikeout profile give Cleveland a significant starting-pitcher advantage over Kay.

That pitching advantage is incorporated into a substantial favorite price, however. With Chicago getting approximately +136 and owning the more favorable postseason-system profile, the White Sox are attractive enough for a free play.

🎯 Play to: CHI WHITE SOX +125.

🏒 NHL

FREE PLAY — PITTSBURGH PENGUINS MONEYLINE -178 over WINNIPEG JETS — 7:30 ET

Pittsburgh gets a solid combination of system and situational support Monday night.

Our NHL database shows that since 2023, home teams with a rest advantage are 684-463 on the moneyline, winning 59.6% of their games for a +4.1% ROI. The sample of 1,147 games makes this considerably more meaningful than a small high-percentage trend, although the modest ROI makes it supporting evidence rather than a standalone reason to bet Pittsburgh.

The scheduling advantage is particularly relevant here. Winnipeg is playing the second half of a road back-to-back after Sunday's 3-2 win at Detroit, while Pittsburgh was idle Sunday after beating Montreal 6-5 in overtime Saturday.

Goaltending strengthens the Pittsburgh case. Stuart Skinner stopped 33 of 35 shots Sunday for Winnipeg, and Clay Stevenson is confirmed to make Monday's start. Stevenson has very limited NHL experience, while Winnipeg remains without Connor Hellebuyck. Pittsburgh should therefore get an opportunity to attack the Jets' goaltending depth at home.

The Penguins have also opened the season with considerable offensive production, scoring 13 goals in their first two games. Evgeni Malkin has scored in both, while Pittsburgh's defensemen have been contributing offensively as well. The Penguins' power play has already produced four goals through two games.

Pittsburgh also has an exceptional historical home profile against Winnipeg, winning 21 of the last 24 meetings in Pittsburgh. We don't give head-to-head history nearly the weight of the current personnel and scheduling situation, but it points in the same direction.

There are reasons not to overrate Pittsburgh's 2-0 start. The Penguins blew a four-goal advantage against Montreal before escaping 6-5 in overtime, and the current sample is far too small for our NHL Luck Gap methodology to carry meaningful weight. Pittsburgh is also missing some personnel, including Bryan Rust and Ryan Graves.

Still, Winnipeg's back-to-back, its downgrade from Skinner to Stevenson in goal, Pittsburgh's rest advantage and the large-sample NHL system all align.

🎯 Play to: PITTSBURGH PENGUINS MONEYLINE -185.

text:
An Oregon State freshman has nine touchdown catches in five games.

The last two players to start a major college career like that were Randy Moss and Michael Crabtree.

He had exactly one scholarship offer.

His name is Jesse Legree and he plays for the Oregon State Beavers.

Tonight against the Colorado State Rams he caught five passes for over 150 yards and three touchdowns. They went for 50 yards, 38 yards and 52 yards. He sat most of the second half because the game was over.

Oregon State won 56 to 26.

Here is the stat that got everybody's attention.

The last three players with nine or more touchdown catches through their first five games at college football's top level are Jesse Legree in 2026, Michael Crabtree at Texas Tech in 2007, and Randy Moss at Marshall in 1997.

That is the whole list.

Crabtree caught 22 touchdowns that year, became the first freshman ever to win the Biletnikoff Award as the best receiver in the country, and went tenth overall in the NFL draft.

Moss caught 26 that year for the Marshall Thundering Herd, finished fourth in the Heisman voting, and is in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Now understand who the third name is.

Legree is listed at 5-foot-10 and 172 pounds. He went to St. Frances Academy in Baltimore. He spent most of high school at defensive back and did not move to receiver until his senior year.

Not one school in America offered him a scholarship to play receiver. Oregon State offered him anyway, and nobody else offered him anything.

A program on the other side of the country, in a town he had never heard of.

He enrolled early, in January, and went to work.

Five games in, he is second in the country in receiving yards, tied for first in the country in touchdown catches, and averaging 26.6 yards every time he catches the ball.

He has gone over 100 yards in all five games. That ties the Oregon State record, shared by Mike Hass and Brandin Cooks.

He has won Pac-12 Freshman of the Week four straight times. Nobody in the history of the conference has ever done that.

His quarterback Braden Atkinson on what it is like to throw to him:

"You give him the ball and he'll make three, four, five people miss. All I have to do is give him a five-yard pass and he gives me 75 yards in the stats."

Here is the part nobody will put on a graphic. He wants to be a therapist when football is finished.

Be honest about where this actually sits. It is five games. Colorado State and UTEP are not Ohio State. November has not happened yet.

But a couple of weeks ago his head coach JaMarcus Shephard won the first game of his life as a head coach, and he said this:

"Everybody needs to start paying attention. Because there's something going on here in Corvallis."

Nine touchdowns in five games.

Randy Moss. Michael Crabtree. And the kid nobody wanted at receiver.

 Menelaus marries Helen and Tyndareus cedes the Spartan kingdom to him. So Menelaus's marriage and his possession of the Spartan kingship are narratively linked. Modern work on Homeric/mythic succession has noticed exactly the same pattern: royal marriage can function as a mechanism by which sovereignty is acquired.  And that's absolutely what's at stake here.

Then Agamemnon practically hands us the decoder ring in Iliad 9. When he's trying to buy Achilles back into the coalition, he doesn't merely offer him one of his daughters.

He offers:
daughter + marriage + seven cities + their productive territory + the obedience of their inhabitants.

Homer has Agamemnon say that the people there will honor Achilles and obey his themistes, his ordinances/judgments.  Scholarship specifically points to this scene as evidence that marriage could accompany the transfer of territorial authority.

And Homer does indeed treat Helen at Troy as Paris's wife: Priam is presented to her as the father of her husband, the duel is supposed to determine who possesses Helen and her property, and after Aphrodite retrieves Paris, Homer describes Helen going to him and the two lying together as husband and wife.

That makes the strategic interpretation considerably nastier for the Atreids.

Troy already sits on the northern Aegean/Hellespontine gateway and is plugged into Dardanians, Thracians, Phrygians and the Anatolian network.

Now a Trojan prince forms a marital relationship with the Spartan royal woman at the southern end of the Greek maritime system.

text:
A South Texas rancher lost his son in a street fight in 1884, and his revenge was to pay a railroad to go around the town. 

Helena was the seat of Karnes County, sitting on the old Chihuahua Road, and it had a reputation. 
The local specialty was a knife fight with the two men's left wrists tied together, which tells you most of what you need to know about the place. 

In 1884, Emmett Butler, son of the cattleman William Butler, was shot and killed there. Nobody was ever convicted.

Butler was one of the largest landowners in the county, and when the San Antonio and Aransas Pass Railway came surveying, he made an offer: free right of way across his land, on the condition that the tracks miss Helena entirely.

The railroad took the deal. A new town called Karnes City grew up at the depot, and in 1894 it took the county seat.

Helena emptied out within a generation. 
The stores closed, the families left, and the square went back to grass and prickly pear. • 

The 1873 courthouse is still standing though, restored and open as a museum, which makes Helena one of the few ghost towns in Texas where you can walk up the courthouse steps and go inside.
