Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use
Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.
With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.
And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.
Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.
This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.
So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.
Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.
Because it does.

text:
Pours coffee, cracks knuckles, takes a deep breath ...

After a weekend with lab folks at the Curve & nearly 2 decades at the intersection of tech & Congress, allow me to explain:

*1. Not a vending machine*
 @timoreilly used to describe the problem as people treating gov like a vending machine: put in money, get out results. It doesn't work that way.

Tech is especially vulnerable to this vision. We're on at least the third generation of tech folks ignoring the groundwork required to build relationships and then showing up with a policy ask and a "where do I write the check?" vibe to their advocacy. Ask Bill Gates. Ask Mark Zuckerberg. Today they look like elder statesmen compared to their initial brushes with DC.

It's understandable why the current exec branch-heavy political dynamic & transactional nature of this particular exec branch reinforces the vending machine theory, but that doesn't hold when it's time to engage the states or Congress.

*2. It's the constituents, stupid*
I was the Health Legislative Assistant for the Chair of the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means during the health reform effort from 2007-2010. That meant a LOT of meetings with people from every interest group, insurance company, consumer group, provider group, etc., you can imagine.. but one thing each of those (most very well paid) lobbyists knew was not to show up to Pete Stark's office without a constituent from CA-13. It was a rule in the office: no constituent, no meeting. I distinctly remember my embarrassment in the early days before I had full comprehended the rule when Pete interrupted my meeting with the Texas Hospital Association to ask who among them was a constituent, and then *literally* kicked them out when they said no one. (I never made that mistake again).

This weekend at the Curve, one state staffer explained that their legislative session runs from Jan to April and lately the AI folks have been showing up, but only in April. They come in at the last minute with an ask. No relationships. No understanding of the political context. No field building in districts.  No offers to help on other issues. Just an ask. 

It's a similar story in Congress where the newly politically engaged have mostly engaged the White House, had sporadic high level engagement on the Hill, but almost nothing in the districts and states. While it's true that committee chairs and leadership decides what comes to the Floor, counting votes requires a lot more than that. And it's tough to win the vote of a Member if they are going to have to go back home and get tough questions that they don't have the answer to. 

And that's really the point. They should not be the ones taking those questions, the ones advocating for the policy should be. Getting to the Member to ask for their vote should be the *end* of a long process that starts in the states and districts, not the beginning. You don't start with the Member and ask for them to go home and do the hard work of selling your policy to their constituents, especially on issues that are going to affect absolutely every American. It may sound cliche and old school and idealistic but THANK GOD this is still how it works in America: YOU HAVE TO START WITH THE PEOPLE.

*3. Spend your money ON THE GROUND*
Back to my Pete Stark story...
You know who could really get his ear and make a case that he would listen to? The local small business person in Newark. The healthcare worker in a hospital in Berkeley. The line worker in Fremont. And yes, the big healthcare network that served a majority of his constituents or the car manufacturers that employed many of them.

This is a little bit of an old school story, and yes tons has changed in Washington, but it is still true that if you want to convince a Member of Congress, the best way is to convince their constituents.

And as far as I can tell, the AI companies have not put any of their efforts towards this work. I got excited when I say @AnthropicAI open a pop-up storefront in NY a while back, passing out "thinking caps" ... but alas that was just a short-term urban hipster outreach project, not something meant for mainstream. Yet, 10,000 storefronts on Main Streets across the country could do so much more for both the perception of the company, the issues AND for the substantive do-gooding that these companies assert their technology will bring. As one other state staffer said over the weekend, "help plumbers use AI!".

Truly, if every plumber in America (and around the world for that matter) was seeing value to their businesses and their families from access to AI and genuine, respectful outreach from the companies meeting them where they are and truly ASKING what they need, then they and their neighbors would be engaging with their lawmakers in a much more empowered, informed way. That doesn't mean they automatically embrace whatever the companies' position is, but potentially does mean that they do not have the visceral immune system response of rejecting cloistered Silicon Valley big brains that seek to control the universe with very little acknowledgement or understanding of their lives, their communities and YES of their political power. 

---

SO yes, @sama right now what you and a wide cadre of very smart people building very important tech are doing in Washington and state capitals across the country (and in countries around the world) is not working. And that's because the current approach is not sufficiently acknowledging that in a democracy, every lawmaker has a temporary assignment. They were sent to do a job by their constituents and they report to them. While campaign contributions can buy lots of face time and influence, it doesn't help if the folks you buy time with are involuntarily retired in November. Lawmakers understand that. 

If the AI world is ready for a reset, I would strongly suggest some serious grassroots outreach. Open some storefronts (a "Charleston AI" on every court square!). Sponsor some Little League. Donate insane amounts of tokens to libraries across the country and make sure they have good Internet and modern computers to run them. HIRE LOCAL PEOPLE to run workshops. Train teachers. Help to modernize local governments. Lay the ground work. Build relationships. And listen.

What is the ceiling of this OSU football team? Well, it may be cliché, but clichés get used as much as they do because they're true and accurate. So, let's use a cliché and say they are 100% capable of going 1-0 every week.

That's a very difficult thing to do when navigating a long season full of ebbs and flows, so you have to simplify it into those terms. To use another cliché, how do you eat an elephant? One bite at a time. Same concept! Then, if you don't go 1-0 on a particular week, you regroup, identify your failures, correct them, and move on to the next opponent and the next opportunity to go 1-0.

Having said all of that, one of the aspects that made Coach Morris such a slam dunk as the right choice for OSU is that he has built a very impressive network of relationships with the high school coaches in Texas. And now his sales pitch isn't as an underdog, trying to find players on the margins. He can walk in with much more firepower than he's ever had.

And he understands timing. We've definitely seen that in his play-calling, and we saw it last week with all the recruiting he did. He knows this program has momentum, he knows it needs to catch up some in recruiting, so he used that momentum to offer as many impactful players as he could.

Independent developers have successfully launched Grand Theft Auto IV on a jailbroken PlayStation 5 console using a custom Xbox 360 software emulator. This technical milestone was achieved by porting PowerPC instruction translation tools directly to the current hardware environment, allowing the original software build to execute locally without relying on any external cloud streaming platforms.

Initial performance tests confirm functional open-world gameplay across Liberty City, including proper simulation of the Euphoria physics engine and main mission scripts. The frame rate still fluctuates during heavy traffic scenes, and minor shader rendering bugs remain visible, yet the software maintains basic system stability without fatal crashes.

Sony still does not offer native backwards compatibility for this classic title on modern systems.

text:
We probably cannot be truly free and dependent. Our modern lives are all about dependence on others for our shelter, transportation, food supply, fuel, electricity, communications, medicines and health care.  We like the things the modern world offers, but there's a hook hidden in those tasty morsels. We cannot individually provide ourselves these luxuries and we are unwilling to give them up, so we bargain away freedom in exchange. As someone fairly wise with his words often says, things can be fine until the assholes show up. There are always enough assholes on both sides of those compromises to spoil it for everyone. 
There are two priorities for AI to solve early on; How do you share the wealth of a society with the people who make up that society when their contributions to wealth generation are no longer needed? And how can societies enjoy the fruits of liberty in the post scarcity world without the assholes ruining everything for everyone?

Literary Titan Says Rebellion to Tyrants “connects technological governance to moral responsibility and civic trust.”

Literary Titan, a professional service organization of editors, writers, and professors, issued a 5-star review of Rebellion to Tyrants Is Obedience to God: Ending the Danger of the Corporate AI Surveillance Machine, by Laurie Thomas Vass. (Gabby Press, September 2026).

Vass explains that the danger to citizen liberty of corporate AI is both in the unregulated, uncontrolled deployment of the technology, itself, plus the danger of the technology fusing power with corrupt agents of government.

“The technology itself is amoral” said Vass, “because the technology cannot choose between good and evil. If the rogue technology escapes human control, and falls into the hands of immoral agents, then the technology becomes a totalitarian tyranny over human liberty, much like the police surveillance system in China.”
Vass explains how metro economic regions must continually create economic growth in order to outrun the dangers of corporate AI.
She argues that metro regions must begin thinking of themselves as a technology innovation growth business, whose business mission is high rates of capital investment in new technology ventures that stimulate economic growth.
Literary Titan asked Vass why she connects AI governance to questions of individual liberty and self-government.
Vass replied, “I trace the 3000 year Western Civilization ethical framework of individual trust and fair dealing among citizens to the principles of liberty and self-government of George Mason and Thomas Jefferson.”
“The Western Civilization ethical basis of self-government, in a representative republic, is to treat other citizens as you would wish to be treated,” she added
“Over the long term, in our new regional economic development model, we expect to see greater rates of capital investment in new small technology ventures that have the potential to grow into large corporations,” said Vass.

“The technology company model we have in mind is SAS Institute, in Cary, N. C.,” she added, “which started out as 4 N. C. State students and staff, who created, what is now, the largest private corporation in the world.”

text:
Eugene Fodor dies at 60; violin virtuoso (LA Times, March 5, 201)

Eugene Fodor, a swashbuckling violin virtuoso who was a media darling of classical music in the 1970s but whose substance abuse fractured a fairytale career, has died. He was 60.

Fodor died of liver disease Feb. 26 at his home in Arlington, Va., said his wife, Susan Davis. He had struggled with addictions to alcohol, cocaine and heroin, she said.

At 24, Fodor became the first American to win top honors on violin at the International Tchaikovsky Competition in 1974. He shared the silver medal with two Russians; no gold was given that year.

Upon returning home, the Colorado native was greeted at the Denver airport by his parents, girlfriend — and horse.

The media dubbed him “the Cowboy violinist” and in two years’ time Fodor appeared on the Johnny Carson show almost a dozen times.

He was an “irresistible combination of Western dude and musical prodigy,” according to a 1989 New York magazine profile.

Such pop-culture celebrity put the dashing Fodor at odds with the classical music world, “almost crowding out his exploits as a violinist,” Martin Bernheimer, then a Times music critic, wrote in 1975.

Fodor’s technique dazzled. He often played showy pieces by Italian composer Niccolo Paganini, moving audiences to interrupt his performance of Paganini’s First Concerto to give him a standing ovation.

Fittingly, Fodor first came to prominence after winning Italy’s Paganini international violin competition in 1972.

Critics were skeptical of a serious musician who went shirtless in publicity photos and accused him of being interested only in pieces that showcased his pyrotechnics.

“We didn’t take him seriously,” the late Daniel Cariaga, then a music critic for The Times, told CBS News in 1996. “That can be almost fatal because if the critics don’t take you seriously, then eventually the audience doesn’t.... You can’t come back from that.”

When Fodor was arrested in 1989, the story made the front page of the New York Times, giving him the “most attention he’d had in close to a decade,” New York magazine reported that same year.

At a motel on Martha’s Vineyard, Mass., Fodor was arrested on charges that included breaking and entering, and possession of heroin and cocaine. The judge refused to accept the musician’s offer of his 300-year-old violin to guarantee bail.

A week later, Fodor entered a rehabilitation clinic and eventually was sentenced to probation.

His cocaine use “was sort of a crutch” to relieve the pain of not having the career that “would make me happy,” he told CBS News in 1996.

The fallout permanently damaged his career, although he continued to tour for decades, often playing pieces that critics considered “fiendishly difficult.”

Eugene Nicholas Fodor Jr. was born into a musical family on March 5, 1950, in Denver. His great-great-grandfather founded a music conservatory in Hungary.

Growing up on an 80-acre ranch near Denver, Fodor “begged for the violin” when he saw his older brother playing, his mother, Antoinette Fodor, told The Times in 1989.

At age 10, Eugene made his solo debut with the Denver Symphony and, after winning a nationwide contest sponsored by the Kiwanis clubs, he began touring at 12.

Early success came at a price, Fodor later said.

His father, also named Eugene, played violin as a hobby and worked in construction. He was ambitious for his son and overly strict at home, which caused the younger Eugene to act out in school and turn to drugs, Fodor said in the New York magazine article.

In the late 1960s, Fodor studied with two influential violin teachers — Ivan Galamian at Juilliard and Josef Gingold at Indiana University.

At USC, Fodor had the great violinist Jascha Heifetz as a teacher for a year beginning in 1970. When Heifetz insisted that students keep their hair short, Fodor tucked his long locks inside a wig. After being spotted giving a concert without the wig, Heifetz kicked Fodor out of class.

His seven-year first marriage, to Davis, ended in 1985. A second marriage also ended in divorce. He remarried Davis last fall.

In addition to his wife, Fodor is survived by their three children, Daniella Davis of Newport Beach, Lindsay Davis of Manhattan Beach, and Dylan Davis of Washington, D.C.; a brother, John of Denver; a sister, Deborah of Virginia; and two grandsons.

His Guarneri violin, made in 1736, is for sale in Europe.

Valerie J. Nelson, “Violin Virtuoso Battled Addictions,” Los Angeles Times, March 5, 2011, AA6.

text:
Bad news for Volkswagen could be good news for your driveway. I have a friend that loves his ID.4 and I am not trying to sound like a car salesman, but 👇👇👇

The October offers caught my eye: $12,500 in customer cash on leftover 2025 ID.4s, plus roughly $1,100 toward charging. The 2026s have $10,000 off. Depending on the version, you’re looking at up to about 291 miles of range in a roomy, five-seat crossover.

That’s enough to get my attention. But before heading to the dealer, I’d want a few things nailed down:

• The out-the-door price, in writing, with the cash applied.
• Whether a state EV rebate can stack with the offer. (Colorado does)
• What the charging incentive covers—including a home Level 2 setup.
• What that model year needs for Tesla Supercharger access.

And if I ask for the purchase price, give me the purchase price. A “special” monthly payment doesn’t tell me what the car actually costs.

A comfortable EV you can charge overnight at home starts looking pretty appealing with that kind of discount. Just make sure the numbers hold up when you sit down to buy.

text:
We were looking at a software last week that would let leads book directly on our schedule.

We decided not to for two main reasons:

1- pest control can easily be sold over the phone. We don't need an inspection on the home 99% of the time. Sounds like a perfect use case for AI to book jobs right?

Not really. In industries like plumbing and HVAC where all the scheduler needs to do is book an inspection, it works great. 

We are fully working through a sales cycle and need to close the deal, not just book an inspection. 

2- Colorado has a "click to cancel" law. If you can sign up for a recurring service online, you have to allow customers to also cancel online in one click. 

Since none of our customers currently sign up online, we don't have to offer this simple cancellation. We give a discount on the initial service if they agree to a one or two year plan. If they cancel before that term is up, they need to reimburse that as a cancel fee. 

Also, when they call in to cancel, if we can have a conversation with them, we can usually find a better plan for them, resolve concerns, or find another way to keep them happy as customer (and continue providing them value). 

We lose that with a click to cancel. 

In a race to add AI and other softwares, I encourage everybody to fully consider how each change will affect the company. 

It's really easy to break laws you might not even know about. In this case, we may have closed more leads but opened us up for much higher attrition.

🎥 The #Monroe_Doctrine is being operationalized with speed and force: #countries_such_as_Iran are to be #ruthlessly_sacrificed_to_Americas_strategic_competition_with_China👇👇

👈 #Akbar_Ganji

✅1) The claim
America’s principal strategy is aimed at China, a rival that must not be allowed to pull ahead of the United States. China needs oil. The pressure on Venezuela, Greenland, Panama, and Iran belongs to that same competition. It is not a personal or sudden decision by Trump.

✅2) Evidence, in the words of Trump and his administration

🔹Panama
• Inauguration, January 2025: “China is operating the Panama Canal. And we didn’t give it to China. We gave it to Panama, and we’re taking it back.”
• To reporters: “We’re going to take it back, or something very powerful is going to happen.”
• Rubio, February 2025: absent immediate changes, the United States would “take measures necessary to protect its rights under the Treaty.”

🔹Greenland
• January 2026: “I love the people of China. I love the people of Russia. But I don’t want them as a neighbour in Greenland.”
• The same period: “If we don’t do it, Russia or China will, and that’s not going to happen when I’m president.”
• 9 January 2026: “I’m going to do something in Greenland, whether they like it or not… I’d like to make a deal the easy way, but if we don’t do it the easy way, we’re going to do it the hard way.”
• September 2026, after the security agreement: “No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland.”

🔹Venezuela
• 16 December 2025, Truth Social: the pressure would continue “Until such time as they return to the United States of America all of the Oil, Land, and other Assets that they previously stole from us.”
• After Maduro’s capture, 3 January 2026: the United States would “run” Venezuela, and “we’re going to be taking out a lot of wealth out of the ground.”
• 24 January 2026, New York Post: “Let me put it this way, they don’t have any oil. We’re taking the oil.”
• Meeting with oil executives: if the United States did not move, China or Russia would, and he told both they would not be there.
• United Nations, September 2026: “We’re taking a lot of oil from Venezuela. … To the victor belong the spoils.”
• Rubio: Venezuela’s oil industry is not to be left in the control of America’s enemies, and China is not to destabilize the American backyard.

🔹Iran’s oil
• Financial Times, 29 March 2026: “To be honest with you, my favourite thing is to take the oil in Iran.”
• The same interview: “I don’t think they have any defense. We could take it very easily.” “Maybe we take Kharg Island, maybe we don’t. … It would also mean we had to be there for a while.”
• June 2026, Truth Social: he would soon take Kharg Island and other Iranian oil sites and take complete control of their oil and gas market “just like Venezuela.”
• 13 September 2026, in Ireland: America would eventually get out of Iran, “unless we decide to stay and keep the oil, like Venezuela.”
• 1987, to Barbara Walters: “Let ’em have Iran. You take their oil. That’s what I’d do.”
• May 2026, on the seizure of tankers: the ship was taken, the cargo was taken, and the oil was taken, and he said the United States had become like pirates.
• Bessent, October 2026: “Iran loaded ZERO crude oil onto tankers in September. The Trump Administration is cutting off the Iranian regime’s most critical source of revenue.”

✅3) China, the principal rival; a policy from Obama to the present
• Obama, 2011: the “pivot to Asia,” a shift of military and economic priority from the Middle East to the Pacific.
• Obama, 2015: “If we don’t write the rules, China will write the rules out in that region.”
• National Security Strategy 2017: China and Russia as “revisionist powers.” The trade war began in the same period.
• National Security Strategy 2022: China is “the only competitor with both the intent to reshape the international order and, increasingly, the economic, diplomatic, military, and technological power to do it.”
• Blinken: “the most serious long-term challenge to the international order — and that’s posed by the People’s Republic of China.” The CHIPS Act and semiconductor export controls continued that competition.
• National Security Strategy 2025: the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine. “We will deny non-Hemispheric competitors the ability to position forces or other threatening capabilities, or to own or control strategically vital assets, in our Hemisphere.”

✅4) Latin America; only what has occurred
🔹Chile: José Antonio Kast was inaugurated on 11 March 2026.
🔹Colombia: Abelardo de la Espriella, backed by Trump, won on 21 June 2026 and took office on 7 August 2026.
🔹Venezuela: Maduro was captured on 3 January 2026. Delcy Rodríguez, from the same camp, is interim president, and no election date has been set. This is not a right-wing change of government; it is control of oil.
🔹Cuba: the blockade has been tightened and Venezuelan oil assistance cut off. Trump and Rubio are pursuing regime change; a new right-wing president does not yet exist.
🔹Brazil: the first round on 4 October 2026 produced no majority; Flávio Bolsonaro about 47 percent, Lula about 45 percent. The runoff is on 25 October 2026. A new president has not yet been elected.

✅5) Conclusion
The evidence shows that competition with China has been a constant of American policy since 2011, and that Trump’s second term has extended it to the canal, the island, the oil, and the backyard. The explicit statements about taking Venezuela’s oil and Iran’s oil, Kharg included, are two instances of one logic. That Iran is not the principal target, but a cost of this competition, is an inference from that evidence, not a separate quotation from the White House. This inference stands apart from Israel’s effective pressure on the United States and on Trump to bomb Iran. On that basis, it is naive to suppose that America’s problem with Iran can be resolved simply: Iran must not become an ally of China, and its cheap oil must not be placed at China’s disposal. Independence and national sovereignty are of no account to the United States. America’s interests take precedence over the interests of every other country in their own affairs.
The charge of imperialism is not confined to one camp. Michael McFaul (@McFaul), U.S. ambassador to Russia under Obama, a Democrat, and now a professor at Stanford, has called the Venezuela oil deal imperialism both on Twitter and in interviews. On 29 August 2026 he wrote that Trump had taken America back to the nineteenth century and was behaving like a typical imperial empire of that century, and that the deal was naked imperialism: taking another country’s assets in the south by military force. On 3 September 2026, answering the White House, he wrote: “That’s called imperialism. We are profiting from the use of force in another country.” He has also written: “Straight up colonialism. We invaded not to restore democracy, but to take their oil.” And on 22 September 2026: “This is straight up 19th century imperialism.”
From the other side, Robert Kagan, a leading neoconservative theorist of military intervention and a co-author of the Project for the New American Century statements, said the same in his conversation with Bill Kristol (@BillKristol). He treats the Trump administration as predatory and imperialist, having taken Venezuela’s oil and Greenland for America by open, naked force, and says this colonial appetite is insatiable. In that interview he called the Greenland arrangement “the caricature of American imperialism,” said the security agreement is more likely “the predicate for further encroachment” than its end, called Venezuela “straight expropriation of another nation’s wealth for the benefit of the United States,” and said of Greenland: “He wanted to commit an act of territorial aggression against Greenland.” A Democrat who served Obama, and a neoconservative who long argued for military intervention, use the same word for the same policy.
The military attack on Iran had, and has, nothing to do with freedom, human rights, or democracy (whenever Trump senses that Iran’s leaders are coming to terms with him, he offers them astonishing praise). This attack is for oil, domination, colonialism, imperialism, racism, and Israel’s interests, and for nothing else. Only that.
John Rawls, in The Law of Peoples, wrote more than once that there was no need for the atomic bombing of Japan in the Second World War. Japan was already close to surrender. The bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, aimed primarily at civilian populations, were very great wrongs. Truman was a racist. He regarded the Japanese as savages and barbarians, and said they should be treated as such; and it was on that ground that Japan was atomic-bombed. Trump is a racist of the same kind. Quite apart from the racist statements he has made, again and again, against Africans and Hispanics, he has called Iran and Iranians mad, savage, and violent, and has called the Islamic Republic “the number-one sponsor of terror.” He has said that he must destroy them, wipe them from the face of the earth, and send them back to the Stone Age (“We’re going to bring them back to the Stone Ages where they belong”; “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again”; “Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly… Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival”). He has also called Iranians “animals,” spoken of “horrible genes, not like our own,” and called Iran’s leaders “scum” and “sick people.” Racism is not an added charge. It is already in the record, from Truman to Trump.

🎥 دکترین مونرو به سرعت و شدت در حال عملیاتی‌شدن است: کشورهایی مانند ایران باید بی‌رحمانه قربانی رقابت استراتژیک آمریکا با چین شوند👇👇

👈 اکبر گنجی

✅۱) ادعا
استراتژی اصلی آمریکا معطوف به چین است؛ رقیبی که نباید از آمریکا پیش بیفتد. چین به نفت نیاز دارد. فشار بر ونزوئلا، گرینلند، پاناما و ایران در امتداد همین رقابت است، نه تصمیم شخصی و ناگهانی ترامپ.

✅۲) شواهد از زبان ترامپ و دولتش

🔹پاناما
• تحلیف، ژانویه ۲۰۲۵: «چین کانال پاناما را اداره می‌کند. ما آن را به چین ندادیم؛ به پاناما دادیم و پسش می‌گیریم.»
• به خبرنگاران: «چین کانال را می‌چرخاند. توافق نقض شده و ما پسش می‌گیریم، وگرنه اتفاق بسیار قدرتمندی می‌افتد.»
• روبیو، فوریه ۲۰۲۵: اگر نفوذ چین کم نشود، آمریکا «اقدامات لازم» را می‌کند.

🔹گرینلند
• ژانویه ۲۰۲۶: «مردم چین و روسیه را دوست دارم، اما نمی‌خواهم در گرینلند همسایه‌ام باشند.»
• همان دوره: «اگر ما نکنیم، روسیه یا چین می‌کنند. تا وقتی من رئیس‌جمهور باشم، این اتفاق نمی‌افتد.»
• سپتامبر ۲۰۲۶، پس از توافق امنیتی: «هیچ دشمن آمریکا اجازه نخواهد داشت در گرینلند حضور نظامی برقرار کند.»

🔹ونزوئلا
• پس از بازداشت مادورو، ژانویه ۲۰۲۶: «شرکت‌های بزرگ نفتی آمریکا وارد می‌شوند، میلیاردها دلار خرج می‌کنند و مقدار عظیمی ثروت از دل زمین بیرون می‌آوریم.»
• همان دوره: «نفت ما را بردند. ما آن را پس می‌خواهیم.»
• دیدار با مدیران نفتی: «اگر ما نمی‌کردیم، چین یا روسیه می‌کردند. به هر دو گفتم آنجا نخواهید بود.»
• سازمان ملل، سپتامبر ۲۰۲۶: «مقدار زیادی نفت از ونزوئلا برمی‌داریم. غنیمت از آنِ پیروز است.»
• روبیو: «اجازه نمی‌دهیم صنعت نفت ونزوئلا در کنترل دشمنان آمریکا باشد. چین قرار نیست حیاط‌خلوت ما را بی‌ثبات کند.»

🔹نفت ایران
• فایننشال‌تایمز، ۲۹ مارس ۲۰۲۶: «کار مورد علاقهٔ من گرفتن نفت ایران است.»
• همان مصاحبه: «شاید خارگ را بگیریم. فکر نمی‌کنم دفاعی داشته باشد. خیلی راحت می‌توانیم بگیریمش»؛ و ماندن در آنجا لازم می‌شود.
• آوریل ۲۰۲۶: «اگر اختیار با من بود، نفت را می‌گرفتم، نگه می‌داشتم و کلی پول درمی‌آوردم.»
• ژوئن ۲۰۲۵: «می‌توانستیم نفت را نگه داریم؛ همان‌طور که دربارهٔ عراق می‌گفتم.»
• ۱۹۸۷، به باربارا والترز: «بگذار ایران برای خودشان باشد؛ تو نفتشان را بگیر.»
• مه ۲۰۲۶، دربارهٔ توقیف نفتکش‌ها: «کشتی را گرفتیم، بار را گرفتیم، نفت را گرفتیم. مثل دزدان دریایی شده‌ایم.»
• بسنت، اکتبر ۲۰۲۶: ایران در سپتامبر هیچ نفت خامی بار نزد؛ محاصره درآمد نفتی را قطع کرده است.

✅۳) چین، رقیب اصلی؛ سیاستی از اوباما تا امروز
• اوباما، ۲۰۱۱: «چرخش به آسیا»؛ انتقال اولویت نظامی و اقتصادی از خاورمیانه به اقیانوس آرام.
• اوباما، ۲۰۱۵: «باید آمریکا، نه کشورهایی مثل چین، قواعد اقتصادی این قرن را بنویسد.»
• سند امنیت ملی ۲۰۱۷: چین و روسیه «قدرت‌های تجدیدنظرطلب». جنگ تجاری از همین دوره شروع شد.
• سند امنیت ملی ۲۰۲۲: چین تنها رقیب دارای قصد و ظرفیت تغییر نظم بین‌المللی.
• بلینکن: «چین جدی‌ترین چالش بلندمدت برای نظم بین‌المللی است.» قانون تراشه و کنترل صادرات نیمه‌رسانا ادامهٔ همان رقابت بود.
• سند امنیت ملی ۲۰۲۵: «فرع ترامپ» بر دکترین مونرو؛ منع رقبای بیرونِ نیم‌کره از کنترل دارایی‌های حیاتی در حیاط‌خلوت آمریکا.

✅۴) آمریکای لاتین؛ فقط آنچه رخ داده
🔹شیلی: خوزه آنتونیو کاست، ۱۱ مارس ۲۰۲۶ تحلیف شد.
🔹کلمبیا: آبلاردو دِ لا اسپریِیا، مورد حمایت ترامپ، ۲۱ ژوئن ۲۰۲۶ پیروز شد و ۷ اوت ۲۰۲۶ کار را آغاز کرد.
🔹ونزوئلا: مادورو ۳ ژانویه ۲۰۲۶ بازداشت شد. دلسی رودریگِس از همان اردوگاه رئیس‌جمهور موقت است و انتخابات تاریخ ندارد. اینجا تغییر حکومت راست‌گرا نیست؛ کنترل نفت است.
🔹کوبا: محاصره تشدید شده و کمک نفتی ونزوئلا قطع شده. ترامپ و روبیو پروژهٔ تغییر رژیم را دنبال می‌کنند؛ رئیس‌جمهور جدید راست‌گرا هنوز وجود ندارد.
🔹برزیل: دور اول ۴ اکتبر ۲۰۲۶ بدون اکثریت تمام شد؛ فلاویو بولسونارو حدود ۴۷ درصد، لولا حدود ۴۵ درصد. دور دوم ۲۵ اکتبر ۲۰۲۶ است. رئیس‌جمهور جدید هنوز انتخاب نشده.

✅۵) نتیجه
شاهدها نشان می‌دهند رقابت با چین از ۲۰۱۱ سیاست ثابت آمریکا بوده و ترامپِ دوم آن را به کانال، جزیره، نفت و حیاط‌خلوت کشانده است. حرف صریح دربارهٔ گرفتن نفت ونزوئلا و نفت ایران، از جمله خارگ، دو مصداق یک منطق‌اند. اینکه ایران هدف اصلی نیست و هزینهٔ این رقابت است، استنتاج از همین شواهد است؛ نه نقل‌قول جداگانه‌ای از کاخ سفید. این استنتاج مستقل از فشار مؤثر اسرائیل بر آمریکا و ترامپ برای بمباران ایران است. بر همین اساس، ساده‌اندیشی است که گمان شود مشکل آمریکا با ایران به سادگی حل می‌شود: ایران نباید متحد چین شود و نفت ارزانش در اختیار چین قرار گیرد. استقلال و حق حاکمیت ملی برای آمریکا فاقد اهمیت است، منافع آمریکا بر منافع تمامی کشورهای جهان برای خودشان تقدم ارزشی دارد.
حملهٔ نظامی به ایران هیچ ارتباطی با آزادی و حقوق بشر و دموکراسی نداشت و ندارد (ترامپ هرگاه احساس کند رهبران ایران در حال راه‌آمدن با او هستند، از آن‌ها تعریف‌وتمجیدهای شگفت‌آوری می‌کند). این حمله برای نفت و سلطه و استعمار و امپریالیسم و نژادپرستی و منافع اسرائیل است و بس. فقط و فقط همین.

text:
Dark Output: What National Accounts Miss When Artificial Intelligence Shifts Value from Prices to Capabilities -  “Dark output” is defensible as a label for identifiable measurement gaps, provided that it does not become an unspecified monetary residual added to GDP.

The decisive distinction separates economic value, consumer surplus, firm productivity and margins, and measured GDP and official productivity, because these objects can move in different directions without any accounting contradiction.

Lower prices can reduce nominal output while preserving real output; lower labour requirements can raise productivity and profits while leaving final expenditure unchanged; better services can increase welfare without a recorded quality adjustment.

The strongest case concerns unpriced household capabilities, inadequately measured service quality, and some complementary intangible investment, whereas provider revenue, retained profits, and infrastructure expenditure already have accounting counterparts.

Current welfare surveys, production-based imputations, task-exposure estimates, and industry productivity statistics measure different objects, so their magnitudes cannot be combined into a single estimate of AI’s economic contribution.

The appropriate response is a coordinated set of production, quality, time-use, distributional, and welfare accounts, with assumptions and geographic coverage disclosed separately.

AI’s Accounting Gap Is Becoming a Policy Risk
The consequential choice in artificial intelligence is whether governments and institutions will judge production, investment and public benefit through the same statistic. On 17 November 2025, the US Census Bureau broadened its business survey question on AI, creating a break in the adoption series; on 2 October 2026, a Bureau of Economic Analysis research spotlight described an association between AI use and stronger output while preserving the distinction between correlation and causation. Those decisions expose the governing problem: measures designed for different purposes are being treated as interchangeable evidence. The fiscal and industrial risk is that expenditure will be mistaken for productive deployment, profits for consumer benefit, and unpriced capabilities for missing GDP. The remedy is complementary accounts that establish what changes, who benefits and which gains become recorded production.

The largest estimates answer different questions
The US evidence becomes more informative when its units remain separate. Census research using the Business Trends and Outlook Survey supplement collected during November 2025–January 2026 reported firm AI use at 17.9% on a firm-weighted basis and 31.2% when weighted by employment, with a reference window of the previous two weeks. Reported worker-task AI use reached 22.6% and 40.6%, respectively, over the previous six months. The employment-weighted figures describe employment located in reporting businesses; they do not describe the proportion of individual workers personally using AI. The different reference windows also prevent the gap from being interpreted as a direct measure of informal adoption. The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks — US Census Bureau research working paper — April 2026.

The valuation evidence measures a different object. The April 2026 Stanford Digital Economy Lab paper What is Generative AI Worth? reports mean monthly willingness to accept compensation for losing access at $98.00 in its July 2025 wave and $124.50 in March 2026; Table 2 gives corresponding medians of $3.39 and $11.48. Its annualised, mean-based welfare aggregates rise from $116.2 billion to $172.3 billion, using estimated US user populations of 98.78 million and 115.33 million within an ages 18–64 population expansion. Those totals depend on stated choices, external user counts and annualisation. The distance between the mean and median matters because the typical respondent and the aggregate valuation answer different questions; neither is a measure of production. What is Generative AI Worth? — Stanford Digital Economy Lab — April 2026.

The production-oriented adjustment is different again. BEA research published in June 2026 estimates that including advertising- and marketing-supported free content would increase average annual US real GDP growth by 0.22 percentage point during 2022–25, under its barter-transaction methodology. The estimate includes AI but is not AI-only, and it is an experimental calculation rather than an adopted revision to headline GDP. SemiAnalysis’s approximately $1.5 trillion labour-cost exposure estimate, published in May 2026, likewise identifies potentially affected tasks rather than output already missing from the accounts. Adding these figures would combine adoption, welfare, production adjustments and exposure into a total with no coherent accounting meaning. The Progression of “Free” Digital Content to AI: Impacts on US Economic Growth and Productivity — BEA — June 2026; AI Dark Output: The Visible Cost of Invisible Output — SemiAnalysis — May 2026.

Infrastructure spending establishes inputs, not successful use
The System of National Accounts records qualifying investment because assets are produced or acquired, while downstream productivity depends on what those assets subsequently enable. A data centre, a software investment and a redesigned workflow occupy different positions in that transmission mechanism. Institutional analysis therefore needs to establish whether assets enter service, whether complementary inputs are operational and whether deployment produces accepted outcomes. The distinction is consequential for procurement: a system generating more documents may increase activity while leaving the cost of verified, usable documents unchanged.

The productivity J-curve literature supplies a mechanism for delayed gains without guaranteeing their arrival. Complementary investment in training, data and organisational processes can consume resources before mature deployment produces observable improvements, while inadequate measurement of those intangibles can distort the timing of recorded productivity. That mechanism supports collecting better evidence; it does not authorise institutions to treat every disappointing productivity observation as deferred success. The relevant test is whether spending becomes persistent use and whether persistent use improves completed production. The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies — American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics — January 2021.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics productivity framework makes the operational distinction explicit: labour productivity concerns real output per labour hour, while multifactor productivity also accounts for other productive inputs. Generation time alone supplies neither numerator nor denominator. Preparation, review, correction and integration belong in the workflow, and time released from a task can support additional output, better quality or unused capacity rather than lower payroll. Procurement and corporate governance need that reconciliation before converting reported task savings into a claim about financial returns or economy-wide efficiency. Labor Productivity and Costs: Concepts — US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Quality determines whether a real gain becomes visible
The System of National Accounts can accommodate a falling price without recording a fall in real output when the deflator captures the price change correctly. For an unchanged service, lower receipts are a nominal result, not proof of less production. A quality improvement at a constant price presents a different problem: the real gain depends on whether the output measure recognises the change. “Dark output” is useful at this specific point of failure, where an inadequate service index obscures volume or quality; it becomes rhetorical when lower prices are declared invisible by definition. Measuring the Economy: A Primer on GDP and the NIPAs — Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The UN guidance on improving AI visibility identifies the difficulty of separating capabilities embedded in software and broader products. Within-firm use intensifies that difficulty because there may be no separate transaction for the task being improved. Yet internal use does not automatically escape GDP: it can support recorded final output, reduce input requirements or contribute to recognised own-account production. Statistical reform must identify which of those mechanisms operates before assigning an unobserved value to the activity. Improving the visibility of Artificial Intelligence in the National Accounts — United Nations national accounts guidance.

The Office for National Statistics offers a practical precedent for maintaining measures with different purposes. Its public-service productivity methodology incorporates quality adjustments while explaining differences from national accounts measures, including healthcare output. The institutional lesson is that an additional measure can illuminate outcomes without silently redefining the core production series. An AI service index should follow the same discipline: specify the accepted output, publish the quality variables and expose the sensitivity of the result to alternative adjustments. Public service productivity: total, UK QMI — Office for National Statistics — May 2026.

Welfare cannot finance a budget until income changes
GDP-B addresses benefits that transaction prices do not fully reveal, but a welfare estimate is not an equivalent addition to taxable income. Households may gain access to useful capabilities while market receipts remain unchanged or decline; producers may retain cost savings while buyers receive no immediate price reduction. Fiscal analysis must trace recorded income, employment and public-service expenditure rather than translate a willingness-to-accept aggregate into presumed budget capacity. The accounting boundary is a constraint on the inference, not a denial of the benefit.

The System of National Accounts also prevents visible financial gains from being relabelled as invisible production. Higher profits funded by lower unit costs are recorded outcomes, while model-provider receipts can represent intermediate purchases whose value must not be counted again alongside the customer’s final output. The distributional question is therefore separate from the production question: who receives the saving, whether prices change, how compensation and hours respond, and whether access expands. A larger margin and a larger consumer surplus can each be economically significant without describing the same gain. Measuring the Economy: A Primer on GDP and the NIPAs — Bureau of Economic Analysis.

International comparison fails when the boundaries differ
The OECD Handbook on Compiling Digital Supply and Use Tables provides a route to additional detail within the national accounts framework, distinguishing products, producers and how transactions occur. That structure can support more visible AI production, but it does not make a household valuation survey interchangeable with a business adoption survey. International comparison requires common definitions of the reporting unit, population, reference window and treatment of embedded software; transferring US willingness-to-accept estimates to another economy would bypass those requirements. OECD Handbook on Compiling Digital Supply and Use Tables — November 2023.

The UN guidance on free digital products develops satellite-account options while preserving the distinction from the central framework. A production-oriented free-content account and a GDP-B welfare account can therefore coexist without sharing a valuation method or being added together. The useful international objective is a reproducible crosswalk showing what is already recorded, what is reclassified, what improves real-volume measurement and what remains a separately estimated benefit. Without that reconciliation, more statistical detail can enlarge the scope for incompatible comparisons. Recording and Valuing “Free” Digital Products in an SNA Satellite Account — United Nations national accounts guidance — September 2022.

The next two years will test whether institutions measure outcomes
Over the next 12–24 months, the cost of retaining a single-metric interpretation will fall on identifiable participants: taxpayers where public procurement rewards generated activity rather than accepted services; adopting firms where gross time savings conceal verification and integration costs; workers where released task capacity is confused with realised employment displacement; and households where improved access remains absent from assessments of benefit. The Business Trends and Outlook Survey’s wording change demonstrates how even an adoption series can shift when the measurement boundary changes. Institutions need equivalent transparency when moving from expenditure to claims about performance.

The proposed response is a connected set of production, deployment and welfare accounts, with task-level time observations, quality-adjusted service indices and firm disclosures that reconcile AI expenditure to accepted output and labour requirements. The OECD digital supply-and-use framework supplies an institutional foundation, but implementation still requires validated definitions and observations. If institutions leave that work undone, infrastructure spending will remain easier to establish than the productive use it supports, and user benefits easier to claim than to compare. The medium-term consequence is weaker procurement, weaker fiscal inference and a distribution of gains that remains unresolved even where the transactions themselves are visible.

PRESS STATEMENT

GOV AIYEDATIWA MOURNS OVER ONDO AIR CRASH, DIRECTS SUPPORT FOR SEARCH AND RESCUE OPERATIONS

The Governor of Ondo State, His Excellency, Hon. Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa, has received with deep sadness the news of the crash of a Nigerian Air Force aircraft in Igbokoda, headquarters of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, in the early hours of today, Monday, October 5, 2026.

According to preliminary reports confirmed by the Nigerian Air Force Director of Public Relations and Information, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, the aircraft, an ATR-42 with tail number NGR 931, was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when it crashed in a swampy area opposite the Naval Base in Igbokoda. The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr. Festus Keyamo, has confirmed that 25 passengers and 7 crew members were on board.

On behalf of the Government and good people of Ondo State, Governor Aiyedatiwa expresses his heartfelt sympathy to the Chief of Air Staff, the entire Nigerian Air Force family, and the families of all personnel and passengers on board the ill-fated aircraft. Our thoughts and prayers are with them at this difficult time.

The Governor has been in contact with the leadership of the Nigerian Air Force, the Ilaje Local Government Chairman, Hon. Maurice Oripelaye, and security agencies on ground.

On the night of 3–4 October, a boat carrying 120 people was reported off Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue. The maritime prefecture for the Channel and the North Sea says the rescue centre at Jobourg sent the salvage tug Abeille Liberté, with naval firefighters aboard, and lifeboats from Saint-Vaast and Barfleur. Life jackets were handed out. The boat was not turned round. The prefecture’s own account is that it reached British waters. The stated reason is safety: the watercraft are overloaded, assistance is offered, and the occupants are not forced off for fear of a capsize.

Ship-tracking screenshots posted that evening show the result. At 19:47, off Portsmouth, Abeille Liberté was plotted beside RNLI lifeboat 16-17 and a coastguard vessel. Twenty-four minutes later the same cluster sat off Shanklin. Isle of Wight reports said the boat had left the Cherbourg area under escort of the French Abeille Liberté, and that Bembridge and Yarmouth lifeboats, with a coastguard helicopter, met the French escort and the migrant boat. Two RNLI boats were later seen entering the Solent.

Abeille Liberté is not a frigate. It is a state salvage tug, tasked under the operational control of the maritime prefect, a naval officer. The distinction matters less than the outcome. A French public vessel, under a naval chain of command, accompanied an illegal crossing until British assets completed it. This was not a one-off. On 22 September the same tug, with French lifeboats and a navy helicopter, shadowed more than 60 people from the Normandy coast until English waters. Nobody stopped them and the UK government didn’t care.

Paris calls this rescue. The effect is a relay. French assets watch the boat across French waters. British assets collect the people once the line is crossed, and the passengers are processed as asylum claimants. France has been explicit that it will not compel people off these boats. The same justification applied week after week, that rule is blanket permission to continue.

Britain is paying for the other half. London has pledged up to £660 million to fund French beach patrols through 2029. The returns deal that sent about 1,400 people back expired on 1 October and will not be renewed. A rescue ends at the nearest safe port. A handover in English waters, repeated until it is government policy, is a transfer. The plot off Shanklin is the visa paperwork.

text:
For most of recorded human history, mankind was ruled by monarchs. Europe, India, West Asia, East Asia, it hardly mattered. Hereditary rule was not some historical aberration. It was the default political arrangement of civilisation.

There were terrible kings, incompetent kings and occasionally completely insane kings. Yet monarchy survived for millennia because, for all its faults, it offered something political systems value enormously: continuity.

Democracy is not particularly new either. India had republican traditions among the ancient ganas and sanghas, Vaishali being the most famous example, while Rome experimented with republican government centuries before Washington existed.

What America did brilliantly was transform democracy into an extraordinarily powerful political ideal: liberty, equality before law, individual rights and government deriving legitimacy from the governed.

The problem begins when equality before law quietly becomes the assumption that everyone possesses equal political judgement.

Democracy ultimately asks the scholar and the idiot, the taxpayer and the freeloader, the person who has studied an issue for twenty years and the person who discovered it through a WhatsApp forward that morning, to exercise exactly the same political power.

We have simply decided that questioning this arrangement is immoral.

And now the cracks are becoming impossible to ignore.

America increasingly resembles two countries occupying the same territory, with completely different cultures, institutions, media ecosystems and ideas of what America itself should be. India manages an even more extraordinary arrangement, where thirty-plus political, linguistic and cultural worlds somehow conduct one giant election every five years and pretend that this automatically produces national consensus.

Then there is democracy’s greatest joke: it was supposed to destroy hereditary privilege, but in much of the world it merely taught hereditary privilege how to contest elections.

Kings became political families. Kingdoms became constituencies. Succession ceremonies became party tickets.

We abolished dynasties and then started voting for them.

My suspicion is that democracy has perhaps another fifty years in its present form before technology, polarization, demographic pressures and increasingly incompatible populations force something fundamentally different to replace it.

And when this grand experiment finally exhausts itself, I would not be surprised if humanity rediscovers the political institution it spent the last two centuries congratulating itself for having escaped.

History has a peculiar sense of humour.

The monarchy may yet have the last laugh.

-No resources were transferred but remember; Alberta’s Crown resources belong to Alberta via the 1930 NRTA. This is fact.

text:
You should offer the world a piece of the pie in exchange for eased tensions.. 

The way to ease a real source of friction between the United States and the countries that finance its debt is to offer them a stake in the AI boom in exchange for writing down what they hold.

Foreign governments and central banks own a large share of U.S. Treasuries. That is a financial relationship, not an alliance and not a truce, but it is a standing claim on the American balance sheet. The AI boom is the one new American asset big enough to bargain with. Washington should capture part of that upside and then trade the captured stake for debt relief.

There are two ways to build the stake.

The government can levy a high tax on the manufacture and sale of humanoid robots, so that a slice of the revenue from automating physical work flows to the Treasury instead of only to the firms that build the machines. That tax has to be set against the risk that it slows adoption or pushes production offshore; it works only if the robots are actually built and sold here in volume.

Or the government can take large equity positions in AI companies, buying shares rather than only regulating the industry. Those shares are a claim on future profits. They are worth something to a creditor only if the companies succeed, and the government has to accept that it will be both shareholder and referee.

Either route produces the same bargaining chip: a defined pool of AI-related value, held as cash from the robot tax or as shares from the investments. The United States then offers that pool to the foreign official holders of its debt. They forgive or stretch a stated amount of Treasuries and receive equity, royalties, or a revenue claim in return. The piece of the pie goes to the creditors, not to the technology. They take it only if the AI claim looks at least as valuable as the bonds they give up.

The deal has to stay narrow. Private holders cannot be forced to swap, so the offer is limited to official holdings and has to be voluntary. It also has to be ring-fenced and modest, so that advertising a write-down does not reprice the rest of the Treasury market and wipe out the fiscal gain. Done that way, debt relief is a transaction: American AI upside for a smaller foreign claim on American debt.

text:
Of course Iranian actors have agency, and U.S. policy is hardly the only variable shaping Iranian politics. But acknowledging that agency does not mean denying or discounting the impact of the world’s most powerful country on the internal politics of a country it has subjected to years of broad, collectively punishing economic warfare and, over the past year, multiple military wars.

For decades, one of the central arguments within the Islamic Republic has been over what kind of relationship with the United States is actually possible. A powerful political current, stretching from Rafsanjani and Khatami to Rouhani and the reformists, argued that the hostility was not immutable: Iran could negotiate with Washington, make concessions, reduce tensions with the West and gain economically and strategically in return.

At times, figures from this camp openly criticized Iran’s nuclear and missile programs and regional policies, and challenged political rivals, particularly influential within the security establishment, who argued that Washington was fundamentally hostile to the Islamic Republic and that concessions would therefore produce greater vulnerability rather than accommodation.

And this was not some politically irrelevant minority. These arguments helped elect presidents, shaped major newspapers and public debate, influenced parts of the foreign-policy and national-security establishment, and ultimately produced the JCPOA.

Even after the U.S. withdrawal from that agreement, maximum pressure and now war, advocates of diplomacy have remained influential enough that their opponents still have to fight these arguments out publicly. 

You can see it in Iranian political and media debates today: whether negotiations were a mistake, whether another agreement with Washington is possible, whether Iran gave up too much, and whether greater deterrent power or renewed diplomacy offers the better path to security.

That is precisely why U.S. policy matters so much to Iran’s internal politics. Since 2018 especially, Washington has repeatedly handed one side of this debate evidence for its case.

The United States withdrew from the JCPOA after Iran had accepted major restrictions on its nuclear program, restored and expanded sanctions, pursued maximum pressure, and ultimately went to war. 

Each of those events made it harder for advocates of accommodation to answer the most basic question their opponents could put to them: what, exactly, did Iran gain from restraint?

This is not a story in which Washington mechanically “creates” Iranian hardliners or deprives Iranians of agency. It is about how political arguments gain and lose credibility.

When one faction says compromise can produce security and economic dividends, while another says Washington will pocket Iranian concessions and continue escalating anyway, what the United States actually does inevitably affects which argument is easier to make.

The remarkable thing is that the pro-diplomacy current has survived politically despite how much has happened since 2018. Its opponents have had to fight tooth and nail to discredit it even now. 

But U.S. policy has made their job considerably easier. To treat that as somehow separate from Iranian domestic politics is to miss one of the most important ways external pressure actually operates inside Iran.

On this broader question of how U.S. policy has shaped Iran’s internal politics and empowered the forces most hostile to accommodation, this recent piece by @NickKristof is well worth reading:

text:
Expensive technology doesn’t always mean better value — but sometimes the extra money pays for engineering that genuinely cannot be delivered cheaply.

From a $300 magnesium gaming mouse to a high-end JVC projector, premium products can justify their prices through lighter materials, more advanced optics, lower latency, better construction and longer-term durability. In these cases, the cost is connected to a real technical objective rather than simply a luxury label.

But premium pricing becomes much harder to defend when the upgrade is mostly cosmetic. Expensive packaging, decorative finishes and luxury materials mean little if the underlying product fits poorly or performs no better than a much cheaper alternative.

Another limitation is that better hardware cannot replace skill. A high-end gaming controller or precision kitchen knife may offer measurable advantages, but those benefits become most valuable when the person using them has the experience to exploit them.

Sometimes the premium is also about longevity. Products such as Dyson’s Solarcycle Morph lamp cost far more than ordinary alternatives. Still, part of that price pays for engineering designed around durability, controlled lighting and a very long operating life.

The real question, then, is not whether expensive tech is worth it. It is whether the extra money buys meaningful engineering, better performance, craftsmanship, or longevity — or simply a more expensive version of something ordinary.

The Profile in Question

Social Media as a Double-Edged Sword

Social media platforms like Instagram are fantastic for staying connected with friends and family. They offer a window into the lives of people you care about, allowing you to see what they’re up to without having to pick up the phone or send an email. But there’s a downside too.

Once you start engaging with someone's content—whether it’s liking their posts or commenting—you leave behind digital footprints that are hard to erase. Your activity becomes part of your online history, and it can be tracked back to you if needed.

Privacy Concerns

Then there’s the elephant in the room: privacy. Instagram is owned by Meta (formerly Facebook), a company known for its extensive data collection practices. While these practices might not always be transparent or entirely beneficial to users, they do raise questions about how your information could potentially be used.

When you decide to follow @carla_onallfours—or any other Instagram profile—your activity becomes part of Meta’s vast database. Are you okay with the idea that your likes and comments might be analyzed or even sold?
What Changes for You?

If you were considering following @carla_onallfours—or any other Instagram profile—this warning might make you think twice before hitting that “follow” button. Is there really value in adding another account to your feed? Are the benefits worth the potential privacy risks?

The Hard Truth

Why do we need these kinds of warnings at all? Because social media can indeed become a trap. Once you start engaging with certain accounts or pages, it becomes increasingly difficult to disengage without leaving visible traces of your online activity.

So before you click that link and follow @carla_onallfours, ask yourself: is the content really worth the risk? Are you prepared for the consequences?
The Fine Print

What Is Stored

What Is Excluded
