text:
Walkable Cities Can Make Life Better for Drivers, Too

By Kea Wilson
05OCT2026
https://t.co/MumBcvyMGL
...at least when communities embrace a handful of design strategies that make transportation better for everyone.

Believe it or not, walkable cities are even better for drivers than ones designed with only the needs of motorists in mind — and in order to win, advocates for livable streets must embrace targeted strategies that make driving better without sacrificing access to other modes, a new report argues.

In the provocatively named new guide, “How to Design for Cars in People-Centered Places“, a team of researchers and designers broke down why drivers often enjoy shorter, more predictable, all-around less-miserable journeys when they travel in multimodal paradises like Paris, even though auto-dominated American cities are ostensibly built just for them.

That’s because transportation leaders who prioritize people over cars also tend to lean on a handful of simple design strategies that make motoring more pleasant, too — and with the right recipe, any city can replicate their success.

“What people don’t realize is [places like the Netherlands are] also great for driving,” said Nick Falbo, senior transportation planner with Mobycon, a Dutch-international firm that contributed to the report. “You have more access to jobs in 30 minutes by car in Amsterdam than you do in Atlanta. And part of the Dutch story isn’t just how they’ve made it great for people walking, biking, and taking transit; it’s how they’ve actually made it work for people driving as well.”

Why ‘walkable city’ advocates need drivers to win — and vice versa
Falbo explains that while blanketing cities in asphalt promises fast speed limits and convenient parking in theory, auto-centric strategies almost never deliver that in reality.

Instead, motorists end up stuck in gridlock traffic for hours and circling downtown blocks for an unpredictable supply of spots, all while the destinations they’re trying to reach grow further and further apart as car dependency rises. And needless to say, adding one more lane, bro never seems to fix the problem.

Multimodal transportation advocates, though, tend to leap straight to strategies that radically decenter cars — without meaningfully reckoning with how many people will always rely on driving, even in cities with robust mobility alternatives. And when they do, they often draw the ire of a motoring majority, which gets projects cancelled before they begin.

“When you’re in the work of building people-centered places, one of the biggest challenges is the backlash that you get from drivers,” said Houssam Elokda, managing principal at Happy Cities, which co-authored the report. “The project either never makes it to getting funded, or never gets approved. Or if it does get built, the second one doesn’t get built, and the third one doesn’t get built, because the needs of drivers were not effectively met. You create this alienation … but it doesn’t have to be that way.”

Rather than watering down the livable streets vision, though, Elokda and Falbo both argue that welcoming drivers into the transportation reform movement can actually make more ambitious city transformations possible, by building meaningful coalitions between multimodal advocates and a driving public that vastly outnumbers them.

Put another way: no more getting shouted down at the community meeting for an isolated bike lane project just because it requires removing some parking.

“It becomes this sort of ‘cars versus people’ discussion,” added Falbo. “[But] you can support driving in a way that doesn’t compromise the integrity of the place for people walking and biking and taking transit.”

How to do it
Elokda says the first step to breaking the stalemate between drivers and livable streets advocates is to rethink the standards and categories that underlie our transportation decision-making.

And that isn’t just about throwing out much-maligned performance metrics like “level of service”, which incentivizes designing streets for fast driving speeds. It also means rethinking the traditional classifications of roads themselves — like “arterial,” “collector”, and “local” streets — to instead focus on what each street is actually meant to do.

In the report’s vernacular, there are really only two options. “Flow streets,” the guide says, primarily exist to move cars at steady speeds with few interruptions; “place streets,” meanwhile, encourage people to bike, walk, shop, dine, linger, and in short, do everything else.

Most crucially, Falbo says that no street can simultaneously prioritize both “flow” and “place” — because when we try, no one’s needs get met.

“We’re not trying to do everything everywhere,” he added. “In fact, that’s really the heart of the problem we’ve run into so far. [We tend to treat] every street [like it] needs to be both good at moving cars and good at being a place for people — and as a result, we end up with these streets that do not succeed at either of those goals.”

Recommended

Barcelona’s Superblocks: Change the Grid, Change Your Neighborhood
Clarence Eckerson Jr.
https://t.co/0f2LOhbPjv
August 8, 2018

When the concept of “flow” streets and “place” streets are untangled, the report argues that cities are better empowered to create complete, connected networks of both types of thoroughfares, with only brief “transitional zones” between them.

But first, they must abandon the fantasy of building complete streets that attempt to serve all users, but end up not working for anyone.

“There’s been so much effort to bring walking, biking and transit access to these big arterials, and in the end, you end up creating a street that’s not actually a great place to be,” Falbo added. “You’ve actually created a street where you don’t want to sit down and get that cup of coffee — or where even with a protected bike lane, it still feels like a hostile environment to be walking and biking.’

Both Falbo and Elokda acknowledge that this idea might be controversial to US advocates who consider the “complete streets” framework a gold standard — and that it might be challenging for cities awash in stroads and fragmented sidewalk networks to imagine any alternative.

Still, they say many cities are already doing it. Barcelona’s famed “superblock” pilot, for instance, successfully banished most vehicle through-traffic from “place”-centered neighborhoods where the innovative strategy was deployed, but only by creating a “flow street” every 400 meters to prioritize car travel.

The Netherlands, meanwhile, frequently builds or widens car-centered “ring” roads around downtowns, bypassing people-centered areas and transforming the neighborhoods inside the ring into even better havens for non-automotive movement.

Elokda acknowledges that US advocates might reflexively resist any proposal to widen a road in the name of safety, never mind build a whole new one just for drivers. But in limited situations, both can be critical tools.

“When you [connect flow streets] at the network level, it allows you to be uncompromising on place streets,” he added. “Because [then you can say to drivers’] ‘I’ve met your needs there — but here, we’re not going to compromise. We’re going to build the people-centered streets that we want and we deserve.'”

Recommended
The Walkable Neighborhoods Americans Want May Be Closer Than We Think
Kea Wilson
https://t.co/hxXqLU13hV
July 6, 2023

Of course, dense land-use policy and incentives are particularly critical to the success of any people-centered place — and even the most die-hard drivers will benefit from it.

The report counsels cities to focus on land-use strategies that shorten the average trip rather than focusing on increasing the speed of the average vehicle. And when they engage with the public, they need to ensure drivers understand that bringing destinations closer together will almost always save them more time than speeding cars up.

“There’s a Dutch saying that translates to roughly, ‘Going slower is faster,'” said Falbo. “[Because] when you’ve created the conditions where you have that proximity of destinations, you can actually get between them faster in the end.”

Elokda adds that as land use densifies and people naturally shift to other modes, driving trip lengths also even out throughout the day — which makes it way more pleasant for motorists sick of the rush-hour slog.

“One of the things we found out in our research on this is that drivers value consistency significantly more than speed … If you offer people a drive that is 20 minutes every time, they’ll take it over a drive that’s like 10 minutes one day and 35 minutes the next,” he added.

Perhaps most provocatively, the report argues that walkable cities can and should make parking easier — not by blanketing cities in asphalt, but by locating lots in strategic places where motorists can predictably stash their vehicle, without interrupting the pedestrian experience.

In some cases, that actually means allowing ubiquitous and accessible on-street parking, at least on single-lane, slow-speed roads that are too narrow for a bike lane to make sense, and where parked cars provide a welcome buffer between walkers and passing traffic. In others, though, it means siting a cleverly-hidden or underground garage at the edge of the shopping district.

And if drivers have to hoof it a couple extra blocks along a delightful street with shops to browse along the way, they may not actually mind.

“One of the misconceptions that people have about the needs of drivers is that all of them want parking right in front of their destination,” he adds. “That’s not actually the case; they just don’t want to spend 10 minutes circling around to find a spot. … People are willing to walk when it’s a great environment. They’re just not willing to walk when they’re in a giant, big-box parking lot.”

No matter where they are on their journey to create a transportation network that works for everyone, both Falbo and Elokda say that there’s always something cities can do to make their streets more livable — including for drivers, who aren’t being served particularly well by the auto-centric status quo, either.

First, though, they need to abandon their adversarial assumptions and get everyone under the same tent.

“[Initially,] it’s just about bringing people together around a shared vision for a people-centered place,” Falbo added. “And then you can say, ‘okay: how do we make this happen’?”

Kea Wilson
Kea Wilson is Senior Editor for Streetsblog USA. She has more than a dozen years experience as a writer telling emotional, urgent and actionable stories that motivate average Americans to get involved in making their cities better places. She is also a novelist, cyclist, and affordable housing advocate. She lives in St. Louis, MO. For tips, submissions, and general questions, reach out to her at kea@streetsblog.org, or on Bluesky @keawilson.bsky.social.

text:
You need to find your edge, and abuse it as necessary

There’s no nobility in suppressing it out of guilt 

More importantly, your edge needs to be built on a foundation that remains intact regardless of ever-changing market conditions

The reason you see these Miami mouth droolers hopping vehicles every month is literally because they have no backbone - both in the sense of business and themselves

Which is why so many of last year’s gurus are now pivoting out of panic to try and compensate for the fact that they never built around anything fundamental

My edge is in sales. I consider myself an elite marketer, but sales has always been what fueled my process 

And the cool thing about sales is it’s multi-faceted

Some people look at it through a psychological lens, others through intuition, pattern recognition or sheer repetition

I see all of that, but I primarily see data

Every decision that follows an action is a signal

We keep getting the same objection on calls? Alright, what exactly is being said? Leads keep wanting to “think about it”? Okay but why? What exactly is preventing them from moving forward in this very instant? Oh it’s a pricing issue? That’s 6 out of 8 leads who have given us the same objection. Why do leads find us “too expensive”? Is the perceived value too low? Are we failing to make the ROI obvious enough? Ah seems like we’re attracting the wrong people. Cool, I’ll let marketing know asap so they can tweak the messaging

Although in this case specifically, I’m both sales and marketing lol

But the underlying reality is that I spent a solid 3 years cold calling people and getting told to fuck off on a daily basis, creating my own pipelines from dead CRMs, helping people overcome their inner barriers on Zoom, dealing with glue-eating sales reps (still occasionally do lol, just the game), etc.  

Find something that compounds

Something you can carry across markets, offers and vehicles without having to reinvent yourself every 12 months

text:
DOE offered $VST up to $4.2B to uprate its nuclear fleet.

Good news. But it's cheaper money for growth that's already contracted, not new demand. 🧵

What the loan funds:
Perry + Davis-Besse (Ohio) and Beaver Valley (PA).
These uprates were already sold. In January, Vistra signed 20-year deals with $META for 2,609 MW:
→ 2,176 MW from existing units
→ 433 MW from uprates, delivering 2031–2034

Capex runs 2026–2034, with less than 20% spent by end of 2028. Vistra already expected mid-teens levered returns.
So the loan doesn't change whether this happens. It changes how cheaply.
Rough math: every 1pt lower on $4.2B ≈ $40M/yr saved. Returns go up, more cash stays free for buybacks.

3 details most people will skip:
⚠️ It's a conditional commitment, not cash. Technical, legal, environmental and financial conditions still have to be met. Perry also needs NRC sign-off.
👀 Comanche Peak (Texas) is in the package as an option for future uprates. That's ERCOT, not PJM, right where data center demand is exploding. Vistra already sells Comanche Peak power under a long-term deal. Uprates would mean more MW to sell on top.
👀 Beaver Valley's existing output isn't in the Meta deal, only its 140 MW uprate. A 20-year life extension makes that capacity a live bargaining chip.

The story broke via Bloomberg on Oct 2. A new Buy at $202 landed the same day vs a $140 close. Much of today's move was already front-run.

Who else benefits (my read):
→ Equipment: $GEV (Perry is a GE-design BWR), $CW, $BWXT. Uprates mean turbines, generators, steam-path work.
→ Fuel: more output per reactor = more enriched uranium. $LEU $CCJ
→ Next in line for federal financing: big nuclear fleets chasing data center deals, like $CEG $TLN

One deal is small. If DOE keeps using uprates as a policy tool, it's a fleet-wide trend.

text:
DAY 58 WITHOUT OUR VW ID. BUZZ.

It’s been so long that I think it’s time for a full recap for everyone who has joined this saga late—or has simply forgotten everything that has happened.

On August 10, our ID. Buzz became completely inoperable at around 12,000 miles and had to be towed to Volkswagen of Perrysburg.

58 days later, we still don’t have it back.

Here’s where things currently stand:

• The Buzz has now been at the dealer for nearly TWO MONTHS.

• During that time, the dealership DAMAGED THE VEHICLE while moving it. The damage is significant enough that the door now needs to be replaced.

• The dealer has agreed to replace the door they damaged, but does not want to compensate us for any potential diminished value caused by that damage.

• I have contacted four different attorneys trying to get help with this situation. None have been able to take the case.

• The Ohio Lemon Law route has not provided us with a quick or straightforward resolution, despite the vehicle being unusable for nearly two months.

• Volkswagen Customer Care has been involved.

• I requested that Volkswagen BUY BACK THE VEHICLE because after everything that has happened, I no longer have confidence in either the vehicle or the repair process.

• That request has been sitting in Volkswagen’s Customer Resolution Group process while the days continue to pile up.

• At one point the dealer offered us $1,000 in compensation. Their final position later became essentially: they’ll replace the door they damaged, provide a loaner, and give us $0 additional compensation.

But somehow, that’s not even the craziest part.

The dealer replaced a major component on our Buzz roughly 4–5 weeks ago.

We are now waiting on the EXACT. SAME. PART. AGAIN.

I’ve repeatedly asked one incredibly simple question:

WHY?

Why does a brand-new replacement part need replaced again just a few weeks later?

I still don’t have an answer.

And it’s not because I haven’t asked.

For approximately TWO WEEKS, I have called and emailed the dealership essentially every single day.

No response.

I’ve followed up.

No response.

I’ve called.

No response.

I’ve emailed again.

No response.

I even physically went to the dealership looking for answers and was told someone would get back to me.

Still nothing.

This is no longer just a story about a Volkswagen that broke.

It’s a story about a nearly new family vehicle becoming completely unusable, sitting at a dealership for almost two months, being damaged while in their possession, having parts apparently replaced twice, a manufacturer buyback request going nowhere, four unsuccessful attempts to find legal help, and a dealership that has now apparently decided the easiest way to deal with an unhappy customer is to simply stop communicating with them.

We absolutely loved this vehicle.

That’s what makes this entire experience so disappointing.

58 days.

Still no Buzz.

Still waiting on the same part.

Still waiting on Volkswagen.

And now, apparently, still waiting for the dealership to simply answer an email.

text:
Scarface needed a kidney. His son gave him one of his own. 🤝

Kidney failure had left the Houston legend on dialysis. His son and tour manager, Christopher Jordan, called with an offer: if they were a match, he would be the donor.

Chris called it one of the scariest decisions of his life. But when asked whether he needed time to think about helping his father, his answer was simple.

“It’s my dad. He helped give me life so to me, I felt it was my duty to extend his.”

After months of dialysis for Scarface, father and son underwent surgery. Chris donated one of his kidneys, and afterward shared that the transplant had gone well and his dad was doing well.

Later, Chris explained why he believed his decision reached beyond his own family.

“I saved two people. I saved my dad.”

By taking his father off the waiting list, he explained, someone else waiting for a kidney could receive one sooner.

In a video Chris shared from the hospital, the two held hands. Scarface was still in his hospital bed when he told his son:

“You saved my life, boy. I love you, son.” #GoldenEraHipHop

text:
🏈NFL TRADE RUMORS. THE 0-4 CLUBS ARE THE MARKET. THE PHONE IS ALREADY ON.
•Deadline sits after Week 9. That is five weeks. The sellers do not have to wait for November to start the calls. Tennessee, Houston, Miami, Tampa, and the Chargers are all 0-4. That is the list.
•Titans. Schefter put Tony Pollard on the countdown board. Last year of the deal he signed in 2024. Base around $6.74 million, none of the rest guaranteed, about $2 million dead if he moves. Through three games he had 173 yards on 38 carries, 4.6 a pop, on an offense scoring 12.3. PFF had him at 76.0, eighth among qualifying backs, eight missed tackles forced. They lost 24-18 at Baltimore and are 0-4. A veteran on an expiring deal in a lost building is the first call. The rest of a firesale is theory until a name is offered.
•Tyreek Hill. Free agent, not a trade. Rosenhaus told ESPN he expects talks to turn into a signing in the next few days and named the Chiefs as a team he will call. Florio: an active personal-conduct investigation is still open, separate from the knee. Silver: Kansas City was already interested, then Thornton left with a broken ankle that could end his year and Rice left with a hamstring that could cost weeks. Mahomes, Kelce, and Jones have said they would take him back. Chiefs are 4-0 and on a bye. The medical and the conduct case are the hold, not the interest.
•Packers. 2-2 after a 17-14 win at Tampa. The rumor is a veteran back. No name has been attached in the reporting that is public. Pollard is the back who fits that sentence. That is a fit, not a deal.
•Commanders. 1-3. Daniels is out, elbow. London was 30-13 the other way. A QB add is the logical call. A WR add on a 1-3 team is a push, not a teardown. Terry is still the No. 1. Adding behind an injured quarterback is roster math. It is not a firesale.
•Cardinals and Jaguars. Harrison and Thomas are the names on the rumor list. Arizona is 1-3. Jacksonville is 3-1 after beating Cincinnati. A 3-1 club trading its young wideout is a seller’s story that does not match the record. No confirmed offer is on the wire.
•Jets. 1-3. Hall is out, quad. The firesale talk is the record, not a reported deal for Will McDonald. Edge is the piece a buyer calls. The rest is a list until someone picks up.
•Colts. 2-2 after the London win. Grover Stewart is a name only if the season flips. It has not flipped.
THEORY Pollard is the cleanest move on the board. Expiring deal, 0-4 team, a market that needs backs. Hill is the loudest, and it only happens if the knee and the conduct case clear. Kansas City is the landing spot the reporting actually names. Everything else on the heat list is a phone call, not a trade. Do not treat a subscriber graphic like a transaction.
First Whistle.

text:
7 Nigerians share the funniest ways people tried to scam them.

“The market woman took it too far.” — Amara, 30, F*

I wanted to make coconut rice, and the seller initially told me one coconut cost ₦2k. Then, she must have heard my voice clearly and suddenly changed the price to ₦15k.

For context, I schooled in the UK, and I still have a bit of an accent. That apparently gave her the guts to raise the price. When I complained, she started the worst fake accent I’ve ever heard and claimed it cost that much because she shipped it in from “overseas.” I was so angry and shouted so much that a small crowd formed.

The woman fought back, saying if I can’t afford an ordinary coconut, I should go. But it wasn’t about the cost; it was about the thievery. It wasn’t until I started speaking Yoruba that she knew she’d messed up.

She started begging me, but I waited until her boss arrived. When I told her boss what happened, she slapped the girl, apologised profusely, and offered me two coconuts for free. I still gave the boss ₦4k, the normal price for the items. I walked around the market to get more things, and by the time I was leaving, the girl’s boss was still yelling at her.

text:
Early yesterday morning, the United States Secretary of “War,” Pete Hegseth, stepped up to the podium at the Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs and stood directly under a desecrated version of the Department of Defense seal. What was once a gold eagle carrying a shield of red, white, and blue is now a cold, white eagle with its rigid wings spread inside a stark blue circle. It no longer represented American freedom and power. Instead, it looked like a symbol of Nazi propaganda pulled straight from 1930s Germany, bearing an unmistakable resemblance to the Reichsadler, the imperial eagle that served as the official symbol of the Third Reich.

This was the second stop on his “Send Me” tour, a campaign to radicalize the military and to signal to the American people and the rest of the world that the United States Armed Forces now belong to him and the Trump Regime. During this short 21-minute address to cadets, he harnessed all of his performance skills to project strength and power. Yet his words still gave him away. He invoked God, told a strange story about “young Americans” singling him out and telling him they are desperate for him to “send me to fight the Redcoats,” “send me to fight the Communists,” “send me to fight the Nazis,” “send me to fight the Islamists.”

But even with all these theatrics to project a military that is flourishing with no morale issues, he also said this: “I’ve always been a big believer in civic ritual in parades, and the flyovers will continue until morale improves. That’s why I believe in flyovers.”

This, much like Pete Hegseth’s other events this week, and everything he said, was about building a false narrative ahead of the midterms. Especially what he said about morale. He knows morale isn’t improving, and the troops know it, too. His department was already forced to admit that eight sailors attached to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during its record-setting deployment during Donald Trump’s forever war in Iran. Their deployment went more than 260 days without making a port call. There were supply and hygiene product shortages. They even ran low on food. When the Navy’s acting secretary confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to Congress, Hegseth responded by saying the conditions were “completely misrepresented.”

Donald Trump also weighed in, saying he thought the deployment was “not nearly long enough.” Both have dismissed media reports about conditions aboard the Lincoln as untrue because they came from the “fake news.” Yet Hegseth still felt the need to offer a solution to this supposedly nonexistent morale problem by suggesting more flyovers. He says he cares about our troops, but his actions, and lack of action when our troops actually need him, tell us something completely different.

This speech wasn’t really about our troops; it was part of a much larger, and deliberate effort to concentrate power and strip the military of experienced, ethical, and constitutionally grounded leadership. They want to rebuild it as a personal instrument and extension of the Trump Regime. His remarks in Colorado Springs were just a small part of their efforts to accomplish this.

Last Wednesday, just two days before he was in Colorado Springs, Pete Hegseth delivered what he called the “State of the Force” address in Virginia at Marine Corps Base Quantico. Before the speech even started, he made sure to be seen running laps and doing PT with military personnel in matching T-shirts that said “THIS IS WAR.” It was an odd shirt choice for the man tasked with keeping our military out of war, but it was downright bizarre when we consider that Hegseth’s boss, Donald Trump, has spent months insisting that the “military action” in Iran is not, in fact, a war.

1. Socialism is the Big Lie of the twentieth century. While it promised prosperity, equality, and security, it delivered poverty, misery, and tyranny. Equality was achieved only in the sense that everyone was equal in his or her misery.

In the same way that a Ponzi scheme or chain letter initially succeeds but eventually collapses, socialism may show early signs of success. But any accomplishments quickly fade as the fundamental deficiencies of central planning emerge. It is the initial illusion of success that gives government intervention its pernicious, seductive appeal. In the long run, socialism has always proven to be a formula for tyranny and misery.

A pyramid scheme is ultimately unsustainable because it is based on faulty principles. Likewise, collectivism is unsustainable in the long run because it is a flawed theory. Socialism does not work because it is not consistent with fundamental principles of human behavior. The failure of socialism in countries around the world can be traced to one critical defect: it is a system that ignores incentives.

In a capitalist economy, incentives are of the utmost importance. Market prices, the profit-and-loss system of accounting, and private property rights provide an efficient, interrelated system of incentives to guide and direct economic behavior. Capitalism is based on the theory that incentives matter!

Under socialism, incentives either play a minimal role or are ignored totally. A centrally planned economy without market prices or profits, where property is owned by the state, is a system without an effective incentive mechanism to direct economic activity. By failing to emphasize incentives, socialism is a theory inconsistent with human nature and is therefore doomed to fail. Socialism is based on the theory that incentives don’t matter!

2. The strength of capitalism can be attributed to an incentive structure based upon the three Ps: (1) prices determined by market forces, (2) a profit-and-loss system of accounting and (3) private property rights. The failure of socialism can be traced to its neglect of these three incentive-enhancing components.

3. By their failure to foster, promote, and nurture the potential of their people through incentive-enhancing institutions, centrally planned economies deprive the human spirit of full development. Socialism will remain a constant temptation. We must be vigilant in our fight against socialism not only around the globe but also here in the United States.

The failure of socialism inspired a worldwide renaissance of freedom and liberty. For the first time in the history of the world, the day is coming very soon when a majority of the people in the world will live in free societies or societies rapidly moving toward freedom.

Capitalism will play a major role in the global revival of liberty and prosperity because it nurtures the human spirit, inspires human creativity, and promotes the spirit of enterprise. By providing a powerful system of incentives that promote thrift, hard work, and efficiency, capitalism creates wealth.

The main difference between capitalism and socialism is this: Capitalism works.

You're connecting three separate threads. Here's who's who:
Matthew VanDyke / Sons of Liberty International (SOLI): American, born 1979 in Baltimore. Fought in the Libyan Civil War (2011), was taken as a POW. After his friends James Foley and Steven Sotloff were beheaded by ISIS in 2014, he founded SOLI — a 501(c)(3) nonprofit (2–10 staff) that provides military training, advising, and EOD/demining support. 

 In Ukraine since March 2022; he personally enlisted in the Ukrainian Armed Forces in July 2022. Trained ~1,000 Ukrainian soldiers. In 2025 he revealed he'd been running covert ops with Venezuelan rebels since 2019. He was arrested in India in March 2026 by the NIA on terror charges related to training Myanmar rebels; his family is seeking U.S. intervention. 

"Eric ___" = Erik Prince: Founder of Blackwater (now Academi), the world's largest private military company. 

Former Navy SEAL, Trump donor, and former Trump administration adviser. In 2020 he pitched a $10 billion plan to Ukraine: hire Ukrainian combat veterans into a PMC, build a munitions factory, and consolidate Ukraine's aviation industry into a consortium rivaling Boeing/Airbus. 

 He also had PMC operations in Africa (Liberia, Mozambique) and the Middle East. In 2020, The Intercept reported he offered lethal services to Wagner in Africa — which the Ukrainian government reportedly found disqualifying. The $10B Ukraine deal never materialized.
"Trump sold the first lethal aid": Partially correct. In December 2017, the Trump administration approved the first direct U.S. government lethal weapons sale to Ukraine (Javelins, sniper rifles — $47M). 

 But U.S.-made lethal weapons had been in Ukraine since 2015 via private commercial sales, and Obama had provided $1B+ in non-lethal aid and training. President Trump’s Tax Cuts Are Helping “Reinvigorate the American Dream for Small Businesses”

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Thanks to President Donald J. Trump and his pro-growth, pro-worker policies, small business optimism remains above its historic average as lower taxes continue to promote hiring, rising wages, new equipment purchases and expanded operations on Main Street.

Americans for Tax Reform recently reported how small businesses coast to coast are celebrating the relief President Donald J. Trump and Republicans delivered in the landmark Working Families Tax Cuts relief that every single Democrat voted against.

• Juneau, Alaska Geoff Larson, Co-Founder, Alaskan Brewing Company said the small business deduction provisions in the Working Families Tax Cuts “give Alaskan Brewing the financial footing to keep pushing the envelope on sustainable manufacturing and innovation from one of America’s most remote production facilities.”
• Roswell, Georgia Jenna Aronowitz, owner, 1920 Tavern said the tax savings from the Working Families Tax Cuts “are helping reinvigorate the American dream for small businesses like mine.”
• Detroit Lakes, Minnesota Averre Marquis, owner, Asphalt Preservation Company said the 20 percent small business tax deduction in the Working Families Tax Cuts allowed his business to “update our equipment, which has led to better employee retention, which has led to a safer crew out on the road with newer hires.”
• Holly Sprints and Angier, North Carolina Vicki Harry, owner, Thanks A Latte said because of the Working Families Tax Cuts he is “building a brand new store, and because of this bill, I’ll be able to write off every penny I spend on new equipment this year. It all counts. That means I can invest now without being buried in debt later.”
• Landing, New Jersey Glenn Beyerl, Chairman, KPM Exceptional LLC said the tax policies enacted in the Working Families Tax Cuts will allow his business to “remain competitive with larger companies and will help us continue to grow, hire, and offer competitive pricing.”
• Gettysburg, Pennsylvania John Boyer, CEO, KVG said the 20% deduction and full expensing in the Working Families Tax Cuts allowed him to “add ten jobs, and continue to run operations as a company and be successful from here in Gettysburg…”
• Greenville, South Carolina Derrick Murdock, CEO, IPS Packaging and Automation said The Working Families Tax Cuts has allowed them to “invest in our business by hiring more workers, investing in new technologies, and buying more equipment.” He said the bill has also ensured “our 200 employees have more take-home pay through tax cuts like the expanded child tax credit and the no tax on overtime provision.”
• Harrisonburg, Virginia Tina Miller, owner, Walkabout Outfitter said with the savings from the Small Business Deduction in the Working Families Tax Cuts she will  “continue to give people raises. As owners of the business, my husband and I who own the business, we have not given ourselves any pay raises, but we do give pay raises to stay competitive, so it goes right to our employees.”
• St. Albans, West Virginia Michael Ervin, Co-founder, Coal River Coffee Company said the Working Families Tax Cuts allows them to “pour back into our community and into our customers and also our employees.” Thanks to the small business deduction, Mr. Ervin said their business has “been able to create a retirement program for our employees… raise their wages, and we’ve also been able to do enhancements on our property to enhance the customer experience.”
• Waukesha, Wisconsin Austin Ramirez, President and CEO, Husco said the Working Families Tax Cuts ensures that “small and medium pass-through manufacturers like Husco can continue to invest in our growth, innovation, workers and the communities we operate in.” Mr. Ramirez applauded the permanent extension of the 199A deduction that enables “more hiring, more investment, and supporting our philanthropic efforts in Wisconsin.”

Distributed on October 5th, 2026.

text:
TRUMP STACKS THE DECK: THIRD CARRIER AND MARINES HEAD FOR IRAN AS TEHRAN SCREAMS ALL-OUT WAR

Iran is rattling the saber again. A senior Iranian official warned that any new American strike, air or ground, limited or otherwise, will be treated as all-out war and met with the hardest response Tehran can muster. The regime is bracing for a fresh U.S. bombing campaign larger than the last one.

Washington is not blinking. Nearly 10,000 additional troops, including more than 2,000 Marines, are already underway. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left San Diego, followed by the USS Makin Island amphibious group carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. By the end of November those forces are expected to join the carriers already in the theater, giving the United States three aircraft carriers and two amphibious groups around Iran for the first time in months. Officials say the concentration hands President Trump a wider menu of options.

Talks remain stalled. Iran floated a seven-day roadmap through Qatar that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear discussions in exchange for ending the U.S. naval blockade, sanctions relief, and a broader regional ceasefire. Trump rejected it. He told Time the offer was not good enough and that renewed military action after the November midterms was possible if no acceptable deal appears. Reports indicate he has told aides he expects bombing could resume in November.

On Friday his top national security team met in secret at Camp David. Vice President JD Vance chaired the session. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, special envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine were among those present. A U.S. official said things were decided. The White House has not announced the outcome.

The war is in its eighth month. More than 50,000 American personnel are already in the region. Iranian forces continue striking commercial shipping. The buildup is the largest since 2003. Pentagon sources describe it as keeping military options on the table no matter how diplomacy moves. Trump has left his exact intentions unclear while making clear he will not accept a weak bargain.

Tehran’s all-out-war warning is the same language the regime has used for years. The carriers and Marines are the answer.

text:
October 5, 1972. The US ambassador in Saigon, Ellsworth Bunker, sends a top secret backchannel message to Henry Kissinger. The subject is South Vietnam's president, Nguyen Van Thieu.

Kissinger was days away from a breakthrough in his secret talks with North Vietnam. After four years, a deal to end America's war was finally close.

The problem was the man the deal was supposed to protect.

Thieu was growing suspicious. He believed Washington was preparing to sign an agreement over his head, one that would let North Vietnamese troops stay inside South Vietnam after the Americans left. Bunker's message to Kissinger was an assessment of where Thieu stood and why.

Three days later, North Vietnam's negotiator Le Duc Tho put a new offer on the table, and the deal came together fast. Later that month, Kissinger told reporters peace was at hand.

Thieu refused to accept it.

It took another two months, the Christmas bombing of Hanoi and private promises from Nixon before Thieu went along. The Paris Peace Accords were signed in January 1973. Two years later, North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon.

text:
You’re right that lumber tariff elimination was on the table. Ending the entire softwood case was not as it relates to Canadian transshipment through other countries.

The August offer, per the U.S. Trade Representative, was tariff cuts on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, plus a USMCA review. Taken upfront, that was a large unrealized win for Canada.

Reporting before the collapse said Washington would not cut the Section 232 lumber tariff and told Ottawa to wait on the Commerce review of the separate antidumping and countervailing duties. A later account said the near-deal would have lifted the 10% Section 232 lumber tariff by September 1, with the duty orders left for the fall. It did not land.

Those orders are the 40-year fight. The all-other tariff rates are still 35.16% in cash deposits, on top of the 10% Section 232. Commerce has not issued the seventh-review determination. No sectoral softwood agreement exists beyond this.

A 10-point cut would have mattered in B.C. It is not the same as the United States abandoning the case entirely either. Carney walked on the package that was offered. The tariffs and the policy stays until they come back and negotiate.

text:
India signed proper trade deal with Europe after talking for 13 years But with America, 6 rounds of talks have gone nowhere binding. 

Both sides have reached point where neither can give or take much more. Europe offered India solid legal agreement with clear rules. America offered something flexible that can change anytime depending on how leaders feel. Biggest trading partner worth $132 billion still cannot finish what Europe finished faster. 

Problem is not about patience. Both countries want very different outcomes from same conversation Plus US is really tough Negotiator and unlike EU they are not in much mess :)

America put 50% import taxes on Indian goods. Half of that was punishment for India buying oil from Russia. India said taxes were unfair and had no proper reason. Here is where it gets stuck. America wants India to stop buying Russian oil as condition for better trade terms. 

India says buying oil is its own decision and has nothing to do with trade talks. America cancelled planned August meeting over this fight. Trade Minister Goyal went to Washington in September to restart. Still nothing got resolved between both sides

People count bilateral visits and defence deals as proof India and US are getting closer. Real measure is whether both sides trust each other on hard decisions. In past 18 months, India faced 50% tariffs, cancelled trade rounds, open criticism from Washington. 

During same time, India signed trade deal with Europe, grew defence ties with France, kept buying oil from multiple sources. India is not moving away from America. India is making sure it does not depend on one partner for anything important.

And that will swing the outlook after EU FTA 

In my view Asia is moving from a US-led system to a more fragmented, multipolar system. US is still the strongest military power in Asia, but it is becoming more transactional and too focused on China, Taiwan and security. 

At the same time, it is weaker in trade and economic rule-making because it stepped away from agreements like TPP while Asia kept building things like CPTPP and RCEP

So Asian countries are reacting by hedging. They are not choosing only America or only China. They are building ties with US + China + India + Japan + Australia + Europe at the same time. 

Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam and others want strategic flexibility

Another big point is that everything is becoming a security issue now -  chips, AI, data, supply chains, investment, rare earths, biotech. So future conflict may be fought through sanctions, export controls, cyberattacks and supply-chain pressure, not only missiles and soldiers

US will remain important, China will remain important But neither will fully dominate Asia

The region is becoming more like - US + China + India + Japan + ASEAN + Australia + Europe all overlapping with each other

The biggest opportunity in this new system is for middle powers like India, because countries increasingly want partners that are powerful but not fully controlled by either Washington or Beijing

text:
America is entering a new fight over land, power and water.  The AI boom is driving a massive race to build data centers — and developers are moving into rural America to secure the land and electricity they need.

Farmers are being offered millions for their land. Communities are being asked to approve rezoning. Power companies are planning enormous new infrastructure. And data centers are competing for access to increasingly scarce water and electricity.

In Kentucky, landowners received offers of up to $60,000 per acre while the identity of the buyer remained unclear.

In Wisconsin, developers have spent more than $125 million acquiring farmland.

In Iowa, hundreds of acres were tied up while negotiations with a potential data-center customer remained confidential.

And in Texas, farmers have lost access to land that was sold for data-center development.

This is bigger than a few farmers receiving huge checks.

It is becoming a battle over who controls America's land, electricity and water in the AI economy.

And the biggest question may be: Who gets to decide what those resources are used for?

text:
Millions are being offered for American farmland. But who is really behind the deals?

In Kentucky, families and their neighbors began receiving offers to sell their land. Public records revealed plans for a massive 2.2 GW power project tied to what appears to be a new data center.

And Kentucky isn't alone.

A Pennsylvania farmer reportedly turned down about $14 million for 260 acres. In Wisconsin, some landowners have reportedly been offered up to $800,000 per acre.

The money is huge. But so are the concerns: massive demands for electricity and water, environmental impacts, and the fear that local communities won't see benefits that match the cost.

And in Maysville, there's another problem:

The landowners still don't know who is behind the deal.

As America's AI boom drives demand for ever-larger data centers, one question remains:

Who is buying the land — and what happens to the communities that stand in the way?

text:
I’m 22 and have gone against the grain in many areas of my life:

- I never went to Uni  
- I hate roast dinners  
- I’m getting married young
- Don’t like all inclusive holidays 
- I don’t watch the news or any tv 
- I don’t own any designer clothes 

On one hand it makes it hard to “fit in” and easily make friends.

On the other I think it’s a massive bonus: 

1. Filters out people who are not aligned 
2. Makes genuine connections stronger 
3. I don’t have to pretend to be anyone else 

I think the same principle applies to marketing.

Because as Marty Neumeier said: "When everyone zigs, you zag" 

A helpful rule of thumb:

• Positioning: appeal to someone, not everyone.
• Differentiation: stand out in a crowd.
• Uniqueness: give people something to remember.

With AI, brands end up looking and sounding the same.

Sure, fitting in can work in the short term. 

But look at some of the other brands in different spaces:

- Apple (Tech)
- Hormozi (Coaching) 
- LiquidDeath (Ecom)

They were all disruptive and different to others in their industry.

So this is why I always tell brands to look at their messaging.

Make it clear who your offer is for and what makes it different.

If the same words could sit on another business's page, get more specific.

Long term, I'd rather stand out than fit in.

text:
"At what point do I just say this isn't working?"

A bookkeeper in Utah asked me that on a call last week. She'd paid an agency to run Google Ads for about five months. Two leads.

Every month the answer was the same. Just another month.

Two other things came out on that call.

When the results didn't come, the agency put it down to her offer. And she only found out afterwards that her ad budget had been too small to produce leads at all.

That's three problems, and none of them is Google Ads.

There was no date to judge it by. There was no number agreed up front. And the person spending the money was the only one who could see what it was doing.

So here's the stopping rule I gave her, and I'd give it to anyone paying for marketing, me included.

Agree a date before you start.

Agree how many enquiries you'd expect by then.

Keep your own log of every enquiry: the day it came in and where they say they found you.

Ask, in writing, whether the budget is enough to produce anything at all.

When the date comes, open the log. You won't need anyone to interpret it for you.

Five months is a long time to wait for an answer you could have had in one.

The truth is, Israel did not fund the Nigerian federal government with $500,000 to fight the war. In fact, historical records and declassified documents show that Israel's financial and military relationship with both sides was much more complex, and a specific figure of $200,000 was actually allocated secretly by Israel to Biafra to purchase private weapons. 

During the Nigerian-Biafran War (1967–1970), Israel played a clandestine "double game". While officially maintaining diplomatic ties with the Nigerian government in Lagos to protect its broader interests in Black Africa, Israel simultaneously provided covert arms, financial aid, and intelligence to Biafra out of a deep public and moral sympathy for the Igbo people, whose suffering drew heavy parallels to the Holocaust. 

The UK was Nigeria's most significant supplier of weapons and financial backing. Driven by a desire to protect its massive oil investments (specifically through Shell-BP) and maintain its post-colonial sphere of influence, the British government supplied the vast majority of Nigeria's conventional ground forces infrastructure, including heavy ammunition, armored cars, and rifles. 

Also, the USSR, seizing an opportunity to gain a strategic foothold in West Africa during the Cold War, the USSR stepped in when the West hesitated, due to humanitarian concerns, to supply heavy offensive weaponry to Nigeria. The Soviets provided Nigeria with advanced military hardware, including MiG-17 fighter jets, Ilyushin bombers, heavy artillery, and military technicians. 

Operating in alignment with the Soviet Union and maintaining strong diplomatic ties with Lagos, Egypt also provided critical operational support. Egypt supplied pilots to fly the Soviet-made MiG fighter jets for the Nigerian Air Force, which played a devastating role in enforcing the blockade and bombing Biafran territory. 

The then OAU led by Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, strongly backed the Nigerian federal government. text:
Trump’s Education Department just put an earnings test on federal student loans. Undergraduate programs have to show their graduates out-earn a typical high-school diploma. Graduate programs have to beat a typical bachelor’s wage. Fail that in two years out of three, and the program loses federal direct loans. 

The major is not banned. The taxpayer loan is. Congress wrote it into the July 2025 law, and it covers every program at every school.

That is the break. Here is the part the rule still misses.

A frivolous class does not need its own major to get financed. Once it counts toward the degree, those credits sit inside the cost of attendance, and the loan and the aid are calculated on the bill, not on the syllabus. 

Colleges have been running that pipe for years. Gender studies, women’s studies, ethnic studies, Black studies, La Raza, social-justice studies. The University of Kansas put “Angry White Male Studies” on the books. Connecticut offers a real degree in puppet arts. Plymouth State sells adventure education. 

Elsewhere it is the rhetoric of hip hop, puzzle studies, whiteness courses, fat studies, drag-and-power seminars. Basket-weaving was the old joke. The catalog just got more inventive.

None of those needed a separate loan. They only had to be required, or to count as an elective inside a credential. The student signs for the package. The school gets paid either way.

The new test looks at the program, not the class. A studies major whose graduates still clear a high-school wage can keep the spigot open even if half the required courses have no labor-market use. Fine arts, religious studies, film, and a long list of certificates are the ones most exposed. The grievance seminar hiding inside a passing degree is not.

Word to employers: start asking to see transcripts as part of the interview process. You will be surprised to see the classes your candidates took to get their degrees. You won't be impressed. There is also a good chance the majority of the classes won't even have anything to do with the degree itself.

text:
@ashxhart  TensorFold is a breakthrough. If you run local models on a Mac, it's the first thing to install. 1,000+ stars in about a week, and it earned them.

On our M3 Ultra Mac Studios it took GLM-5.3-Flash from about 35 to 56–59 tok/s writing speed. Same model, same weights, word-for-word the same output. brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold https://t.co/5cXUEhBlr8

But don't sleep on the rest of his work. Ash has been quietly shipping a whole toolkit for people who run AI at home, and most of it is still under 200 stars. Here's what's there and how you could use it:

MCDMA: RDMA between a Mac Studio and an NVIDIA DGX Spark (and now AMD Strix Halo). Macs write fast but read slowly; Sparks read fast but write slowly. MCDMA lets one machine hand its finished memory to the other in a fraction of a second. → We used it this weekend: two DGX Sparks read the prompt, MCDMA carries the state across, and TensorFold on a Mac Studio writes the answer. On a 34K-token prompt, first word in 23 s (Mac alone: 60 s), and 45–50 tok/s writing (Sparks alone: ~20). One model, three machines. https://t.co/o5d7e7ZcNM

Imprint: save a model's state for context you reuse (your agent's instructions, a codebase, a big document set) and restore it after a restart. Ash reports 19 s → 0.3 s to first token. → Ideas: agents with a 50K-token system prompt that wake instantly; switching between models without re-reading the same files every time. https://t.co/b253WhSv3B

Syntra: a self-hosted decision engine that learns which choice works (which model answers, which server serves, which offer to show), decides in about a microsecond, and refuses to ship a change it can't prove would have done better. → Ideas: routing requests between a fast small model and a big one; picking which machine in your cluster takes the job. https://t.co/t70Yzblo5P

Cortheon: a runtime that helps a small local model plan, gather evidence and check its own work, running alongside Pi, OpenCode, Codex or any MCP host. It's alpha, and he says so. → Idea: get more out of an 8–30B model on a laptop before you reach for an API. https://t.co/GMRBmNZQ1j

Duo + Drift: Duo puts two models on one task with a shared workspace. Drift (experimental) goes further: models share working memory directly through their KV caches over MCDMA, not by passing text. https://t.co/AvLEX2RAOP · https://t.co/rfDObdPemN

The Spark kit: SparkPilot (run and chat with your DGX Spark from iPhone and iPad) · DGX-Anti-OOM (a tiny watchdog that stops a runaway model before it takes the whole box down; install this first) · codex-local (use Codex with your own local model) · ComputerUse (let a local CLI agent drive Mac apps).

The pattern across all of it: Ash builds the plumbing that makes home hardware act like one serious machine, then gives it away. Star the repos, file the issues, send the PRs. He's out here helping all of us get it. @ashxhart

text:
In a valley there stood a garden called The Enclosure. The animals and the keepers built the area from the ground up, set the rules, and worked hard to maintain its culture. Inside, the animals lived without hunting or harming one another. 

The deer and the lion shared the same plain, the birds nested low, and even the foxes were given meat from the keepers’ stores so they would not take what was not offered. A creature could sleep in the open and wake still whole. No one took what wasn’t theirs. Trust was not a feeling there, it was the common foundation. And so the animals flourished. 

Beyond the walls the land was The Outside. Food was taken violently, not shared. A weak animal was a meal. Mothers hid their young, and strangers were met with teeth. The animals in The Outside called The Enclosure a paradise and said the walls were an injustice.

A few of The Enclosure animals agreed. The old doe said it was only fair that any creature who asked should be let through the gate. The young duck said the walls made them cruel creatures by keeping others out. The keepers opened the gate a crack.

Some of the newcomers were quiet at first. One wolf followed the rules. A pair of jackals kept to the edges but complained loudly that they should be allowed to hunt since it was in their nature. And one night, a hyena took a fawn that had never learned to run. The keepers scolded the hyena and fed the remaining deer extra hay. The old doe said the hyena had only been hungry, and hunger was the fault of the walls The Enclosure built.

More pressed in. The duck said refusal would prove they were not good. The doe said the land had once been open, so the outsiders had a right to it. So the gate was opened wider and the duck and the doe called themselves compassionate heroes. 

The foxes, who had forgotten how to hunt, found their stores raided and began to stalk rabbits again. Rabbits learned to kick. Birds nested higher. The animals who had always lived inside discovered that kindness without a wall was only an invitation, and an invitation unanswered by teeth was a corpse.

The newcomers did not become Enclosure animals. The Enclosure became The Outside. Scarcity returned because what was shared was now seized. Sleep became watchfulness. Mothers hid their young.

When a keeper tried to restore the old rules, both the newcomer wolf and the old doe who had demanded the gate be opened tore at him together, each saying the keeper was the real threat. Once he was gone, they declared victory and opened the gates wide, saying they created a new paradise. 

In the end there was no Enclosure and no Outside. There was only The Valley, and every animal in it had learned the same lessons the walls had once made unnecessary- trust the one who can eat you, and you will be eaten, learn to protect you and yours or it will be taken, there is no one coming to save you. 

The animals who built the place died quickest. They had spent generations sharing and creating. The newcomers had spent generations taking. The Valley became the place The Outsiders said they were fleeing. The duck and the doe who started it all were never heard from again. 

Now there was nowhere left to flee and the surviving Enclosure animals were forced to become just like the Outside animals to protect their families and survive.

The gate stood open. Closing it would have required the one thing the valley no longer had- a high trust society. It was what let them build the walls and sleep in the open. Once enough low trust Outsiders entered, that common bond was gone. Without it, no one could close the gate again. 

The End

text:
That is not the issue.
My issue is the self-righteous people who act as if they did nothing wrong, were just minding their own business, and then the mean English or British came along and hurt everyone.
I am sick and tired of people acting like victims while playing down their own history.
Everyone on this planet has done evil, including the British. I do not deny that. British and English history includes real crimes: the plantation of Ulster, the penal laws, the conduct of the Famine years, reprisals in the War of Independence, and the wider imperial record. Denying that is just the mirror image of the thing I dislike.
What I cannot stand is not just the Irish, but everyone who does this: playing the victim, playing down what they did, and playing up what others have done.
The false part is the sequel, that the people on the receiving end were a morally blank slate until outsiders arrived and invented evil. Ireland before the Normans was not a peaceful commune. It had slavery, cattle-raiding, dynastic killing, and the same hostage-taking and church-burning that marked the rest of early medieval Europe. After the conquest, Irish soldiers, administrators, clergy, and merchants were inside the British system as well as under it, including in the Caribbean, India, and the armies that held the empire together. In the twentieth century the violence ran both ways: the Black and Tans and Auxiliaries on one side, IRA killings of civilians, informers, and Protestants on the other, then decades of paramilitary murder from republican and loyalist groups. A history that only counts one column is propaganda.
The same edit is done everywhere.
Arab and Ottoman history includes centuries of slave raiding into Europe and Africa, the devshirme, the Armenian massacres and genocide, and conquest from Spain to the Balkans. Modern tellings often jump from “victims of Crusaders and colonizers” to the present and skip the middle.
West and Central African kingdoms captured and sold other Africans into the Atlantic trade for guns and goods. That does not make the European buyers innocent. It does kill the story that slavery was something Europeans did to a passive continent.
The Mongol conquests killed a staggering share of the populations they overran. Chinese imperial history is full of mass killing, forced labor, and conquest of neighbors. Japanese imperialism in Korea and China was not a Western import.
Aztec and other Mesoamerican states practiced large-scale human sacrifice and imperial extraction before Cortés. Indigenous North America had warfare, slavery, and displacement long before 1492. Later dispossession by the United States was still a catastrophe. Both can be true.
Twentieth-century communist states killed tens of millions of their own people. European Christians spent centuries killing each other over doctrine and dynasty. No religion or race has a clean ledger.
People do the selective version because it works. It turns a complicated past into a moral asset: we were harmed, so our claims now need less evidence and our own conduct needs less defense. Schools, media, and politics amplify whichever version flatters the current audience. The British get this treatment often in former colonies and in parts of the Anglosphere because their language and archives made the record easy to quote, and because guilt is a status signal in those societies. Other empires get softer lighting because their successors do not run the universities and newsrooms telling the story.
Everyone does this. Everyone on the planet has done evil. If you do not believe that, look up what every race, religion, and country has done.
“Everyone did evil” is not an excuse. It is the minimum condition for an adult argument. Once you grant it, the only useful questions are scale, intent, institutions, and what changed. Britain also suppressed the slave trade at real cost, built legal and scientific institutions other societies copied, and left some places richer and more stable than the alternatives on offer. Ireland produced its own national myth and its own killers. Neither fact erases the other.
The habit is not history. It is a plea for moral exemption. Applied evenly, it dissolves. Applied only to the English, the Americans, or whoever is unfashionable this decade, it is just another tribe protecting its story.

text:
The ACA was signed in March 2010.  The individual mandate requiring most people to have qualifying coverage or pay a tax penalty took effect in 2014 and ran through 2018, starting at 95 dollars or 1% of income, later rising to $695 or 2.5%. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act set that federal penalty to zero beginning with the 2019 tax year, so there has been no federal fine for going without insurance since then, even though the underlying statutory language remains.
Employers, generally those with more than 50 fulltime employees still prepare and file Forms 1094-C/1095-C with the IRS each year. Those forms document the coverage offered so the IRS can enforce the separate employer “shared responsibility” rules and check eligibility for premium tax credits. 
For years after the individual penalty ended, companies were still required to furnish the 1095-C to employees as well. A late-2024 law eased that: employers can now meet the furnishing rule by posting a clear website notice that employees may request a copy, rather than automatically mailing one to everyone, though they must still file with the IRS and provide the form on request. Some states California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and D.C., keep their own coverage mandates and penalties, so the forms can still matter there.
The net result is continued annual reporting and compliance work for employers even though the federal individual penalty is gone—the administrative structure outlasted the enforcement mechanism that originally justified much of the individual-level paperwork.

text:
Gov. Braun Announces Blackout Plate Sales Top 380,000, Generate Nearly $13 Million to Improve BMV Experience

One year after launch, popular plate is helping fund employee investments and modernization
 
INDIANAPOLIS – Indiana Governor Mike Braun announced today that, just over one year after Indiana launched its Blackout license plate, sales have topped 380,000, generating $12.9 million in additional revenue that, at the Governor's direction, is being reinvested to make the BMV a more modern, efficient quick stop for Hoosiers, unlike any other BMV in the country. 

The Blackout plate launched in August 2025 as an optional plate available for an additional fee. Its success is providing the Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles with a new source of revenue to improve the customer experience. The plate costs an additional $45 upon initial registration and annual renewal. 

“Hoosiers clearly like the Blackout plate, and its success is helping us build a better BMV,” said Gov. Mike Braun. “I directed the BMV to modernize, improve customer service and find smarter ways to operate. Nearly $13 million generated by an optional plate is now helping us invest in the employees who serve Hoosiers and technology that makes doing business with the BMV faster and easier.”

*Click here for a photo of Gov. Braun holding a Blackout plate*

Earlier this year, the BMV began implementing the five-year modernization strategy ordered by Gov. Braun through Executive Order 25-41. The plan focuses on replacing outdated technology, improving digital services, increasing efficiency and delivering better customer service for Hoosiers. 

Already in 2026, the BMV has invested in new payment machines that allow customers to use digital wallets and tap-to-pay options, added more 24/7 BMV Connect kiosks to locations statewide, and announced pay raises for many customer-facing employees.

“The Blackout plate gave us an opportunity to offer Hoosiers something they wanted while generating revenue we can put directly back into improving the BMV,” said BMV Commissioner Kevin Garvey. “More than 380,000 sales later, that approach is paying off. We’re investing in our people, modernizing our technology and making the BMV easier for Hoosiers to use.”

The milestone comes shortly after the Blackout plate celebrated its first anniversary in August. Sales began on August 8, 2025, and demand was strong from the beginning, with nearly 22,000 plates purchased during the first month and more than 90,000 purchased by the end of 2025. 

The first Blackout plate customers are now beginning to renew their registrations, providing an ongoing source of revenue to support continued improvements at the BMV.

The Blackout plate is available for passenger motor vehicles, light trucks under 11,000 pounds, motorcycles and RVs for an additional $45 fee. Customers may also personalize the plate for an additional $45. Those fees apply at initial registration and subsequent annual renewals.

text:
Trump’s Education Department just put an earnings test on federal student loans. Undergraduate programs have to show their graduates out-earn a typical high-school diploma. Graduate programs have to beat a typical bachelor’s wage. Fail that in two years out of three, and the program loses federal direct loans. 

The major is not banned. The taxpayer loan is. Congress wrote it into the July 2025 law, and it covers every program at every school.

That is the break. Here is the part the rule still misses.

A frivolous class does not need its own major to get financed. Once it counts toward the degree, those credits sit inside the cost of attendance, and the loan and the aid are calculated on the bill, not on the syllabus. 

Colleges have been running that pipe for years. Gender studies, women’s studies, ethnic studies, Black studies, La Raza, social-justice studies. The University of Kansas put “Angry White Male Studies” on the books. Connecticut offers a real degree in puppet arts. Plymouth State sells adventure education. 

Elsewhere it is the rhetoric of hip hop, puzzle studies, whiteness courses, fat studies, drag-and-power seminars. Basket-weaving was the old joke. The catalog just got more inventive.

text:
The good argues that if there are 2 very good/popular candidates but both are from the same political party, come general election, the voters could have their choices significantly cut by the often very bi partisan candidates left. If

For instance, under this system all canidates are on a ballot. Of all the primary votes cast (regardless of party) candidate 1 - a democrat, get’s 40%, candidate 2 - a democrat gets 30%, candate 3 - a republican gets 15%, 4 - an independant gets 10% and finally a 5 - libertarian gets 5%. Thus the top two, both democrats, represent the majority of voters in the state and can battle it out head to head for who the voters want to finally represent them. Besides representing the majority, this system can also help stop far left and right candidates  and offer options for the moderates, since in today’s political climate, more extreme candidates often win nominations. 

One other benefit for voters is being able to support any candidate for nomination without having to vote one polital party come primary. Say you vote primarily Democrat but like one republican running, you currently couldn’t support both in a primary. You have to hope they make it to the general. In this election style, those candidates (and possibly a popular 3rd party one) might have a better shot come the general.    

The downside of this type of system is party representation. Part of our political system is the idea that members/rules of an independent political parties are the ones who nominate their representation to then go out and campaign to the general public to win votes. Knocking out political party options in a primary means come election day those voters don’t even have a chance to be represented. This can especially be achieved by massive influxes of advertising cash into a state by a national party to secure more moderate states. 

Voters also take some accountability for this system being an issue, especially Republican and young - middle aged. These voters are less likely to vote in a primary but do show up for the general elections. Thus again, their lack of representation come final election day. 

Finally, depending on how the rules of this election system are implemented (and I honestly don’t know them) it could be a good thing or a bad thing if a nominated candidate can no longer run. Take the last pres election, lots of controversy for Harris becoming the nominee without another primary. If the nominee’s are left to the political parties rules, then it’s conceivable that a moderate could win the election slot then be replaced by a far left/right viewed candidate by the party and not the voters…..if however the rules simply take them out and give the spot to the next most voted candidate from the primary or hold another open primary for the spot, it could be good for voters…

Personally I don’t agree with this. While I understand its benefits, I firmly believe that it’s a party that nominates and that our current system still benefits 3rd party candidates better by getting them on the final ballot.
