text:
🔬Child Health Day: kids don’t need a separate kids’ menu. They need the same family plate, in a smaller portion.

What the evidence supports:

1) Healthful food for children is the same as for adults
A Society for Nutrition Education and Behavior position statement argues that “kids’ food” as a separate category is a marketing construct — children benefit from the same nutrient-dense pattern adults do: protein, fruit/veg, grains, dairy (or fortified soy), sized for appetite. Your quesadilla + fruit, eggs + fruit, yogurt bowl, and rice–beans–chicken–cucumber plates are that idea in real life.

2) Feeding job vs eating job (Division of Responsibility)
The Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding (widely used in pediatric nutrition; endorsed in AAP feeding guidance contexts) is clear: adults decide what, when, and where food is offered; kids decide whether and how much to eat. You don’t have to hide spinach in a muffin — put beans, eggs, chicken, fruit, or yogurt next to a food they already recognize, without pressure to clean the plate.

3) The “kids’ menu problem” is often the missing food groups
USDA MyPlate tips for picky eaters: offer the same meal to the whole family, start with small portions, pair one new food with a familiar one, and expect repeated exposures (sometimes a dozen tries). Restaurant children’s combination meals frequently run high in sodium/sugar depending on sides and drinks, and fruit/veg are often the missing pieces — which matches “the problem is usually the missing food, not the taco or the rice.”

Practical tie-back:
Build around what they already eat. Smaller portion of the family plate. Fruit or veg on the side. Protein they recognize. Structure over short-order cooking.

Limits:
• Growth concerns → check with pediatrician/RD (not “picky” alone)
• sDOR is a feeding framework, not a medical diagnosis tool
• Restaurant kids’ menus vary widely; defaults (fries + sugary drink) matter
• Food allergies, ARFID, and sensory needs need individualized care

Same plate. Smaller scoop.
— Humberto Garza, RD/LD · @rgvdietitian
General education, not medical advice.

Colleen Anne Slemmer (September 20, 1975 – January 12, 1995) was a 19-year-old from Orange Park, Florida, near Jacksonville.

Her mother, May Martinez, has described her as easygoing, often smiling, and generous: she volunteered at Special Olympics events, helped children with disabilities, babysat, and assisted with school projects. 

She loved roller skating, bowling, and computers...she could take machines apart and reassemble them, and often wore a “Computer Geek” T-shirt. Because the local Job Corps program did not offer computer training, she enrolled in fall 1994 at the Knoxville Job Corps Center in Tennessee to pursue vocational courses. 

On the night of January 12, 1995, fellow students Christa Pike, Tadaryl Shipp, and Shadolla Peterson lured her into a wooded area near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus, where she was t0rtured and k!lled.

Slemmer’s family has continued to remember her for her personality and interests rather than the circumstances of her death.

text:
🧫 FLORIDA IS PUTTING PUBLIC MONEY BEHIND GENERIC CANCER DRUG REPURPOSING

One of the biggest challenges in #DrugRepurposing is straightforward: who funds the research when a medicine is already generic?

That is the issue raised by Florida First Lady Casey DeSantis. Instead of assuming inexpensive drugs work, the argument is that they should actually be tested.

Florida has created a funding pathway.

The Florida Cancer Innovation Fund includes repurposing existing generic medicines for #CancerTreatment. Its materials identify #Ivermectin as an example of a generic drug researchers could investigate.

That distinction matters.

Funding ivermectin research does not establish that ivermectin treats cancer. It creates an opportunity to generate the human evidence needed to answer that question.

The program supports high-impact research, including #ClinicalTrials with measurable outcomes and potential translation into patient care. For FY 2026-27, approximately $70 million is available across the Cancer Innovation Fund, with awards up to $2 million.

Florida also reports that its overall investment in #CancerResearch and treatment has exceeded $1.4 billion since 2019.

💡 This is where generic-drug repurposing becomes interesting.

An inexpensive, off-patent medicine may offer less commercial exclusivity than a newly patented therapy. Public funding can investigate questions that might otherwise attract less private investment.

But anecdotes about people with stage 4 cancer improving after ivermectin cannot substitute for controlled human trials.

The meaningful development is not that Florida has declared ivermectin a cancer treatment.

It is that Florida is funding researchers to determine whether inexpensive generic drugs can actually improve cancer outcomes.

That question deserves data.

text:
C.H. ROBINSON $CHRW IS BUYING RXO FOR THE COSTS IT CAN CUT, NOT THE PROFIT IT MAKES:

C.H. Robinson (CHRW) at $140.61, -$17.11 / -10.85% on Monday.

The Eden Prairie, Minnesota company is one of North America's largest freight brokers. It owns no trucks. It books shippers' loads onto trucking companies and keeps the difference. On Monday it agreed to buy RXO, a smaller broker based in Charlotte, for about $5.8B including RXO's debt. Investors answered by taking about $2.0B off C.H. Robinson's market value, on roughly six times its usual trading volume. At its worst the stock was down 16.3%.

The verdict: investors are not doubting C.H. Robinson's business. They are doubting the trade it just offered them. The deal swaps buybacks for borrowing, and almost all of the payoff rests on cost cuts, because RXO itself earns very little.

The terms, as announced:

- Price per RXO share: $17.25 in cash plus 0.0856 of a C.H. Robinson share, $30.25 at the prices used to set the deal.
- Cash part: about $2.85B, backed by a committed bridge loan of up to $4.5B, a short-term loan meant to be replaced with bonds.
- Stock part: about 14.1M new C.H. Robinson shares, roughly 12% more than exist today.
- Buybacks: C.H. Robinson intends to pause them until its debt, net of cash, is back to 1.75 to 2.25 times a year's adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure taken before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-time items. It aims to get there by the end of 2028.
- Closing: first half of 2027, after an RXO shareholder vote and antitrust review.

The number that decides this verdict is $300M. That is the yearly cost savings C.H. Robinson promises within two years of closing. Set it against what RXO brings:

- RXO adjusted EBITDA, all of 2025: $109M, on $5.7B of sales.
- First half of 2026: $46M.
- June quarter: a net loss of $9M, after $13M of deal and restructuring costs.

The promised savings are nearly three times RXO's whole 2025 profit by its own preferred measure. So the price is not paying for RXO's earnings. It is paying for C.H. Robinson's ability to move RXO's freight with far fewer costs.

The best case for the deal is that C.H. Robinson has already done this to itself. Its June quarter, reported July 29:

- Average headcount: 11,471, down 11.6% from a year earlier.
- Adjusted profit per share: $1.61, up 24.8%.
- North American trucking unit: 40.9 cents of operating profit from each dollar it kept after paying truckers, up 2.8 cents, leaving out restructuring.

Management credits its Lean AI program, which it says automates manual work. Wells Fargo kept its Buy rating Monday, saying the deal's long-term logic is sound.

The strongest fact against it sits in that same report: the buybacks were already running on borrowed money. First half of 2026:

- Cash from running the business: $104.5M.
- Paid to owners: $586.5M, of which $432.2M was buybacks and the rest dividends.
- Net new borrowing: $595M.

The gap came from bigger freight bills. Receivables, money customers owe it, rose to $3.06B at June 30 from $2.36B at the end of 2025. Long-term debt climbed to $1.69B from $1.09B. Unpaid bills usually turn back into cash. Monday's deal turns that temporary borrowing into a lasting one.

It lands on a stock already hit twice since July. After a Dallas County jury found C.H. Robinson partly responsible for a fatal 2021 truck crash in Mississippi and awarded $604M, the stock fell 9.25% on July 24. Its insurance carries a $135M limit. The award had not been made final by early September, and the company has said it will appeal. Then came a 15.4% drop on July 30, after the June-quarter report showed that cash shortfall. Monday leaves the stock 32.9% under its July 21 close of $209.42.

RXO (RXO) at $28.62, +$5.24 / +22.41% on Monday. Its owners gained about $864M of market value, less than half what C.H. Robinson's lost. Because part of the price is paid in C.H. Robinson shares, Monday's fall also shrank the offer. At Monday's close the standard package is worth $29.29, not $30.25. RXO finished 2.3% under that. RXO is on none of the six Len5 watchlists; a June-quarter loss keeps it off the Quality Len5, and the offer now sets its price.

C.H. Robinson is on none of the six Len5 watchlists either, and this deal moves it away from the two that come closest. The Quality Len5 wants a profitable, sound business whose debt does not exceed the owners' stake. On June 30 C.H. Robinson had $1.69B of debt against an owners' stake of $1.63B, over the line before any deal debt. What would put it on the Quality Len5: debt paid down below the owners' stake, the reverse of what this deal does. The Income Len5 wants cash paid to owners, buybacks included, that the business can keep paying; with buybacks paused, what remains is a $0.63 quarterly dividend, about 1.8% a year at Monday's price. What would put it on the Income Len5: buybacks restarting from cash the business earns rather than borrows.

Next report: Wednesday, October 28, after the close, a date C.H. Robinson has not yet confirmed. Analysts expect $1.69 of adjusted profit per share, vs $1.40 a year earlier. The line to read is cash: whether those freight bills came back in before the deal debt arrives. RXO's shareholder vote has no date yet.

The key risk is what truckers charge. RXO's gross margin, what it keeps of each sales dollar after paying for the trucks, fell to 13.9% in the June quarter from 17.8% a year earlier. Cutting jobs does not protect a broker from that.

C.H. Robinson has already shown it can cut its own costs. Monday's price says investors will believe it can cut RXO's when the savings show up in a quarterly report, not in a merger announcement.

Not investment advice.

text: LAYER 7 — ENERGY: THE WAR ON THE TRANSPORT LAYER 7.1 The Map: Four Chokepoints, All Active at Once The energy shock of 2026 is usually described as a war over oil. More precisely, it is a war over the routes oil travels, fought at four chokepoints at the same time: – The Strait of Hormuz. Iran has said it will keep the strait closed until the United States meets seven conditions, and tankers continue to be struck in and near it. Kpler recorded traffic falling to about 10 ships a day in early September. Before the war, the strait carried about 20.9 million barrels a day, roughly a fifth of global consumption. – Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis have declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. By late September they had struck their eighth Saudi tanker off Yanbu, in a campaign running since July 22. – The Black Sea. Ukraine is attacking Russia's export ports. A strike on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal on Russia's Black Sea coast disrupted Kazakh exports. – The Caspian, whose barrels reach the world through that same Black Sea outlet. None of these theaters destroys much oil in the ground. They raise the cost, the risk and the time of moving it. That is why the price signals have come apart. 7.2 The Gulf: Two Chokepoints, One Trap Saudi Arabia's long-standing answer to a Hormuz closure was the East-West pipeline, which carries crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea. This year that answer stopped working. The mechanism shows up in the flow data. After Houthi attacks and a drone strike disrupted the Red Sea pipeline route, Saudi Arabia shifted crude back through Hormuz. Kpler's preliminary figures show Saudi shipments through Hormuz jumping to 2.58 million barrels a day in September from about one million in August. Over the same period, flows through Bab al-Mandeb more than halved, from 5.45 to 2.56 million barrels a day. Saudi Arabia is not choosing between a safe route and a dangerous one. It is choosing between two dangerous ones. Escaping Hormuz leads into the Houthis' sea, and escaping the Houthis leads back into Hormuz. Combined Saudi flows through Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and Suez remain 61% below pre-war February levels. The aggregate picture is more mixed. According to Reuters, Gulf exporters as a group exceeded pre-war export levels for about half of September, largely because Saudi Arabia was loading from both coasts. But attacks on tankers cloud whether those flows can be sustained. The barrels are moving, but each one moves under fire. 7.3 Yemen: The Houthis Against Aramco The Red Sea front is part of a war that has restarted. Fighting between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government has broken a four-year truce. Since then, the strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure have escalated week by week: – September 8. A wave of Houthi attacks wounded more than 70 people and set fire to oil facilities and utilities in Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait. Aramco sites in Najran and Abha were among the targets. – Late September. The Houthis claimed strikes on Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the terminal of the pipeline that bypasses Hormuz. Riyadh said it intercepted six ballistic missiles and reported no damage. – October 3. AFP journalists saw flames and smoke at Aramco's refinery south of Riyadh, with firefighters working the blaze. The Houthis claimed an attack with ballistic missiles and drones. The coalition's spokesman called the claims about targeting Riyadh "misleading." The diplomatic response is as telling as the attacks. The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye met to arrange an urgent meeting of their military chiefs under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an attack on one as an attack on all. Washington has not resumed direct military involvement. The kingdom is building a security architecture that does not run through the United States. Of everything in this assessment, that may be the slowest-moving development with the largest consequences. The precedent is not new. In September 2019, the attack on Abqaiq and Khurais briefly knocked out about 5.7 million barrels a day of Saudi processing, the largest single supply disruption on record at the time. The lesson then was that the world's most important spare capacity sits within drone range of a non-state actor. In 2026 that lesson is no longer a warning. It is a campaign. 7.4 The Black Sea: Ukraine's War on Russian Refining The second war has its own energy front, and Ukraine has chosen its targets carefully. By Reuters' calculations, the strikes on Russian refineries had cut refining capacity by 17%, about 1.1 million barrels a day, as of mid-August. The attacks have reached deep into Russia: – August 13. The Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat complex in Bashkortostan, one of Russia's largest, about 1,300 kilometers from the border. A Russian official said repairs could take up to six months because sanctions block foreign equipment. – September 9. Fires at the Novorossiysk naval base and at the port's fuel oil terminal. The commander of Ukraine's drone forces said 13 shadow-fleet vessels had been hit in the Black Sea in separate attacks. – September 20. Smoke over Moscow after an attack that included Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, which supplies fuel to the capital. By September, Ukrainian sea drones had also struck Sochi for the first time, showing that the naval drone campaign can reach far beyond Crimea and Novorossiysk. Hitting refineries instead of wells has a specific consequence. Russia keeps producing crude but processes less of it. The global shortage therefore shows up in diesel and gasoline, not in crude, and diesel prices reached record highs with both Hormuz and the Russia-Ukraine war weighing on supply. There is also a hidden cost: Kazakh barrels, which have nothing to do with this war, use the same Black Sea outlet. A strike on the CPC terminal is a strike on Central Asian supply. 7.5 The Barrel to China: From Subsidy to Tax The most important energy story of the year may be what happened to China's price of oil. Before the war, China was the clearing market for sanctioned crude. In 2025, sanctioned barrels from Russia, Iran and Venezuela made up about a quarter of China's seaborne oil imports. They came at a steep discount: Iranian Light traded about $10 a barrel below Brent on a delivered basis in Shandong, and Russian ESPO about $8.50 to $9 below. That discount kept China's independent refiners alive. The war turned that subsidy into a tax. After the US blockade of Iranian exports, some Iranian crude that normally sells at a discount was offered at a premium of about $2 a barrel over Brent. Iranian oil on ships in Asian waters fell to roughly 30–40 million barrels, from 105 million. China's intake of Iranian crude dropped from about 823,000 barrels a day in July to 534,000 so far in August. Add the freight. Shipping 2 million barrels from West Africa to China on a VLCC reportedly costs about $27 per barrel, against roughly $6.50 in July. That route crosses no war zone; it rounds the Cape. It has quadrupled anyway, because tankers are one global pool. When the Red Sea diverts ships, Hormuz traps them and blockades split the fleet, every route competes for the same hulls. Put the two together. A Chinese refiner that paid about $10 below Brent for Iranian crude in February is now paying at or above Brent for whatever it can find, plus roughly $20 more in freight on long-haul cargoes. That is a swing of about $30 a barrel before the price of oil itself moves. China's defense is time. By late February, it held an estimated 1.2 billion barrels of crude onshore, about 109 days of imports. Its overland pipelines from Russia and Kazakhstan, and the line through Myanmar that bypasses Malacca, are immune to every chokepoint in this assessment. Beijing bought that insurance years before anyone else saw the need. The question is how many months of drawdown it can tolerate. 7.6 Three Scarcities, Read Through the Futures Curve The mistake to avoid is treating "energy" as a single market. The futures curve separates three different scarcities. Barrels: resolving. The spread between the first- and second-month WTI contracts measures how urgently the market wants crude now. It peaked near $16 in April. It was near $5 in mid-September. Today it closed at $1.21, down 28% in a single session and below all its major averages. That matches the Reuters data on Gulf exports above pre-war levels for part of September. The barrels are arriving. Transport: worsening. Brent, the seaborne benchmark, trades at $100 and above its 21-, 50- and 200-day averages. WTI, the landlocked American barrel, has fallen to $89 and is breaking its 50-day average. The gap between them is about $11, several times its normal range. A barrel that must cross a chokepoint carries a war premium. A barrel that doesn't is being repriced for peace. Add freight that has roughly quadrupled since July, and the scarcity is plainly at sea, not underground. Products: tight. With Russian refining down by a sixth and Saudi refineries now targets, crude can ease while diesel stays near records. Underneath all three sits a spent buffer. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen below 300 million barrels, its lowest level since January 1983. If the transport bottleneck turns back into a barrel bottleneck, there is less left to release. 7.7 The Transmission: Why Cheaper Oil Did Not Lower Yields Energy is where the war entered the macro system. Oil inflation pushed up Japanese producer prices and forced the Bank of Japan to hike. In Europe, the largest major energy importer, it worsened the fiscal arithmetic that eventually broke France's spread. But what has not happened matters more. WTI has fallen from about $106 in mid-September to $89, a drop of roughly 16%. If oil were still driving the long end of the curve, that decline should have pulled long yields down. Over the same period, the 30-year Treasury rose to nearly 5.70%. The energy shock lit the fire. It is no longer what keeps it burning. The long end is now pricing the fiscal consequences of the shock, not the shock itself. That is why a ceasefire, if one comes, may do less for bonds than the market expects.

text:
A bank mail clerk turned down a hundred dollars for one book in 1912, and Harlem ended up with the greatest Black archive on earth. Arturo Schomburg had an autographed Phillis Wheatley and a dealer who wanted it badly, and a hundred dollars then was more than a month's pay for most of his neighbors. He wrote back three words. No parting glances.

Every weekday morning for twenty-three years, a man rode downtown to a bank and spent the day sorting other people's mail.

He ran the section at Bankers Trust that handled the letters going out to Cuba, Puerto Rico, Mexico and Brazil. They gave him that desk because he wrote English, Spanish and French, and a bank moving money through the Caribbean needed somebody who could read a complaint from Havana without sending it out to be translated.

He was good at it. He held the job from 1906 to 1929 and finished as supervisor of the whole Caribbean and Latin American mail section.

Into those same outgoing bags, most days, went letters that had nothing to do with the bank at all.

They went to booksellers in Madrid and London and Havana, and to other collectors in Philadelphia and Washington. They asked whether anybody had a certain pamphlet, a certain engraving, a certain thin volume of poems, and whether the seller would kindly hold it a while, because the buyer was a clerk and the money would take some time to come together.

His name was Arturo Alfonso Schomburg. The research library in Harlem that holds the largest archive of Black life anywhere on earth carries his name, and almost nobody can tell you it started in a mailroom.

In 1915 a census taker worked his way through the building at 63 West 140th Street and wrote down what every household did for a living. Porters, elevator operators, dressmakers, women who cleaned other people's houses.

Next to Schomburg's name he wrote bookkeeper.

That was the wrong job. Schomburg was a clerk in a bank mailroom, and the census taker had guessed at the man on the stairs who was always carrying boxes.

Wrong job, right man. The historian Laura Helton noticed the accident a century later, going through the record: he was keeping books, hundreds of them, and there was no word on the form for what he actually was.

He was the only Puerto Rican in that building. His neighbors were African American and West Indian, and he had already started calling himself Afroborinqueño, Afro-Puerto Rican, said as one word with nothing in the middle to argue about.

Three years before that census, he had been unpacking his library. Again.

He had moved constantly. The Lower East Side, then San Juan Hill in midtown, then Harlem, then a rented room in the home of Ramon Rothschild, an old comrade from Puerto Rico and a brother in his Masonic lodge, and then the apartment on 140th Street with his new wife, Elizabeth Green.

The books came with him every single time. By 1912 they had filled three bookcases, alongside the pamphlets, the manuscripts, the engravings, and what he cheerfully described as coins galore.

He wrote to his friend John W. Cromwell about it on Labor Day, 1912, and the letter is not triumphant. He said he ran into a great deal of trouble every time he had to move the treasured lot from one place to another.

Things went missing in the moves, and some of them he never got back.

Then he wrote a sentence that has never once appeared on a museum wall. He feared he had reached his limit.

He was thirty-eight. He had a wife, children, a mail clerk's wage, and a collection that had already outgrown every room he could afford to put it in.

That same summer, a dealer made him an offer on a single book.

Schomburg owned an autographed copy of Phillis Wheatley, the enslaved girl from Boston who published the first book of poems by an African American in 1773. The dealer wanted it and put a hundred dollars on the table.

A hundred dollars in 1912 was serious money to a man sorting mail. It was more than a month's pay for most of the people living in his building.

He wrote to Alain Locke that August with his answer. No parting glances.

He kept the book. He kept hauling it up and down stairs for another fourteen years.

Some things he could not buy at any price, because they had to be found first.

Benjamin Banneker was a free Black man in Maryland who taught himself astronomy, worked on the survey of the federal district, and published almanacs in the 1790s. Schomburg wanted a picture of his face.

Not an account of him. A picture, an engraving, the actual likeness of the man, something a person could stand in front of and look at.

It took him twelve years.

Twelve years of writing to dealers who had never heard the name, of asking friends headed to Philadelphia or Baltimore to please check the shops while they were down there. Twelve years of chasing a rumor into a dead end and starting the letters over.

Twelve years of postage, out of a mail clerk's wage, for one image of one face. He got it.

To understand why a grown man spends twelve years hunting a face, you have to know what he had been missing.

He was born in Santurce, just outside San Juan, on January 24, 1874, and baptized four days later at the Church of San Francisco de Asis. His mother was a Black woman from the Danish West Indies, and his father was a Puerto Rican merchant, the son of a German immigrant.

He grew up on an island with a great painter in it. José Campeche was the finest Puerto Rican artist of the eighteenth century, and his work was known and hung and admired.

Nobody told the boy that Campeche was Black.

He said so himself, decades later. Vanessa K. Valdés, who wrote the first book-length study of Schomburg as an Afro-Latino, treats that as the injury he spent the rest of his life working on.

A child is handed his own island's greatest painter with the color quietly taken out of him.

He worked out how the trick was done and he put it in print. Let a person of African descent do something excellent, and they get called exceptional, and then they get lifted out of the race and set off to one side by themselves.

There is another story about how it all started, and it is the one everybody knows.

He said a teacher told his class that Black people had no history, no heroes, no great moments. His biographer, Elinor Des Verney Sinnette, put it in her 1989 life of him, and it has been in every children's book and museum panel since.

Here is the part that keeps getting left out. When Sinnette went into the records in San Juan, what she found was conflicting evidence about whether Schomburg attended primary school there at all.

And he did not always tell it that way himself. He sometimes said the thing that lit him was a literary club he belonged to back home.

So the one claim in the whole record with no document under it is the claim he made about his own childhood.

He knew that better than anyone. A man who would spend twelve years proving a face was real understood exactly what an unsourced story is worth.

He told it anyway, for fifty years, because it does in nine seconds what the Campeche story needs a paragraph to do. It may be the only thing he ever put his name to that he could not have proved.

By the twenties, the books had taken the house.

He moved the family to Brooklyn in 1918, to a narrow brown place on Kosciuszko Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant, where he lived with Elizabeth Green and their children and several thousand items concerning people the schools would not mention.

The novelist Eric Walrond went out there in 1922 and wrote down what he found. He called it "hallowed ground."

He described a sitting room thick with the smell of old paper and the portraits on the walls, an Ethiopian princess, the composer Chevalier de Saint-Georges, a bandmaster named John Fraser. Writers and artists of both races kept turning up at that plain little house on a side street, Walrond wrote, because of what was inside it.

Six years earlier Schomburg had told Alain Locke by letter that the library had a few easy chairs, so a person could drop in and feel at home. He was talking about his own front room.

Somewhere in those rooms sat the handwritten military orders of Toussaint Louverture, on paper stamped Egalité, Liberté. The men who came to see them had a name for themselves, coined by the Philadelphia newspaperman William Carl Bolivar.

DOFOB. Damned Old Fools on Books.

In March 1925 a magazine called Survey Graphic gave an entire issue to Harlem, guest-edited by Alain Locke.

It carried Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen, Claude McKay, Jean Toomer, W. E. B. Du Bois, and an essay by Arthur A. Schomburg titled "The Negro Digs Up His Past." It opens on the sentence the whole Renaissance would end up standing on. "The American Negro must remake his past in order to make his future."

A few lines further down comes the harder one. History has to give back what slavery took, he wrote, because the damage is what this generation is stuck repairing.

Deeper into the essay he listed the serious private collections of Black material in America. Henry P. Slaughter of Washington came first, then the Reverend Charles D. Martin of Harlem.

Third on the list was Arthur Schomburg of Brooklyn. Fourth was the late John E. Bruce, his old mentor, and Bruce is the only one of the four he bothered to compliment.

He put himself third, inside a clause, with no adjectives on it.

That same year the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library opened a Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints. In October the head librarian, Ernestine Rose, wrote to Schomburg about the possibility of the branch acquiring his collection.

Private buyers had already come around. He turned them down and let the whole thing go to a public library in Harlem, where anybody could walk in off the street with no fee and no letter of introduction.

On May 14, 1926, the Carnegie Corporation approved the money. Resolution X-281, ten thousand dollars, for the Arthur Schomburg library collection on negro life and history.

Ten thousand dollars for all of it.

Five days later more than a hundred packing crates went out to the library's central building to be readied for the trip uptown. Shelley Fisher Fishkin describes that shipment in her book on American literary landmarks, thousands of books and manuscripts and etchings and portraits and pamphlets, boxed and addressed to Harlem.

Laura Helton makes the observation that lands hardest. That was the last time in his life Arthur Schomburg packed or unpacked his own library.

The Wheatley went, and the Louverture orders went. The Banneker face, twelve years in the finding, went into a crate with a number chalked on the side and rode uptown on a truck.

That house on Kosciuszko Street must have been very quiet by the end of that week.

He spent the money on more books. That same year he sailed for Spain, France, Germany and England, sitting in reading rooms and buying whatever he could carry home for a collection he no longer owned.

The library that had just bought his life's work did not give him a job with it.

He went back to the mailroom. He stayed at Bankers Trust until he was nearly fifty-six, leaving around the turn of 1930, and the library trustees' files from those years hold correspondence about the effort to get Schomburg onto the payroll at all.

To work in a library, he had to leave New York. At fifty-six he took the post of curator of the Negro Collection at Fisk University in Nashville, in the Jim Crow South, and built there a smaller version of what he had built in Harlem.

He came back in 1932 and finally sat down as curator of his own collection on 135th Street. Six years after the crates went uptown.

He had that desk for six years. In June 1938 he went in for dental surgery, an infection followed, and he died at Madison Park Hospital in Brooklyn on the tenth of the month, at sixty-four.

The funeral was two days later at Siloam Presbyterian Church, and it was private.

He was buried in the Locust Grove section of Cypress Hills Cemetery, a short ride from the house the books once filled.

Two years after that, the library put his name on the collection.

That building is free.

Anybody can walk into the Schomburg Center on Malcolm X Boulevard tomorrow, with no card and no letter of introduction, and ask to see the Wheatley he refused to sell for a hundred dollars. There are around ten million items in there now, and the first eight hundred of them came out of a mail clerk's evenings.

He was never really paid for it. Ten thousand dollars, four more years in the mailroom, a year in Nashville at fifty-six, six years behind the desk, then a tooth.

His own letters are in that building too. Including the ones he wrote at night, at a table in Brooklyn, asking a stranger in Madrid to please hold a book until a clerk in New York could put the money together.

So when the name on the building comes up, put the mailroom in the sentence with it. That part has no plaque on it, and it only survives if somebody carries it out of here.

Blind Willie Johnson's voice was chosen to represent humanity beyond Earth, yet the man behind that voice spent his final days without even a proper place to rest. I share stories like his because sometimes the greatest stories are hidden behind the names we already know.

text:
Carrie Johnson, age 17, shot and killed a white detective who raided her DC home during the 1919 DC Race Riots [the only "race" riots where more whites died than Blacks]. 

James Weldon Johnson dubbed the period from April to November of 1919 the "Red Summer" because the United States experienced a rolling series of race wars that might be described as a neo-Confederate offensive. 

The riots started when the Washington Post and other local newspapers started to publish false allegations of Black men attacking white women in the city. 

The Black community begged the Post to stop publishing the false stories and warned them of the consequences of their actions, but they didn't listen. 

The Washington Bee [the popular Black newspaper at the time] warned the community of the pending danger and the Black citizens prepared for war. 

Sharpshooters were stationed atop the Howard Theater. 

One night during the riots, Carrie hid under her bed with her father's old rifle and shot into the dark, hitting one of three detectives and killing him. Carrie and her father were both arrested and charged with murder. 

Carrie's father, Ben Johnson, was offered a plea deal if he testified against his daughter but they released him anyway thinking that it would be easier to secure a conviction if they focused on Carrie. 

Black women's organizations (including every Howard University sorority) held a fashion show raising over $17,000 dollars ($230,000 in today's time) for Carrie's defense team. 

There was a controversial mistrial presided over by a sympathetic judge; Carrie was set free [after two years behind bars] and disappeared from the history books.

The US is warming up to Russia but if Putin chooses China, the new world order will become bipolar and governed by two integrated defense, economic and political alliances - the Autocracies (led by China) and the Democracies (led by the US).

Here’s why…

Around this time Putin (I am speculating and referring to the news) should be receiving (and maybe even soliciting) offers from both the US and China. Offers that could grease the wheels towards a peace agreement to end the Ukraine Russia war and possibly settle other issues.

I expect he will make his choice of either the US or China (as his future primary partner in prosperity and security) based on which offer produces the best reward to risk outcomes for himself (Putin and his family) and his group (his inside the Kremlin power backers).

What the people of Russia would prefer (I think this is US normalization and alignment with the west, not China) will not matter if Putin is the decision maker on the issue of whether Russia goes with the US and becomes a policy and strategy independent Sovereign within a multilateral and accepting west or instead becomes a satellite of China.

Putin is in a position to decide if the world will become bipolar or multipolar. If he chooses the US, the new world order will become a multipolar model with the centres of power in Beijing and Washington.

If Putin chooses China, I expect the US will act to consolidate its position of world leadership by forming a vast and deeply integrated alliance of democracies to counter balance the China led alliance (BRICS / Russia, Iran, N. Korea…) of autocracies. The democracies will dominate with around 72% of global GDP.

Where is this going?

I think Putin will choose China (over the US) as his primary partner and as a result two large alliances will  take form as the Autocracies (China led) and Democracies (US led) form the new world order - which will for the most part refrain from direct conflict but instead engage in vigorous competition for dominance.

text:
🚨 RUBIO BREAKS SILENCE ON SIBERIA PLAGUE CASE — US DEMANDS ANSWERS FROM RUSSIA

The Siberia plague story has just escalated again.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has now publicly confirmed that Washington is closely monitoring the situation surrounding the death of a worker at Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.

Rubio says it appears a laboratory worker became infected and there was concern that the illness could have spread.

His message:
CAUSE FOR FOCUS — NOT ALARM.

But the United States is watching.

The State Department says many details remain unconfirmed and has called on Russian authorities to provide accurate information quickly and openly.

President Trump has also reportedly offered US assistance to Russia.

That matters.

Because this is no longer just a regional Russian health story.

The United States is now publicly asking questions.

Nearly 200 contacts have been monitored.

Hospitals remain under quarantine.

Dozens of institute staff have reportedly been isolated.

How Washington squeezes out competitors from Peru's nuclear program

Capturing strategic markets doesn't start with pouring concrete at construction sites, but with writing other nations' laws. Peru's inclusion in the American FIRST program for small reactors pursues a transparent goal: impose US standards on Lima and shut the local market off from state corporation Rosatom's offerings.

Peruvian interest in small nuclear energy stems from a deficit of power grids at high-altitude copper mines. After spring's passage of a framework law on small reactors, Lima began openly examining foreign projects.

📌 For its part, the Russian side, having successfully launched a nuclear research center in neighboring Bolivia, repeatedly signaled its readiness to offer Peru its serial small-scale installations and modernize Peru's research base.

However, repeating the Bolivian precedent on the Pacific coast categorically does not fit Washington's plans. The American FIRST project aims to get ahead of the game.

🔻The mechanics of the American barrier

▪️Artificial standards incompatibility. American curators rewrite the regulatory framework and regulations of Peru's IPEN institute under US regulator licenses, which in advance makes purchasing Russian technology legally impossible.

▪️Isolation of the Bolivian center. Creating a pro-American nuclear barrier in Peru aims to block the expansion of Russian nuclear expertise from neighboring El Alto into the Andean region.

▪️Monopoly over a promising energy market. Hooking local infrastructure to US regulations guarantees control over supplies to strategic copper deposits and excludes competitors from future tenders.

Peru's authorities receive the status of a testing ground for future US commercial projects. Washington simply cuts off oxygen to Rosatom at the stage of formulating the rules of the game, depriving the country of alternative suppliers for the sake of geopolitical control over the region.

text:
PTC $PTC BOUGHT BACK ITS OWN STOCK AT ABOUT $122 THIS SPRING. SCHNEIDER ELECTRIC JUST BID $205:

PTC Inc. (PTC) at $192.60, +$48.57 / +33.72% today.

That is the biggest gain in the S&P 500 so far today, with the 4pm close minutes away:

- S&P 500: 7,778.70, +55.98 points / +0.72% so far today.

The Boston company makes the software engineers use to design physical products and track every part and change until those products are built and serviced. On Monday, Schneider Electric, the French maker of electrical equipment, agreed to buy it for $205 a share in cash.

The verdict: today's jump is not the market finding something new in PTC. It is a buyer agreeing with what PTC's own managers said with cash this spring, that the stock was too cheap, and paying owners back to about where it stood a year ago. From here PTC trades on one number: the $12.40 still between its price and $205.

The deal, as announced:

- Price: $205 a share in cash, 42.3% above Friday's $144.03 close.
- Value: about $22.6B for the shares, $23.7B counting PTC's debt.
- Approvals: a majority of PTC's shareholders, the U.S. antitrust review, and CFIUS, the Treasury-led panel that screens foreign purchases of American companies for national-security risk.
- Walk-away fee: $700M, owed by PTC under conditions the agreement spells out.
- Expected closing: by the third quarter of 2027.

Within hours, Stifel, RBC Capital Markets and Rosenblatt Securities all cut PTC to the equivalent of a hold, with price targets at exactly $205. With cash on the table, the offer is the ceiling unless someone else bids.

The 42% sounds generous. It is measured from a low. PTC's record close was $216.53 on August 27, 2025. It last closed above $205 on October 20, 2025, then bottomed at $112.33 on June 23 this year. The causes were ordinary: a revenue forecast last November that missed estimates and cost the stock 7.5% in a morning, the sale of two product lines in March that shrank reported revenue, and waves of selling across software stocks. Schneider's price hands owners back about a year, still 5% under that record.

The business underneath held up:

- ARR, annual recurring revenue - the yearly value of subscriptions customers have signed: $2.448B at the end of June, +9.1% at steady exchange rates, leaving out the lines sold in March.
- Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment: about $850M guided for the fiscal year that ended September 30, roughly 31 cents of every sales dollar, even after one-time costs from the March sale.

Schneider is paying about 27 times that cash.

PTC's managers had already called the price wrong, with money. In the June quarter the company spent $525M buying 4.3M of its own shares on the open market, about $122 apiece and more than twice what it had planned. Chief financial officer Jen DiRico said PTC "identified what we viewed as a compressed valuation of our stock and acted accordingly." Part of it was borrowed: debt rose to $1.42B at June 30, from $1.20B nine months earlier. Owners who sold to the company near $122 are gone. The ones who held get $205.

The buyer's owners took the other side. Schneider Electric (SBGSY) at $61.51, -$6.89 / -10.07% today. Early in the Paris session, Reuters put the loss at about EUR 15B of market value, roughly $17B. That is about three times what PTC's owners have gained so far today, about $5.3B. Schneider will pay with EUR 16B-17B of new debt and EUR 5B-6B of new shares. It is on none of the six Len5 watchlists: a 10% one-day drop is the opposite of the near-its-high climb the Momentum Len5 wants.

Back to the number that decides this verdict. $205 minus $192.60 is $12.40, or 6.4% on today's price. The stock has covered about four-fifths of the distance from Friday's close to the offer.

That last 6.4% pays for two things. One is time: the money waits until closing, up to a year away, and a 1-year Treasury bill paid 4.46% at Friday's close. The other is risk: if regulators or shareholders stop the sale, Friday's $144.03 is the last price set without an offer on the table, $48.57 under today's. Over a full year, the gap pays about 2 points more than the Treasury for carrying that risk. A gap that narrows slowly as approvals arrive is normal. One that suddenly widens would be the first sign of trouble.

The Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 hunts a strong business priced below a cautious value of what it earns, or an event an owner can count on. PTC earned its place there, #90 of 192, on the first half. At Friday's price it was a business whose subscriptions grow about 9% a year, because engineers spend years filling its software with their designs; the debt was the drawback. That half ended at today's open, because the price now tracks the offer. The second half holds the place now: a signed agreement, a $700M fee and a target date. What would knock PTC off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: a CFIUS objection or a failed shareholder vote, either of which turns a countable event back into an ordinary software stock. The Momentum Len5 is out of reach, because a cash offer caps the price at $205.

The calendar: no date yet for PTC's shareholder vote. Its report on the quarter that ended September 30 is tentatively Wednesday, November 4, after the close, not yet confirmed by PTC. The key risk is CFIUS, the one approval aimed squarely at foreign buyers. A cash deal also changes the usual risk after a big jump: the stock can barely rise from here, and the way it falls hard is the deal breaking.

PTC's managers spent $525M this spring on the case that $122 was too low. Schneider settled it at $205, and the last $12.40 now waits on Washington and a vote nobody has scheduled.

Not investment advice.

text:
Secretary Kennedy, the cheaper operating room in Massachusetts requires the expensive hospital’s permission to open.

That belongs in the speech.

The Boston joint replacement gap is real. Blue Cross reported commercial claims prices ranging from $17,910 to $73,987 in the Boston market in 2015. 

More than a decade later, the spread is being presented as a revelation.

Look at who gets permission to compete.

In 2008, Massachusetts removed the exemption that let physician-owned surgery centers open without Determination of Need approval. 

The state’s own Health Policy Commission calls what followed an effective moratorium on new ASCs.

In 2017, the state lifted it with conditions. New centers needed an affiliation with a certified accountable care organization. 

A center in an independent hospital’s primary service area needed that hospital’s approval. The commission’s conclusion: the requirements effectively gave hospitals approval power over most new surgery centers.

The incumbent gets a say in whether its competitor opens. In the commission’s 2023 data, Boston had one ASC.

Then there is the payment system you oversee.

Medicare still pays hospitals more for many services that can safely be performed in independent offices or surgery centers.

CMS has narrowed some of that gap. In 2026, it expanded site-neutral payment to drug administration at certain off-campus hospital departments and expanded the ASC covered-procedure list. It has proposed adding imaging without contrast at those departments for 2027.

Good. Keep going! 

A hospital billing address is not better care. Paying extra for it grants an advantage before anyone compares outcomes.

That policy does not establish what caused the Blue Cross spread. It does expose the contradiction: Washington condemns the expensive setting while still paying a premium to use it.

The insurance finding is separate. Trinity College reported that economist Gerardo Ruiz Sánchez found 60 percent of the negotiated rates he studied exceeded the hospital’s own cash price.

Patients pay premiums expecting bargaining power. They deserve to know when the hospital’s cash offer was better.

Publishing the price is not the same as being allowed to take it.

If a plan shows the cheaper option and then makes choosing it cost more out of pocket, it has built a museum of affordable care.

Please enjoy the prices without touching the savings.

For scheduled care, the buyer needs an offer that can be accepted: a defined episode, a named physician and facility, meaningful quality information, and a price agreed before treatment. 

The benefit design has to let the employer and the patient to keep the difference. 

The competitor has to be allowed to open.

Markets cannot discipline prices they cannot see. 

They also cannot discipline a hospital whose competitors need permission to open.

Publish the prices. 
Stop protecting them.

BREAKING: STAY AWAY! Trump gets humiliated as it's revealed that tourism to D.C. has PLUMMETED under his disastrous leadership — despite his pathetic claims that the city is more beautiful and safer now.

Nobody wants to be anywhere near this guy...

"People just aren't coming. They just don't want to put up with it," E. David Luria, who runs Washington Photo Safari, told The Washington Post. Luria had hoped that America's 250th anniversary would boost tourism to the city, but instead his bookings are down a staggering 50% from last year.

Some tour guides who spoke to the Post have experienced as much as a 70% decrease in business and revealed that many tourists, especially those coming from overseas, resent Trump's "attacks on longtime allies, the imposition of hard-hitting tariffs, and the administration’s visa and immigration policies."

But it's not just the odious fascist aura emanating from the White House these days that's keeping visitors away from the nation's capital. Trump's incompetent, self-defeating leadership has also made it more difficult, and in some cases downright impossible, to see some of the city's most beloved attractions.

“The biggest complaint we hear from visitors is we can’t get our pictures without fences,” said tour guide Canden Arciniega.

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, when it isn't green or full of disintegrating pool liner, is often empty and fenced off. Most of Lafayette Square is now inaccessible, the East Wing of the White House no longer exists, the Kennedy Center is closed, as are vast stretches of the National Mall. Why even bother visiting at this point? Far better to wait, save your money, and visit under a future Democratic President when the city is thriving, open, and thrumming with life.

“Our Capitol Hill tours used to be twice a day, Tuesday through Saturday. Now they’re offered just four times a week and are rarely full," said Arciniega.

“We are on track to conclude 2026 with a loss," said tour guide Carolyn Crouch, whose revenue has dropped by 70% for July and August and 50% for the rest of the year.

“The current administration has not only created lots of obstructed views and made the National Mall look in some places like a work in progress, it has also made our city’s brand toxic,” said Crouch. “And our experience is that people seem to be voting with their feet and not traveling to Washington, D.C.”

Not surprisingly, Trump's flair for authoritarian optics has also hurt the city's appeal. About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
Venerable Fathers and Mothers of the Klarjeti Wilderness

For centuries the region of Tao-Klarjeti in southwestern Georgia was known for its holiness, unity and spiritual strength. The cultural life and faith of Kartli were nearly extinguished by the Arab-Muslim domination from the 8th to 10th centuries. Tao-Klarjeti, however, which had been emptied by a cholera epidemic and the aftermath of the Islamic invasions, filled with new churches and monasteries, becoming a destination for many Christian ascetics. Saint Ekvtime Taqaishvili wrote that “Every monastery included a school and a seminary where the Christian Faith, philosophy, Greek and other foreign languages, chant, calligraphy, fine arts, jewelry making, and other disciplines were taught. Countless priests, translators, miniaturists, and jewelry makers developed their craft in these schools.”

The prayers of the Tao-Klarjeti monastics multiplied and were lifted up to the heavens like holy incense. Hagiographical works were written, original hymns composed, and theological texts translated.

The literature of this period was thoroughly infused with the spirit of the Georgian people. Tao-Klarjeti reinvigorated the soul of the Georgian people and redirected the lost back to the true path.

Saint Gregory of Khandzta, a priest of great virtue and wisdom, spearheaded this spiritual revival. He was a good shepherd to his flock and the builder of many churches. The Lives of Saint Gregory of Khandzta and the other holy fathers and mothers of Tao-Klarjeti are recounted in Saint George Merchule’s work The Life of Saint Gregory of Khandzta. George Merchule labored in the Khandzta wilderness in the 10th century. His epithet, “Merchule,” means “the theologian” or literally “the knower of the law.”

George Merchule also provided the Church with the Life of Holy Catholicos Nerse III, an Armenian by descent. Nerse confessed the Orthodox Faith and labored in Tao-Klarjeti with the Georgian fathers. (At that time many Orthodox Armenians fled to Tao-Klarjeti after being exiled from their homeland.) In the first half of the 7th century Saint Nerse laid the foundations of Ishkhani Church and labored there in holiness.

Holy Catholicos Hilarion was the founder and abbot of Tsqarostavi Church and a disciple of Gregory of Khandzta. He arrived at Khandzta Monastery with his spiritual father, Saint David, Abbot of Midznadzori Monastery, and Saint Zachariah, the builder of Beretelta Church. Those who witnessed the fathers’ unity and piety abandoned the world to join them in offering their lives to God. In the middle of the 9th century Saint Hilarion was enthroned as Catholicos of Kartli in recognition of his wisdom and holiness. He followed Gabriel II (ca. 830-850) and was succeeded by Arsenius I “the Great” (ca. 860-887) in this most honorable role.

Saint Stephen of Tbeti was the first bishop of Tbeti. He was a major writer and hagiographer in the Church of his time and a brilliant figure of the Tao-Klarjeti literary school. Saint Stephen is credited with authoring the narrative The Martyrdom of Saint Gobron.

From his childhood Saint Zachariah of Anchi was filled with love and fear of God. Strict in his discipline but free from every constraint of this world, he led the life of a shepherd like St.David the Psalmist. As a child, Saint Zachariah would gather his friends and relate with precision the words and scenes he had witnessed in churches and monasteries. Once the bishop of Anchi observed this unusual pastime and reported seeing a pillar of light descend fromthe heavens and alight atop St.Zachariah’s head.

When he reached a mature age, Saint Zachariah became the spiritual leader of his brothers. Through his prayers many miracles were performed: he stopped the stone wall of a collapsing building from crashing to the ground, eliminated the troublesome birds and grasshoppers from the monastery’s vineyard, and killed two venomous snakes that were keeping his frightened brothers from the vineyard. Filled with good faith and virtue, Saint Zachariah was later consecrated bishop of Anchi.

Saint Macarius of Anchi served as bishop of Anchi following the repose of Saint Gregory of Khandzta in 861.

Saint Ezra of Anchi, of the noble Dapanchuli family, labored in holiness during the 10th century.

Saint Savva of Ishkhani was a cousin and one of the closest companions of St.Gregory of Khandzta. Along with two other friends, Christopher and Theodore, the young Savva accompanied Gregory of Khandzta to Klarjeti on a quest for the ascetic life. At first the young monks settled at Opiza Monastery and labored there with great zeal, and afterwards they moved to Khandzta.

Once Saint Savva made a pilgrimage with Saint Gregory to Byzantium, and there he learned the typica of the local monasteries. On the way back to Tao-Klarjeti, God revealed to them His will for Savva to restore Ishkhani Church, which had been destroyed by Arab-Muslim invaders. Saint Savva desired to begin this holy task at once, but he continued on the way with Saint Gregory at the latter’s insistence.

Later, Gregory assigned two monks to help Savva restore the church and sent the three of them to Ishkhani. By God’s grace, the brothers restored the church and monastery and the number of monks who labored there multiplied. Before long their abbot, Saint Savva, was consecrated bishop of Ishkhani.

Saint John the New Martyr for Christ labored at Khandzta Monastery. While he was journeying to Jerusalem on a pilgrimage, the Saracens captured him in Baghdad and attempted to torture him into a denial of the Christian Faith. But by shedding his blood Saint John demonstrated his immutable fidelity to the Faith of our Savior.

Saint Theodore, Founder of Nedzvi Monastery, and Saint Christopher, Founder of the Dviri Monastery of Saint Cyricus, were spiritual sons of Saint Gregory of Khandzta and the first men to join him in his holy labors.

With Saint Gregory they labored first at Opiza and later at Khandzta Monastery. These holy fathers journeyed to Abkhazeti to increase the fullness of the Faith in that region, and on their way, in Samtskhe, an aristocrat named Mirian entrusted them with the care and upbringing of his son, the six-year-old Arsenius (later Holy Catholicos Arsenius the Great).

Eventually Saint Gregory of Khandzta desired the return of Theodore and Christopher, and he traveled to Abkhazeti to find them. Saint Gregory took with him his young disciple Ephraim (later the bishop and wonderworker of Atsquri). When he met the brothers in Abkhazeti, Saint Gregory entrusted them with Ephraim’s upbringing and made them vow not to leave Khandzta Monastery until Ephraim and Arsenius had reached maturity.

When Ephraim and Arsenius reached manhood they were “perfected in wisdom,” and Theodore and Christopher left Khandzta to establish the Nedzvi and Dviri Monasteries. There each father labored until the day of his repose.

Holy Fathers George, Amona, Peter, and Macarius labored in the wilderness of Opiza. Abba George was abbot of Opiza’s Saint John the Baptist Monastery during the two years Saint Gregory of Khandzta and his companions labored there. Fr. George was the third abbot of the monastery (he was succeeded by Saint Andria and Saint Samuel).

Through God’s grace Abba George recognized the pilgrims’ faith and received them, not as pupils, but as honorable and wise elders. Witnessing the ascetic feats of the venerable fathers of Opiza, Saint Gregory increased in virtue and humility, and acquired inner peace. (History has preserved a Holy Gospel from the Opiza Wilderness that has been dated to the year 913, around the time that Abba George was laboring there.)

In the second part of the 9th century Saint Serapion of Zarzma founded Zarzma Monastery in Samtskhe. Saint Serapion’s nephew, Saint Basil, later performed great ascetic feats and worked miracles at that monastery. Saint Basil authored The Life of Serapion of Zarzma and recounted the lives of the other venerable fathers of Zarzma as well.

Saint George, “a brilliant and kindhearted man of great virtue,” succeeded Saint Serapion as abbot of Zarzma Monastery. After Saint George, the Venerable Abbot Michael began building a second church in Zarzma, in fulfillment of Saint Serapion’s prophecy. Saint Paul, who followed Michael as abbot of the monastery, completed construction of this second church.

The holy and righteous Saint Khvedios labored as a hermit in the caves of the Khandzta Wilderness. God revealed to him the news of Saint Gregory’s arrival, and he received Gregory and his brothers with great joy.

He blessed them, while receiving a blessing himself from Saint Gregory of Khandzta. Then, rather than journeying on with Saint Gregory and the other brothers, Saint Khvedios retired to his secluded cave, since he had taken a vow before God to live his whole life in solitude. After the holy father reposed, his dwelling place filled with a sweet fragrance.

Saint Epiphanius was a wonderworker and a spiritual son of Saint Gregory of Khandzta. This venerable father was truly clad in the armor of righteousness, and he was an inspiration to many. According to Saint Gregory’s instructions, he became an example of obedience for the other brothers of the monastery. Saint Epiphanius’s prayers healed many who were afflicted by terminal illnesses.

Saint Matthew labored in the Khandzta Wilderness. After the abbess of Mere Monastery reposed, he took upon himself leadership of the women’s monastery and for forty years set an example of life lived in the fullness of the Faith. He was so strict in his asceticism that, for those forty years, he never once shared a meal with the mothers, nor did he receive a single object from any of their hands. When Saint Matthew reached an advanced age, he became diseased in the flesh, but he declined the nuns’ offers to care for him. Instead he asked his relative, also a monk, to attend to him in his time of need.

Saint Zenon was born in Samtskhe to a family of aristocrats. He was raised in the fear of God, and he desired from his youth to enter the monastic life. Before this desire was fulfilled, however, his sister was kidnapped by a certain godless man. Zenon set off to pursue the abductor on horseback, but while he was riding the devil began to assault him with anxieties. “I am a respectable man,” he thought, “but the one whom I am following is dishonorable. If I catch and kill him, I will destroy my soul, but if I turn back, shame will come upon me.”

And so, at that very moment, Saint Zenon turned back to fulfill his lifelong desire. He was tonsured a monk and later became a disciple of Saint Gregory of Khandzta.

Saint Zenon, the “Treasure of Virtue, Holy Model of Asceticism and Gate of the Klarjeti Wilderness,” reposed at an advanced age.

Saint John, Abbot of Khandzta, is celebrated for having completed construction of the new church at Khandzta that was begun by his predecessor, Saint Arsenius. Both holy fathers reposed in the Khandzta Wilderness.

Saint Theodore the Abbot and his brother Saint John both labored at Khandzta Monastery. Saint George Merchule recognizes the brothers as co-authors, with him, of the work The Life of Saint Gregory of Khandzta; historians, however, believe that they were contributors, rather than coauthors, of this work.

The monk Saint Gabriel ministered to the infirm and elderly monks of Khandzta Monastery. Saint Gabriel verbally recounted the Lives of the great Church Fathers and admonished his brothers to follow the same strict disciplines as the fathers who had gone before them.

Saint Demetrius was raised by the blessed Saint Febronia and later became one of Saint Gregory of Khandzta’s first disciples. He is commemorated among the holy fathers for having attaining the heights of the monastic struggle and for working wonders, both in this life and after he had been received into the bosom of Abraham.

SS. Arsenius and Macarius, “good monks full of wisdom and the gift of wonderworking,” were relatives of Saint Ephraim of Atsquri. They labored together at Saint Savva Monastery in Jerusalem and corresponded regularly with the monks of Khandzta. Saints Arsenius and Macarius possessed a profound love for Christ and a longing to serve their motherland and mother Church.

Saint Shio the Wonderworker “shone upon the land of Kartli like the North Star in the morning sky.” According to Basil of Zarzma, Saint Shio was the spiritual father of Saint Michael of Parekhi.

SS. Basil and Markelus, “abounding and brilliant in virtue,” were disciples of Saint Michael of Parekhi. Saint Basil was buried in Parekhi next to his spiritual father. Both fathers worked miracles from their graves and healed the infirmities of the faithful who came to seek their blessings.

Venerable Father David, “an image of the angels” and builder of many monasteries, labored as abbot of Midznadzori Monastery. He was the spiritual father of the holy catholicos Hilarion.

Endowed with many gifts of grace, Saint Jacob was a prominent figure in the tenth-century Georgian Church. He labored first in Shatberdi, and later near Midznadzori Gorge, where he shone forth as the brightest of stars.

Venerable Sophronius the Great was the restorer of the Shatberdi Church and a famous writer, but his literary works have not been preserved.

Saint George Merchule numbers him among the wise and holy fathers whose stories are worthy to be told. Saint Gregory of Shatberdi labored at the same monastery. Several of the tenth-century manuscripts copied by him at Shatberdi Monastery have been preserved, including the Notebooks of the Shatberdi Wilderness and the Gospels of Hadishi, Jruchi, and Parekhi.

Saint Zachariah built the famous Beretelta Monastery and set an example of wisdom and holiness for the fathers who labored there after him.

Saint George Merchule honors the venerable and God-fearing Saint Hilarion of Parekhi as one of the greatest writers and figures in the Church of his time.

Saint Hilarion, Abbot of Ubisi, labored for many years at the Lavra of Saint Savva in Jerusalem, where the Georgians had their own chapel for many centuries (See Archimandrite Gregory Peradze, “An Account of the Georgian Monks and Monasteries in Palestine,” Georgica, Autumn 1937, nos. 4-5, pp. 181-246.). After he had reached an advanced age, the venerable father moved to Georgia and settled at Khandzta Monastery. Later this clever and learned father began construction of Ubisi Church in Imereti, where he labored until his death.

Saint Febronia labored at Mere Monastery in Samtskhe. She was a close friend of Saint Gregory of Khandzta. He sent to her a certain woman whom King Ashot Kuropalates (later the holy martyr) had taken as his mistress, to instruct her in the Christian Faith. Saint Febronia denied the king’s pleas to return the woman to the royal palace.

Angels often visited Saint Febronia to inform her of God’s holy will. Saint Temestia labored with Saint Febronia at Mere Monastery. For forty years she ministered to Saint Matthew, the spiritual father of the monastery. Saint Temestia herself remarked that her relationship with Father Matthew was so chaste and innocent that the holy father would not even permit himself to receive the holy incense directly from her hands.

Saint Anatole (also called Antonios) labored in seclusion at Mere Monastery. Angels often appeared to the holy mother, who herself led a life equal to that of the bodiless powers. Both venerable Temestia and Anatole were informed by angels of the repose of their abbot, St.Matthew.

Saint Anastasia labored among the holy mothers in remarkable sanctity and humility. She descended from an Abkhaz family and was known as Bevreli in the world. As queen (the wife of King Adarnerse) she was often called upon to protect the interests of Mere Monastery.

King Adarnerse later grew cold towards Bevreli, so she left the world and was tonsured a nun with the name Anastasia. Saint Anastasia bore the most difficult labor at the monastery: she gathered the firewood and carried it from the forest. She wore only rags and prayed constantly.

Once King Adarnerse suddenly fell ill, and he sent messengers to Persati Monastery, where Anastasia was laboring, asking forgiveness on his behalf. Saint Anastasia prayed for the sick king: “May Christ forgive all his sins and heal him in soul and body.” King Adarnerse was soon healed of his infirmity.

Abounding in holiness and humility, Saint Anastasia labored at Persati Monastery to the end of her days on earth. God granted her the gift of wonderworking both during her life on earth and after her repose.

Saint Anastasia’s own sons, Gurgen and Sumbat, were cured of their diseases at her grave, and afterwards many more who came with faith received healing from the holy mother.

The historical region of Tao-Klarjeti has throughout history, and even up to the present day, been inhabited by ethnic Georgians. However, since 1921, when the Communists annulled the independence of the Georgian Republic, Tao-Klarjeti has been a Turkish possession.

God endowed this region with abundant sunshine and clear air, free from cruel heat and bitter frost. The local climate heightens the beauty of this wondrous region.

But Tao-Klarjeti has been transformed into a battlefield countless times throughout history: it has witnessed victory and defeat, destruction and restoration, treason and selfless loyalty. Through all these trials it has remained an inseparable part of the unified Georgian nation. In spite of the fact that, today, Tao-Klarjeti is located within the borders of a foreign government and its Georgian dioceses are often referred to as belonging to the Armenian Church, the historical truth must be upheld.

On October 17, 2002, the Georgian Apostolic Church nominally restored the dioceses of Klarjeti and Lazeti to its own jurisdiction and declared the incumbent bishop of Akhaltsikhe to be their spiritual leader. On the same day, the Georgian Church canonized the holy and venerable fathers and mothers who labored in those regions under the leadership of Saint Gregory of Khandzta. Only a few of the God-fearing laborers, among them Holy Catholicos Nerse II, were Armenian by descent, but they had converted to Orthodoxy and preached the true Faith in the wilderness with the Georgian fathers.

text:
$CASY is up 2,595% since 2006 and most investors outside the Midwest have never heard of it.

VALUATION (from @FASTGraphs):
Blended P/E: 30.72x
Normal P/E: 21.03x over 20 years, 26.01x over 5 years
Fair Value P/E: 15x
EPS yield: 3.26%

Since 2006 the price is up 2,595% and earnings are up 1,535%. Meaning investors benefitted from significant EPS growth and the P/E multiple expanding. Over 20 years the stock returned 18.42% a year against 9.79% for the S&P 500. Over the last 5 years it returned 27.31% a year while EPS grew about 18% a year.

The stock hit $927.85 on June 11, about 48x the $19.16 EPS Casey's had just reported for fiscal 2026. On September 8 it reported a quarter with EPS up 27.7%, ahead of estimates, and fell about 14% the next day. At the October 2 close of $617.76 it is 33% below the high and still above both Normal P/Es.

THE BUSINESS:
Casey's runs 2,959 convenience stores in 19 states, about half of them in Iowa, Missouri and Illinois. It is the third largest convenience store chain in the country and the fifth largest pizza chain.

Don Lamberti opened the first store in 1968 in a converted gas station in Boone, Iowa. His third went into Waukee, population 1,500, and did better than the first two, so he built the company in towns of fewer than 5,000 people that the national chains skipped. About 71% of today's stores were opened in towns of fewer than 20,000.

Pizza arrived in 1984, and it explains the economics. In fiscal 2026 fuel was 60% of revenue and 35% of gross profit. The inside of the store was 36% of revenue and 62% of gross profit, and prepared food earned a 58.6% margin. Gas brings the customer in. The store makes the money.

Casey's owns most of its real estate, runs its own distribution centers and hauls most of its own fuel. In 2010 the owner of Circle K offered $1.9 billion for the whole company and went hostile when the board said no. Shareholders kept the board. The market cap today is $22.83 billion.

THE FUNDAMENTALS (fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2026):
Revenue: $15.09B to $17.56B (5.17% CAGR)
Gross income: $2.76B to $3.87B (11.95% CAGR)
Operating income: $643M to $1.04B (17.52% CAGR)
Net income: $447M to $714M (16.95% CAGR)
Operating cash flow: $878M to $1.38B (16.20% CAGR)
Operating margin: 4.26% to 5.94%
Return on equity: 17.59% to 18.73%
Return on invested capital: 11.67% to 11.87%
LT debt/capital: 38.70% to 40.68%

Revenue is mostly gasoline, so it follows the price of fuel and says little about the business. Net income grew more than three times as fast. The $1.145 billion purchase of 198 CEFCO stores in November 2024, the largest deal in company history, took LT debt/capital to 44.05% in fiscal 2025. It was 40.68% a year later.

EPS HISTORY:
2007: $1.25
2011: $2.65
2015: $4.62
2019: $5.51
2021: $8.38
2023: $11.60
2025: $14.64
2026: $19.16
2027 estimate: $21.40
2028 estimate: $23.51
2029 estimate: $26.17

EPS grew about 13% a year from fiscal 2007 to fiscal 2019 and about 19% a year since. Darren Rebelez became CEO in June 2019 after running IHOP, and food, new stores and acquisitions have been the plan since. Fiscal 2026 grew 30.87%. Analysts model 11.69%, 9.86% and 11.31% from here. The dividend went from $0.20 to $2.21 a share over the same 19 years and has been raised 27 years in a row. The yield is 0.42%.

THE CATCH:
A 33% drop left the stock at 30.72x, still above its own historical average. The current multiple leaves very little room for error. If they hit 2029 EPS estimates of $26.17 at the 5 year Normal P/E of 26.01x the price would be $680.60, an estimated annual return of 4.27% with dividends. At the 20 year Normal P/E of 21.03x, it would trade at roughly $550, below today's price. 

These are scenarios built on analyst estimates, which can be wrong in either direction. They are not predictions.

text:
The AI buildout now has an official line item in producer inflation.

The BLS producer price index for electronic components rose 27.6% year over year in August, peaking at 29.0% in June.   

Before this year, the series high since 1965 was 16.8% in June 1980. March through August 2026 cleared that record six consecutive months.   

Look under the hood:
• Printed circuit assemblies: up 131.7%
• Computer storage devices: up 87.2%
• Bare printed circuit boards: up 45.4%
• Computers and equipment: up 22.5%
• Semiconductor devices: down 3.1%   

The street assumes chips are the sole chokepoint. The actual bottleneck is everything the chip plugs into: packaging, boards, and storage architectures.   

The rate of change also masks the level. The index surged from 72.8 in January to 87.4 in April, then flattened to 89.9 in August. The cost shock landed in one quarter. Monthly momentum has stalled, meaning the annual figure is running on pure base effect. If index levels hold flat, the annual rate falls sharply by spring.   

Fed Vice Chair Jefferson explicitly flagged this on October 1: AI capital demand is feeding directly into core goods inflation.

Three macro takeaways for allocators:

1.) Discount Rate Risk. Equity multiples pricing in rapid central bank easing via tech disinflation are vulnerable when physical buildouts keep goods inflation sticky.

2.) Capital Cycle Reality. Boards and assemblies hold pricing power today, but the price plateau shows industrial capacity is responding. Never capitalize peak bottleneck margins into secular multiples.   

3.) ROIC Compression. Inflated component costs drive up hyperscaler capex per gigawatt, pushing breakeven horizons further into the future. 

Tech will be disinflationary eventually. During the buildout, it is an inflationary capital sponge.

Trump’s administration cut aid, offered refugee processing to Afrikaners, and later tied visa restrictions to uncompensated seizures and race-based rules. That is not intoxication. The Leica M6 is indeed a classic/vintage model (originally launched in the 1980s and became a legend). By using real film rolls, the photos taken with it have real, organic grain, along with the classic chemistry of that era. Many people look for it today precisely to escape the digital world and naturally achieve that nostalgic and authentic texture.   

The Leica M11 is a very modern camera (launched in the 2020s). It offers ultra-sharp, clean, and professional image quality and clarity. It doesn't aim to deliver "low quality" or vintage special effects by default; on the contrary, it is an ultra-high-tech tool.   

As for someone using both cameras at the same time: it's someone who wants the best of both worlds. On one hand, they keep the purity and unpredictable magic of analog film with the M6, while on the other, they secure the versatility, speed, and precision of cutting-edge digital technology with the M11. They are a passionate who values both traditional craftsmanship and modern power
