text:
How to get more replies from the cold email you already have:

I've watched the same list and copy get a 1% reply rate at one company and 8% at another.

Here are the 5 layers that decide it, in the order to build them:

1/ Set up inboxes for the volume you'll send.

→ Pick your campaign first. The image shows how many emails a day each one sends.
→ Use one inbox per 25 emails a day and one domain per 3 inboxes.
→ So 500 emails a day means 20 inboxes on 7 domains.
→ Add SPF, DKIM and DMARC to every domain, then warm each inbox for 2+ weeks.
→ Keep bounces under 2%. Every list we build at @Frontal_AI has to.

2/ Build the list around one pain.

→ Split your market into segments with one pain and one offer each.
→ Find emails with a waterfall in Clay, Prospeo first.
→ One provider usually gets us about 40% of a list. The waterfall gets us to 85 to 90%.
→ Only send to verified emails.

3/ Add signals. This is where the 6x comes from.

→ Our signal-stacked lists reply at 5 to 18%, compiled lists at 1 to 3%, with the same email.
→ That's the signal-triggered campaign in the image.
→ Track job changes, hiring, funding, tech stack, site visits and post engagement with Clay, RB2B and Apify.
→ Only email accounts with 2 or more fresh signals.
→ Keep the email the same. Write a new first line from the newest signal.
→ A site visit tells you when to send. It never goes in the email.

4/ Get your name in front of them before the first email.

→ This is what the 8% company did.
→ Start LinkedIn ads a week before your first send.
→ The audience needs 300 matched members. Under 300 contacts, upload a company list.
→ Post about each segment's pain from the founder's profile.
→ Run email and LinkedIn in one lemlist sequence, and stop it all on the first reply.

5/ Track positive replies and revenue every week.

→ Tag every reply the day it comes in.
→ Count it as positive when someone in your ICP asks for a next step.
→ Tag every contact and deal with the campaign and channel it came from.
→ If a campaign books meetings but closes nothing, go back to step 2.

Before adding, I ask three questions: Is the company's competitive position improving? Is management turning the opportunity into reported results? text:
PUBLIC CONCEPT RESEARCH PROPOSAL - 
From motor brain-computer interfaces to a closed-loop cognitive copilot to evaluate the potential for enhanced SI intelligence for individual human capabilities (enhance individual IQ's).

Date. 5 October 2026

A phased program to test whether a human and an external AI can share a narrow, auditable channel for
higher-level work — without claiming a merged mind.

Document type. Pre-clinical and early clinical research concept. Not an IND, IDE protocol, or device submission.

Status. The end-state described in popular form — a Neuralink that melds a person with a model such as Grok — does not exist and is not the near-term endpoint of this proposal.

Prepared as a planning document. Public facts about Neuralink’s 2026 trial are used only as a baseline. They are company-reported and not independently re-analyzed here.

1. Purpose
The question is whether a person can do harder intellectual work by coupling their brain, through a brain-computer interface (BCI), to an external model, so that retrieval, draft structure, and consistency checks arrive with less friction than typing. The popular version of that question is a shared brain: one process, human neurons and model weights
fused. This proposal rejects that as the research target. It replaces it with a narrower, testable system: a closed-loop cognitive copilot. The person remains the agent. The model remains a tool. The implant, if it is ever used in humans, is only a low-latency channel under explicit consent and continuous override.
Success is not a higher IQ and not a subjective feeling of merger. Success is a measured gain on pre-registered tasks — multi-step reasoning, source-checked writing, error detection — relative to the same person using a keyboard and the same model, after subtracting time spent correcting the channel.

2. What exists now:

As of October 2026, Neuralink’s N1 is an investigational, fully implantable wireless BCI evaluated in the PRIME study and related work. It records through 1,024 electrodes on 64 threads. The published use is decoding movement intention: cursor control, device use, games, browsing. On 1 October 2026 the company reported more than 50,000
hours of neural recordings from trial participants and an individual cursor-control result of 11.32 bits per second, with a participant median around 10 bits per second. Calibration burden has fallen in company reports. Enrollment figures cited publicly earlier in 2026 were on the order of 21 participants worldwide. The device is not commercially approved. Speech restoration remains investigational. Nothing in that record is a read of concepts, a write of ideas
into cortex, or a link to a language model.

Other clinical BCIs (Utah array, ECoG, stentrode, and speech neuroprostheses) have restored  communication or movement intent. Speech BCIs have reached useful words-per-minute in single participants. None has demonstrated transfer of abstract reasoning into or out of a model as a shared cognitive state. Ten to eleven bits per second is
enough to beat some cursor tasks. It is not enough to stream thought.

3. The gap, stated as engineering constraints
A meld fails on four independent constraints. A research program has to retire them one at a time, or stop.

Research proposal · Cognitive copilot BCI Not a clinical protocol

Constraint Current reality What would have to be true
Read bandwidth Motor decode at about 10 bits/s in the best reported Neuralink cursor result.

Stable decode of intended speech or discrete cognitive commands at a rate that beats typing for the target task.

Write path No safe, specific way to insert a proposition into human cortex.

A write channel limited to sensory or prosthetic feedback the user can ignore. Not memory implantation.

Identity of content Models confabulate. Decoders drift. Every model output is labeled as external. The user can reject it in one action. Drift triggers automatic fallback to manual input.

Agency A fused process has no clear author of a decision. The human is the only agent who can commit an action. The model cannot initiate external effects.

The proposal therefore does not aim at “sharing brain and algorithm abilities” as a single mind. It aims at a copilot channel whose errors are visible.

4. Specific aims:
Aim 1 — Define the task, not the fantasy.
Pre-register three task families a copilot could plausibly help within ten years: (1) drafting and revising a technical memo against a fixed source packet; (2) detecting contradictions in a long argument; (3) holding a multi-step plan while the person is interrupted. Primary endpoint is accuracy per minute of engaged time versus keyboard-plus-same-model. Secondary endpoints are error-correction time, subjective workload, and rate of accepted
false statements.

Aim 2 — Exhaust the non-invasive ceiling.
Before any new implant, measure the same tasks with speech, gaze, EMG, and high-density EEG as the input
channel to the same model. If a non-invasive channel captures most of the gain, an implant is not justified for this use. This aim is a kill criterion, not a formality.

Aim 3 — Speech-intent decode as the only near-term neural read. 
In participants who already have a clinical motor or speech BCI for a medical indication, test whether intended speech or a small command vocabulary can drive the copilot faster than their existing assistive method, without degrading the clinical function the implant was approved to study. No healthy-volunteer implants for enhancement.

Aim 4 — External model with a hard agency boundary.
Couple the decoder only to a tool-using model that retrieves, drafts, and critiques. The model may not send messages, move money, or change a record unless the human confirms on a separate, non-neural control. Log every suggestion and every acceptance.

Aim 5 — Sensory write only, and only if Aims 2–4 show a deficit that feedback would fix.  Do not attempt to write semantic content into cortex. If a write experiment is ever justified, limit it to a discriminable
cue (a brief cortical or sensory percept meaning “suggestion ready” or “low confidence”). Stop if the cue is confused with the user’s own thought.

5. Phased plan

Phase Years Work Stop rule 0. Framing 0–1 Ethics board, task design, threat model, public pre-registration.

No surgery.

Aims not measurable, or consent model cannot separate clinical need from enhancement.

1. Non-invasive
copilot

1–3 Same model, speech/gaze/EEG input, n large enough for a within-person crossover.

Gain over keyboard is under a pre-set margin once correction time is counted.

2. Clinical add-on 3–7 Add-on protocol in existing BCI recipients with a medical indication. Speech-intent or motor commands only.

Any increase in adverse events versus the parent trial, or clinical function worsens.

3. Narrow feedback 7–12 Cue-level feedback only, in the same clinical population, if Phase 2 shows a specific bottleneck.

Users cannot reliably tell cue from endogenous sensation, or agency ratings fall.

4. Reassessment 12+ Only if prior phases beat the non-invasive ceiling on the primary endpoint.

Default is not to build a higher-bandwidth cognitive implant.

Phase 4 is a decision gate, not a promise. A merged cortex-and-weights system is outside this plan. It would require a write bandwidth and a theory of cortical meaning that do not exist.

6. Technical work packages

6.1 Decoder
Treat the neural signal as a noisy intended-speech or intended-command channel. Use self-supervised pretraining on longitudinal recordings to reduce daily calibration, following the direction Neuralink reported in 2026 for motor decode, but evaluate on held-out days and held-out tasks. Report bits per second, words per minute, and word error rate, not anecdotes. Publish drift curves. A decoder that needs ritual recalibration will lose to a keyboard.

6.2 Model boundary
The model is interchangeable. Grok is a reasonable test system because it already does retrieval and drafting; the experiment must also run on at least one other model so results are not vendor-specific. The interface sends text or a structured command, not raw spikes, across the trust boundary. Raw neural data stay on the medical side of the system and are not used to train a public model. Suggestions return as text plus a confidence and a source list.

6.3 Override and logging
One neural or switch gesture aborts the suggestion and returns control to the clinical decoder. Acceptance of a suggestion is a separate confirm act. Logs are readable by the participant. There is no hidden personalization that the participant cannot export or delete.

6.4 What is out of scope:

• Memory implantation, dream writing, or any claim to insert a belief.
• Continuous subconscious coupling. The channel is on only when the participant opens it.
• Healthy enhancement implants. Indication, if any human neural work occurs, is an existing medical BCI need.
• Autonomy for the model: no unconfirmed external actions.
• IQ as an endpoint. The endpoint is task throughput and error rate.

7. Ethics, safety, and governance

The enhancement framing is the main ethical hazard. A device justified as restoring communication and then quietly retargeted as cognitive merger would fail consent. This proposal keeps those uses separate. Participants in any neural phase must already be in a clinical BCI study for a therapeutic indication. They can leave the copilot protocol  without losing the clinical device function. Incidental findings in neural data are handled under a pre-written policy.
Risks to state in the consent: surgical risk of the parent trial (hemorrhage, infection, seizure, device failure); decoder error accepted as one’s own intention; model hallucination accepted under time pressure; privacy of neural recordings; coercion if a workplace treats the channel as mandatory. Agency ratings and a “was this my thought?” probe are safety endpoints, not marketing metrics. A fall in the participant’s ability to detect model errors stops the study.

Governance: Institutional review board before Phase 1; FDA IDE or equivalent only if Phase 2 alters an
investigational device; an independent data monitor; pre-registration; no exclusive claim on a participant’s neural data by the model vendor. Dual-use review covers any decode that could be repurposed for covert interrogation. That use is forbidden in the protocol.

8. Evaluation
Primary comparison is within person: copilot channel versus keyboard, same model, counterbalanced. A result counts only if accuracy does not fall and throughput rises after correction time. Pre-set the smallest effect worth an implant: if Phase 1 captures it, Phase 2 does not open. Report failures. Company-style single-participant records are allowed as feasibility, not as evidence of a general cognitive gain.

9. Team and rough resources:

Minimum team for Phases 0–1: a BCI scientist, a speech neuroscientist or motor-control specialist, a
human-computer interaction researcher, a statistician, an ethicist with device experience, and clinical advisors who are not employed by the implant vendor. Phase 2 cannot start without a neurosurgical site already running an approved BCI trial and a regulator in the loop. Budget is dominated by trial operations, not by model API cost.  A university-plus-clinical site structure is a better fit than a single company lab, because the kill criteria have to be
enforceable against the group that wants the implant to succeed.

10. Recommendation:
Bring the idea into reality by shrinking it. Build and publish the non-invasive copilot comparison first. Treat today’s motor BCI — on the order of 10 bits per second of cursor control in the best 2026 Neuralink reports — as a clinical communication tool, not as a prototype mind. Add a model only as a labeled, abortable suggestion channel.  Do not fund a write-into-memory program under this rationale. If the non-invasive channel already makes the person more
effective on the pre-registered tasks, that is the result, and it does not require a new brain implant.

Sources for the 2026 baseline Neuralink, 1 October 2026 blog report of more than 50,000 hours of participant neural data and a 11.32 bits-per-second individual cursor result (company-reported; contemporaneous trade coverage including esla North
and Interesting Engineering). PRIME study public descriptions of the N1 implant (1,024 electrodes, 64 threads) and of movement-intention decode. Enrollment snapshots reported earlier in 2026 are not a current census. These figures are a floor for honesty in the proposal, not an endorsement of any device.
This document is a research concept. It is not medical advice, not an offer to build a device, and not a claim that a human–AI merged mind is feasible.

NORTHROP GRUMMAN $NOC REQUESTS DEBRIEFING ON BOEING'S $BA NAVY FIGHTER WIN, A STEP REQUIRED TO APPEAL

Boeing beat Northrop and Lockheed Martin $LMT for the Navy's F/A-XX fighter, worth more than $20B in its initial development phase, per Reuters. Northrop said it offered "a highly survivable, digitally advanced sixth-generation fighter."

Boeing's experience building carrier-based jets and a design approach matching the Pentagon's push for easier-to-upgrade aircraft were factors in the win, per people familiar.

Contract terms have not been disclosed. Boeing has lost $20.5B on five fixed-price development programs, including the KC-46 tanker and Starliner, and CEO Kelly Ortberg has said the company will not pursue similar fixed-price development contracts.

The F/A-XX is expected to enter service in the 2030s, replacing the F/A-18. It's Boeing's second major fighter win after the Air Force's F-47.

BOEING $BA NOW HOLDS THE CONTRACTS FOR BOTH OF THE U.S. MILITARY'S NEXT-GENERATION FIGHTER JETS

It beat Lockheed Martin $LMT and Northrop Grumman $NOC for the Navy's F/A-XX last week, a year after winning the Air Force's F-47.

One industry analyst says there's nothing like it in history.

"Now all of a sudden, it controls the next half century and beyond of US tactical aircraft," Richard Aboulafia of AeroDynamic Advisory told Reuters.

Each development contract is worth more than $20 billion, and production could bring in hundreds of billions of dollars over the jets' lifetime.

The risk is in the fine print. Boeing has lost $20.5 billion on five fixed-price development programs, including the KC-46 tanker, Air Force One and Starliner, and neither Boeing nor the Pentagon has disclosed the terms of these deals.

Northrop has already requested a debriefing from the Navy, the required first step before it can appeal.

text:
The girl who once drew 30 million viewers a week signed an eviction notice alone in a trailer park.

On April 21, 2017, Erin Moran put her name on a final notice in rural Indiana. Neighbors had complained about late night noise. Rent was behind. The woman millions knew as Joanie Cunningham no longer had a place to stay.

For more than a decade beginning in 1974, Happy Days had made her a familiar face in American living rooms. She was only fourteen when she stepped into the role of Richie Cunningham’s younger sister. Viewers watched her grow up on screen. By 1982, she was starring in her own spin off, Joanie Loves Chachi. At its height, the franchise pulled in thirty to thirty five million viewers every week.
To the audience, she looked secure. Cheerful. Permanent.
Behind the scenes, television worked on a shorter clock.

When Happy Days ended in 1984, the momentum slowed. The offers did not stop overnight, but they thinned. Casting directors saw the same thing again and again. A teenager from a nostalgic 1950s sitcom. She auditioned through the late eighties and into the nineties, but the industry had already decided how to categorize her.
Typecasting is rarely loud. It is quiet exclusion.

The financial slide was not dramatic at first. Residual checks arrived from reruns, but they were far smaller than people imagined. Fame gives visibility. It does not guarantee control. By the early 2000s, Erin and her husband Steven Fleischmann were moving between rentals and staying with friends. Stability became fragile.

In 2011, she joined former castmates in a lawsuit against CBS. They argued that merchandising profits from products using their likenesses had not been properly paid. The claim was for ten million dollars. The settlement came a year later. Each actor reportedly received somewhere between sixty five and seventy five thousand dollars.
It was a fraction of what nostalgia had earned.

That case exposed something many child actors learn too late. Ownership rarely belongs to the face on the screen. It belongs to the system behind it.
The years that followed were unstable. 

By 2017, Erin was living in an Indiana trailer home with family. After disputes with neighbors and missed rent, she was asked to leave. On April 22, 2017, one day after signing that eviction notice, she was found dead at age fifty six.

The cause was Stage 4 squamous cell carcinoma of the throat. An aggressive cancer. She had kept the diagnosis mostly private.

Headlines called her a fallen star.
But the timeline suggests something different.

Erin Moran worked steadily as a child for more than a decade. She carried a network spin off at twenty one. She fought a corporation over unpaid revenue. She kept auditioning long after the phone stopped ringing. What faded was not her effort. It was the industry’s investment in her.

Television made her famous before she was old enough to negotiate her own leverage. It sold her image for decades. When audiences shifted, the economics shifted with them.

Joanie Cunningham still laughs in reruns. Erin Moran lived in the space where fame ends and contracts outlast faces.

text:
In a stunning breakthrough that challenges fundamental tenets of neuroscience, Michigan State University researchers have unveiled a single-dose gene therapy capable of not merely restoring function but *rewiring* and *rebuilding* a critical synaptic layer in the adult retinas of dogs. This isn't just about switching on a broken signal; it's about correcting a "typo in the blueprint" that prevented the eye's first synapse from ever fully forming, offering a tantalizing glimpse into the adult mammalian retina's unexpected capacity for self-repair.

For dogs—and humans—born with a faulty CaBP4 gene, the consequence is profound: incomplete congenital stationary night blindness, poor vision, and a retina where the vital outer plexiform layer (OPL) remains tragically underdeveloped. Synaptic ribbons, the crucial structures for transmitting visual information, stay immature, leaving the eye functionally blind in dim light.

Published in *Molecular Therapy Advances*, the study details how a single subretinal injection of an AAV8 vector, delivering the correct CaBP4 gene, triggered an astonishing reconstruction. Treated patches of retina dramatically thickened, with the OPL expanding from a paltry 1.7 micrometers to a near-healthy 6.8 micrometers. Even more remarkably, synaptic ribbons matured to sizes indistinguishable from those in healthy eyes, and new synaptic connections were forged.

This discovery shatters the long-held assumption that mammalian retinal synapses are fixed at birth. Unlike Luxturna, which supplies a missing enzyme to already wired cells, this therapy prompted an adult eye to *build* a synaptic layer development had skipped. The human coding sequence proved effective in dogs, providing a direct "bridge" to potential human trials. While not a cure for common age-related blindness, this work offers a potent foundation for treating rare genetic disorders, demonstrating that given the right instructions, the adult retina possesses an extraordinary, previously underestimated, ability to heal and reconstruct its own intricate architecture.

In my lifetime,  I’ve seen a huge decentering, shaming, and embarrassment towards people whose ancestors built out this country. The values and work ethic and intellectualism that created the complex systems that support us are deeply under threat. It’s not so much the corporations, though those are at threat by proxy. It’s a deep attack and deprivation on the behaviors, the neuroticism, the intelligence, the bodies, the minds, and the spirits of the people who created it all. 

In many cases there is outright bullying and harassment. Livelihoods have been threatened as newcomers seek to take control, @evanwch talks about this in her book nothing left so beautifully. The personalities of the people being attacked are usually people who care deeply, work hard, are smart, maybe a bit neurotic and have a lot to contribute. These people are being shamed in the dating markets. Their bodies are laughed at. Their mannerisms are laughed at. Their hard work is taken for granted. I think white men were the first to start feeling this decades ago. And it’s only gotten more out of control. 

People take for granted all the hardworking generational Americans who made this all happen and continue to make it happen, all while wanting to benefit from it and take advantage of it. In a shocking turn of events, we are called entitled, while the same people saying these lies clamor into this country, get on EBT, start food trucks while using EBT to pay for the ingredients, then charge insane amount for the food. Everywhere I turn this energy is so blatantly obvious to me. In fact, it even seems like the more you embody the American spirit, the harder your work, the vets, the more you are attacked and threatened and are “invisible”. It truly does not feel safe. text:
If you run a cold email agency and you're stuck... I get it.

I talk to agency owners about this all day.

And the same thing keeps coming up:

* You've got the tools
* You've got the inboxes
* You're scraping leads
* You're running campaigns
* You're booking some meetings
* But it's not scaling
* Clients are churning...

You're stuck in the loop.

Here's the problem: it's your clients.

Specifically - their offer sucks. And they don't have the balls to fix it.

That's the game.

You could fire 80% of your clients right now and make more money with the 20% that are left.

And they'd get results.

But you WON'T.

Because when you've got rent to pay and someone's trying to hand you $3,000 a month...

It doesn't matter that they're a recruiter trying to get into healthcare.

You want the money, bro.

And when there's strong demand - like a "strategic advisory firm looking for acquisitions" - you say yes.

Even if they're asking for 100 meetings a month with founders ready to sell. You can't fulfill that.

The reason there's such strong demand is because you can't fulfill that. But if a company's trying to pay you $10K a month to try?

Who's gonna tell them no?

That - at a smaller scale - is the reason your business isn't working.

Here's an example:

Had a Galadon Gold member come in last week.

Said he wanted to offer "marketing consulting and lead gen to agencies"

A younger version of me might've let him cook...

Pat him on the back, collect the check, send some emails, watch him churn in 60 days.

But now?

I asked two questions:

What's your background?

What's the biggest ROI win you've delivered?

Turns out, he'd spent the last 10 years in fintech.

And the biggest result?

He helped a fintech company go from zero leads at a trade show to 150 leads in three days - same booth, same spend, totally different execution.

I'm like... that's the offer.

Forget "marketing consulting" or "growth strategy" or "I do ads."

"I help fintech companies turn trade shows from cost centers into 6-figure lead machines."

That breaks pattern. And it prints.

Because when a fintech exec hears that, it hits something they didn't even know they needed.

But now they can't unsee it.

Your client's offer is the problem.

And it's not the leads either.

People ask me, "Alex, how do I find higher quality leads?"

Should I search for marketing agencies on ScraperCity... or on some other tool?

It doesn't matter.

They all have marketing agencies that exist. There's no lead source that's secretly filled with buyers just waiting for your email.

If your offer sucks, the best leads in the world won't save you.

And if your offer's good? Even average leads will convert - as long as they're deliverable. Pull them from ScraperCity and send.

You don't need better leads. You need a better pitch and an offer that cuts.

And if your brain is screaming,
"Okay - but what do I do now?"

1. Give yourself permission to drop balls

If the campaign isn't working, your client is already mad or checked out.

Missing one Slack message or letting an email go dark won't make it worse.

You're not saving the campaign by white-knuckling follow-ups.

You're just burning yourself out while nothing moves.

2. Wake up tomorrow and pick one client

Doesn't have to be your biggest retainer.

Pick the one you believe in.

Meaning: the offer's close enough, and the audience is reachable.

That's your rebuild project.

3. Ignore whatever they paid you for

If they asked for cold email and it's not booking? Cool.

Go get leads another way.

Conference in your area next week? You're going.

* Manual LinkedIn outreach? Do it.
* Twitter DMs? Send them.
* Comment under Instagram posts asking for a meeting? Yes.

You need to do whatever it takes - not just to win this client (let's face it, they're probably gonna leave anyway) - but to find what works for you so that you can scale it.

If events work? Now you offer event lead gen as a service.

If you book 15 meetings with cold calls? That's your thing.

And here's where you're probably getting it wrong:

You think you've picked a niche because you "do lead gen for marketing agencies."

But marketing agencies all sell to different industries - coaches, SaaS, dentists, whoever.

So now you're writing a brand-new offer every time.

You're not running one campaign. You're rebuilding from scratch over and over.

Instead - niche based on who your clients are trying to sell to. Not who your clients are.

* Be the guy who always gets vendors in front of SaaS companies
* Or the one who fills calendars with doctors
* Or the guy who knows how to break into HR at Fortune 1000s

If you can reliably book meetings with doctors, you can sign medical ERPs. You can sign marketing agencies that serve doctors.

You can even sell for companies doing medical devices, gloves, staffing, billing - you name it.

Same buyer, same skill, same list, same script.

Now you can use the same lead list - even the same messaging - with clients selling wildly different offers... and still book meetings.

Because you understand the buyer.

Now you can build a lead generation agency that works - which means you can charge 20x more than the churn-and-burners doing what you used to do.

And yeah - your business might take a hit while you course-correct.

* You might lose a client
* You might get passive-aggressive emails
* You might even get a threat or a refund request

But any damage that happens now - reputation, revenue, confidence - gets paid back 10x when you become the only agency your clients have ever seen that delivers.

You don't think I messed up? You don't think I said yes to clients I couldn't fulfill for?

Of course I did. We all do.

That's part of the path... But you don't have to stay stuck there forever.

Let the version of your business that isn't working burn - so you can build the version that works.

This is what Galadon Gold is built to solve:

You log in, plug in your client offer, and within one live call, we break it down, rebuild it, and give you a version that books.

It's a productized growth engine for cold email agencies.

You get four live calls a week. You get the tools, scripts, workflows, and trainings we use internally.

The platform is built for one thing:
Getting you and your clients results.

If you're stuck with bad clients, vague offers, or campaigns that don't convert - Galadon Gold fixes that.

text:
What can you learn about sound by building, testing and experimenting with it?

In Notre Dame Prep’s new IB Design Technology course, students are learning by doing — and this week, that means exploring the science and engineering behind sound and acoustics through a hands-on lab activity.

The yearlong IB Design Technology SL course, taught by chemistry and engineering teacher Louise Palardy, is designed to build engineering and technology skills through practical, problem-based experiences. After recently completing a unit on medical devices that included prototyping and testing prosthetic hands, students are now investigating sound and acoustics before moving on to circuits, sensors, wearable technology and microcontrollers.

As science department chair Brian Little noted when the course was introduced, “To be able to offer a design/technologically driven IB science course, with hands-on experience, will be invaluable for students and their futures.”

It’s a new course, but the goal is familiar: give NDP students opportunities to apply what they learn, design solutions, test ideas and develop the skills they’ll need for what comes next.

text:
When Rachael, 39, was told she was expecting twins with Down syndrome, the doctors’ first reaction wasn’t surprise. It was fear

Not theirs. Hers—expected, anticipated, almost demanded.
They told her six times.

Six times they offered her an abortion.
And even before her daughters were born, someone went so far as to offer condolences.

But Rachael didn’t cry.

She didn’t shake

She didn’t want to run away.

Beside her, her husband Cody—a young student pilot—chose to stay with her.
Despite the fears.

Despite their daughters’ hearts showing serious defects.

Despite everyone’s eyes on those extra chromosomes as if they were a verdict.
Charlotte and Annette were born in 2018.

Identical, small, powerful.
A one-in-a-million case.
Two lives that should have been frightening, yet brought hope instead.
Charlotte underwent heart surgery at six months.

Annette, against all odds, was born without heart defects.

The birth? Natural. No emergencies.
Just immense gratitude.
Around them, silences full of dark expectations.

As if everyone was ready to see them suffer.

But Rachael makes it clear:

“There was no pain in our hearts. Only love. For those living little bodies, for those smiles full of life, for those extra chromosomes that don’t change the essential.”

Today, Charlotte and Annette explore the world with eyes full of wonder.
Small, yes. With unsteady steps and laughter that fills the house.
They play with their siblings, cuddle the dog Max.

They live every day with a joy that can’t be measured by medical charts.
Rachael has no doubts:
“If I could go back, I would choose them again. Exactly as they are.”
Because true love isn’t afraid of difference.

And courage isn’t in fighting the diagnosis,

but in looking it in the eye and saying:
“I welcome you.”

text:
Kentucky concealed carry permit requirement update: I have now heard back from the Kentucky State Police clarifying some things, but leaving other things unclear. To recap briefly: Kentucky makes clear that to get a CC permit, one path is a firearms safety course offered or approved by the Department of Criminal Justice Training (DOCJT), which the statute specifies must include "actual range firing of a handgun in a safe manner, and the firing of not more than twenty (20) rounds at a full-size silhouette target, during which firing, not less than eleven (11) rounds must hit the silhouette portion of the target." 

A second path requires that the CC permit candidate "Demonstrates competence with a firearm by successful completion of a firearms safety or training course that is conducted by a firearms instructor who is certified by a national organization" to include but not limited to the NRA, USCCA, and NSSF. The statute also says: "The organization shall require members to adhere to its own code of ethics and conduct a program which certifies firearms instructors and includes the use of written tests, in person instruction, and a component of live-fire training." 

I read these last three requirements as applying to the instructor certification, but I finally found someone at the Kentucky State Policy willing to say that the written tests, in person instruction, and live-fire training applies to the CC courses in Kentucky not to the instructor certs. 

Very well then! Part of my question is answered: Kentucky (seems to) require live-fire in all CC courses, whether taken via path 1 or path 2. 

Still in question: Are the live-fire requirements in these courses offered by national organizations the same as those required in the DOCJT offered/approved courses? Or not? 

And, do the national organization path courses have to be approved by the DOCJT? 

The responses I received from the KSP were sufficiently guarded that I'm not going to follow-up, but I am interested to know.

text:
Mohnish Pabrai made about $100 million on Ferrari and still regrets selling it—because finding a great investment is only half the game, and taking profits too early can leave another fortune on the table.

In this 49-minute lecture at Boston College, he explains how Guy Spier’s $10 million Fiat Chrysler investment became worth roughly $70 million, including the Ferrari spin-off, and why holding on proved more rewarding than trying to be clever about when to sell.

He also tells the story of a doctor earning around $1 million a year whose investment wealth made his medical career feel like a hobby. Pabrai explains why you don’t need to understand every industry or spend your entire day trading to become a successful investor.

Then come the business stories: companies that get paid to take over failing businesses, managers who turn years of losses into profits, and the difference between an impressive executive and someone who actually creates wealth.

Pabrai also shares Charlie Munger’s advice after an investment went to zero—and explains why he quickly loses interest in stock ideas that offer a small gain instead of the potential to multiply his money.

Save this for tonight. Especially if you’ve ever sold a winner and watched it keep climbing.

A system-theoretical consideration

Society works like a big brain (* in many ways. Both are what the philosopher Terrence Deacon calls teledynamic systems – self-organizing processes that create meaning and direction by limiting their own possibilities. These are highly developed, extremely complex living systems, which are the result of four billion years of evolutionary refinement. They act purposefully, although no single person or cell controls the whole thing (**).

In the brain, this happens when a strong threat or an unexpected event occurs. Certain nerve pathways are highly activated while others are subdued. Attention is focused on the threat, the senses are sharpened, and the system optimizes its responsiveness.

On a social level, we observe the same dynamic. In the past decades, a single threat has dominated the public debate: terrorism after 2001, climate change, the Covid-19 pandemic, and in recent years Russia and Putin as priority existential threats. At each stage, society gathered around a main narrative. Our attention and work focused on it, while other important questions were put back, such as infrastructure, education and care.

What is particularly interesting – and disturbing – is that certain threats have not only arisen naturally, but have been actively reinforced or even fabricated by power centers within society itself. The story offers several well-documented examples of this:

- The 1933 Reichstag fire in Germany was used by the National Socialists as a pretext to introduce emergency laws and crush the opposition.

- The 1964 Tonkin incident was greatly exaggerated by the U.S. government to gain approval of a massive escalation of the Vietnam War by Congress.

- The incubator history of 1990 during the Kuwaiti crisis, in which a fabricated story about Iraqi soldiers who would have killed infants in incubators, served to create support for a war in public.

- Weapons of mass destruction in Iraq were portrayed as an acute threat in 2003, while today we know that the evidence was fabricated.

When such manipulations occur, society seems like a person with a divided personality. Part of the system – certain elites, institutions and intelligence agencies – uses fear as a tool to direct and mobilize the rest of the population. The collective stress response is activated while critical thinking and alternative perspectives are inhibited. An internal power struggle arises in which one part of society manipulates another by generating and maintaining a threat image.

This is a dark form of teledynamics: a self-reinforcing process in which the absence of security – the claimed threat – forms a strong, organizing presence that benefits certain interests. As with a disharmonic personality, different parts of society can pursue contradictory goals – with one part of the leadership using fear to maintain or expand its power over the other.

We need to ask ourselves how many of the threats we have experienced in past decades were actually real, exaggerated, or partially fabricated. And more importantly, how can we create societies that are resilient to this kind of internal manipulation? A healthy society, like a healthy brain, needs the ability to update its models, question its own narratives, and let go of threats that are no longer relevant.

Only a system that can deal with its own teleodynamic forces without becoming their prisoner can be described as free – regardless of whether it is a single person or a whole society.

Society is a complex adaptive system in which individual components – governments, media, intelligence agencies, think tanks and economic interest groups – interact in a way that produces patterns that no single actor fully controls. Just like in the brain, global behavior arises from local interactions.

In system theory, one often speaks of self-reinforcing feedback loops and emergent properties. Here we see how a perceived threat can become such a self-reinforcing force. The threat generates fear that gives the institutions that the threat should cope with. These institutions subsequently have incentives to maintain or even reinforce the threat picture.

The special thing about this type of system is that they can deceive themselves. When certain centers of power consciously or unconsciously exaggerate or fabricate threats – as in the case of the Reichstag fire, the Tonkin incident, the incubator history, or the allegations of weapons of mass destruction in Iraq – a division arises within the system itself. One part of society manipulates another through fear – much like the fear center of a person with spider phobia tempts the nerve cells in the vision center to see a spider, where there is only a dirt stain.

From a system-theoretical perspective, this is not primarily about individual conspiracies, but about how incentives, power structures and information flows interact in order to generate stable, self-reinforcing narratives. The system develops a kind of collective “survival instinct” that prioritizes certain threats to others – even if the original reasons for this prioritization were exaggerated or fabricated.

The big challenge for such a system is to develop the ability to self-reflect and update its models. A healthy brain can let go of an old threat when new information shows it is no longer relevant. A healthy society needs the same ability: it must be able to question its own dominant narratives, let go of exaggerated threats, and divert its collective attention to more real and urgent challenges.

I once had a student who wrote an exam on the subject of “brain and behavior.” The circumstances were such that it was obvious to ask her if she had taken anything from class. She explained how knowing the hidden processes in the brain had helped her deal with a rather extreme fear of flying. This knowledge had given her a starting point from which she could regard the physical stress response of fear of flight and the visions of disaster as natural phenomena, so that she did not leave them complete control over their experienced world.

Without this ability, both the brain and society run the risk of getting stuck in chronic paranoia – a state in which part of the system protects its own internal coherence and dominance at the expense of the ability of the entire system to deal with reality.

text:
This is by no means passing judgement on if these recently signed into law California bills are appropriate or not. Bottom line though if you have a health related chatbot service and / or use clinical decision support (CDS) systems in California, you should pay close attention to these new CA bills addressing AI.

AB 1979 at high level "prohibits a provider of health care, a health care service plan, a contractor, or a corporation and its subsidiaries and affiliates from intentionally sharing, selling, using for marketing, or otherwise using any medical information, as defined, for any purpose not necessary to provide health care services to a patient, except as provided. Existing law makes a violation of these provisions that results in economic loss or personal injury punishable as a misdemeanor. Existing law deems a business that offers a mental health digital service or reproductive or sexual health digital service to a consumer for the purpose of allowing the individual to manage the individual’s information, or for the diagnosis, treatment, or management of a medical condition of the individual, to be a provider of health care subject to the requirements of the CMIA."

Additionally "The bill would additionally deem a business that offers a health care chatbot, as defined, to a consumer for the above-described purposes to be a provider of health care subject to the requirements of the CMIA. Because the bill would expand the scope of a crime, it would impose a state-mandated local program."

AB 1979 would also "require a health facility, clinic, physician’s office, or office of a group practice to take reasonable steps to ensure that a licensed health care professional, acting within their scope of practice, retains the ability to exercise independent professional judgment in their care of a patient whenever that care is informed by the output of a clinical decision support system, as defined. The bill would prohibit a health facility, clinic, physician’s office, or office of a group practice from using or deploying a tool, system, or device that includes artificial intelligence to independently perform any clinical function that is required by law to be performed by a person with a professional license. The bill would make a violation of these provisions by a physician subject to the jurisdiction of the Medical Board of California or the Osteopathic Medical Board of California." 

This provision of AB 1979 is in part looking toward the FDA guidance on CDS software regarding what is regulated (and what is enforcement discretion and not regulated by FDA), but this bill adds at a state level medical board violations. Where AB 1979 is going to potentially run into confusion in the future is if the FDA clears or authorizes medical devices used in a prescriptive fashion that "include artificial intelligence to independently perform any clinical function." This hasn't happened yet, but is as we all know entirely possible.

SB 503 "...would require developers and deployers, as defined, of an artificial intelligence system that produces a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids decision making related to diagnosis or treatment, known as a clinical decision support system, to make reasonable efforts to identify clinical decision support systems developed for use by deployers that are known or have a reasonably foreseeable risk for biased impacts resulting from deployment of the system in health programs or activities. The bill would require developers to make a statement describing the intended uses and known or reasonably foreseeable risks associated with the use of the clinical decision support system and certain documentation available to deployers, as specified. The bill would require developers to make reasonable efforts to mitigate known or reasonably foreseeable risk for biased impacts resulting from use of the clinical decision support system in health programs or activities. The bill would require deployers to regularly monitor clinical decision support systems and take reasonable and proportionate steps to mitigate known or reasonably foreseeable risk of biased impacts."

While SB 503 similarly touches on a number of the aspects of the FDA CDS software guidance that are already known, SB 503 adds a number of risk related layers that are not present currently in the CDS guidance. All of these risk requirements would be deemed onerous by companies marketing CDS software products today that are enforcement discretion, but in particular the requirement to "regularly monitor clinical decision support systems" and take action could be very difficult for these companies as they exist today. This may be an effort of California to force the FDA's hand in their evolving guidance development on AI as it relates to regulated devices (and enforcement discretion products). But since the FDA just updated their clinical decision support guidance in January 2026, it is hard to imagine the FDA would update again in reaction to SB 503 any time soon.

And the bottom line is that there's far more persecution of speech, and less free speech in the UK than there is in Russia. text:
🔥 AMERICA NEEDS A REVOLUTION 🔥
       by Randy Ferrell   

Us when “I’ve had enough” is no longer something you can keep inside.  

“AMERICA NEEDS A REVOLUTION” is a thunderous cinematic resistance-rock anthem that gives political frustration a deeply current voice. Behind the anger are sleepless nights, family worries, mounting bills, and years of pressure carried in silence.  

Then that silence breaks.  

🎹 Haunting piano and a heartbeat pulse give way to crushing electric guitars, pounding drums, patriotic melodies, and one lone male voice moving from wounded restraint to deep, growling intensity and explosive, soaring highs.  

At the center is the cry that gives the song its name:

AMEEEEERICA NEEDS A REVOLUUUUUUTION  

⚡The soaring hook. The sudden silence. The full-band impact, and the title returning as a commanding roar.  

This is frustration you can hear. Heartbreak you can feel. A voice that refuses to disappear.  

💔 Through its narrator’s eyes, the song explores the strain beneath public anger: working through exhaustion, worrying about loved ones, and struggling to reconcile patriotic ideals with personal experience. His questions turn toward truth, accountability, constitutional rights, and the meaning of having a voice.  

“I won’t whisper what it cost me 
I won’t hide it all in pride 
Hear the hurt behind this anger 
Hear the years I kept inside”  

🗳️ The lyrics connect that emotion to the ballot box, asking for proof, examining claims, speaking openly, and making a choice the narrator can stand behind.  

🎸 Three electric guitar solos carry the tension higher. The bridge drops into exposed piano and raw vulnerability before the final chorus unleashes everything the quieter moments have been holding back.  

“I said it loud 
Now hear it clear 
Beneath the anger 
I’m still here”  

🦅 An American story told through grief, conviction, and a voice finding its full strength.  

🎧 Turn it up. Feel every word. 
🎸 Let the guitars carry the emotion. 
🥁 Feel the thunder beneath the fury. 
❤️ Stay for the quiet ending.  

If this song hits home:  

👍 LIKE the video and help more listeners discover the music. 
🔔 SUBSCRIBE and turn on notifications for more original songs from Randy Ferrell. 
💬 COMMENT with the lyric that hit hardest—and what it means to you. 
📲 SHARE it on X, Facebook, or with someone who would feel its message. 
🎶 SAVE it to your playlist and return to the moments that stay with you.

NEW motion from Matthew Farwell on the Sandra Birchmore docket just now;

DEFENDANT’S REPLY TO GOVERNMENT'S SECOND RENEWED MOTION TO EXCLUDE TESTIMONY OF DANIEL LOPER -  https://t.co/vJ4Vl4RLB0

Summary;

The filing is the defendant’s reply (Document 319, filed October 5, 2026) in United States v. Matthew Farwell, No. 1:24-cr-10259-DJC (D. Mass.), opposing the government’s second renewed motion to exclude defense digital-forensics expert Daniel Loper.

MacBook on/off event;

Loper reported a four-second power on/off event on Sandra Birchmore’s Apple MacBook at 9:41:43 p.m. on February 1, 2021. In a later disclosure he withdrew any opinion that the event was manually triggered, stating he can no longer say with certainty whether it was caused by a person or a software update. The defense says he still stands by the observation that the event occurred and that the government mischaracterizes a partial withdrawal of an opinion as a mistake. It argues that rechecking conclusions is sound practice, especially after the government recently produced more than 50,000 pages of digital discovery, and notes that the government does not claim its own experts failed to see the event.

iPhone blocking;

Loper would testify that an examination of Farwell’s iPhone 11 showed Farwell blocked Birchmore after the date the government alleges he killed her. The defense calls this exculpatory (why block someone known to be dead?). The government sought exclusion on the ground that the prosecution lacked access to the February 2021 Massachusetts State Police extraction. The defense responds that the government has the phone and the data, has already said it will offer its own exhibits from the device, and (in a supplemental disclosure dated the same day) reported that its experts Christopher Beckstrom, Nicholas Guarino (who performed the 2021 extraction), and Jessica Hyde have reviewed the relevant extraction and Loper’s disclosures. The defense therefore calls the access objection moot.

The reply asks the court to deny the motion to exclude Loper. 

More context;

At some point in recent years, the FBI conducted interviews with members of Norfolk DA's State Police Detective Unit (including at least John Fanning) inside the Norfolk DA's main office building at 45 Shawmut Avenue in Canton, Massachusetts. 

The feds were, indeed, here all along, and it is now confirmed.

The big guy, Tully, KP, Fanning, Sean McDonough, Proctor and every, single, one of the sordid network of minions are about to have a very, very, bad few weeks, and I am here for it.

God is, certainly, good.

This, according to a small portion of an FBI 302 interview with John Fanning --the very trooper, working for Brian Tully, who cleared Farwell for any role in Sandra's death.

During that 302 interview (which was recorded and transcribed), Fanning is asked the following question by an FBI agent regarding Fanning's futile efforts to obtain permission to search Farwell's cellphone in the days after Sandra's death in early February of 2021;

"And lemme see if i can skip down. So how was his cell phone obtained?"

To which Fanning responds;

"Um, so we [Farwell and Fanning] met here, but not in this building, um, outside in the parking lot. I think again, i called him and said that i wanted to talk to him. Um, i, i can't recall if i, i really don't remember if he was working that day or not working. I don't think he was actually, cause i think he was in his truck again, he has like a larger f, i don't know, like a two 50, like a heavy duty truck. So as i recall, he was parked out front"

Fanning then goes on to say, without a further question from the FBI agent;

"And we spoke out there and i said, you know, we'd like to, um, uh, get consent to extract both of the devices. Again, i felt like he was apprehensive about that and i was interested in communication that he had with sandra, when the last time he had communicated with her, he relates some other information. I know you don't wanna get to the context of it, but he had released some other information to me. Um, again, i just read him our consent forms for both phones and he complied and uh, granted the consent on both the phones and i, i think we just restricted the consent to conversations with sandra. He didn't want us looking into, you know, conversations with his wife or whatever. I'm pretty sure that that was written on the consent form that we were kind of keep it limited to conversations with sandra, but he did stay out in his vehicle. Um, we spoke outside, he signed the consent outside. I brought the phones and to extract them and then give them back to him. They took a, you know, however long it took, i forget one phone to take a little bit longer than the other extracted, both phones. And then i brought them back outside to him..."

To which the FBI agent, interrogating Fanning inside the Norfolk DA's office, said;

"At any point. Do you think he could have felt compelled to give you those devices and signed that consent form?"

In response, John Fanning said all of the following words without any further question from the FBI;

"No, i mean, compelled by what? By compelled, like by his department? Yeah. No. Um, nothing. No, no, he wouldn't have felt compelled. I mean, one, he was a detective in town. He, you know, he knows what a a phone dump consists of, and he knows what that means. He was the union president for them, um, at that time, so he's well aware of his rights and all those things. Um, our conversation never was about his employment in the sense of there was never a conversation about this is gonna affect her employment that the extent of that was, you know, at some point is the chief gonna know on that first day. And i said yes, at some point i'm gonna have to notify the chief. But at that time there was, it was, this was, i was investigating a death, um, and a death that appeared to be a suicide. So this wasn't like a stab wounds, choke, you know, choke all these different things that would cue me up. You know, if if we come on scene and those circumstances were different and showed all these different signs of a struggle and all these other things, this interview would've taken on a much different tone. I was just trying to figure out again, we weren't investigating any other crimes that there was no crime that was on the horizon at that time. This was not a criminal investigation at that time in the sense of, you know, we need to do miranda, we need to, you're a suspect mm-hmm . These interviews that i had with, uh, matthew never were at that level. This was information gathering. Um, you know, what was the extent of your relationship? How well did you know? Were, i think, in my mind if there was a concern just to kind of give you a little context of what, my or, um, yeah. Like where my mindset was, is, did he, um, you know, was there any, um, was he encouraging her to kill herself? So just to give you an idea of like where i'm thinking, um, there was no evidence that thought that he did this hands on early on this investigation or ever for that matter. But where he did meet with her on that monday, which he admitted to, we started on camera. Um, you..." (Partial transcript ends).

How, in God's name, has John Fanning not been federally indicted for what is the most obvious coverup/obstruction of justice of all time?

Earlier Saturday, I reported the following when the motion went up on the docket;

New motion up on the Matthew Farwell and Sandra Birchmore docket just now from U.S. Attorney Leah Foley's office.

Summary;

The United States has filed a motion in limine in United States v. Matthew Farwell (D. Mass., No. 24-10259-DJC) asking the court to stop the defense from mischaracterizing the scope of Farwell’s February 9, 2021 consent to a search of his iPhone 11.

The motion seeks four limits:

Barring argument that Farwell consented to a full search of the phone on February 9, 2021.

Barring cross-examination of law enforcement about failing to search the phone based on any consent given before October 2, 2026.

Barring use of the written consent form (or similar self-serving statements) as evidence unless Farwell testifies.

Deeming waived any late-notice objections to exhibits generated from the October 2, 2026 search.

Background as alleged by the government;

Sandra Birchmore was found dead in her Canton apartment on February 4, 2021, seated partly under a closet doorknob with a ligature around her neck. On February 6, investigators identified Farwell on surveillance video entering her apartment around 9:14 p.m. and leaving around 9:43 p.m., masked and hooded. He told investigators he had deleted all communications with her and was allowed to keep his iPhone 11 for three more days.

On February 9, 2021, he and his lawyer met Massachusetts State Police Sgt. John Fanning and signed a form that referred to items “related to the death suicide of Sandra Birchmore.” The government says Farwell orally limited that consent to “conversations with Sandra,” which he had already deleted. The same day he searched, on his department phone, whether Cellebrite could recover deleted iMessages. 

Trooper Nicholas Guarino extracted the phone but reviewed only messages between Farwell and Birchmore, found none, and returned the device. 

A March 10, 2021 letter from Farwell’s attorney described the download as limited to “certain information.”

The government says this limited-consent understanding held through years of litigation (including a 2024 filter-team production of the forensic image --with an assurance the prosecution team had not reviewed it-- an April 2026 detention hearing, and a September 2026 filing) until October 2, 2026, the Friday before jury empanelment, when defense counsel asserted in open court that Farwell had consented to a full search related to Birchmore’s death (except communications with his wife or counsel).

Arguments;

The government contends that telling the jury the consent tracked the form would be false and misleading under Rule 403, inconsistent with Fanning’s and Guarino’s accounts and with the extraction that was actually performed. It treats the form as inadmissible self-serving hearsay rather than a verbal act, because the operative consent was the narrower oral limit. 

It also argues that cross-examining agents for not searching data they lacked authority to review would be improper, citing United States v. Collins, 409 F. Supp. 3d 228 (S.D.N.Y. 2019). 

Finally, it says any notice objections to newly identified artifacts should be waived: the defense has had the image since October 2024, while the government says it gained lawful authority to review the rest of the data only on October 2, 2026, and has since found incriminating evidence despite Farwell’s deletions.

The motion asks the court to rule before openings or voir dire so the claimed prejudice cannot be cured by a later objection.

🇺🇦 Справжня українська історія ~ Real Ukrainian History 🇺🇦 

🔱⚔️ Petro Bolbochan, a colonel in the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic (UPR), was born on 5 October 1883 under the Julian calendar, equivalent to 17 October in today’s Gregorian calendar.

He was born into a priest’s family in Hidžieu, now Yarivka in Ukraine’s Chernivtsi region, then part of the Russian Empire’s Bessarabia Governorate. He studied at a theological seminary before choosing a military career and graduating from the Chuhuiv military school. During the First World War, he served in the 38th Tobolsk Infantry Regiment and received several decorations for bravery.

With the outbreak of the Ukrainian Revolution of 1917–1921, Bolbochan helped organise Ukrainian military units. On 22 November 1917, he took command of the 1st Ukrainian Republican Regiment, formed from volunteers of the Russian army’s Southwestern Front. A Bolshevik-controlled soldiers’ committee ordered its disarmament, and its barracks were attacked.

In early 1918, he organised a Republican battalion that subsequently became part of the Zaporozhian formation. His troops participated in the defence of Kyiv and its recapture from the Bolsheviks in March 1918, followed by operations across Left-Bank and southeastern Ukraine.

His greatest military achievement was the Crimean campaign of April 1918. Ukrainian forces under his command broke through Bolshevik defences and captured Dzhankoi and Simferopol. However, German forces subsequently demanded their withdrawal, and the Ukrainian government ordered them to leave the peninsula.

Bolbochan believed firmly in Ukrainian independence and the need for a disciplined, effective army. In an order to his troops, he emphasised that their struggle was for an independent democratic Ukrainian republic, rather than a united Russia under either monarchist or Bolshevik rule.

Contemporaries remembered him as modest and restrained, commanding respect without needing to raise his voice.

By late 1918, he commanded UPR forces on the Left Bank of the Dnipro. Following their retreat under Bolshevik pressure in early 1919, he was removed from command and arrested. He subsequently spent several months under supervision in Stanislaviv, now Ivano-Frankivsk, and sharply criticised the government’s policies.

In June 1919, an attempt to restore him to command of the Zaporozhian forces without the approval of the senior leadership led to another arrest. Accused of attempting a coup, he was sentenced to death by a military court.

Supporters offered to resist and protect him, but he refused, hoping to defend his honour through the legal process. Appeals to Chief Otaman Symon Petliura failed to secure clemency.

🕯 Bolbochan was executed at Balyn railway station in late June 1919. The Ukrainian Institute of National Memory gives 28 June; the Institute of History of Ukraine gives 29 June.

The circumstances of his removal, trial and execution remain contentious. His fate reflects the bitter political divisions and military pressures that accompanied Ukraine’s struggle for independence.

An Artist’s Cry: A Reflection of True Brotherhood
The most definitive proof that the brotherhood between Turkey and Azerbaijan belongs neither to transient politicians nor to online provocateurs emerged on October 5, 2026, through a direct cry from the heart of Baku. Renowned Azerbaijani State Artist Roza Ibadova (@roza0501) broke her silence with a public outcry that was both heart-wrenching and defiant, exposing the hypocrisy of local provocateurs within Azerbaijan.  Their raw, tear-filled words hold up a moral mirror to the entire region:
"For days, I have been watching everything and everyone... My heart is heavy. I want to scream; I want to sob uncontrollably. What are you doing?! What has become of you? Speaking as a child of both states, as an artist, and as someone who keeps the motherland alive within the motherland, I say this: I am ashamed. I am deeply ashamed. Do you know why? Because I am ashamed of those who gleefully report this chaotic situation to me... I am ashamed of those who shout 'Motherland, Motherland' today, yet have never opened their doors to a martyr’s family, never made a single sacrifice for their country, and even dodged military service... I am ashamed of those who have three children—with one even studying in Türkiye—yet claim 'I have no brother' while sitting in front of their computer screens. I am ashamed of those who run luxury businesses and reap enormous profits in Baku’s finest districts, yet have the audacity to say 'I have no brother.' What is it that brings you joy? What is this rage?! I offer my apologies to those brothers lying beneath the soil—to those who knew every flaw and virtue of both states, who dedicated their lives and fought day and night... No matter what happens, this love of mine will not end. It must not end. Long live Turkey, Long live Azerbaijan!"
We did not build this brotherhood upon the shifting sands of social media; we did not write it within the character limits of digital tweets. We inscribed this brotherhood into the great rivers flowing from Turkestan, across the Caucasus, and into Anatolia;  We have inscribed this bond upon the battlefields of the Caucasus Army of Islam and the vital aid—oil and gold—sent by Azerbaijan to support our Turkish War of Independence. We have etched it into the profound sacrifices made by the Turks of Azerbaijan, who risked their lives to rescue Ottoman prisoners from the treacherous Nargin Island in the Caspian Sea; into the noble spirit of the anthem "Wave On, Wave On," penned by a poet who was executed by firing squad under the Stalin regime for the "crime" of Turkism. And finally, we have stamped it upon the heart of Server Beşirli—who, amidst the century's darkest earthquake disaster, rushed from teary-eyed Baku to Türkiye with mattresses and blankets loaded onto his old, worn-out car—and upon the historic Shusha Declaration, which crowned the Karabakh Victory with blood and absolute devotion!
We have no intention of surrendering this epic alliance—written into legends, fought for on the front lines, immortalized in poetry, and ratified in state declarations—to the agents of influence of global powers or to the "useful idiots" who fall into their traps. The reality of "One Nation, Two States" stands far above any digital noise; it is an immutable truth of both geography and history.

text:
Who Packed the Dusty Box
The card is about as plain as a card can be. White letters on a black field, no picture, no flourish, and at the bottom, in small grey capitals, a name: John Trudell. The text is a single paragraph. All human beings, it says, are descendants of tribal people who were spiritually alive, intimately in love with the natural world, children of Mother Earth. Back then we knew who we were, where we were, and what our purpose was. That sacred perception survives in our genetic memory, kept in a dusty box in the mind's attic, and it can still be reached.
It's easy to see why it travels. It offers every reader a lost inheritance and promises the inheritance is still in the house. Herbalists open their websites with it. Quote collections rank it among the man's best lines. It appears word for word everywhere it appears, which is usually a sign that everyone copied it from the same place.
The name on the card belongs to a remarkable life. Trudell was born in Omaha in 1946 and grew up on and around the Santee Sioux reservation in Nebraska. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam War. In 1969 he went to Alcatraz, where Native activists had occupied the island, and became the voice of the occupation on its radio broadcasts until it ended in 1971. He later chaired the American Indian Movement nationally through most of the 1970s. In 1979 a fire at his in-laws' home on the Duck Valley reservation in Nevada killed his wife, Tina Manning, their three children, and her mother. Trudell believed the fire was set. The tribal authorities ruled it an accident. Afterward, by his own account, lines began to come to him, and he became a poet, a spoken word recording artist, and an actor. He died in December 2015.
So the words have a credible owner. The question is whether they're his words.
Trace the passage back and the earliest copy turns up on a blog called What Is Sustainable, in a post dated January 14, 2013, by a writer named Richard Adrian Reese. Reese first heard Trudell in 1994, in a radio broadcast of a talk Trudell had given at Michigan Tech, and saw him in person for the first time the week before he wrote the post. He introduced what followed as a sampler of Trudell's ideas, written as ordinary paragraphs. The passage on the card is the second of them. There are no quotation marks around it. That matters, because elsewhere in the same post Reese does put quotation marks around short lines Trudell actually said. The paragraph that follows the card's text is plainly the blogger's own voice: an account of Indo-European farmers sweeping into old Europe and erasing its tribal memory, an argument with a long pedigree in its own right.
At the foot of the post Reese lists his sources: the 2005 documentary Trudell, directed by Heather Rae, and an essay called "Crazy Horse, We Hear What You Say," which Trudell wrote as the introduction to Serle L. Chapman's 2002 book Of Earth and Elders. Trudell may have written these exact sentences there, and if so the card is simply right. But on the evidence that circulates online, the most careful reading is that the card's paragraph is a listener's summary of a poet's teaching, and the summary was later lifted into quotation marks and signed with the poet's name. That isn't a forgery. It's the most ordinary way a voice gets lost: an admirer's paraphrase becomes the quote.
Who wrote the words decides what kind of claim they make. Trudell was an oral artist who preferred performing to writing, and he had a precise vocabulary. One of his best documented teachings concerned the phrase the card opens with. A human being, he taught, has two parts. "Human" is the body, made from the minerals and fluids of the living world. "Being" is the spirit, the link to the power of the universe. In his mouth, then, "all human beings" is not a casual opening. It already contains a claim about spirit. Read that way, the card's line about a sacred perception is the second half of a single idea: the body descends from the earth, and the being remembers.
The phrase that does the most work on the card is also the one with the most surprising history. "Genetic memory" sounds like the language of modern laboratories. It is older than the gene. In 1870 the physiologist Ewald Hering lectured in Vienna on memory as a general function of organized matter, arguing that heredity and remembering were one process. The novelist Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon, carried the lecture into English and built on it. In 1881 the French psychologist Théodule Ribot argued that psychological memory and genetic memory share one mechanism and differ only in that one reaches consciousness. The German biologist Richard Semon later divided memory into genetic and nervous kinds. The idea belonged to an era that believed creatures could inherit what their parents had learned, the view tied to the name Lamarck, and it faded as genetics matured. Modern psychology mostly treats it as mistaken. The one modern result people raise against that verdict came from a 2013 study in which mice trained to fear a smell had descendants that were unusually sensitive to that same smell. It concerns a reaction to one odor, and researchers still argue over what it shows. It's a long way from a sacred perception of reality.
Here is where the most tempting answer comes in, and it fails. If a card like this can scatter readers in so many directions, the obvious fix is better words: language so clear that nothing in it can mislead. That hope is very old. In 1668 John Wilkins, one of the founders of the Royal Society, published a scheme for a philosophical language in which every concept would have its fixed place, so that a word could not mean more than it should. Nearly three centuries later Jorge Luis Borges mocked the dream by inventing a Chinese encyclopedia that divides animals into absurd categories, among them those that have just broken the water pitcher. The joke lands because every perfect language turns out to carry its maker's sorting of the world. Governments have pursued a humbler version. The United States Plain Writing Act of 2010 requires federal agencies to write clear government communication that the public can understand and use, and agencies file reports on how well they comply.
Plainness would not have rescued this card, because it already has plainness. A schoolchild can read every word of it. What it lacks is the one thing no choice of words supplies: a trail back to the person who spoke. Clear words with no source can travel just as far as murky ones, and further, because nothing in them invites the reader to check. The word "spirit" glows on the card because there's nothing beside it to measure it against. Put the paragraph back where it came from, among a fan's notes on a poet's talks and alongside Trudell's teaching about the human and the being, and the word settles into place.
Even the image at the card's close has a past. Sherlock Holmes, in the second chapter of A Study in Scarlet in 1887, describes the brain as a little empty attic that a sensible person furnishes only with useful tools, throwing out the rest. The card turns the picture around: the box nobody thought useful is the one worth carrying down. Nothing suggests the card's writer had Holmes in mind, and the likeness proves nothing. It's simply a reminder that an attic holds things put there by other people, at other times, for their own reasons.
So who packed the dusty box? The ideas belong to John Trudell. They are a poet's teaching that the body comes from the earth and the spirit remembers, spoken many times in many rooms. The sentences, as they now circulate, may well belong to a listener who wrote them down in 2013. The phrase "genetic memory" comes from Victorian biology. The promise that the box can still be opened is not a finding of any science. It's a belief, held by a man who had good reason to know what can be lost. The card is worth keeping. It just needs a label on the box.
